rows: Lie with eyes under the bar, feet flat about hip to shoulder width. Pull the shoulder blades back and down, keep a moderate arch, glutes and head on the bench. Full overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width so forearms are vertical at the bottom; bar low in the palm over the wrist.

Brace, unrack to straight arms over the shoulders. Lower under control to the lower chest near nipple line, elbows about 45 to 70 degrees from the torso. Touch without bouncing, then press up and slightly back to lockout over the shoulders, exhaling near the top.
Upper back pinned; drive the feet without lifting the hips. Wrists stacked over elbows. No 90 degree elbow flare or bounce; use a spotter or safeties set just below chest height.

Set up as for a flat bench press: eyes under the bar, shoulder blades retracted, feet planted. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width, roughly index fingers at or just inside the edge of the knurling (about a fist narrower per side than your normal grip). Wrists straight and stacked over the elbows.

Unrack and lower the bar to the lower sternum, keeping the elbows tucked about 15 to 30 degrees from the torso and the forearms vertical. Touch lightly, then press up and slightly back to a full lockout, finishing with hard elbow extension.

Shoulder width is narrow enough; hands touching or very narrow grips only bend the wrists and stress the elbows. Elbows travel down and in, not out. The bar touches lower on the chest than a normal bench; keep the same tight upper back.

Lie on a flat bench with shoulder blades retracted and feet planted. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped clearly wider than your normal grip, up to index fingers on the 81 cm ring marks (the widest legal powerlifting grip). Forearms will angle slightly outward at the bottom.

Unrack and lower the bar to the mid chest; the wide grip shortens the bar travel. Elbows sit about 60 to 75 degrees from the torso. Touch lightly with no bounce, then press straight up to lockout over the shoulders.

Greater pec and front delt demand, less triceps. Keep the shoulder blades pinned so the shoulders do not roll forward at the bottom. Stop short of ring-plus grips; skip it if wide grips aggravate the shoulder or AC joint.

Lie on a flat bench with shoulder blades retracted and feet planted. Take a full underhand grip, thumbs wrapped, about shoulder width to slightly wider. A spotter should help with the unrack because the grip makes it awkward.

Unrack and lower the bar on a lower path than a normal bench, to the lower chest or upper abdomen, with elbows tucked about 20 to 30 degrees from the torso. Press up and back toward the face to lockout over the shoulders.

Emphasizes the clavicular (upper) chest with low shoulder stress. Never use a thumbless grip here. Start light; wrists stay straight and the bar sits in the heel of the palm. Use safeties set just below the lowest bar position.

Set an adjustable bench to about 30 degrees (up to 45). Sit with hips back on the seat, eyes under the bar, feet planted and shoulder blades retracted. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width.

Unrack and lower the bar to the upper chest just below the collarbones, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees from the torso and forearms vertical. Press straight up to lockout over the shoulders, the bar path more vertical than on a flat bench.

Around 30 degrees keeps the upper chest in charge; steeper angles shift work to the front delts. Do not over-arch, which flattens the incline into a flat press. Keep the hips on the seat and the bar away from the neck.

Set a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees and hook the legs under the pads. Lie back with eyes under the bar, shoulder blades retracted. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width; a spotter should hand off the bar.
Lower the bar to the lower chest under control, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso. Touch lightly, then press back up to lockout over the shoulders; the range is shorter than a flat bench.

Biases the lower (sternocostal) pec fibers and is gentle on the shoulders. Keep the shoulder blades pinned. The head is below the hips, so always use a spotter or Smith safeties at heavy loads and rack carefully.
Set up exactly as for your competition bench: eyes under the bar, shoulder blades pinned, arch set, feet planted for leg drive, competition grip width (index fingers no wider than the 81 cm rings).

Lower the bar to your normal touch point and hold it motionless on the chest for 1 to 3 seconds (until a press command if training for a meet), staying tight. Then press explosively to lockout without letting the bar sink or heave first.
Stay braced through the pause; do not relax the lats or let the bar sink into the chest. Same touch point and elbow angle every rep. Expect to use about 5 to 10 percent less than touch-and-go loads.
Set up as for a competition bench with your normal grip, arch and leg drive. Named after powerlifter Eric Spoto.
Lower the bar slowly along your competition path and stop it about 2 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches) above the chest without touching. Hold the bar dead still for 1 to 2 seconds, then press to lockout.

The bar must stop, not hover and drift. Keep the same elbow tuck and bar path as your competition bench so the pause lands at your touch point. Builds control and strength off the chest; use about 10 to 15 percent less than your touch-and-go bench.

Lie on a flat bench with your normal grip and shoulder blades retracted. Extend the legs straight out in front with the feet off the floor, or heels just lightly resting, so leg drive is impossible. Keep a small natural arch rather than a full competition arch.
Unrack (a hand-off helps), lower the bar to your normal touch point with control and press back to lockout, keeping the body balanced on the bench without help from the legs.
Removes leg drive to isolate upper body pressing and expose weak points. Brace the trunk to stop the body shifting side to side. Use about 10 to 20 percent less than your normal bench and a spotter.

Lie on a flat bench inside a power rack and set the safety pins at your sticking point, usually 5 to 10 cm above the chest. Set the bench so your eyes are under the bar, get your normal grip, arch and leg drive.

Press the bar off the pins to lockout, then lower it under control until it settles fully onto the pins. Let it come to a dead stop for about 1 second to kill momentum, then press again from that position.

Overloads the range above the chest. Lower softly; do not crash into the pins or relax on them. Keep the same bar path as the competition bench. Not the same as a dead bench, which starts from pins set at chest-touch height.

Set the safety pins in a power rack so the bar rests about 1 to 2 cm above your chest at full arch, at the same spot it normally touches. Lie under it, set grip, arch and feet, and get fully tight before the first rep.
Start each rep from a dead stop on the pins with no eccentric, pressing to lockout. Lower the bar back to the pins, release tension briefly, then re-tighten and press again.

Builds starting strength off the chest without the stretch reflex, so expect lower loads than a normal bench. Re-set the shoulder blades and breath before each rep. Keep wrists stacked and elbows at your competition angle.
Lie on a flat bench with your competition setup. A partner holds, or you strap down, a stack of 1 to 5 boards (usually 2x4 or 2x6 lumber screwed together) on the sternum where the bar touches.

Unrack and lower the bar until it touches the boards, pause briefly without relaxing, then press back to lockout. Each extra board shortens the range and shifts emphasis toward lockout and the triceps.

Keep the elbows tucked at your normal bench angle; do not let them flare as loads climb. Use a spotter or safeties. Loads heavier than your full-range max stress the elbows, so keep reps low and volume modest.

Lie on the floor inside a power rack with the bar set on the hooks or safeties at about arm's length above the chest. Bend the knees with feet flat, or keep the legs straight. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped at your bench width, shoulder blades retracted against the floor.
Unrack and lower the bar until the backs of the upper arms rest on the floor, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso. Pause 1 second with no bounce, then press to lockout over the shoulders.
Limits shoulder range and removes leg drive, overloading the mid and top range and the triceps. Let the elbows land softly. Set the rack hooks or safeties where you can re-rack from the floor.
Set up as for a normal flat bench press. Decide the tempo before the set, written as eccentric-pause-concentric seconds, for example 3-1-1 (3 seconds down, 1 second pause on the chest, 1 second up).

Lower the bar on your normal path to the chest over the full prescribed count, keeping the elbows and touch point consistent. Hold motionless if a pause is prescribed, then press to lockout at the set speed.
Count the eccentric honestly and stay tight the whole way down. Builds positional control and technique. Reduce the load about 10 to 20 percent from normal reps.

Lie on a flat bench with hips and knees bent about 90 degrees and the feet either crossed in the air or resting on the end of the bench, which flattens the lower back. Retract the shoulder blades and take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width.
Unrack and lower to the mid chest with control, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees, then press to lockout while keeping the lower back flat and the body still.

Removes arch and leg drive for a longer range and more chest work. Keep the shoulder blades retracted even without an arch. Not the same as a Larsen press, which keeps the legs extended. Use lighter loads and a spotter.

Loop matching resistance bands around each bar sleeve and anchor them low to the rack base, band pegs or bench legs so they stretch as the bar rises. Set up with your normal bench grip, arch and leg drive. Equipment is barbell plus bands.
Lower the bar to the chest under control against the bands pulling it down, then press hard and fast to lockout as band tension rises toward the top.
Teaches acceleration through the whole rep and overloads lockout. Check both bands are identical and centered on the sleeves. The bands speed the eccentric, so control the descent and stay tight.

Hang matching bands from the top of a power rack and loop them around the bar sleeves so they support part of the load at the chest. Load more than your max on the bar and set up with your competition grip and arch.
Lower the bar to the chest; the bands take the most weight off at the bottom and less as you press, so close to the full load is felt at lockout.
Lets you handle more than your full-range max with less stress at the chest. Know roughly how much weight the bands take off at the bottom. Keep the competition groove and touch point.

Hang chains from each bar sleeve, usually with a lighter lead chain, so several links pile on the floor when the bar is on the chest and lift off as it rises. Set up with your normal grip, arch and leg drive.
Lower the bar as links settle on the floor and the load drops, then press as links lift and resistance builds toward lockout.
Accommodating resistance that also adds a little sway to the bar. Check both sides carry the same amount of chain. Press each rep with maximal intent.
Load the bar to about 40 to 60 percent of your one-rep max, often plus bands or chains. Use your competition setup, rotating grip width slightly between sets (within the rings).
Lower the bar quickly but under control to the chest and press as explosively as possible to lockout. Typical prescription is 8 to 10 sets of 3 reps with 30 to 60 seconds rest.
Every rep should move fast; end the set if bar speed drops. Stay as tight as with heavy weights. Do not bounce off the chest; the speed comes from the press, not a rebound.

Pull a Slingshot (an elastic double sleeve) over both arms so it sits just above the elbows and across the front of the chest. Set up on the bench with your normal grip and arch. Equipment is barbell plus Slingshot.
Lower the bar to the chest; the sleeve stretches and stores energy, assisting out of the bottom. Press to lockout as normal.

Lets you overload the top half and handle heavier weights with less shoulder stress at the chest. Fit it snugly, seams lined up with the elbows. Keep the same bar path as a raw bench and use a spotter.

Lie on a flat bench and take a wide overhand grip, thumbs wrapped, about 1.5 times shoulder width. Use light weight and either a spotter or safeties set just above neck height. Shoulder blades retracted.
Lower the bar slowly toward the base of the neck or upper chest line, elbows flared about 80 to 90 degrees from the torso, then press back up to lockout over the shoulders.
A high-risk bodybuilding variation popularized by Vince Gironda for upper chest stretch. Keep loads light and always use safeties. Avoid with shoulder problems; stop the bar a few cm above the neck.

Lie on a flat bench under a Swiss (football or multi-grip) bar racked in a rack. Take a full neutral grip (palms facing in) on the middle set of handles, about shoulder width. Retract the shoulder blades and plant the feet.
Unrack and lower the bar to the mid or lower chest with elbows tucked about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso. Press to lockout over the shoulders.
The neutral grip is shoulder-friendly and increases triceps involvement. Keep wrists straight on the handles. Narrow handles bias triceps, wider handles bias chest. Equipment is a Swiss bar.
Lie on a flat bench under a cambered bench bar, whose center bends down toward the chest by several cm. Grip at your normal bench width and set safety pins because the hands travel below chest level.
Lower the bar so the camber sinks toward the torso and the hands go a few cm below chest height, giving a deeper stretch, then press back to lockout.
Adds range of motion and pec stretch. Start light and progress slowly. Stop above the point where the shoulders roll forward or the front of the shoulder hurts. Equipment is a cambered bar.
Hang kettlebells or plates from mini bands on each end of a flexible bamboo or Earthquake bar. Lie on a flat bench with a normal grip and shoulder blades retracted.
Lower the bar slowly to the chest over about 3 seconds while controlling the oscillating load, then press steadily back to lockout and pause until the weights settle.
Trains shoulder stability and rotator cuff control, useful in rehab and as a warm-up. Move slowly and keep the bar level. Use light weights and keep the grip firm.
Lie on a flat bench under a Duffalo bar, which has a moderate bend in the middle (less camber than a cambered bench bar). Grip at your normal bench width and set safety pins.
Lower the bar to the chest; the bend lets the hands travel a few cm deeper than with a straight bar. Press back to lockout over the shoulders.
A middle ground between a straight bar and a cambered bar, often used to reduce shoulder strain while keeping a slightly bigger stretch. Keep the shoulder blades pinned. Equipment is a Duffalo bar.
Lie on a flat bench under a thick axle bar (about 5 cm diameter, non-revolving sleeves) and take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped at normal bench width. The bar sits deep in the palms.
Unrack and lower to the chest under control, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees, then press to lockout over the shoulders.
Squeeze the bar hard to stop it rolling in the hands. Keep wrists stacked over the elbows. Use lighter loads than a standard bar. Equipment is an axle.

Set a flat bench under a Smith machine so the bar lines up over the lower to mid chest. Set the safety stops just below chest height. Lie down with shoulder blades retracted and take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width.
Rotate the bar to unhook it, lower it along the fixed vertical path to the lower chest with elbows about 45 to 60 degrees, then press to lockout. Rotate the bar back onto the hooks at the end.
Bench position sets the touch point, so check it before loading. Keep the shoulder blades retracted. Useful for training close to failure without a spotter.

Set an incline bench at about 30 degrees under the Smith machine so the bar lands on the upper chest just below the collarbones. Set the safety stops and take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width.
Unhook the bar, lower it to the upper chest with elbows about 45 to 60 degrees, then press back to lockout and rehook.
A stable path for upper chest focus. Keep the hips on the seat and the chest high. Shift the bench if the bar drifts toward the neck or mid chest.

Place a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees under the Smith machine so the bar lines up with the lower chest and secure the legs. Set the safety stops and take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width.
Unhook the bar and lower it to the lower chest, elbows about 45 degrees, then press back to lockout. Rehook at the end.
Lower chest focus without needing a spotter. Keep the shoulder blades pinned. Make sure the safety stops are set before starting.
Lie on a flat bench under a Smith machine with the bar over the lower chest. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width and set the safety stops.
Unhook the bar and lower it to the lower sternum, elbows tucked about 15 to 30 degrees from the torso and forearms vertical. Press to full lockout.
The fixed path lets you focus on the triceps. Keep the wrists straight; do not go narrower than shoulder width. Do not let the elbows flare.

Sit on the end of a flat bench with dumbbells on the thighs, lie back and kick them up to the chest. Hold them at the sides of the chest with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped, palms facing the feet (or angled about 45 degrees), shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.

Press the dumbbells up and slightly in until the arms are straight over the chest, dumbbells a few cm apart. Lower under control until they reach chest level or just below with a stretch, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees from the torso.
Keep forearms vertical. Do not clang the dumbbells at the top. To finish, bring them to the chest and sit up using the knees, or lower them to the floor under control.
Set a bench to about 30 degrees (up to 45). Kick the dumbbells up as you lie back and hold them at the upper chest, palms forward or slightly angled in, shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.
Press the dumbbells up over the upper chest until the arms are straight. Lower slowly to the sides of the upper chest, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees from the torso.
Too steep an incline turns it into a shoulder press. Keep wrists stacked over elbows. Control the bottom stretch and keep the hips on the seat.
Set a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees and secure the legs. Hold the dumbbells on the chest as you lie back (a partner can hand them over), palms facing the feet, shoulder blades retracted.
Press the dumbbells up over the lower chest to lockout, then lower them under control to the sides of the lower chest, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso.
Biases the lower chest. Keep the shoulder blades back. At the end bring the dumbbells to the chest and have a partner take them rather than dropping them from a head-down position.
Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells at the sides of the chest with a neutral grip (palms facing each other). Shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.
Press the dumbbells straight up over the chest, keeping palms facing in. Lower under control with elbows tucked about 30 degrees from the torso until the dumbbells reach chest height.
Easier on the shoulders, with more triceps involvement. Keep the dumbbells parallel and wrists straight. Keep them apart; pressing them together turns it into a squeeze press.
Lie on a flat bench holding two dumbbells (hex dumbbells work best) with a neutral grip, pressed firmly together over the mid chest. Shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.
Squeeze the dumbbells hard against each other and lower them together to touch the mid chest, elbows tucked close to the torso. Press back up to lockout while maintaining the inward squeeze.
The constant squeeze keeps pec adduction tension through the press. Do not let the dumbbells separate. Use moderate weight and a 2 to 3 second lowering.

Lie on a flat bench holding one dumbbell at the side of the chest with an overhand or neutral grip. Hold the bench edge or rest the free hand on the abdomen. Feet planted wide for balance, shoulder blades retracted.
Press the dumbbell up to lockout over the shoulder while keeping the torso square and the hips down. Lower slowly back to chest level, elbow about 45 degrees. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Brace the core to resist rotation toward the weight. Do not let the working shoulder lift off the bench. Builds unilateral strength and anti-rotation control.
Lie on a flat bench with shoulder blades retracted and feet planted, and press both dumbbells to lockout over the chest with an overhand grip.
Keep one arm locked out while lowering the other dumbbell to chest level and pressing it back up. Alternate sides each rep.
The locked-out arm stays still and stacked while the other works. Keep the torso square without rolling. Adds time under tension on both sides; exhale on each press.
Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, holding dumbbells over the chest with a neutral or overhand grip. Shoulder blades retracted against the floor.
Lower the dumbbells until the backs of the upper arms touch the floor, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso. Pause 1 second, then press back to lockout over the chest.
Limits range to protect the shoulders and builds lockout strength. Let the elbows land softly; do not bounce them off the floor. A good option with no bench.
Lie on a flat bench and hold dumbbells with an underhand grip, thumbs wrapped (palms facing your head). Press them to lockout above the lower chest, shoulder blades retracted.
Lower the dumbbells to the lower chest, elbows tucked close to the sides about 20 to 30 degrees. Press back up and slightly toward the face to lockout.
Biases the upper (clavicular) chest with little shoulder strain. Start light to learn the grip. Keep the wrists straight and the dumbbells parallel.
Set a bench to a low incline of about 15 to 20 degrees (often the first notch). Hold dumbbells at the sides of the chest with an overhand grip, shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.
Press the dumbbells up over the upper chest to lockout, then lower slowly to a deep stretch at chest level, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso.
Biases the upper chest while keeping front delt involvement lower than a 30 to 45 degree incline. Full range with control. Keep the hips on the bench.
Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells over the chest with a neutral grip (palms facing each other) and elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees. Shoulder blades retracted, feet planted.

Open the arms in a wide arc, lowering the dumbbells until they are level with the chest or slightly below and the upper arms are about in line with the torso, keeping the elbow angle fixed. Squeeze the chest to bring them back together over the chest along the same arc.
Do not turn it into a press by bending the elbows more. Stop at a comfortable stretch, not a forced one. Use much lighter weights than presses.
Set a bench to about 30 degrees. Hold dumbbells above the upper chest with a neutral grip and elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulder blades retracted.
Open the arms wide in an arc until you feel a stretch in the upper chest, dumbbells about level with the chest, then squeeze them back together over the upper chest.
Keep the elbow angle constant. Control the eccentric. Avoid lowering far below chest level if the front of the shoulder hurts.
Lie on a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees with legs secured. Hold dumbbells over the lower chest with a neutral grip and elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees.
Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in an arc until you feel a stretch, then squeeze them back together over the lower chest.
Biases the lower chest. Keep the movement slow and controlled. Use light weights because the shoulder is stretched, and have a partner take the dumbbells at the end.

Lie along a flat bench (or across it with only the upper back supported and hips low). Hold one dumbbell with both hands cupped under the top plate in a diamond grip, arms extended over the chest with elbows slightly bent.

Keeping the elbow angle fixed, lower the dumbbell back behind the head in an arc until the upper arms are about in line with the torso and you feel a stretch in the chest and lats. Pull it back over the chest along the same arc.
Keep the elbows soft and fixed. Brace so the ribs do not flare and the lower back does not arch. Use a weight you can control through the full stretch.
Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells over the chest with a neutral grip, shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.

Lower the dumbbells in a wide fly arc with elbows slightly bent until they reach chest level. At the bottom, tuck the elbows and press the dumbbells back up as in a bench press. Repeat with the fly on each eccentric.
Gets the stretch of a fly with the stronger concentric of a press, so you can go heavier than a fly. Control the bottom position. Keep the shoulder blades back.
Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, holding dumbbells over the chest with a neutral grip and elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees. Shoulder blades retracted against the floor.

Open the arms in a wide arc, keeping the elbow angle fixed, until the backs of the upper arms lightly touch the floor at about 45 to 60 degrees from the torso. Without resting, squeeze the dumbbells back together over the chest.
The floor caps the range, making it a shoulder-friendly fly. Keep the elbow bend fixed. Do not relax or bounce the arms on the floor; touch and go.
Lie on a flat bench holding very light dumbbells (or plates) with an underhand (palms-up) grip at the hips, arms nearly straight with a slight elbow bend. Shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.

Sweep the dumbbells out to the sides and overhead in a wide semicircle close to the floor plane, rotating the palms to face up the whole way, until they meet behind the head. Reverse the arc back to the hips.
Use very light weights; the long lever stresses the shoulder at the overhead position. Keep a slight bend in the elbows and the ribs down. Stop the arc short if the shoulders pinch.

Sit on a Swiss ball with dumbbells on the thighs, then walk the feet forward until the head and upper back rest on the ball. Hips lifted level with the knees in a tabletop bridge, knees at 90 degrees over the ankles, feet hip to shoulder width apart. Hold the dumbbells at chest level with an overhand grip.
Press the dumbbells over the chest to lockout, then lower to chest level with elbows about 45 degrees, keeping the hips up and level the whole time.
Squeeze the glutes to hold the bridge; do not let the hips sag. Use lighter weights than on a bench. Widen the feet for more stability, narrow them to progress.

Rest the head and upper back on a Swiss ball in a tabletop bridge, hips level with the knees and feet hip to shoulder width apart. Hold dumbbells over the chest with a neutral grip and elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees.
Lower the dumbbells out in a wide arc, elbow angle fixed, until they reach about chest level, then squeeze them back together over the chest, keeping the hips level.
Keep the glutes squeezed so the hips do not sag. Use light weights; the ball reduces stability. Move slowly to stay balanced.

Stand tall with feet hip width apart. Hold one or two smooth weight plates (often 2 x 5 kg) vertically between the palms at mid-chest height, fingers pointing forward, elbows bent and the plates touching the sternum.
Squeeze the palms together hard and press the plates straight forward at chest height until the arms are fully extended. Hold 1 second, then return them to the chest while keeping the squeeze.
The inward squeeze is the exercise; do not let the plates slip down. Keep the shoulders down and the ribs stacked over the hips. Use light plates and a slow tempo.
Lie on your back on a flat bench or the floor with knees bent. Hold one weight plate flat between the palms (palms pressing the rim or the faces of the plate) at mid-chest, elbows bent and tucked.
Squeeze the palms into the plate and press it straight up over the chest to full arm extension. Lower it under control back to just above the sternum, keeping the squeeze.
The squeeze creates constant inner chest tension. Keep the plate level and the shoulder blades on the bench. Use moderate plates and a 2 to 3 second lowering.

Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a kettlebell (or one in each hand) in the rack position with the handle diagonal across the palm, the bell resting on the back of the forearm and the upper arm on the floor about 45 degrees from the torso.
Press the kettlebell up until the arm is straight over the shoulder, wrist neutral. Lower under control until the upper arm touches the floor, pause briefly, and press again.
Keep the wrist straight so the bell does not flop backward. Do not bounce the elbow off the floor. To get in and out, roll to the side holding the bell with both hands.
Lie on a flat bench holding a light kettlebell upside down by the handle, bell pointing to the ceiling, forearm vertical and grip tight. Shoulder blades retracted and feet planted.
Press the kettlebell up to lockout over the shoulder, keeping it balanced upside down, then lower slowly to chest level with the elbow about 45 degrees from the torso.
A crushing grip and vertical forearm keep the bell upright and fire the rotator cuff. Use a light bell and move slowly. Start with one arm so the free hand can protect the face.

Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the mid chest (around nipple line) and set the start position for a full stretch. Sit with the back flat against the pad, feet flat, shoulder blades retracted, and grip the horizontal or neutral handles with a full grip.

Press the handles forward until the arms are straight without locking hard. Return slowly until the hands are about level with the chest and the pecs are stretched, without letting the weight stack touch down.
Keep the shoulder blades on the pad; do not let the shoulders roll forward at lockout. Wrists straight, elbows about 45 to 60 degrees. Control the eccentric.
Adjust the seat so the vertical (palms-facing) handles line up with the mid to lower chest. Sit with the back and head against the pad and the feet flat.
Press the handles forward until the arms are straight without locking hard. Return slowly until you feel a stretch across the chest, keeping the shoulder blades on the pad.
Palms face each other, elbows tucked about 30 to 45 degrees. Easier on the shoulders than the wide grip and adds triceps. Do not let the shoulders roll forward at lockout.

Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the upper chest just below the collarbones. Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat and shoulder blades retracted, and grip the handles with a full grip.
Press the handles up and forward until the arms are straight. Return slowly until the hands are about level with the upper chest and the pecs are stretched.

Seat too low puts the handles high and turns it into a shoulder press; seat too high flattens the angle into a flat press. Keep the shoulders down and the elbows about 45 degrees from the torso. Control the return.
Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the lower chest. Sit back against the pad with feet flat and shoulder blades retracted, and grip the handles with a full grip.
Press the handles down and forward until the arms are straight. Return slowly until the hands reach the lower chest with a stretch.
Biases the lower chest. Keep the back flat against the pad and wrists straight. Do not let the weight stack slam between reps.

Load plates on each arm of an iso-lateral (independent-arm) chest press. Adjust the seat so the handles sit at mid chest. Sit with the back flat on the pad, shoulder blades retracted, and grip the handles.
Press both arms forward along their converging arcs until the arms are straight, or press one arm at a time. Return slowly to a full stretch with the hands level with the chest.
Each arm works independently, so watch for side-to-side imbalances. Keep the shoulders on the pad and avoid partial reps. Load both sides evenly.
Load plates on each arm of an iso-lateral incline press. Set the seat so the handles start level with the upper chest. Sit with the back against the pad and the feet flat.

Press both handles up and forward until the arms are straight. Lower under control until the hands are just above the upper chest and the chest is stretched. The arms can also be worked one at a time.
Keep the shoulder blades back and down on the pad. Drive through the palms, not the fingers. Do not let the elbows flare straight out to the sides.
Load plates on each arm of an iso-lateral decline press. Set the seat so the handles start level with the lower chest. Sit with the back against the pad and the feet flat or on the foot bar.
Press the handles down and forward until the arms are straight. Return under control until the lower chest is stretched. The arms can also be worked one at a time.
Targets the lower chest. Keep the shoulder blades pinned and the chest up. Control the return; do not let the weight pull the shoulders forward.
Set a chest press machine so the handle lines up with the mid chest. Sit with the back against the pad, grip one handle and brace the free hand on the seat or thigh.
Press the handle forward until the arm is straight while keeping the torso square to the machine. Return slowly to a full stretch. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Resist twisting toward the working arm. Keep the shoulder blade on the pad. Good for correcting left-right imbalances.

Adjust the seat so the handles or arm pads are at chest height and the upper arms are about parallel to the floor. Sit with the back flat against the pad, chest up, and hold the handles with a slight bend in the elbows (or forearms on the pads with elbows at 90 degrees).
Bring the handles together in front of the chest in a wide arc, squeezing the pecs, and pause briefly. Return slowly until you feel a stretch with the hands roughly in line with the shoulders.
Keep the shoulder blades back so the front delts do not take over. Do not let the arms travel too far behind the body. Use a controlled tempo and no momentum.
Sit on the pec deck as usual but hold only one handle, the arm at chest height with a slight elbow bend. Brace with the other hand on the seat or the opposite arm of the machine.
Sweep the working arm across in an arc to the midline, squeezing the pec, then return slowly to a full stretch. Switch sides after the set.
Keep the torso square; do not rotate to finish the rep. Allows a slightly longer range than the two-arm version. Keep the shoulder down.

Select a counterweight on an assisted dip machine (more weight means more help). Grip the dip handles with a neutral grip, kneel or stand on the platform, and start with arms straight and shoulders depressed.
Lean the torso forward about 20 to 30 degrees and bend the elbows to lower until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor and the elbows near 90 degrees. Press back up to straight arms.
Keep the shoulders away from the ears. Reduce assistance over time to progress to bodyweight dips. A forward lean biases chest, an upright torso biases triceps.

Adjust the seat so the handles start about level with the chest or just below with the elbows bent about 90 degrees. Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat or on the footrest, and grip the neutral handles.
Press the handles down until the arms are fully straight beside the body. Return slowly until the elbows reach about 90 degrees.
The upright, supported torso makes this primarily a triceps press. Keep the elbows close to the body and the shoulders down. Avoid letting the shoulders roll forward at the top of the return.

Set both pulleys at the highest position with D-handles. Grab one in each hand and step forward to the middle of the station in a split stance, torso leaning forward about 15 to 20 degrees, arms out to the sides with a slight elbow bend.

Bring the handles down and together in a wide arc in front of the lower chest or hips, keeping the elbow angle fixed. Squeeze briefly, then return slowly along the same arc until the arms are in line with the shoulders.
The high-to-low path biases the lower (sternocostal) chest. Keep the chest up and shoulders down. Do not turn it into a press by bending the elbows.
Set both pulleys at the lowest position with D-handles. Step forward into a split stance with the arms low and out to the sides, palms facing forward, elbows slightly bent.
Sweep the handles up and together in an arc to about upper chest or chin height, keeping the elbow angle fixed. Return slowly to the start until you feel a stretch.
Biases the upper (clavicular) chest. Keep the shoulder blades back and down and avoid shrugging. Use lighter weight and a slow eccentric.
Set the pulleys at about shoulder height with D-handles. Step forward into a split stance with the arms out to the sides at shoulder height and elbows slightly bent.
Bring the handles together in a horizontal arc in front of the mid chest. Squeeze briefly, then return slowly to the start until the hands are just behind the line of the shoulders.
Targets the mid chest. Keep the torso upright with a slight lean and the elbow angle fixed. Do not let the shoulders roll forward as the hands meet.
Set one pulley at shoulder height (or high or low for angle) with a D-handle. Stand side-on in a split stance, holding the handle with the arm out to the side and a slight elbow bend.
Sweep the handle across the body in an arc to the midline or slightly past it, squeezing the pec. Return slowly to the start without twisting the torso.
Brace the core to resist rotation toward the cable. Allows a longer range than the two-arm version. Keep the shoulder down and back.
Place a flat bench centered between two low pulleys with D-handles. Lie on the bench holding the handles above the chest, palms facing, elbows slightly bent.
Open the arms in a wide arc until the hands are about level with the chest, then squeeze them back together over the chest.
Cables keep tension at the top of the movement, unlike dumbbells. Keep the elbow angle fixed and the shoulder blades back. Use a controlled tempo.
Set an incline bench at 30 to 45 degrees between two low pulleys. Lie back holding the handles above the upper chest, palms facing, elbows slightly bent.
Open the arms in an arc until you feel a stretch in the upper chest, then squeeze the handles back together over the upper chest.
Targets the upper chest with constant tension. Keep the elbow angle fixed. Do not let the shoulders roll forward at the top.

Set a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees between two low pulleys with D-handles and secure the legs. Lie back holding the handles above the lower chest, neutral grip, elbows bent about 15 to 20 degrees.
Open the arms in a wide arc until the hands are about level with the chest and you feel a stretch, then squeeze the handles back together over the lower chest.
Biases the lower chest with constant cable tension. Keep the shoulder blades pinned and the elbow angle fixed. Sit up carefully at the end; hand the handles back slowly.

Set both pulleys at about chest height with D-handles. Face away from the station in a split stance, handles at the sides of the chest with an overhand or neutral grip, elbows about 45 degrees from the torso and a slight forward lean.
Press the handles forward and slightly together until the arms are straight in front of the chest. Return slowly until the hands are back beside the chest with a stretch.
Brace the core so the cables do not pull you backward. Keep the shoulder blades back and wrists straight. A good standing press that trains core stability too.
Set one pulley at chest height with a D-handle. Face away in a split stance with the opposite leg forward, holding the handle beside the chest with the elbow about 45 degrees from the torso.
Press the handle straight forward to full arm extension while keeping the hips and shoulders square. Return slowly to the start. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Resist rotation toward the cable side. Keep the shoulder blade back at full extension. Trains pressing strength with anti-rotation core demand.
Place a bench (flat or upright) between two pulleys set at chest height. Sit with the back against the pad or upright, handles at the sides of the chest with an overhand or neutral grip.
Press the handles forward until the arms are straight, then return slowly to the start with a stretch.
A stable seated alternative to a machine press. Keep the back flat against the pad and the shoulder blades retracted. Control the return.
Set both pulleys at about shoulder or head height. Kneel tall or half-kneel in the middle of the station, holding the handles with the arms out to the sides and elbows slightly bent.
Bring the handles together in an arc in front of the chest, squeezing briefly, then return slowly to the start.
Kneeling removes leg drive and body sway, making it stricter. Keep the glutes squeezed and the torso upright. Do not lean back to finish the rep.
Anchor a resistance band behind you at chest height (door anchor or post), or wrap a looped band around the upper back. Hold the handles at chest level with the elbows bent and in a split stance.
Press the handles forward until the arms are straight, then return slowly to the start against the band tension.
Tension increases as you press, so focus on the finish. Keep the core braced and wrists straight. Step further from the anchor for more resistance. Equipment is a resistance band.
Anchor a band behind you at chest height. Hold the handles with the arms out to the sides at chest level and elbows slightly bent, in a split stance.
Bring the handles together in a wide arc in front of the chest, squeezing briefly, then return slowly to the start.
Keep the elbow angle fixed throughout. Control the return; do not let the band snap the arms back. Equipment is a resistance band.
Wrap a resistance band across the upper back, holding one end under each hand. Get into a push-up position with hands slightly wider than shoulder width.
Lower the chest toward the floor, then push up against the band, which adds resistance at the top of the movement.
Keep the body in a straight line. Use a light band to start. The band should cross the shoulder blades, not the neck. Equipment is a resistance band.

Set gymnastic rings a few cm off the floor (or higher to make it easier). Grip the rings with a neutral grip, arms straight under the shoulders, and get into a push-up plank with the body straight and feet hip width.

Lower the chest between the rings with the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso until the hands are at the sides of the chest, rings kept close to the body. Press back to straight arms, turning the rings out (palms forward) at lockout.
The unstable rings demand more stabilizer work than floor push-ups. Keep the rings from drifting apart. Squeeze glutes and brace. Raise the rings to scale. Equipment is gymnastic rings.
Start in a push-up position (or on the knees to scale) on a smooth floor with each hand on a slider or towel, hands under the shoulders and body in a straight line.
Slide one or both hands out to the sides in a wide arc, keeping a slight elbow bend, as the chest lowers toward the floor. Pull the hands back together by squeezing the chest to return to the start.
Very demanding on the chest and shoulders; start from the knees and slide a short distance. Keep the hips in line and do not let the chest crash. Equipment is gliding discs or sliders.

Set one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a corner. Stand facing the free end in a staggered or square stance, holding the end of the bar at chest height with both hands interlaced or cupped, elbows bent and close to the body.
Press the bar up and forward in its natural arc until the arms are straight, then lower it slowly back to the chest.
The angled path is shoulder-friendly and suits people who find flat pressing painful. Brace the core and lean slightly into the bar. Keep the ribs down; do not arch back. Equipment is a landmine.

Set a barbell in a landmine attachment. Stand or kneel facing the free end, gripping the end of the bar with both hands flat on either side of the sleeve, fingers pointing up and palms pressing hard into the bar.
Keeping the inward squeeze, press the bar up and forward to full extension, then lower it under control back to the chest.
The inward squeeze recruits the inner chest. Keep the elbows tucked and squeeze the whole time. Brace the core to avoid leaning back. Equipment is a landmine.
Set a barbell in a landmine attachment. Stand in a split stance facing the free end with the opposite leg forward, holding the end of the bar at the shoulder with one hand.
Press the bar up and forward until the arm is straight, then lower it slowly back to the shoulder. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Brace to resist rotation toward the bar. Keep the shoulder blade back and the wrist straight. A shoulder-friendly unilateral press. Equipment is a landmine.

Grip parallel dip bars with a full neutral grip, bars about shoulder width or slightly wider, and jump or step up to a support position with arms straight, shoulders depressed away from the ears. Bend the knees and cross the ankles or let the legs hang slightly forward.

Lean the torso forward about 20 to 30 degrees and lower by bending the elbows, letting them travel back and slightly out, until the shoulders are just below the elbows (upper arms about parallel to the floor or a little deeper). Press back up to straight arms, keeping the lean.

The forward lean biases the chest; an upright torso shifts work to the triceps. Keep the shoulders down and back; do not sink so deep that the front of the shoulder strains. Scale with a band or assisted machine.
Attach a plate or dumbbell to a dip belt around the hips (or hold a dumbbell between the feet, or wear a vest). Mount parallel bars with a full neutral grip, arms straight and shoulders depressed.
Lean forward about 20 to 30 degrees and lower under control until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor. Press back up to straight arms without swinging the load.
Master 10 or more strict bodyweight dips first. Add load in small jumps and keep the same depth and lean as bodyweight dips. Do not let the weight swing or bounce out of the bottom.

Set gymnastic rings at about hip height, grip with a neutral grip and jump to a support position with arms straight, rings pressed into the sides of the body and turned out slightly (RTO). Shoulders depressed, legs together.

Lower under control, keeping the rings close to the body and the torso leaning slightly forward, until the shoulders are just below the elbows. Press back to the support position, turning the rings out at the top.
Much harder than bar dips because the rings move. Do not let the rings drift wide. Build a solid 30 second ring support hold first. Equipment is gymnastic rings.

Grip a single straight bar (pull-up bar set low, or the top of a dip station) with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width and jump to a support position with the bar at the hips, arms straight and shoulders depressed. Lean the chest slightly over the bar.
Bend the elbows and lower the chest toward the bar while the legs swing slightly forward to counterbalance, until the bar touches just below the chest. Press back to straight arms.
A key skill for the muscle-up transition. Keep the elbows tucked back, not flared, and the shoulders away from the ears. Control the descent; do not drop onto the bar.

Stand with your back to a straight bar at about hip height, reach behind and grip it with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width. Jump to a support position with the bar behind the hips, arms straight and legs slightly in front.
Bend the elbows and lower the body until the bar is near the lower back and the shoulders are in deep extension, then press back to straight arms.
Places the shoulders in extreme extension, so build shoulder extension mobility first. Move slowly and keep the shoulders depressed. Start with a shallow range.
Jump or step up to the top support position on parallel bars, arms straight, full neutral grip, shoulders depressed. Use a box to reach the top if needed.
Lower slowly over 3 to 5 seconds, leaning forward about 20 to 30 degrees, until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor. Step or jump back to the top and repeat; do not press up.
Builds strength for full dips. Control the entire descent at a steady speed. Keep the shoulders down and back.

Loop a resistance band across both parallel bars. Grip the bars with a full neutral grip and place the knees or feet on the band, then rise to the top support position with arms straight. Equipment is a dip bar plus band.
Lean forward about 20 to 30 degrees and lower until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor, with the band helping most at the bottom. Press back to straight arms.
Use a lighter band over time to progress. Keep the shoulders down and back. Do not let the band bounce you up out of the bottom.

Stand about 2 to 3 m from a solid wall or partner, feet shoulder width apart and knees soft, holding a 2 to 6 kg medicine ball at chest height with both hands on the sides of the ball, thumbs behind, elbows bent and close to the body.
Step forward and explosively push the ball straight out from the chest, extending the arms fully and finishing with the thumbs pointing down. Catch the rebound at chest height, absorb, and repeat.
Throw with maximal intent; the goal is speed, not load. Push from the legs through the chest and arms. Stop the set when throw speed drops.
Get into a push-up position with one hand on top of a medicine ball and the other on the floor, both hands about shoulder width apart, body straight from head to heels and feet hip width.
Lower the chest toward the floor, keeping the hips level, then press back up. Switch the ball to the other hand after the set or roll it across between reps.
The ball adds instability and an uneven range of motion. Keep the hand over the top of the ball. Brace to keep the hips from rotating.
Start in a push-up with one hand on a medicine ball and the other on the floor, body straight.
Perform a push-up, then explosively push off the ball and move both hands across so the other hand lands on the ball and the first lands on the floor. Perform another push-up and cross back.
Move quickly but land softly. Keep the hips in line throughout. Start slow and progress to explosive transitions.
Place both hands on the sides of a stability ball at chest height, fingers pointing down or forward, and step back into a push-up position with the body straight.
Lower the chest to the top of the ball while keeping it stable, then press back to straight arms.
Squeeze the ball inward to control it. Keep the elbows about 45 degrees from the torso. Start on the knees or against a wall if needed.
Kneel in front of a stability ball and walk the hands forward until the shins or feet rest on the ball and the hands are under the shoulders on the floor, body straight.
Lower the chest toward the floor while keeping the ball still, then press back to straight arms.
The further the ball is toward the feet, the harder it gets. Brace the abs and glutes to stop the hips sagging. Keep the head neutral.
Turn a BOSU ball dome side down and grip the edges of the flat platform with both hands about shoulder width. Step back into a push-up position with the body straight.
Lower the chest to the platform while keeping it level, then press back to straight arms.
Keep the platform from tipping side to side. Brace the core. Can also be done dome side up for an easier balance challenge.

Place the hands flat on the floor slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers spread and pointing forward, wrists under or just outside the shoulders. Step the feet back hip width apart onto the balls of the feet so the body forms a straight line from head to heels. Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes.

Lower the body as one unit, elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso and forearms near vertical, until the chest is a fist height or less from the floor and the upper arms are at least parallel to it. Press the floor away to straight arms, letting the shoulder blades move freely, and exhale on the way up.
No sagging hips or piked butt; chest and hips move together. Head neutral, eyes just ahead of the hands. Scale with an incline or knee push-up; progress with a decline, deficit or load.

Kneel on a mat with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width under the shoulders. Walk the hands forward until the body forms a straight line from the knees to the head, hips extended (not bent at the waist). Cross the ankles if comfortable.
Lower the chest toward the floor with the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso until the chest is a few cm from the floor. Press back up to straight arms, keeping the hips in line.
Keep a straight line from knees to shoulders; do not leave the hips back. Use it to build to full push-ups. Move to an incline push-up when 15 or more clean reps are easy.

Place the hands on the edge of a bench, box or Smith bar slightly wider than shoulder width, arms straight under the shoulders. Walk the feet back until the body forms a straight line from head to heels, feet hip width.
Lower the chest to the edge of the bench with the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso, then press back to straight arms.
The higher the surface, the easier it gets; lower it gradually to progress toward floor push-ups. Keep the body rigid and the hips in line. Touch the chest, not the chin, to the edge.

Stand about an arm's length from a wall, feet hip width apart. Place the palms flat on the wall at shoulder height, slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers pointing up, and lean in so the body is straight from head to heels.
Bend the elbows to about 45 degrees from the torso and lower the chest toward the wall until the nose is a few cm away. Push back to straight arms.
The easiest push-up regression, for beginners, older adults and rehab. Step further from the wall to make it harder. Keep the heels down and the body straight; do not push with the hips.

Place the feet on a bench or box (about 30 to 60 cm high) and the hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder width under the shoulders, so the body forms a straight line angled down toward the head.
Lower the chest (upper chest or chin area) toward the floor with the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso, then press back to straight arms.
Raising the feet shifts more load to the upper chest and front delts and increases the percentage of bodyweight lifted. Keep the hips from piking or sagging. Higher surfaces make it harder.
Get into a push-up position with the hands together under the chest, thumbs and index fingers touching to form a diamond. Body straight from head to heels, feet hip width.
Lower the chest to the hands with the elbows tracking back close to the body, then press back to straight arms.
Hard on the wrists and elbows; turn the hands slightly out if needed. Keep the elbows close and the hips in line. Scale from the knees or with the hands on a bench.
Get into a push-up position with the hands about 1.5 times shoulder width apart, fingers pointing forward or slightly out. Body straight, feet hip width.
Lower the chest toward the floor with the elbows bending out to the sides about 60 to 75 degrees from the torso, then press back up to straight arms.
More chest and front delt, less triceps than a standard push-up. Do not go so wide that the shoulders hurt. Keep the core braced throughout.
Get into a push-up position with the hands directly under the shoulders or slightly narrower, fingers forward, body straight from head to heels.
Lower the chest with the elbows tucked close to the ribs, pointing back, until the chest nearly touches the floor. Press back to straight arms.
Keep the elbows tucked to target the triceps. Hands narrower than a standard push-up but not touching (that is a diamond push-up). Keep the hips in line.
Get into a push-up position with the hands about twice shoulder width apart, fingers pointing out to the sides. Body straight, feet slightly wider than hip width.
Shift the weight toward one hand and lower the chest to it, bending that elbow while the other arm stays almost straight. Press back to center and repeat to the other side.
A progression toward the one-arm push-up. Keep the straight arm straight and the hips square. Scale by using a smaller range or reducing the width.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Lower the chest to the floor, then explode up hard enough for the hands to leave the floor, clap quickly, and land with soft elbows, flowing straight into the next rep.
Land with bent elbows to absorb the impact, not with locked arms. Keep the body rigid. Master regular plyo push-ups first. Scale by clapping on the knees.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight. Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes.
Lower the chest under control, then press explosively so the hands leave the floor. Land softly with bent elbows, sink into the next rep and repeat.
Focus on speed and height, not the number of reps. Keep the body in a straight line. Stop the set when speed drops.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight. Brace hard; this is an advanced move.

Lower the chest, then explode up so the hands and feet leave the floor at the same time, extending the arms forward like Superman for a split second. Pull the hands back under the shoulders and land softly with bent elbows and knees.
Very advanced; build up with plyo and clap push-ups. Land with soft arms to absorb the impact. Keep the body rigid in the air.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight.
Lower the chest, then explode up so the whole body leaves the floor. In the air, pike the hips and touch the hands to the toes, then land back in the push-up position with soft elbows.
An expert-level plyometric move. Master the superman push-up first. Practise on a soft surface. Keep the core tight during the pike.
Get into a push-up position with the hands about twice shoulder width apart. Body straight.

Lower the chest to the floor between the hands, then shift the body horizontally toward one hand while staying low, straightening the opposite arm. Shift back across to the other hand, then press up to the start.
Stay low throughout the slide. Keep the hips level and the core braced. A strength progression toward the one-arm push-up.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight.
As you lower the chest to the floor, lift one foot and bring the knee out to the side toward the same elbow. Press back up as you return the leg. Alternate sides each rep.
Keep the hips low and level, do not rotate. Bring the knee as close to the elbow as possible. Adds core and hip mobility work.
Start in a downward dog position with the hands shoulder width apart, feet wider than hip width and the hips raised high to form an inverted V.

Bend the elbows and swoop the chest down and forward close to the floor between the hands, then push up through straight arms into an upward dog with the hips low and chest lifted. Push the hips back up to return to downward dog.
A flowing, traditional Indian wrestling exercise that also stretches the spine and shoulders. Keep the movement smooth. Breathe in on the swoop and out on the return.
Start in a downward dog position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width, feet hip width apart and hips high.
Bend the elbows and swoop the chest down and forward toward the floor into an upward dog with the arms straight. Then reverse the exact same path, swooping back down and pushing back to downward dog.
Unlike the Hindu push-up, the return retraces the same swoop rather than pushing straight back. Keep the movement smooth. Engage the core throughout.

Get into a push-up position with the hands turned out or back (fingers pointing toward the feet or sides) and placed beside the lower ribs or waist. Lean the body forward so the shoulders are well in front of the hands, protract the shoulder blades and posteriorly tilt the pelvis.
Keeping the forward lean, lower the chest toward the floor with the elbows close to the body, then press back to straight arms while maintaining the lean and protraction.
Builds straight-arm and front-delt strength for the planche. Keep the shoulders ahead of the hands the whole time. Warm up the wrists and biceps tendons, which are heavily loaded.
Get into a push-up position with the feet wider than shoulder width for balance. Place one hand under the center of the chest and put the other arm behind the back or on the hip.
Lower the chest toward the hand with the elbow close to the body, keeping the hips and shoulders square to the floor. Press back to straight arm.
Resist rotating the hips toward the floor. Widen the feet to make it easier. Progress from archer push-ups or an elevated one-arm version.
Get into a push-up position with one hand placed forward (near the head) and the other back (near the waist), about shoulder width apart side to side.
Lower the chest to the floor, keeping the body straight and the hips level, then press back up. Switch the hand positions after each set or rep.
Each arm works at a different angle, building unilateral strength. Keep the hips square. Alternate the lead hand evenly.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the feet hip width apart.
Perform a push-up, then at the top rotate the body into a side plank, lifting one arm to the ceiling so the body forms a T. Return to the push-up position and repeat to the other side.
Rotate the whole body as one unit, pivoting on the feet. Keep the hips lifted in the side plank. Stack the shoulders over the supporting hand.

Get into a push-up position and have a partner place a weight plate flat on the upper back between the shoulder blades, or wear a weighted vest. Hands slightly wider than shoulder width, body straight.
Lower the chest to the floor with the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso, keeping the weight balanced. Press back to straight arms.
Keep the plate on the upper back, not the lower back. Maintain a rigid plank. Increase the load gradually.

Place two push-up handles, dumbbells, plates or blocks on the floor about shoulder width apart and grip them so the hands are raised above the floor. Get into a push-up position with the body straight.
Lower the chest below the level of the hands for a deeper stretch, then press back up to straight arms.
The extra range builds strength and chest stretch. Keep the shoulders packed at the bottom. Equipment is push-up handles or blocks.
Get into a push-up position on the hands (or on the knees or forearms to scale) with the hands under the shoulders and the body straight.

Perform a normal push-up, then at the top keep pushing the floor away so the upper back rounds slightly and the shoulder blades spread apart (protract). Return the shoulder blades to neutral and repeat.
The plus targets the serratus anterior, which stabilizes the shoulder blades. Keep the elbows straight during the plus. Do not shrug toward the ears.
Make fists and place them on the floor or a mat about shoulder width apart, resting on the first two knuckles with the wrists straight. Get into a push-up position.
Lower the chest to the floor, keeping the wrists straight and stable, then press back up.
Keeps the wrist neutral, which suits those with wrist pain. Use a padded surface. Keep the forearm, wrist and fist in a straight line.
Place the hands on the floor shoulder width apart, supported only on the fingertips and thumbs with the palms off the floor and fingers spread like a tent. Get into a push-up position.
Lower the chest to the floor while keeping the fingers strong and the palms lifted, then press back up.
Builds finger and grip strength. Start on the knees or with fewer reps. Stop if the fingers start to collapse.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight.
Lower the body all the way to the floor, then lift the hands off the floor briefly (or extend them out to the sides). Place them back down and press up to straight arms.
Ensures full range on every rep. Keep the body rigid as you press up from the floor; the chest and hips should rise together. Used in military fitness tests.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the body straight.
Lower the body slowly to the floor over 3 to 5 seconds, keeping the body rigid. At the bottom, drop the knees and push back up to the start, then repeat the slow lowering.
Builds strength for full push-ups. Keep the descent at a steady speed. Keep the elbows at about 45 degrees.

Hold a full or straddle planche: body horizontal and parallel to the floor, supported only on straight arms with the hands beside the hips, fingers turned out, shoulders leaning well forward of the hands and protracted.
Bend the elbows to lower the body toward the floor while keeping it horizontal and the legs off the floor, then press back up to the planche without letting the hips drop.
An elite calisthenics move. Build up through planche leans, tuck planche and straddle planche push-ups. Protect the wrists and biceps tendons with gradual progression.
Get into a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width and the feet slightly wider than hip width for balance.
Perform a push-up, then at the top lift one hand to tap the opposite shoulder while keeping the hips still. Return the hand and repeat, alternating sides.
Keep the hips level; do not rock side to side. Widen the feet to make it easier. Combines pressing strength with anti-rotation.
Get into a push-up position and lift one foot off the floor, keeping the leg straight and in line with the body.
Perform push-ups while holding the leg up a few cm off the floor, keeping the hips square to the floor and the elbows about 30 to 45 degrees from the torso. Switch legs after the set.
The lifted leg reduces the base of support and increases core and glute demand. Squeeze the glute of the raised leg. Keep the hips level.
Place two low boxes or plates about shoulder width apart. Start in a push-up position with the hands on the boxes.
Drop the hands off the boxes to the floor between them, absorbing the landing with bent elbows, then explode back up onto the boxes.
Absorb the landing quickly and rebound fast. Start with low boxes. Keep the body rigid. An advanced plyometric drill.
Place two kettlebells on the floor about shoulder width apart, handles parallel. Grip the handles and get into a push-up position with the body straight.
Lower the chest between the kettlebells for a deeper range, then press back up to straight arms.
The handles keep the wrist neutral and add range of motion. Check the kettlebells are stable and not rolling. Keep the elbows at about 45 degrees.
Start in a forearm plank with the elbows under the shoulders, forearms parallel and palms flat on the floor, body straight from head to heels and feet hip width apart.
Press up through the hands to straighten the arms into a high plank, leaning the shoulders forward over the hands. Then lower back down onto the forearms with control.
A demanding triceps exercise from old-school calisthenics. Keep the body rigid and the hips from piking. Scale by starting on the knees.

Grip a fixed bar with a full (thumb-around) overhand grip, hands 1-2 fist widths outside shoulder width so the forearms are near vertical at the top. Hang with elbows fully straight, legs together or ankles crossed, glutes tight and ribs pulled down into a slight hollow.

Start by depressing the shoulder blades (shoulders move away from the ears), then drive the elbows down and slightly back toward the ribs until the chin clears the bar and the upper chest approaches it. Exhale through the top. Lower over 2-3 seconds to a full dead hang with the elbows straight before the next rep.
Pull the bar to you, chest up; do not crane the chin. No kick, swing or half reps. Scale with bands, negatives or the assisted machine; progress with a dip belt once 8-10 strict reps are easy.
Grip the bar with a full underhand (palms toward you) grip at shoulder width or slightly narrower. Hang with straight elbows, shoulders set, glutes and abs braced and the legs still, ankles together.

Depress the shoulder blades, then pull the elbows down and back toward the hips, keeping them in front of the torso, until the chin passes over the bar and the chest is near it. Lower in 2-3 seconds to full elbow extension without relaxing into a passive shrug at the bottom.

Supination puts the biceps in a stronger line of pull, so most people get more reps than with an overhand grip. Keep wrists straight, not curled. Avoid half reps; if the elbows ache, switch to a neutral grip.

Grip the bar overhand about 1.5 times shoulder width (roughly where the bar's knurling or bend starts on many stations). Hang with straight arms, shoulders set and legs together. The upper arms start at about 45 degrees out from the head.

Depress the shoulder blades, then pull the elbows down and out to the sides, bringing the upper chest toward the bar until the chin clears it. Lower slowly to a full hang. Range of motion is shorter than a standard pull-up and the biceps contribute less.
Do not lean far back to cheat; the torso stays nearly vertical. If the front of the shoulder pinches, bring the grip in a hand width. Going extremely wide reduces range without adding lat work.
Grip the bar overhand with the hands 15-20 cm (6-8 in) apart, inside shoulder width. Hang with straight arms, legs together and the core braced; the elbows will point forward rather than out.

Depress the shoulder blades and pull, driving the elbows down and forward of the torso, until the chin is over the bar. Lean the chest back slightly near the top so the bar meets the upper chest. Lower under control to straight arms.

Keep the wrists straight and stacked over the elbows; a narrow overhand grip strains the wrists and elbows in some lifters, so switch to a neutral grip if they complain. Keep the legs quiet. More shoulder extension and biceps than the wide-grip pull-up.

Grab the parallel handles of a pull-up station (usually 50-60 cm apart) with palms facing each other and a full grip. Hang with straight elbows, shoulders set and legs together, body still between the handles.

Depress the shoulder blades, then drive the elbows down beside the torso toward the back pockets until the chin rises above the handles. Lower slowly through the full range to a dead hang with straight arms.

Often the most shoulder- and elbow-friendly grip, and the brachioradialis helps, so strength usually sits between pull-up and chin-up. Keep the elbows close rather than flared. Avoid swinging between the handles; squeeze the glutes.

Hang a plate, kettlebell or dumbbell from a dip belt (or wear a weight vest; a dumbbell held between the feet is a lighter option). Step up, take a full overhand grip just outside shoulder width and settle into a still hang with the load centred between the legs.

Brace, depress the shoulder blades and pull until the chin clears the bar, keeping the load hanging quietly. Lower under control to straight elbows and pause briefly at the bottom to kill any swing before the next rep.

Add load only when 8-10 strict bodyweight reps are easy, and in small jumps (1.25-2.5 kg). Every rep goes to full extension; no kipping. Cross the ankles and squeeze the glutes so the weight does not swing.
Hang a plate, dumbbell or kettlebell from a dip belt or wear a vest. Take an underhand grip, thumbs wrapped at shoulder width and settle into a still dead hang with the ribs down and core braced.

Depress the shoulder blades, then drive the elbows down toward the ribs until the chin passes over the bar with the chest tall. Lower over 2-3 seconds to full extension without letting the weight swing, and reset before the next rep.

Load in small jumps and keep full range on every rep. Heavy underhand pulling stresses the biceps tendon and inner elbow, so rotate with neutral-grip weighted pulls if elbows ache. Common strength test: added load for a 1-5 rep max.

Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width. From a dead hang, lift straight legs to hip height so the hips are flexed to 90 degrees and the body forms an L, knees locked, toes pointed, pelvis tucked under (posterior pelvic tilt).

Holding the L, depress the shoulders and pull until the chin clears the bar, then lower to straight arms with the legs still level. Keep the legs at hip height for every rep of the set; the hips must not drop as you pull or lower.
Pulling with the legs forward removes any kip and makes the abs and hip flexors work isometrically. Scale with bent knees (tuck pull-up). If the legs drop below horizontal, end the set.
Grip the bar overhand very wide, about twice shoulder width. Hang with both arms straight, shoulders set and the core braced in a slight hollow.

Pull toward one hand, bending that elbow while the other arm stays straight (or nearly so) and acts as an outrigger, until the chin is over the working hand. Lower under control to the centred hang and alternate sides, or complete all reps on one side.

A progression toward the one-arm pull-up: push down less with the straight arm over time, or let that hand slide or open to a fingertip assist. Keep the hips square. Stop the set when the straight arm starts bending to help.

Stand under and in line with the bar so it runs front to back over your head. Grip it with the hands touching or close together, one in front of the other, palms facing each other, and hang with straight arms.
Pull up so the head passes to one side of the bar, bringing that shoulder close to it, then lower to full extension. On the next rep pull the head to the other side, alternating every rep.

Brace the core and squeeze the legs together to stop the body spinning. Switch which hand is in front between sets so both sides get the same work. Pull high enough that the shoulder nearly touches the bar.

Drape two strong towels (or martial-arts gi lapels) over the bar about shoulder width apart. Grip each towel in a vertical, neutral fist, hands high on the fabric, and hang with straight arms and the core braced.
Crush the towels and pull until the hands reach chin level and the head rises above the bar line, elbows driving down beside the body. Lower slowly to straight arms while keeping a full grip.
Grip is usually the limiter, which is the point: it builds crushing grip for climbing, grappling and strongman. Scale with one towel and one hand on the bar. Check towels for tears before every set.
Grip the bar overhand about twice shoulder width. Pull up to the top of a wide pull-up with the chin over the bar and the chest close to it.

Staying at bar height, shift horizontally toward one hand so that arm bends fully while the other straightens. Slide across to the other hand the same way, then return to the centre and lower under control to a full hang. One full traverse equals one rep.

Keep the chin at or above the bar throughout the traverse; dropping turns it into archer pull-ups. Move slowly and keep the body still. Prerequisite: comfortable archer pull-ups and 12-15 strict pull-ups.
Grip the bar at shoulder width with one hand overhand and the other underhand. Hang with straight arms, ribs down and the core braced to resist rotation.
Depress the shoulders and pull until the chin clears the bar, keeping the chest square to the bar, then lower to a full hang. Switch which hand is underhand every set.
The body wants to twist toward the underhand side; resist it with the abs and glutes. Useful for blending pull-up and chin-up stress or when grip is limiting with a heavy load.
Place a box or bench under the bar. Take an overhand grip just outside shoulder width and step or jump to the top position: chin over the bar, elbows fully bent, shoulders down.
Remove the support and lower yourself as slowly as you can, aiming for a 3-8 second descent, until the elbows are fully straight. Step back up to the top rather than pulling, and repeat for 3-6 reps.

Control the whole descent, especially the bottom third where most people drop. Keep the shoulders packed, not shrugged. Excellent for a first strict pull-up; eccentrics cause soreness, so keep volume modest at first.

Loop a long resistance band around the bar, pass one end through the other loop and pull it snug (a girth hitch). Step one knee or both feet into the bottom loop, then take an overhand grip just outside shoulder width and hang with straight arms, band stretched.

Depress the shoulders and pull until the chin clears the bar; the band helps most at the bottom where it is most stretched. Lower under control to straight arms while keeping the foot or knee secured in the loop.
Use the lightest band that allows clean reps and step down to thinner bands over time. Do not bounce off the band's recoil at the bottom. Keep the band-side leg still so the band does not slip.
Select the counterweight: more weight means more assistance. Kneel or stand on the platform and take an overhand (wide or close), underhand or neutral grip on the handles, arms straight.
Depress the shoulders and pull until the chin reaches handle height, elbows driving down beside the body. Lower slowly until the elbows are straight while the platform rises with you.
Reduce assistance gradually; the help is constant through the range, unlike a band. Use the full range on every rep. Do not let the platform bounce you out of the bottom.
Choose the counterweight (more weight means more help). Grip the narrow handles underhand (palms facing you) about shoulder width and kneel or stand on the platform with the arms straight.
Pull the chest up toward the hands until the chin passes the handles, then lower slowly to straight arms.
Start each rep by pulling the shoulders down. Keep the ribs down and do not swing. Reduce the assistance over time as you get stronger.
Choose the counterweight. Grip the parallel handles with the palms facing each other and kneel or stand on the platform with the arms straight.
Pull the chest up toward the handles until the chin passes them, then lower slowly to straight arms.
Usually the most shoulder-friendly grip. Drive the elbows down toward the hips. Keep a long spine and avoid kicking.

Grip the bar overhand slightly wider than the shoulders with a full or hook-thumb grip. Establish a controlled kip swing from the shoulders: arch (chest through the arms, feet behind) then hollow (chest behind, feet in front), arms straight.
