From the arch, snap into the hollow and drive the hips up while pulling with the arms so the chin clears the bar. At the top push the bar away to swing back into the arch, then chain the next rep from the hollow.

Build strict pull-up strength first (5+ reps) to protect the shoulders. Power comes from the hip snap and the push-away, not a wild leg kick. Keep the hollow tight so the swing stays short and controlled.
Grip the bar overhand slightly wider than the shoulders. Hang and prepare a continuous, circular path: the body moves forward-up, over, and back-down like a horizontal loop.

Drive the hips forward and up while pulling, bringing the chin over the bar, then push the body back and down so it swings forward again under the bar. The bottom of one rep becomes the drive of the next with no pause.

Fastest cycling pull-up, used in competition volume. Learn the kipping pull-up and hold 5+ strict reps first. Avoid if shoulder strength or mobility is limited; high volume is hard on the shoulders and hands.
Grip the bar overhand slightly wider than shoulder width. Hang with arms straight; the rep can be performed strict or with a kip.
Pull high enough that the chest contacts the bar at or below the collarbones, driving the elbows back behind the torso. Lower to full elbow extension before starting the next rep.

Drive the elbows back hard and lean the head and shoulders back slightly so the chest, not the chin, meets the bar. In a kip, a stronger hip drive is needed than for chin-over-bar. Standard in CrossFit workouts.
Hang from the bar with an overhand grip at or just outside shoulder width, elbows fully straight and the shoulders relaxed up toward the ears (passive hang).
Without bending the elbows, pull the shoulder blades down and slightly back so the body rises 3-5 cm. Hold for 1-2 seconds at the top, then return slowly to the relaxed hang.

Arms stay straight; movement comes only from scapular depression by the lower traps and lats. Do not shrug or bend the elbows to fake height. Use as a warm-up and to teach the start of every pull-up, 8-15 reps.
Set a box or step under the bar so that standing on it places the bar at about chin height. Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width with a slight bend in the knees.
Jump lightly and use the arms to finish pulling the chin over the bar, then lower under control as slowly as possible until the feet touch the box. Reset and repeat.
Use only as much leg as needed so the arms do most of the work. The slow lowering does most of the strengthening. A beginner progression and a common scaling for conditioning workouts.
Hang gymnastic rings at a height where you can dead hang without the feet touching, about shoulder width apart. Grip the rings with palms facing forward or each other and hang with straight arms.
Pull up, letting the rings rotate naturally from overhand toward neutral or slightly underhand, until the chin passes the rings and the hands are near the chest. Lower under control to a full hang.
Free-rotating rings let the wrists and shoulders find their own path, which many people find friendlier than a fixed bar. Keep the rings close to the body at the top. Brace to control any wobble.
Grip the bar overhand about 1.5 times shoulder width. Hang with straight arms. Requires good shoulder external rotation and thoracic extension mobility.
Bring the head slightly forward and pull up so the bar passes behind the head, stopping when the bar is level with the base of the neck. Lower under control to a full hang.
Skip it if shoulder mobility is limited or there is any pain; the position combines abduction and external rotation under load. Never strike the neck. Use moderate reps rather than heavy loading.
Grip the bar underhand at shoulder width (overhand also works). Hang with straight arms and prepare to lean back strongly; popularised by Vince Gironda.
As you pull, arch the upper back and lean the head and shoulders back so the hips and legs angle forward. Continue until the lower chest or sternum touches the bar, then lower to full extension.
Harder than a normal chin because the finish becomes a row with full scapular retraction. Drive the elbows down and back hard at the top. Expect fewer reps; prioritize quality.
Grip the bar with one hand, usually neutral or underhand. The free hand rests at the side or across the body. Hang with the working shoulder packed down and the legs together.
Pull until the chin clears the bar, resisting body rotation by bracing the core and squeezing the legs together. Lower slowly to a full hang.

An elite skill that typically requires 15-20 strict pull-ups or a weighted pull-up near 50 percent of body weight. Build up with archer pull-ups, one-arm negatives and assisted variations. Some rotation is normal; minimize it with tension.

Grip the bar with one hand (neutral or underhand is easiest), shoulder packed. With the other hand hold a towel or band hanging from the bar, or grip the wrist or forearm of the working arm; the lower the assisting hand, the less help it gives.

Pull mainly with the bar hand, letting the assisting hand supply only as much help as needed, until the chin clears the bar. Lower under control to a full hang, ideally with less assistance on the way down.

Progress by gripping lower on the towel or using fewer fingers. Keep the working shoulder down and engaged and resist rotation with the core. If the free arm is clearly doing most of the work, use archer pull-ups instead.
Grip the bar overhand just outside shoulder width with a full grip. Hang with straight arms, shoulders set, legs together and the core braced in a slight hollow.

Pull up and stop dead for 2-3 seconds at a set point, typically mid-range (elbows about 90 degrees) or with the chin over the bar, holding the body completely still. Finish the rep and lower over 2-3 seconds to a full hang. Pauses can also be placed at two points per rep.
Pause at your usual sticking point to build strength there. Do not let the body sag or swing during the hold. Count the pause honestly; expect 2-3 fewer reps than normal.

Use a box to reach the top of a chin-up (underhand, shoulder width) or pull-up with the chin above the bar, elbows fully bent, shoulders pulled down and the chest close to the bar. Legs hang straight, ankles together.
Remove the foot support and hold this top position for as long as possible, breathing steadily. When the chin drops below the bar, lower slowly to a straight-arm hang (a free negative) and step down.

Keep the chin above the bar without tilting the head back, and keep the shoulders away from the ears. Used in fitness tests and to build first pull-up strength; combine 10-30 second holds with slow negatives.
Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width. Hang with straight arms, shoulders set and the body still in a slight hollow; no swing.

Pull as explosively as possible so the body keeps rising after the arms finish, release both hands briefly at the top to clap (or simply let go and regrip), then catch the bar and absorb the descent with bent arms, lowering back to a hang.
Only for athletes with 12+ strict pull-ups. Progress from explosive chest-to-bar pulls and hand releases. Always regrip with full control and reset each rep.
Grip the bar overhand about shoulder width with a full or slightly false grip. Hang and begin a hollow-to-arch kip (strict versions start from a dead hang).

Pull the bar explosively toward the hips, not the chest, while snapping the hips up. As the bar reaches the lower ribs, lean the shoulders over it and turn the wrists over, then press to elbow lockout above the bar. Lower under control back to a hang.
Strong explosive pull-ups (chest-to-bar) and dips are prerequisites. Avoid chicken-winging one elbow over at a time. Keep the arms close as you transition.
Set gymnastic rings overhead, shoulder width apart. Grip with a false grip so the heel of the hand sits over the ring. Hang with arms straight and the body tight.

Pull the rings to the lower chest, then quickly rotate the torso forward over the hands through the transition, keeping the rings tight to the ribs. Press out of the bottom of the ring dip to straight arms on top of the rings. Lower back down with control.
Keep the rings close to the body. Train false-grip pull-ups and deep ring dips separately. A kipping version exists, but master the strict muscle-up first.

Stand at a securely anchored climbing rope (usually 4.5 m) with mats below. Grip high with both hands. For a foot-assisted climb, wrap the rope around one shin and pin it with the other foot (J-hook), or wrap and step on it (S-wrap).

Pull with the arms while lifting the knees to the chest, clamp the rope with the feet, then stand up and reach higher. Repeat to the target height. Descend hand under hand with the feet controlling the speed.
Never slide down the rope; it burns the hands. Practise the foot lock low before climbing high. Scale with partial climbs or seated rope pulls.

Stand at a securely anchored climbing rope (usually 4.5 m) with mats below. Grip as high as possible with both hands and hang with straight arms; the legs stay off the rope for the whole climb, either straight down, in an L or crossed at the ankles.
Pull with both arms, then reach hand over hand to the next grip without letting the body drop between pulls. Continue to the target height. Descend hand under hand under control; do not slide.
Requires roughly 10+ strict pull-ups and a strong grip. Keep the core tight so the legs do not swing. Practise the first two or three pulls from a seated start before climbing high.
Hang from a bar or rings with an overhand grip. Pull into a tuck front lever: arms straight, shoulders depressed, back roughly horizontal, knees tucked to the chest.
Holding the horizontal body position, bend the arms and pull the bar toward the hips or lower ribs, then extend the arms back to the tuck lever without letting the hips drop.
Keep the hips level with the shoulders. Progress to advanced tuck, straddle and full lever rows. Depress the shoulders strongly and keep the elbows close to the body.

Set the knee pad so the thighs are snug under it with the feet flat. Grip a long bar overhand about 1.5 times shoulder width (where the bar bends), arms fully straight. Sit tall and lean back about 10-20 degrees with the chest up.

Depress the shoulder blades first, then drive the elbows down and slightly back until the bar reaches the upper chest just below the collarbones. Lower the bar slowly until the arms are straight and the lats stretch, shoulders rising slightly at the top.
Do not rock the torso back to move the weight. Think elbows to back pockets. Avoid pulling to the belly or letting the stack crash.
Attach a V-bar (double D) handle to the high pulley. Set the knee pad snug, sit tall and grip the handle with palms facing each other, hands about 15 cm apart, arms straight overhead.

Lean back about 15-20 degrees and pull the handle to the upper chest, driving the elbows down and back close to the ribs. Pause briefly, then return slowly to full extension, letting the shoulders rise for a full lat stretch.
Keep the chest proud and meet the handle with it. Keep tension at the top rather than relaxing the shoulders completely. No momentum or rocking back.
Set the knee pad snug and sit at the pulldown station. Grip the straight bar underhand (palms toward you, full grip) at shoulder width or slightly narrower, arms straight overhead, chest up.

Depress the shoulder blades, then pull the bar to the upper chest, driving the elbows down and back close to the sides, keeping them in front of the torso. Pause briefly, then return the bar slowly to the top for a full stretch.
Keep the wrists straight rather than curled back. Supination gives strong biceps involvement and a long range of shoulder extension. Avoid leaning back more than about 20 degrees or using momentum.

Attach a wide parallel-grip bar or MAG-style handle to the high pulley. Set the knee pad snug, sit tall and grip the handles with palms facing each other, hands about shoulder width or slightly wider, arms straight.

Draw the shoulder blades down and pull the handles toward the upper chest, with the elbows travelling down beside the torso. Lean back about 10-15 degrees. Return to straight arms under control for a full stretch.
A shoulder-friendly middle ground between wide and close grips. Avoid shrugging or rounding forward at the bottom. Pause briefly with the handles at the chest.

Set the knee pad snug and sit with the torso upright under the pulley. Grip a long bar overhand about 1.5 times shoulder width and lean the head slightly forward. Requires good shoulder external rotation and thoracic mobility.
Pull the bar down behind the head toward the base of the neck, keeping the torso vertical and the elbows directly under the bar. Return slowly to straight arms.

Stop the bar at the base of the neck; never yank it into the neck or jut the head forward aggressively. Skip it if the shoulders lack external rotation or it causes pain. Use moderate loads and controlled reps.

Attach a D-handle to the high pulley. Sit at the pulldown station with the knee pad snug, or kneel facing the cable, and grip the handle with one hand, arm fully extended overhead with the palm forward or neutral.

Depress the shoulder blade, then pull the elbow down toward the hip, rotating the palm to face in if desired, until the hand is beside the shoulder. Return slowly to a full overhead stretch, letting the shoulder blade rise.
Pull the elbow to the back pocket. A slight lean toward the working side allows a stronger contraction, but avoid twisting the torso. Useful for fixing side-to-side differences.

Set a D-handle on a high pulley. Kneel on a pad on the working-side knee with the opposite foot forward, hips and knees at 90 degrees, torso tall. Reach up to grip the handle with the working arm straight.
Pull the handle down and slightly back until the hand is beside the shoulder, keeping the ribs down and the hips and shoulders square to the stack. Return slowly to full extension.
Squeeze the glute of the down knee to keep the pelvis neutral. Keep the torso tall rather than leaning. Trains anti-rotation core control as well as the lats.

Attach a straight or neutral bar to a high cable. Kneel tall on a pad facing the stack, about an arm's length away, gripping the bar about shoulder width or slightly wider with arms extended overhead.
Lean back slightly and pull the bar to the upper chest, driving the elbows down toward the ribs. Return under control to straight arms without the cable pulling you forward.
Without thigh pads the core and glutes must stabilize. Keep the hips under the shoulders instead of sitting back on the heels. Useful when no pulldown station is available.

Clip two D-handles to the pulldown carabiner, or one to each of two high pulleys on a functional trainer. Sit with the thighs anchored and grip a handle in each hand, arms straight overhead, palms forward.

Pull the handles down to shoulder height, letting the palms rotate naturally toward neutral as the elbows drive down and slightly behind the torso. Return slowly to a full overhead stretch with the shoulders rising slightly.

Free-moving handles let each arm follow its own path and travel further than a bar allows. Keep the shoulders depressed at the bottom. Stretch fully at the top of each rep and avoid leaning back past about 20 degrees.

Sit in the plate-loaded or selectorized pulldown machine with the thighs locked under the pad. Adjust the seat so the arms are straight and the lats stretched when holding the handles at the top. Grip the independent handles overhand or neutral.
Pull the handles down and slightly back in the machine's arc toward the upper chest, together or one arm at a time, driving the elbows to the sides of the ribs. Return slowly to full extension.
Use the single-arm option to correct side-to-side imbalances. Keep the chest up and the torso still; the machine's arc does the work. Avoid shrugging at the top or cutting the stretch short.
Load the iso-lateral pulldown and set the thigh pad snug. Sit facing the machine and take one handle with the arm reaching up and the lat stretched.
Pull the handle down and slightly back until the hand is beside the shoulder and the elbow is by the side. Return slowly to a full stretch. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Lean a little toward the working side at the top for a deeper stretch. Keep the hips down. Think of driving the elbow toward the back pocket.

Anchor a resistance band high, over a pull-up bar, door anchor or rack. Kneel tall or sit below the anchor and grip the band ends (or handles) with arms extended overhead and slightly forward, band already under light tension.
Depress the shoulder blades, then pull the hands down to shoulder level, driving the elbows toward the ribs and squeezing the lats. Return slowly against the band's pull to a full overhead reach.
Band tension rises as you pull, so the finish is the hardest part; pause there. Good home or warm-up option for 12-20 reps. Check anchor and band for wear before every set.
Attach a triceps rope to the high pulley of a pulldown station. Sit with the thighs anchored and grip the rope ends with a neutral grip just below the knobs, arms straight overhead.
Pull the rope ends down and apart to the sides of the upper chest, elbows driving down and slightly behind the torso. Return slowly to full extension with a full lat stretch.
Spreading the rope lets the elbows travel further back than a bar. Expect to use less weight than a bar pulldown. Avoid excessive lean back; keep the torso at about 10-15 degrees.

Attach a straight bar to a high pulley. Stand an arm's length back, feet hip width, hinge 20-30 degrees at the hips with soft knees, and grip the bar overhand at about shoulder width, arms long and elbows slightly bent and fixed.

Keeping the elbow angle locked, sweep the bar down in an arc by driving the arms toward the hips until the bar touches the thighs. Squeeze the lats, then return slowly until the arms are overhead in line with the torso and the lats stretch.
This is shoulder extension, not a triceps pushdown; the elbows must not bend and straighten. Keep the ribs down and the hips still. Use moderate load and a controlled tempo.
Attach a rope to a high pulley. Stand a step back with a 20-30 degree hip hinge and grip the rope ends with a neutral grip, arms extended forward and up in line with the torso, elbows slightly bent.

With the elbow angle fixed, pull the rope down in an arc toward the hips, spreading the ends so the hands finish beside or slightly behind the thighs. Hold one second, then return slowly to the stretched start.
The rope lets the hands finish behind the body for a stronger lat squeeze than a bar. Keep the torso still and the ribs down. Do not shrug or round the upper back to finish.
Attach a D-handle to a high pulley. Stand facing it or turned slightly side-on, hinge a little at the hips, and hold the handle in one hand with the arm straight overhead and the elbow softly bent.
Keeping the arm straight, sweep the handle down in an arc past the hip, finishing slightly behind the body with the shoulder blade drawn down. Return slowly to the stretched overhead position.
Let the shoulder blade move naturally with the arm. Keep the torso from rotating toward the working side. Good for building the mind-muscle connection with each lat before pulling.

Anchor a resistance band above head height to a rack or pull-up bar. Step back until the band is taut, hinge slightly at the hips, and grip the band with arms straight and angled up in line with the torso.
Keeping the elbows locked in a slight bend, pull the band down in an arc to the thighs, squeezing the lats and drawing the shoulders down. Return slowly to the start without losing tension.
A great warm-up before pull-ups or deadlifts for 15-20 reps. Keep the core braced and the shoulders away from the ears. The arc, not elbow bending, should move the band.
Lie face up on a flat bench with the head near the end. Hold a barbell or EZ-bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip over the chest, elbows bent about 90 degrees.
Keeping the elbow angle fixed, lower the bar back past the head toward the floor until a stretch is felt in the lats. Pull it back over the chest along the same arc.
Use light loads; the bottom position is vulnerable for the shoulders. Keep the elbows from flaring wide. Brace the core so the lower back does not arch off the bench.

Place a flat bench in front of a low pulley with the head end toward the stack. Lie face up with the head near the end, feet flat, and grip a straight bar or rope extended back behind the head, arms nearly straight.
Keeping the elbows slightly bent and fixed, pull the handle up and over in an arc until it is above the chest (or continue to the thighs). Return slowly to the stretched position behind the head.
The cable keeps tension at the top where dumbbells lose it. Keep the lower back on the bench and ribs down. Do not bend the elbows and turn it into a triceps extension.

Adjust the seat so the shoulder joints line up with the machine's pivot point. Fasten the belt if present, place the backs of the upper arms or elbows on the pads and lightly hold the bar behind the head, lats stretched.
Drive the elbows forward and down in an arc until the bar reaches the stomach, squeezing the lats. Return slowly until the arms are fully back behind the head.
Push with the elbows, not the hands; the hands only guide the bar. One of the few lat exercises that removes the biceps. Keep the lower back against the seat and do not shrug at the stretch.
Lie face up on a flat bench or the floor, knees bent. Hold a kettlebell by the horns with both hands, bell hanging down, arms extended over the chest with a slight elbow bend.
With elbows slightly bent and fixed, lower the bell back behind the head until a stretch is felt in the lats (on the floor, the bell lightly touches down). Pull it back over the chest under control.
The floor version limits range and is safer for beginners. Keep the ribs down and abs braced. Hold the handle securely so the bell does not slip over the face.

Sit on a stability ball and walk the feet out until the upper back and head rest on the ball, feet hip width, knees at 90 degrees and hips lifted level in a bridge. Hold one dumbbell over the chest with both hands cupping the top plate.
Lower the dumbbell back behind the head in an arc with slightly bent elbows, keeping the hips up. Pull it back over the chest along the same arc.
Keep the glutes squeezed so the hips do not sag as the weight goes back. Adds core and hip stability demand to the pullover. Use a lighter load than on a bench.

Deadlift the bar to the hips. Stand with feet hip width, toes forward or slightly out, and grip overhand (full grip) just outside shoulder width. Hinge with soft knees until the torso is about 30-45 degrees above parallel, spine neutral, bar hanging at arm's length below the shoulders over mid-foot.

Brace, then pull the bar to the lower ribs or upper abdomen, driving the elbows back at about 45 degrees from the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Lower under control until the arms are straight without changing the torso angle. Breathe between reps.
Keep the spine neutral and the torso angle fixed; standing up as you pull turns it into a shrug. If you must jerk the weight, it is too heavy. Straps are fine when grip limits the back.

Set the barbell on the floor over mid-foot. Stand with feet hip width, hinge until the torso is about parallel to the floor with a flat back and knees bent enough to reach, and grip overhand slightly wider than shoulder width.

Brace and explosively row the bar from the floor to the lower chest or upper abdomen without lifting the torso. Lower it back to the floor and let it settle to a dead stop, re-bracing before every rep.
The torso stays parallel; no hip extension to help. Each rep starts from zero, so it builds starting strength. Named for weightlifting coach Glenn Pendlay. Use plates that put the bar at mid-shin.

Grip the barbell underhand at about shoulder width. Hinge only slightly so the torso is about 20-30 degrees forward of upright, knees soft, bar hanging at mid-thigh. Popularised by bodybuilder Dorian Yates.

Pull the bar toward the lower abdomen or belt line, keeping the elbows close to the body and driving them back behind the torso. Squeeze, then lower under control to straight arms with the bar near the thighs.

Distinct from the reverse-grip bent-over row by the upright torso: it allows heavier loads but shorter range and more traps. Keep the elbows tucked to hit the lats. Avoid excessive body English or standing up to finish.

Grip a barbell underhand at shoulder width. Hinge forward until the torso is around 45 degrees or lower (much more bent than a Yates row), back flat, knees soft, bar hanging at arm's length below the shoulders.
Row the bar to the lower abdomen with the elbows tucked close to the sides, squeeze the lats, then lower it slowly to arm's length without changing torso angle.
An underhand (palms-up) grip increases biceps involvement and the lat bias. Keep the wrists neutral rather than curled. Load moderately: heavy underhand rows can strain the biceps tendon.

Raise a flat bench on blocks or plates so a barbell hangs below it at full arm length without touching the floor. Lie face down with the chin past the end and the legs on the bench, and grip the bar overhand at about shoulder width.
Pull the bar up to the underside of the bench, driving the elbows high and back and squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower to a full hang with straight arms, letting the shoulder blades spread.
Fully chest-supported, so there is no lower-back fatigue or momentum. Keep the chest glued to the bench. If the bench is too low, the range is cut short.
Prone Dumbbell Row on High Bench

Raise a flat bench on blocks so the arms can hang fully without the dumbbells touching the floor. Lie face down with the chin past the end, holding a dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down, palms neutral or facing back.
Row both dumbbells up beside the bench, elbows driving back, until the upper arms are past the torso. Lower slowly to full extension, letting the shoulder blades spread.
Lets each arm move independently with a deeper stretch than the barbell version. Keep the chest on the bench. Change palm and elbow angle to shift between lats and upper back.

Set the Smith bar at about knee height. Grip overhand just outside shoulder width, unrack by rotating the hooks, and hinge to a 30-45 degree torso angle with a flat back, feet hip width and a little behind the bar.
Pull the bar to the lower ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades, then lower under control to straight arms without changing torso angle.
The fixed path removes balance demands, so you can focus on the back. Stand so the vertical bar path brushes the thighs. Rerack carefully by rotating the hooks onto the pins.

Grip the bar overhand with a wide snatch-width grip (roughly index finger to index finger at the outer knurl rings or wider). Hinge until the torso is near parallel, back flat, knees soft, bar hanging at arm's length.
Row the bar to the lower chest with the elbows flared wide, about 75 degrees from the torso, squeezing the upper back and rear delts. Lower to straight arms under control.
Shifts emphasis to the upper back and rear delts. Use 15-25 percent less weight than a standard row. Keep the neck neutral and the torso still.
Grip a barbell overhand just outside shoulder width. Hinge to a 30-45 degree torso angle with a neutral spine and soft knees, bar hanging below the shoulders.
Row the bar to the lower ribs and hold it there for 1-3 seconds with the shoulder blades fully squeezed and the bar touching the torso. Lower slowly to straight arms.
Removes momentum and exposes cheating. Use about 20-30 percent less load than normal rows. The torso angle must not change during the pause; if you have to stand up to hold it, lighten the bar.

Wedge one end of a barbell into a landmine or corner and load the other end. Straddle the bar with feet shoulder width, hinge to about 45 degrees with a flat back and soft knees, and slide a close-grip V-handle (or the handles of a dedicated T-bar) under the bar just behind the plates.
Pull the handle toward the lower chest, driving the elbows back close to the body and squeezing the back. Lower to full arm extension under control without the plates touching the floor.
Keep the chest up and the hips back. Use smaller plates for a longer range. Do not round the lower back to reach the floor.
Load the chest-supported T-bar machine. Stand on the foot platform, lie with the chest against the angled pad, and grip the handles: neutral close, or overhand wide.
Row the handles up toward the chest, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Lower slowly until the arms are straight and the shoulder blades spread.
The chest stays on the pad, sparing the lower back. A wide overhand grip biases the upper back; a close neutral grip biases the lats. Do not lift the chest to cheat.
Load the chest-supported T-bar row. Stand on the foot plate with the chest on the pad and take the wide (overhand) handles with the arms straight.
Row the handles up with the elbows flared about 60 to 75 degrees until the upper arms pass the torso. Lower slowly to a full stretch.
The wide grip and flared elbows shift the work to the upper back and rear delts; the narrow grip works more lats. Keep the chest on the pad and the neck neutral.

Set a barbell in a landmine and load it with small plates. Stand perpendicular to the bar end in a staggered stance, front leg nearest the plates, front forearm resting on that thigh. Grip the thick sleeve end overhand with the far hand, torso about parallel to the floor. Named for coach John Meadows.
Row the bar end up and back, driving the elbow high and slightly out, until the hand reaches hip level. Lower until the lat and upper back fully stretch.
Use straps for heavy sets. Small plates increase range. Keep the hips square and avoid twisting the torso to finish.
Brace one hand on a bench or rack with the feet staggered. Grip a heavy dumbbell in the other hand, ideally with straps, torso slightly above parallel. Named for powerlifter Matt Kroczaleski.
Row the dumbbell powerfully toward the hip for high reps, typically 15-30, allowing slight body English. Lower to a full stretch each rep.
Some momentum is accepted, but control the lowering. Use straps if grip limits the back. A top set of heavy, high-rep rows; not a substitute for strict rows.

Place the same-side knee and hand on a flat bench, back flat and nearly parallel to the floor, other foot on the floor slightly out to the side. Hold a dumbbell in the free hand with a neutral grip, arm hanging straight below the shoulder.
Row the dumbbell back toward the hip in a slight arc, elbow close to the body, until the upper arm is in line with the torso. Lower slowly to a full stretch, letting the shoulder blade glide forward.
Pull to the hip, not the chest, for the lats. Avoid rotating the torso to lift heavier. Keep the neck neutral.

Stand beside a flat bench in a staggered stance, the leg on the working side back. Hinge until the torso is 15-30 degrees above parallel and place the free hand on the bench (three points of contact: two feet and one hand). Hold a dumbbell in the working hand directly below the shoulder, back flat.

Row the dumbbell back toward the hip in a slight arc, elbow close to the body, until the upper arm is in line with the torso. Lower to a full stretch, letting the shoulder blade glide forward without the torso rotating.

Allows heavier loading and a more athletic stance than the knee-on-bench version. Keep the hips and shoulders square to the floor. Pull to the hip for the lats, toward the lower ribs for the upper back.

Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing in. Feet hip width, soft knees, hinge at the hips until the torso is 30-45 degrees above parallel with a flat back, dumbbells hanging below the shoulders.

Brace and row both dumbbells to the sides of the waist, elbows travelling back at about 30-45 degrees from the torso, squeezing the shoulder blades together. Lower slowly to straight arms without changing the torso angle.

Brace hard to keep the torso still; the lower back works isometrically. A neutral grip is easiest on the wrists; pronate and flare the elbows to shift work to the upper back. Avoid rising up as the set gets hard.

Set an incline bench at 30-45 degrees. Lie face down with the chest on the pad and the top of the pad at upper-chest level, feet on the floor or on the seat. Hold a dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down, palms neutral.
Row both dumbbells up, driving the elbows back past the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Lower to a full stretch, letting the shoulder blades protract slightly at the bottom.
The chest stays on the pad to remove momentum and spare the lower back. Elbows flared about 60-75 degrees target the upper back and rear delts; tucked elbows pulling to the hips target the lats.

Set an incline bench at a steep angle (around 60-75 degrees). Stand behind it, feet back, and lean forward so only the upper chest rests on the top of the pad, torso roughly 45 degrees. Hold dumbbells hanging below with straight arms. Named for coach Eric Helms.
Row the dumbbells up toward the lower ribs or hips while keeping the chest in light contact with the pad. Lower slowly to a full stretch.
The pad acts as a cheat detector: if the chest leaves it, the weight is too heavy. Strict variation that removes body English while keeping a free standing setup. Keep the neck neutral.
Place two kettlebells between the feet in a stance wider than shoulder width. Hinge deeply with a flat back and bent knees until the torso is near parallel, and grip both handles.
Row one kettlebell to the hip while pressing the other firmly into the floor for support, then lower and alternate sides in a steady rhythm.
Keep the hips level and avoid rotation; press the non-working bell down hard. The deep, wide hinge loads the back without needing a bench. Great for core stability and back strength.

Stand in a staggered stance or with one hand on a bench. Hold a kettlebell in the other hand by the handle with a neutral grip, arm hanging straight below the shoulder, back flat and torso about 30-45 degrees above parallel.
Row the kettlebell to the hip, keeping the elbow close and the wrist straight. Lower until the arm is fully extended and the lat stretches.
The bell hangs below the handle, so the centre of mass sits under the hand and demands a firm grip and straight wrist. Keep the torso square and the spine neutral.
Hold a kettlebell in each hand with a neutral grip. Feet hip width, hinge forward with a flat back and soft knees until the torso is around 45 degrees, bells hanging below the shoulders.
Row both kettlebells to the waist, elbows close to the sides, squeezing the shoulder blades, then lower to straight arms without changing the torso angle.
Avoid lifting the torso as you pull. Keep the bells close to the legs. Pause briefly at the top of each rep.

Set two hex dumbbells shoulder width apart. Get into a high plank gripping the handles with a neutral grip, wrists stacked under the shoulders, feet wider than hips, glutes squeezed and body in a straight line.

Press one dumbbell into the floor and row the other to the lower ribs, elbow close to the body, while bracing so the hips stay square to the floor. Lower it under control and repeat on the other side.
Hips level, no rotation or hip hike. A wider stance makes it easier; narrow feet make it harder. Use hex dumbbells so they cannot roll. Scale by rowing from the knees or with lighter bells.

Sit at a low cable row station with the feet on the platform and the knees slightly bent. Grip a V-handle (close neutral grip) with arms extended, sitting tall with the torso upright or leaning forward no more than about 10 degrees.

Pull the handle to the lower ribs or upper abdomen, driving the elbows back close to the sides and squeezing the shoulder blades together, chest up. Return slowly until the arms are straight and the shoulder blades reach forward slightly, keeping the spine neutral.
Keep the torso nearly upright, with only a small lean; rocking back and forth turns it into a hip swing. Pause at the contraction. Do not let the lower back round on the return.
Attach a long straight bar to the low pulley. Sit with the feet on the platform and knees soft, grip the bar overhand about 1.5 times shoulder width and sit upright with arms extended.
Pull the bar to the lower chest, flaring the elbows out to about 60-75 degrees from the torso and squeezing the upper back. Return slowly to full extension.
Shifts emphasis to the upper back and rear delts compared with the V-handle row. Do not shrug. Keep the chest tall and the torso still.
Attach a D-handle to the low pulley. Sit at the station with the feet on the platform, knees soft, and grip the handle with one hand, arm extended forward, free hand on the thigh.
Row the handle toward the hip, letting the torso rotate slightly toward the cable at the start and squaring up at the end. Return slowly with a full stretch.
Keep rotation small and controlled. Great for fixing imbalances. Pull the elbow back toward the back pocket and keep the shoulder down.

Set a cable pulley at about chest height with a D-handle (one arm) or two handles. Stand in a split stance facing the stack, front knee soft, hips and shoulders square, and grip the handle with the arm extended.
Row the handle to the side of the ribs, driving the elbow back and squeezing the shoulder blade, while keeping the hips and shoulders square. Return slowly to full extension.
Brace the core to resist rotation. Lower the pulley to bias the lats; raise it for the upper back. An athletic, functional row.
Adjust the seat so the handles are at mid-chest height and the chest pad so the arms are fully extended when holding the handles. Sit tall with the chest against the pad, feet flat.
Row the handles back, driving the elbows behind the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Return slowly to the start until the shoulder blades spread.
Keep the chest on the pad. Avoid shrugging. Use the neutral handles for lats and the wide overhand handles for the upper back.
Set the seat so the handles are level with the lower chest and the chest pad so you reach them with the arms straight. Sit with the chest on the pad and hold one handle.
Row the handle back until the elbow passes the torso, squeezing the shoulder blade back. Return slowly to a full reach. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Keep the chest on the pad and do not twist away from the working arm. Neutral handle for lats, pronated for upper back. Good for evening out left-right strength.
Adjust the seat so the handles align with mid-chest and the arms are fully extended when holding them. Sit with the chest against the pad, feet flat, and grip each handle (neutral or overhand).

Row the handles back, together or alternating, driving the elbows behind the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades. Return slowly to full extension, letting the shoulder blades glide forward at the stretch while the chest stays on the pad.
Independent arms help fix strength imbalances; alternating arms adds an anti-rotation challenge. Keep the chest on the pad and control the stretch. Do not shrug.
Load one arm of the iso-lateral row. Set the seat so the handle lines up with the mid chest. Sit with the chest on the pad and hold the handle with the arm straight.
Row the handle back until the elbow passes the torso, then return slowly to a full reach. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Brace the free hand on the frame. Keep the chest on the pad and the shoulders level. Let the shoulder blade move forward at the stretch and back at the finish.

Adjust the seat so the handles are above head height when reaching up and forward. Sit with the thighs under the pad and chest against the support if present, and grip the handles with a neutral or overhand grip.
Pull the handles down and back toward the chest in the machine's arc, driving the elbows toward the hips. Return slowly to the stretched position, letting the shoulder blades rise.
Combines a pulldown and a row angle. Keep the chest tall and do not lean back. Train one arm at a time to fix imbalances.
Adjust the seat so the handles are at waist height when the arms are extended forward and slightly down. Sit with the chest on the pad, feet braced, and grip the handles with a neutral grip.
Row the handles back toward the hips in a low arc, elbows close to the body, squeezing the lats. Return slowly with control to a full stretch.
The low path biases the lower lats. Keep the chest on the pad and avoid jerking. Pull the elbows into the back pockets and pause for a second at full contraction.

Set a bar in a squat rack or Smith machine at about hip height. Lie underneath with the bar over the lower chest, grip it overhand slightly wider than shoulder width, and extend the body straight from head to heels, heels on the floor, glutes squeezed.

Pull the lower chest to the bar, driving the elbows back at about 45 degrees from the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades together while keeping the body rigid like a plank. Lower until the arms are straight.
Keep the hips from sagging or piking. Raise the bar or bend the knees to make it easier; lower the bar or elevate the feet to make it harder.

Set a bar at about hip height in a rack or Smith machine. Lie underneath with the bar over the lower chest and grip it underhand at shoulder width, body straight from head to heels, heels on the floor.
Pull the lower chest to the bar, elbows close to the body and travelling back toward the hips. Lower slowly until the arms are straight.
More biceps and lat involvement than the overhand version. Keep the body rigid and squeeze the glutes to stop the hips sagging. Adjust bar height to scale.
Set a bar at about hip height and place the heels on a bench or box of similar height. Grip the bar overhand slightly wider than shoulder width and hang with the body straight and horizontal.
Pull the chest to the bar, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower with control to straight arms.
A harder progression of the inverted row because more body weight is lifted. Keep the hips in line with the shoulders. Use a weighted vest to progress further.

Set up for an inverted row with the bar at about hip height. Wear a weighted vest or have a partner place a plate on the chest (a plate needs a hand to hold it, so a vest is preferred). Grip the bar overhand with the body straight.
Pull the chest to the bar, keeping the load secure. Lower until the arms are straight.
Progress by adding load once 3 sets of 12 bodyweight reps are easy. Keep the body rigid. Make sure the load does not slide. Pause at the bar.
Set gymnastic rings at about hip height, shoulder width apart. Grip the rings and lean back with arms straight and the body rigid from head to heels, heels on the floor.
Pull the chest to the rings, allowing the hands to rotate naturally toward neutral. Lower with control to straight arms.
Rings allow a natural wrist path and add a stability demand. Walk the feet forward toward the anchor to make each rep harder. Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top.
Lie under a sturdy table with the chest under its edge. Grip the edge with hands shoulder width apart, thumbs under the table, and extend the body with heels on the floor.
Pull the chest toward the table edge, squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower until the arms are straight.
Make sure the table is sturdy and will not tip. Bend the knees to scale down. Pause with the chest near the table edge and keep the neck neutral.
Stand in a doorway and grip both sides of the frame at chest height. Walk the feet close to the threshold and lean back until the arms are straight and the body is straight from head to heels.
Pull the chest toward the doorway, squeezing the shoulder blades and keeping the elbows close to the ribs. Lower slowly to straight arms.
Feet closer to the threshold increase difficulty. Grip firmly; use a towel looped around the frame if grip slips. Keep the heels planted.
Anchor a resistance band at chest height, or sit on the floor with legs extended and loop the band around the soles of the feet. Grip the ends or handles with a neutral grip and arms extended.
Row the band toward the lower ribs, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades. Return slowly to full extension.
Tension increases as you pull, so the top is hardest; pause there. Keep the torso upright and the shoulders down away from the ears.
Stand with feet hip width over a sandbag. Hinge to about 45 degrees with a flat back and soft knees, and grip the sandbag by its handles or by the fabric (harder on grip), arms straight.
Row the sandbag to the stomach, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower to straight arms with control.
The shifting load challenges stability. Keep the spine neutral. Start light because sand shifting mid-rep can pull you out of position.
Attach a long straight bar to a high pulley. Sit on the bench or kneel tall facing the stack, about an arm's length away, and grip the bar wide overhand with arms extended.
Pull one end of the bar down and back toward that hip, as if paddling a kayak, while the other arm stays long. Return to the start and pull the other side. Alternate sides each rep.
Rotate the torso slightly with each stroke but keep the torso tall. Control the return. Use moderate weight so the torso stays upright.

Lie face down on a flat or low incline bench, chest supported, a dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down. Row both dumbbells to the top so the elbows are behind the torso and the shoulder blades are squeezed.
Isometric version: hold both dumbbells at the top for the target time. Alternating version: hold one dumbbell at the top while the other lowers to full extension and rows back up, then switch sides.
Hold the top position firmly; the holding side must not sag. Keep the shoulder blades squeezed and the chest on the pad. Builds isometric strength in the contracted position.

Attach a rope to a cable set at upper chest to forehead height. Grip the rope ends with a neutral or overhand grip, thumbs toward you, and step back until the arms are straight and the weight is off the stack. Stand tall with a split or hip-width stance.
Pull the rope toward the face, elbows high and wide, spreading the ends apart and rotating the shoulders outward so the hands finish beside the ears with the knuckles pointing back. Return slowly.
Lead with the elbows and finish with the external rotation. Use moderate weight for 12-20 reps; heavy loads turn it into a row. Avoid leaning back.
Anchor a resistance band at face height. Grip the band ends with a neutral or overhand grip and step back until the band is taut with the arms extended in front.
Pull the band toward the face, spreading the hands apart and rotating the shoulders outward so the hands finish beside the ears in a double-biceps position. Return slowly.
Keep the elbows high. Use a light band for 15-25 reps as a warm-up or shoulder-health accessory. Keep the ribs down.

Hold a light dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip. Feet hip width, soft knees, hinge forward with a flat back until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor, arms hanging below the shoulders with a slight fixed elbow bend.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until the arms are in line with the torso, leading with the elbows. Lower slowly to the start.
Use light weights and keep the elbow angle fixed. Avoid swinging or standing up. Keep the neck neutral.
Sit at the end of a flat bench with feet together. Lean forward so the chest is near the thighs, back flat, dumbbells hanging under the legs with a neutral grip and a slight elbow bend.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides with the elbows slightly bent until the upper arms are level with the shoulders. Lower slowly.
The seated position limits momentum. Lead with the elbows. Keep the neck neutral. Pause at the top.
Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie face down with the chest on the pad, feet on the floor, a light dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down, palms facing in.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides with slightly bent elbows until the arms are level with the torso. Lower slowly.
Chest support removes momentum. Use light weights. Lead with the pinkies and think of reaching the hands wide, not up. Keep the chin tucked.

Set the pec deck arms to the rear-fly position. Adjust the seat so the handles are at shoulder height. Sit facing the machine with the chest against the pad and grip the handles with a neutral or overhand grip, arms extended forward.
Pull the handles out and back in a wide arc until the arms are in line with the torso. Pause, then return slowly to the front.
Keep the elbows slightly bent. Avoid shrugging. Control the return.
Set the pec deck handles to the rear position and the seat so the handles are at shoulder height. Sit facing the pad, chest against it, and hold one handle with the arm straight in front.
Sweep the arm out and back in a wide arc until it is in line with the body, then return slowly to the front. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Lead with the back of the hand and keep a slight bend in the elbow. Keep the chest on the pad and do not rotate the torso. Sitting side-on lets the arm travel a little further.
Set two pulleys at shoulder height. Cross the cables and grip the left cable with the right hand and vice versa. Step back to the centre with arms extended in front at shoulder height.
Pull the arms out and back in a wide arc until they are in line with the shoulders. Return slowly to the crossed position.
Keep the elbows soft. Constant tension is the advantage. Avoid arching the back or shrugging.
Set a pulley at shoulder height with a D-handle or no handle (grip the cable ball). Stand side-on to the stack and grip the handle with the far hand, arm reaching across the body at shoulder height.
Pull the handle out and back across the body in an arc until the arm is in line with the shoulder. Return slowly.
Keep the torso still and avoid rotating. Lead with the elbow. Use light weight. Keep a slight elbow bend throughout.
Hold a light resistance band in front at shoulder height with an overhand grip, hands shoulder width apart, arms straight. Stand tall with the ribs down.
Pull the band apart by moving the hands out to the sides until the band touches the chest. Return slowly to the start.
Keep the arms straight and squeeze the shoulder blades. Great warm-up; do 15-30 reps. Vary the grip: overhand, underhand or diagonal. Do not arch the lower back.
Hold the TRX handles with a neutral grip, arms extended forward at chest height. Lean back with the body straight from head to heels.
Open the arms out to the sides, keeping a slight bend in the elbows, pulling the body up until the arms are in line with the shoulders. Lower slowly.
Walk the feet forward to make it harder. Keep the body straight. Do not shrug. Pause at the top with the shoulder blades squeezed together.
Hinge forward or lie face down on an incline bench with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing back (overhand), arms hanging straight below the shoulders.
Row the dumbbells up with the elbows flared out to the sides, about 75-90 degrees from the torso, until the upper arms are parallel to the floor. Lower slowly.
Wide elbows shift emphasis to the rear delts and upper back. Use light to moderate weights. Avoid shrugging. Pause at the top.
Lie face down on an incline bench set to 30-45 degrees, or on the floor, with light dumbbells (0.5-2 kg) or no weight. Chest stays on the pad and the chin is tucked.
Raise the arms in a Y shape, then a T shape, then a W shape, pausing at the top of each. Lower slowly between letters.
Use light loads; this targets the lower traps and rotator cuff. Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down. Thumbs point up on the Y and T. Do 6-10 reps of each letter.
Set a barbell in a squat rack at about chest height when kneeling. Sit or kneel under it, grip underhand or overhand at shoulder width, and rest the heels on the floor or a box in front.
Pull the chest to the bar using the legs only as much as needed, driving the elbows down. Lower under control until the arms are straight.
A scalable bridge between inverted rows and full chin-ups. Use less leg drive over time. Keep the torso upright and the shoulders down.
Grip a pull-up bar overhand at shoulder width with a full grip. Step off a box so the arms are fully straight and the feet are off the floor.
Hang for time, either passively with relaxed shoulders for decompression or actively with the shoulder blades pulled slightly down. Step back onto the box to finish.
Builds grip endurance and shoulder tolerance for pull-ups. Breathe slowly. Use a box to get down rather than dropping, and start with 20-30 second holds.
Stand on a 2-5 cm platform or plates with the barbell on the floor over mid-foot. Hinge until the torso is parallel to the floor, back flat, and grip overhand slightly wider than shoulder width.
Row the bar explosively from the floor to the lower chest without raising the torso, then return it to the floor for a dead stop each rep.
The deficit adds range and stretch at the bottom. Requires good hamstring flexibility to stay flat-backed. Use lighter loads than the standard Pendlay row.
Attach a rope to a low or mid pulley. Lie face up on the floor or a bench with the head toward the stack, holding the rope ends with arms extended toward the pulley.
Pull the rope toward the forehead, spreading the ends and rotating the hands back until the elbows are beside the shoulders. Return slowly to straight arms.
The floor supports the torso, removing body English. Keep the lower back flat. Use light to moderate loads for 12-20 reps.

Set a bar at about hip height. Lie under it, grip the bar with one hand directly over the mid-chest, feet wider than hips, body straight from head to heels; the free arm rests on the chest or reaches to the side.
Pull the chest toward the bar with one arm while resisting rotation, then lower until the arm is straight.
Keep the hips square to the floor. Widen the feet or raise the bar to scale. A key step toward the one-arm pull-up.
Attach a rope to the low pulley of a seated row station. Sit with feet on the platform, knees soft, and grip the rope ends with a neutral grip, arms extended.
Row the rope toward the lower ribs, pulling the ends apart so the hands finish beside the torso and the elbows travel behind the body. Return slowly to full extension.
Spreading the rope adds range and upper-back squeeze. Stay upright with minimal lean. Use slightly less weight than a V-handle row.
Set a pulley at about head height with a D-handle or rope. Kneel in a half-kneeling position facing the stack and grip the handle with the arm extended upward and forward.
Pull the handle down and back toward the chest or shoulder, driving the elbow behind the body. Return slowly to full reach.
Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg to keep the pelvis level. Keep the ribs down. Bridges a pulldown and a row.

Set the bar in a rack at collarbone height. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped just outside shoulder width so the forearms are vertical, bar low in the palm over the forearm bones, wrists stacked. Unrack, step back and stand with feet hip-width, glutes squeezed. Breathe into the belly and brace.

Press the bar straight up, pulling the chin back so it clears the face. Once the bar passes the forehead, move the head and chest forward through the window so the bar locks out over the mid-foot in line with the ears, elbows straight and shoulders shrugged slightly up. Lower along the same vertical path to the front delts and re-brace.

No knee dip or leg drive; that makes it a push press. Squeeze glutes and keep ribs down so the lower back does not lean into an incline press. A bar drifting forward of the face is the most common fault.

Set an adjustable bench at 80-90 degrees inside a power rack and the J-hooks about 5-10 cm above head height when seated. Sit with hips against the pad, feet planted wider than hip-width under the knees. Take an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped just outside shoulder width, forearms vertical.

Unrack (ideally with a lift-off) and lower the bar to the top of the chest. Press straight up, pulling the head back to clear the chin, then bring the head forward under the bar so it locks out over the crown. Lower under control to the collarbone without bouncing and press again; exhale through the top.

Keep the ribs down and the mid-back against the pad; arching off the seat turns it into an incline press. Elbows stay slightly in front of the bar at the bottom. The bench removes leg drive and balance, so it isolates the delts and triceps more than the standing press.

Set the bar in a rack at shoulder height and step under it so it rests on the upper traps as for a high-bar squat. Take an overhand grip 1.25-1.5 times shoulder width so the forearms are vertical when the bar is behind the head. Stand with feet hip-width, glutes and abs braced, head neutral.

Press the bar straight up from behind the head to full lockout over the back of the ears and mid-foot, finishing with a slight shrug. Lower under control to about ear level or the base of the skull, stopping where the forearms can stay vertical, then press again.

Only use it if you have the shoulder external rotation and thoracic extension to keep the forearms vertical and the head neutral; never push the head forward to make room. Start with an empty bar and a shortened range. Moderate loads and controlled tempo; it is an accessory, not a max lift.

Set an upright bench at 90 degrees inside a power rack with the J-hooks just above head height when seated, so the bar can be unracked behind the head. Take an overhand grip 1.25-1.5 times shoulder width. Sit tall with feet planted wide and the back against the pad.

Unrack the bar and lower it behind the head to about ear level, forearms vertical and elbows directly under the bar. Press straight up to lockout with the bar over the crown of the head, then lower back under control to the same stopping point and repeat.

Keep the head neutral and chest up; do not jut the chin forward. Stop the descent where the shoulders still feel stable, which for many lifters is ear level rather than the traps. The seat removes leg drive, so use lighter loads than the standing version and a 2-3 second lowering.

Hold a barbell in the front rack position on the front delts with an overhand grip just outside shoulder width. Stand with feet hip-width, glutes and abs braced; it can also be done seated on an upright bench. Use a load well below your strict press.

Press the bar just high enough to clear the top of the head, about 5-10 cm, then guide it backward and lower it behind the head to about ear level. Press up again just over the head and lower it back to the front of the shoulders. One front-to-back-to-front pass is one rep; the elbows never lock out.

Constant tension on the delts is the point, so stop each press as soon as the bar clears the head. Keep the bar path close to the head and the forearms vertical. The behind-the-neck half needs good external rotation; skip that half or the exercise if it pinches.

Sit on the floor inside a power rack with legs straight and feet about hip-width, or in a wide straddle. Set the J-hooks so the bar is at upper-chest height when seated. Take an overhand grip just outside shoulder width and sit tall with ribs stacked over the pelvis.

Unrack, brace and press the bar straight up to lockout over the crown of the head without leaning back; move the head back to clear the chin and forward under the bar at the top. Lower under control to the upper chest and repeat. Re-rack on the hooks at the end of the set.

With no back support or leg drive any trunk weakness shows immediately, so keep a hard brace. Keep the knees straight and do not rock the torso. If tight hamstrings force a slump, sit on a low plate or bend the knees slightly; named after strongman Zydrunas Savickas.

Sit on the floor with legs straight and feet about hip-width. Hold a dumbbell at each shoulder at about chin height with palms forward or neutral and forearms vertical. Sit tall with ribs stacked over the pelvis and brace the abs.

Press both dumbbells straight up until the arms are locked and the biceps are beside the ears, hands over the shoulders. Lower slowly back to shoulder level and repeat without rocking the torso. Exhale through the top, re-brace at the bottom.

This is as much a trunk exercise as a press; leaning back means the load is too heavy. Keep the legs straight and quiet. Pressing a single dumbbell adds an anti-lateral-flexion challenge for the obliques.

Set an adjustable bench at 80-90 degrees. Rest the dumbbells on the thighs, then kick them up one at a time to the shoulders. Hold them at about ear level with an overhand grip, elbows 30-45 degrees in front of the torso and forearms vertical. Feet planted wider than the hips, back against the pad.

Press the dumbbells up and slightly in until the arms are straight over the shoulders, handles a few centimetres apart rather than clashing. Lower under control for 2-3 seconds until the handles reach ear or shoulder level, then press again.

Keep the back on the pad and ribs down. Forearms stay vertical throughout; do not flare the elbows straight out to the sides. To finish, bring the dumbbells to the shoulders and then to the thighs rather than dropping them from overhead.

Stand with feet hip-width and hold a dumbbell at each shoulder at chin height, palms forward or turned slightly in, elbows slightly in front of the torso and forearms vertical. Squeeze the glutes, brace the abs and take a breath.
Press the dumbbells straight up to full lockout, biceps beside the ears and hands over the shoulders. Lower under control to the shoulders and press again without any knee bend.
Avoid leaning back or using the legs; the trunk has to stabilise more than in the seated version. Keep wrists stacked over elbows. A slightly staggered stance helps if the lower back arches.
Sit on a bench set at 80-90 degrees, or stand. Hold dumbbells in front of the shoulders at chin height with palms facing you and elbows in front of the body, like the top of a curl.

Press up while rotating the palms outward and opening the elbows to the sides, so the palms face forward by the time the arms lock out overhead. Reverse the rotation on the way down, bringing the elbows back in front and the palms to face you at the bottom.

Rotate smoothly through the whole range rather than all at the top. Keep ribs down and avoid arching. Popularised by Arnold Schwarzenegger; the extra front-delt range makes it harder, so use 10-20 percent less than your normal dumbbell press.

Stand with feet hip-width holding one dumbbell at the shoulder at chin height, palm forward or neutral, forearm vertical. Put the free hand on the hip or hold it out to the side. Squeeze both glutes and brace.
Press the dumbbell straight overhead to lockout with the biceps beside the ear, without leaning away from it. Lower slowly to the shoulder and finish all reps before switching arms.

The obliques must keep the torso vertical; resist side-bending toward or away from the weight. Keep the elbow slightly in front of the body, not drifting behind. Useful for correcting left-right strength differences.
Sit on a bench set at 80-90 degrees, or stand. Hold dumbbells at the shoulders at chin height with palms facing each other and elbows pointing forward, forearms vertical.
Press the dumbbells straight up, keeping the palms facing in, until the arms lock out over the shoulders. Lower under control for 2-3 seconds back to the shoulders.

A shoulder-friendly option for lifters who feel pinching with an overhand grip, since the elbows stay in front of the torso. Keep the elbows forward rather than flared. Front delts and triceps work harder than in the overhand press.
Sit on a bench set at 80-90 degrees or stand with feet hip-width. Hold a dumbbell at each shoulder at chin height, palms forward, forearms vertical. Brace the abs.

Press one dumbbell overhead to lockout while the other stays at the shoulder, lower it under control, then press the other side. A harder version holds one arm locked out overhead while the other arm presses.
Keep the torso still and avoid shifting toward the pressing side. The non-working dumbbell stays fixed at the shoulder, which adds time under tension. Count each side as one rep.

Kneel on a pad with one knee down and the other foot forward, both knees at 90 degrees, hips and shoulders square. Hold the dumbbell at the shoulder on the same side as the down knee, palm neutral or forward. Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg.
Press the dumbbell overhead to full lockout, biceps by the ear, keeping the torso tall. Lower under control to the shoulder, finish the set and switch the stance and arm.

Squeezing the down-side glute locks the pelvis and stops lower-back arching; keep the ribs down. Do not lean away from the weight. A good pressing regression for lifters who compensate through the lumbar spine.
Kneel upright on a mat with knees hip-width and hips fully extended so they stack over the knees, shins flat or toes tucked. Hold a dumbbell at each shoulder at chin height with forearms vertical.
Brace and press both dumbbells straight overhead to lockout. Lower slowly back to the shoulders while keeping the hips locked forward and the torso vertical.

Squeeze the glutes hard to keep the hips extended and stop the lower back arching. If you feel the lower back working, the load is too heavy. No leg drive is possible, so it exposes compensations hidden in the standing press.

Sit on a bench set at about 80-90 degrees. Hold dumbbells beside the shoulders at chin height with palms facing forward and the elbows pulled back and out so the upper arms are roughly in line with the torso and the forearms are angled slightly outward.

Press the dumbbells up and slightly back in a short arc until they are over the head, stopping just before lockout. Lower until the handles are level with the top of the shoulders with the elbows out wide, then press again.
Named after Larry Scott; the flared elbows and partial range bias the side delts. Use light weight and keep constant tension. Stop the set if the front of the shoulder pinches.

Clean the kettlebell to the rack position: bell resting on the outside of the forearm, wrist straight, elbow tucked against the ribs and fist at chin height. Stand with feet hip-width, glutes and quads tight. Grip the handle diagonally across the palm.

Press the bell up while the forearm rotates slightly so the palm faces forward at lockout, biceps beside the ear and the bell over the shoulder. Pull it back down into the rack under control, keeping the elbow close, and repeat. Switch arms after the set.
Squeeze the free fist and tense the whole body to help the press. Avoid leaning away from the bell. Keep the wrist neutral, not bent back under the weight.
Clean two kettlebells of equal weight to the rack position with elbows tight to the ribs, bells resting on the forearms and fists at chin height. Stand with feet hip-width and brace hard.
Press both bells overhead together to lockout with the biceps beside the ears and palms facing forward. Pull them back down into the double rack under control and reset tension before the next rep.
Keep ribs down; the double load invites lumbar extension. Elbows track slightly forward rather than flaring wide. Re-clean the bells if the rack position collapses.
Clean two kettlebells to the rack position, then press one overhead so you start with one bell locked out and one in the rack. Stand with feet hip-width and brace.
Lower the top bell while pressing the racked bell at the same speed, so the two pass at about head height. Continue alternating in a smooth see-saw rhythm; each press counts as one rep.

Keep the trunk still while the load shifts from side to side; do not lean away from the pressing arm. Coordinate both arms. Use moderate loads and breathe steadily rather than holding one long breath.

Adjust the seat so the handles start level with the shoulders or chin and the back pad is upright. Sit with the back and head on the pad, feet flat, and take the overhand or neutral handles with forearms vertical.
Press the handles up until the arms are almost locked, then lower under control for 2-3 seconds to the start position without letting the weight stack touch.
Keep the head and back on the pad and the hips on the seat. The fixed path suits high-rep work and taking sets close to failure safely. Neutral handles are easier on sensitive shoulders.
Adjust the seat so the parallel (palms-facing) handles start at about shoulder height. Sit with the back against the pad and the feet flat.
Press the handles overhead until the arms are straight, then lower under control to shoulder height.
Elbows stay in front of the body, which is easier on the shoulders than the wide grip. Keep the lower back against the pad and the ribs down.
Set the shoulder press machine so the handle starts at shoulder height. Sit with the back against the pad and hold one handle; hold the seat with the other hand.
Press the handle overhead until the arm is straight, then lower under control. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Do not lean away from the working arm. Keep the ribs down. Useful for fixing left-right differences.

Place an upright bench (80-90 degrees) inside a Smith machine so the bar descends just in front of the face to the upper chest. Sit with feet planted and take an overhand grip just outside shoulder width, then rotate the bar to unhook it.
Lower the bar to upper-chest or chin level, then press straight up along the fixed track until the arms are nearly locked. Rotate the hooks back onto the safety pegs at the end of the set.
Bench position matters: too far forward or back strains the shoulders because the bar cannot follow a natural path. Control the descent. Set the safety stops just above the chest.

Set an upright bench (90 degrees) in a Smith machine so the bar travels just behind the head. Take an overhand grip 1.25-1.5 times shoulder width so the forearms are vertical at the bottom, then unhook the bar.
Lower the bar behind the head to about ear level, then press straight up to near lockout. Repeat for reps and re-rack using the hooks.
Requires good shoulder external rotation; keep the range pain-free. Keep the head neutral rather than pushed forward. Use moderate loads and set the safety stops at ear height.

Set both pulleys of a cable station to the lowest position and place an upright bench (80-90 degrees) between them, or set the pulleys at shoulder height and stand. Hold a D-handle in each hand at shoulder height, palms forward and forearms vertical.
Press the handles up and slightly together until the arms are extended overhead. Lower slowly back to shoulder level, resisting the cables the whole way.
Cables keep tension at the bottom where dumbbells lose it. Keep the back on the pad. Do not let the cables pull the elbows behind the torso.
Stand on the middle of a long loop or tube resistance band with feet hip-width. Hold each end at shoulder height with palms forward and forearms vertical so there is light tension at the start.
Press the hands straight overhead to lockout as the band stretches, then lower slowly back to the shoulders against its pull.
Resistance is highest at lockout, so keep the ribs down there. Widen the stance or shorten the band to add resistance. A portable, joint-friendly option for home training or warm-ups.

Wedge one end of a barbell into a landmine attachment or a corner. Stand in a staggered stance facing the free end, holding the end of the sleeve at the shoulder in one hand with a neutral grip, elbow in front of the torso, and the foot on the pressing side back.
Press the bar up and forward along its arc until the arm is straight, letting the shoulder blade glide forward at the top. Lower under control back to the shoulder.
The angled path suits lifters who cannot press straight overhead pain-free. Avoid twisting the torso toward the bar. Reach through at the top to train the serratus.

Set a barbell in a landmine attachment. Kneel facing it with the knee on the pressing side down and the other foot forward, both knees at 90 degrees. Hold the end of the bar at the shoulder with a neutral grip, elbow tucked.
Press the bar up and forward to full extension while keeping the hips square and the torso tall, then lower slowly to the shoulder. Finish the set and switch sides.
Squeeze the glute of the down leg to stop the lower back arching. Keep the torso from rotating toward the bar. A good shoulder-friendly pressing progression.

Load a landmine barbell fitted with a Viking press handle, or use a dedicated Viking press machine. Set it so the handles sit at shoulder height. Stand under the handles with feet about shoulder-width, grip them with a neutral grip, elbows under the wrists, and brace the trunk.

Press both handles up along the lever's arc to full lockout overhead, then lower under control back to the shoulders. In competition the legs may dip and drive for reps; strict versions keep the knees locked.

Keep the ribs down and avoid leaning back to chase the arc. The neutral grip and fixed lever path are shoulder-friendly and allow heavy, high-rep pressing. A strongman event that builds pressing endurance.

Set the safety pins in a power rack at your sticking point, usually forehead to top-of-head height. Load the bar on the pins and step under it with your normal press grip just outside shoulder width, forearms vertical, feet hip-width.
Squeeze the bar, brace and press it from a dead stop on the pins to full lockout over the mid-foot, then lower it back to the pins and release tension for a second before the next rep.

Overloads the lockout and sticking point, so loads can exceed your full-range press. Build full-body tension before every rep since there is no stretch reflex. Keep the bar path vertical and the head through at lockout.
Set up as for a standing barbell overhead press: bar on the front delts, full overhand grip just outside shoulder width, forearms vertical, feet hip-width, glutes and abs braced.

Press the bar to about forehead height (or your sticking point) and hold it motionless for 1-3 seconds, then finish the press to lockout over the mid-foot. Some programmes pause at the bottom on the front delts instead to kill the stretch reflex; decide which before the set.
Stay tight during the pause; do not lean back to grind through. Keep the bar still, not drifting forward. Use about 70-85 percent of your normal press loads.

Rack the bar on the upper traps and take a snatch-width overhand grip (hook grip optional), wide enough that the bar sits in the hip crease when standing with straight arms. Stand with feet hip-width, glutes and abs braced, head neutral.

Press the bar straight up from behind the neck to a locked snatch receiving position, shrugging the shoulders up into the bar at the top so it sits over the back of the neck and mid-foot. Lower under control back to the traps.
Builds overhead strength and lockout stability for the snatch. Keep elbows under the bar and the head neutral. Requires good thoracic and shoulder mobility; use light loads first.

Hold an empty or lightly loaded barbell at its exact centre in one hand with an overhand grip, resting at the shoulder like a javelin, bar parallel to the floor and pointing front to back. Stand with feet hip-width, free hand on the hip.
Press the bar straight overhead to lockout while keeping it level, then lower slowly back to the shoulder. Complete all reps and switch hands.
Any tilt shows rotational instability at the shoulder and wrist, so crush the grip and move slowly. Keep the torso upright without leaning. Start with a technique bar, a dowel or a light dumbbell.
Overhead Press From Bottom of Squat

Hold an empty or light barbell in the front rack or with a snatch-width grip on the front delts. Sit into a full, upright deep squat with heels down, knees out over the toes and the bar resting on the shoulders.

Staying in the bottom of the squat, press the bar overhead to lockout so it finishes over the mid-foot with the ears in front of the arms, hold briefly, then lower it back to the shoulders while remaining in the squat.

Named after weightlifter Viktor Sots; it builds strength and mobility in the overhead squat position. Keep the torso vertical and heels down. Use very light loads; it is a positional drill, not a max lift.

Start in a high plank, then walk the feet in and drive the hips up so the body forms an inverted V with the torso at roughly 45-60 degrees to the floor. Hands slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers spread, legs straight or knees soft, head between the arms.

Bend the elbows to lower the top of the head toward a spot 10-15 cm in front of the hands, so head and hands form a triangle. Touch lightly, then press back up to straight arms, pushing the hips back up as you finish.

Keep the hips high so the press stays as vertical as possible. Elbows track back at about 45 degrees rather than flaring out. Put the hands on yoga blocks or parallettes to add range, or elevate the feet to progress toward the handstand push-up.

Place the feet (or knees for an easier version) on a box or bench 40-60 cm high and the hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder width. Walk the hands back toward the box until the hips stack roughly over the shoulders and the torso is close to vertical.
Bend the elbows to lower the head toward a spot just in front of the hands, forming a tripod, then press back up to straight arms while keeping the hips high.

The higher the feet and the more vertical the torso, the more bodyweight you press, making this the bridge to handstand push-ups. Keep the core tight and elbows at about 45 degrees. Control the descent and do not drop onto the head.

Place a folded mat against a wall. Set the hands slightly wider than shoulder width, 15-30 cm from the wall, fingers spread, and kick up into a handstand with the back to the wall and heels resting on it. Arms locked, ribs down, glutes tight.

Bend the elbows to lower under control until the head lightly touches the mat, forming a triangle with the hands, elbows at about 45 degrees. Press back to straight arms without kicking, finishing with the shoulders shrugged toward the ears.
Squeeze glutes and keep ribs down to avoid a banana-shaped back. Lower slowly; never crash onto the head. Scale with elevated pike push-ups, partial range onto stacked mats, or slow negatives.
Place plates, parallettes or blocks 5-15 cm high against a wall, slightly wider than shoulder width. Kick up into a back-to-wall handstand with the hands on the raised surfaces and heels on the wall.
Lower under control until the head passes below the level of the hands (or the shoulders reach hand level on parallettes), then press back to full lockout. Keep the heels on the wall throughout.
Only attempt once strict wall handstand push-ups are solid for 5 or more reps. The extra range loads the bottom position heavily. Lower slowly and keep the elbows from flaring past 45 degrees.
