Kick or press into a freestanding handstand on the floor or on parallettes, hands about shoulder-width, fingers spread, body in a straight hollow line from wrists to toes.

Lower toward the floor while keeping balance through finger and palm pressure, letting the legs move slightly to counterbalance, touch the head lightly or stop just short, then press back to a straight-arm handstand.

Requires a stable 30-plus second freestanding handstand and strong wall handstand push-ups first. Control balance through the fingers. Practise bailing safely by stepping down or rolling out before adding reps.
Place an abmat or folded mat against a wall. Kick up into a back-to-wall handstand with the hands slightly wider than shoulder width, 15-30 cm from the wall, arms locked.

Lower the head to the mat, then tuck the knees toward the chest. Drive the hips and legs explosively up the wall while pressing, so the leg kick carries you through the bottom and the arms finish the lockout. Return to the mat under control and repeat.
Master strict handstand push-ups first; kipping adds speed and impact on the neck. Always use a pad. Time the leg kick with the press so you finish with the arms locked and heels on the wall.
Lie face down with the feet against the base of a wall, toes on the floor, and hands beside the chest as in the bottom of a push-up.

Press up to a plank, then walk the feet up the wall while walking the hands back toward it until the chest is close to the wall in a handstand (hands about 10-20 cm away). Reverse the walk back down to the floor under control.
Keep the core tight and glutes squeezed so the lower back does not sag. Walk only as far as you can control. Return slowly rather than dropping, and keep the arms locked as you shift weight.

For chest-to-wall: lie face down with the feet at the wall and walk the feet up while walking the hands in until the stomach faces the wall. For back-to-wall: kick up with the back to the wall. Hands shoulder-width, fingers spread, arms locked.
Push tall through the shoulders, elevating them toward the ears, and hold a straight line from wrists to toes for time. Walk or step down with control.
Chest-to-wall builds a straighter line than back-to-wall. Keep ribs tucked and glutes squeezed. Build to 60-second holds before handstand push-up work.
Stand with feet hip-width holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, palms facing in, elbows slightly bent (about 10-20 degrees). Lean the torso a few degrees forward so the side delts sit on top.

Raise the arms out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with the elbows, until the upper arms are parallel to the floor and the hands are level with or slightly below the elbows. Pause briefly, then lower slowly over 2-3 seconds to just beside the thighs.
Think of pushing the dumbbells out to the walls rather than up. Do not shrug, swing or rock the torso. Light weight and strict reps beat heavy cheating.
Sit on the end of a flat bench with feet planted and back tall, holding dumbbells at the sides with palms facing in and elbows soft.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, keeping the elbows slightly higher than the hands. Lower under control until just short of the bench and repeat.
Sitting removes leg drive and momentum, making it stricter than the standing version. Keep the shoulders down away from the ears. Stop at shoulder height to keep tension on the side delts.

Stand beside a sturdy upright or rack, grip it with the near hand and lean away so the body is at about 15-20 degrees from vertical with feet together near the post. Hold a dumbbell in the far hand hanging in front of the thigh.
Raise the dumbbell out to the side in an arc until the arm is slightly above parallel to the floor. Lower slowly back to the start and repeat, then switch sides.
The lean increases tension at the bottom of the range. Keep the body rigid and do not swing. Use lighter weight than a standard raise.

Set an incline bench to about 30-45 degrees and lie on your side against the back pad, the bottom arm braced on the bench. Hold a light dumbbell in the top hand hanging toward the floor in front of the body, elbow slightly bent.
Raise the dumbbell up and out in an arc until the arm points roughly toward the ceiling, then lower slowly back to the start. Complete the reps and switch sides.
Loads the side delt hardest in the stretched, bottom position. Keep a fixed slight elbow bend. Use very light weight and strict control.

Set a pulley at the lowest position with a D-handle. Stand side-on with the machine beside you and take the handle in the far hand so the cable crosses in front of the body, hand starting near the opposite hip. Hold the frame with the free hand.

Raise the arm out to the side until the upper arm is parallel to the floor, with a slight fixed elbow bend. Lower slowly until the hand crosses back in front of the hips, then repeat and switch sides.
Constant cable tension makes the bottom of the range effective. Keep the torso still and avoid shrugging. Lead with the elbow rather than the hand.

Set a cable to the lowest position. Stand side-on with feet close to the machine, hold the frame with the near hand and lean away to about 15-20 degrees, gripping the D-handle with the far hand across the front of the body.
Raise the handle out and up in an arc until the arm is just above parallel to the floor, then lower slowly until the hand crosses past the midline. Switch sides after the set.
The lean and cable angle combine for maximum tension in the stretched position. Keep the elbow soft and fixed. Do not use body sway to lift the weight.
Set a pulley at the lowest position with a D-handle. Stand side-on, reach the far hand behind the back and take the handle so the cable runs behind the hips. Stand tall with chest up.
Raise the arm out to the side until the upper arm is parallel to the floor, then lower slowly back behind the hips. Complete the set and switch sides.
The behind-back line lets the arm start in more adduction for a deeper stretch. Keep the chest up. Pause briefly at the top without shrugging.
Set both pulleys to the lowest position. Take the left handle in the right hand and the right handle in the left so the cables cross in front of the body. Step back and hinge slightly forward.
Raise both arms up and out into a Y shape, finishing with the hands slightly above head height. Lower slowly so the cables cross back at the hips.
Lead with the thumbs up and keep the elbows soft. Do not arch the lower back to reach the top. Works the side delts and lower traps.
Adjust the seat so the machine's pivot point lines up with the shoulder joint. Sit with the chest against the pad if present and place the forearms or the outsides of the elbows against the arm pads.
Lift the arms out to the sides until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, pause briefly, then lower slowly until the weights almost touch.
Push through the elbows, not the hands. Keep the shoulders depressed. Machines allow safe drop sets and high-rep work.
Set the lateral raise machine so the shoulder lines up with the pivot. Sit or stand side-on with the working arm against the pad.
Raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder, then lower slowly. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Lead with the elbow, not the hand. Keep the shoulders down away from the ears. Sitting side-on lets you focus on one delt at a time.
Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet together or hip-width and hold one end in each hand at the sides, palms facing in, elbows slightly bent.
Raise the arms out to the sides until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, pause, then lower slowly to the sides.
Resistance increases toward the top, the opposite of dumbbells. Step wider on the band to add tension. Keep elbows slightly bent and do not shrug.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding very light dumbbells or plates at the sides with arms straight and thumbs pointing up.
Raise the straight arms out to the sides and keep going past shoulder height until the hands meet overhead, letting the shoulders shrug up slightly at the top. Lower slowly through the same arc.
Popularised by weightlifter Lu Xiaojun to build delts and upper traps through full upward rotation. Use very light weights and fully straight arms. Keep ribs down at the top.
Stand with feet hip-width holding a light kettlebell in each hand by the handle at the sides, bells hanging below the hands, elbows slightly bent.
Raise the arms out to the sides until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, keeping the bells hanging steady, then lower slowly back to the sides.
The offset bell challenges grip and forearm. Avoid swinging the bells. Go lighter than your dumbbell raise.
Set a barbell in a landmine attachment. Stand side-on to the bar, holding the end with the far hand so it starts in front of the opposite hip.
Raise the bar end up and out to the side in an arc to about shoulder height, then lower slowly back across the body. Switch sides after the set.
The arc gives a unique strength curve with good tension at the bottom. Keep the torso square. Use light loads and controlled tempo.
Stand with feet hip-width holding light dumbbells at the sides with palms facing in and elbows soft.

Raise the arms to the sides to shoulder height, bring them forward to the front at shoulder height, raise them overhead, lower back to front shoulder height, open back out to the sides, then lower to the start. That sequence is one rep.
A high time-under-tension burnout for all three delt heads. Use very light weight. Keep the elbows soft and avoid shrugging.
Stand or sit holding dumbbells at the sides as for a standard lateral raise, often slightly heavier than usual.
Raise the dumbbells only through the bottom half to two-thirds of the range (to about 45-60 degrees from the sides), then lower under control. Use continuous reps without resting at the bottom.
Often used after reaching failure on full reps to extend a set. Keep the movement strict, not a swing. Stay in the range where the delts are working.
Stand with feet hip-width holding dumbbells in front of the thighs with an overhand grip (palms facing the body), elbows slightly bent and fixed. Brace the abs.
Raise both dumbbells straight in front until the arms are parallel to the floor, pause briefly, then lower slowly over 2-3 seconds to the thighs.
Do not swing or lean back. Stop at shoulder to eye level. The front delts already work hard in pressing, so use moderate volume; a neutral grip is easier on irritable shoulders.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding dumbbells in front of the thighs, palms facing the body or thumbs up, elbows slightly bent.
Raise one dumbbell to shoulder height while the other stays down, lower it slowly, then raise the other arm. Continue alternating.
Keep the torso still; do not twist toward the working arm. Control the lowering. A neutral grip (thumbs up) is easier on the shoulders.
Stand with feet hip-width holding a barbell or EZ-bar with an overhand, shoulder-width grip resting on the thighs, elbows slightly bent and fixed. Brace the abs and keep the chest up.
With arms nearly straight, raise the bar in front of you in an arc until the arms are parallel to the floor or up to eye height, pause briefly, then lower slowly over 2-3 seconds back to the thighs.

Brace the core and avoid leaning back or using the hips to swing the bar. Use a light bar; both arms are locked together, so the stronger side cannot cover the weaker as easily. An EZ-bar is easier on the wrists.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a weight plate with both hands at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions (neutral grip), arms extended in front of the hips with a slight elbow bend. Brace the abs.
Raise the plate straight in front to shoulder or eye level, optionally rotating it like a steering wheel at the top, then lower slowly back to the hips.
The neutral grip is shoulder-friendly. Keep the arms nearly straight and the elbow bend fixed. Avoid leaning back to get the plate up; choose a lighter plate instead.
Set a pulley at the lowest position with a D-handle. Stand facing away from the stack with the cable running between the legs, holding the handle in front of the thigh with an overhand grip.
Raise the arm straight forward to shoulder height, pause, then lower slowly to the thigh. Complete the reps and switch sides.
Cables maintain tension at the bottom. Keep the elbow soft and the torso still. Do not let the cable pull you backward.
Attach a rope to a low pulley. Stand facing away from the stack with the rope running between the legs, holding both ends with a neutral grip in front of the hips.
Raise the rope in front to shoulder height with nearly straight arms, then lower slowly back to the hips.
The neutral grip and constant tension make this joint-friendly. Brace the core. Avoid swinging the hips.
Set a bench to 45-60 degrees and sit back with the head and upper back on the pad. Hold dumbbells hanging at the sides with a neutral grip (palms in), arms straight with a slight elbow bend.
Raise the dumbbells forward and up in an arc until the arms are about parallel to the floor, then lower slowly so the hands pass back behind the line of the body to stretch the front delts.
The incline places the front delts on a stretch at the start, unlike the standing version. Use light weight. Keep the back and head on the pad; do not crunch forward to finish the rep.
Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees and lie face down with the chest on the pad and feet braced on the floor. Hold light dumbbells or plates hanging straight down, thumbs up.
Keeping the arms straight, raise them forward past the head until they are roughly in line with the torso, pause briefly, then lower slowly back to hanging.
The bench removes all momentum, so the weight needed is very light. Keep the chest on the pad and the neck neutral. Stop short of any pinching at the top.
Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart and hold one end in each hand in front of the thighs, palms facing the body and elbows slightly bent.
Raise both arms straight forward against the band to shoulder height, pause for a second, then lower slowly to the thighs while resisting the band's pull.
Band tension rises toward the top, so the finish is the hardest part. Keep the elbows soft and avoid leaning back. Useful for home training and warm-ups.
Lie on your side on a flat bench, bottom arm supporting the head and hips stacked. Hold a light dumbbell in the top hand hanging toward the floor in front of the chest, elbow slightly bent.
Raise the dumbbell up and back in an arc until the arm points toward the ceiling, then lower slowly to the start. Complete the reps and switch sides.
Isolates the rear delt with no momentum. Keep the torso from rolling back as the arm rises. Use very light weight and a slow lowering.
Take an overhand grip 1.5 times shoulder width, hinge forward with a flat back and soft knees until the torso is near parallel to the floor, arms hanging straight.
Row the bar toward the upper chest or lower neck line with the elbows flared wide, about 75-90 degrees from the torso, then lower slowly to full arm extension.
Pull the bar higher on the torso than a standard row. Keep the torso still; no hip drive. Use lighter loads than a standard barbell row.
Set a bench to 30-45 degrees and lie face down with the chest on the pad and feet on the floor. Hold very light dumbbells or plates hanging straight down, thumbs pointing up.
Draw the shoulder blades down and back, then raise the straight arms forward and out at about 45 degrees into a Y until they are in line with the torso. Pause for 1-2 seconds, then lower slowly.
Targets the lower traps, with the posterior delts and cuff assisting. Keep the shoulders away from the ears and the chest on the pad. Start with 1-3 kg or no weight at all.
Set a bench to 30-45 degrees and lie face down with the chest supported. Hold light dumbbells hanging straight under the shoulders with thumbs pointing up or forward.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together and raise the straight arms directly out to the sides into a T until they are level with the shoulders. Pause, then lower slowly.
Works the rear delts and mid traps. Lead with the shoulder blades, not the hands. Avoid shrugging or lifting the chest off the pad.
Lie face down on a 30-45 degree incline bench holding very light dumbbells. Bend the elbows to about 90 degrees with the upper arms angled about 45 degrees from the body.
Pull the elbows back and down toward the hips while rotating the forearms up so the arms form a W, squeezing the shoulder blades together. Hold briefly, then lower slowly.
Combines rotating the forearms up (external rotation) with pulling the shoulder blades back and down. Do not let the shoulders roll forward or up. Light loads and slow tempo work best.
Lie face down on a mat with the forehead resting on a folded towel, legs straight and arms extended overhead with thumbs pointing up.
Lift the arms off the floor in an I overhead and hold 2 seconds, lower, then repeat with the arms in a Y at 45 degrees and again in a T straight out to the sides. One cycle is one rep.
Pull the shoulder blades down and back before each lift. Keep the neck neutral and the lift small. Add light plates or perform it on an incline bench to progress.
Lie face down over a Swiss ball with the ball under the chest and stomach, feet wide on the floor for balance and arms hanging down, holding nothing or very light dumbbells.
Raise the arms into a Y overhead and lower, then into a T to the sides and lower, then pull the elbows back into a W and lower. Hold each position for one to two seconds.
The unstable ball adds a core and balance demand. Keep the neck neutral and the body in a straight line. Keep loads very light so form stays crisp.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a barbell with an overhand grip at shoulder width or slightly wider (hands at least outside the hips), arms straight and the bar resting against the thighs.
Pull the bar straight up close to the body by driving the elbows up and out until the elbows reach shoulder height and the bar is at lower-chest level. Pause briefly, then lower slowly to the thighs.

Stopping at lower-chest height with a grip at shoulder width or wider reduces impingement risk; close grips and pulling to the chin load the traps and pinch more. Keep the elbows above the hands. Do not swing the hips to start the bar.
Stand tall holding a barbell overhand with hands roughly 1.5 times shoulder width apart, arms straight and the bar resting on the thighs.
Lead with the elbows and pull the bar up close to the body to about lower-chest height, elbows out to the sides and level with the shoulders. Pause and lower slowly.
The wide grip shifts emphasis from the traps to the side delts and is easier on the shoulders. Avoid shrugging at the top. Keep the bar close to the torso throughout.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs, palms facing the body and arms straight.
Pull the dumbbells up along the front of the body by driving the elbows up and out until they reach shoulder height, with the hands near the lower chest. Lower slowly.
Dumbbells let the hands drift wider for a more natural, shoulder-friendly path. Keep the elbows higher than the wrists. Do not lean back or swing.
Attach a straight bar or rope to the lowest pulley. Stand close to the stack facing it, holding the attachment overhand in front of the thighs with arms straight.
Pull the attachment up the front of the body by leading with the elbows until they reach shoulder height and the hands are at lower-chest level. Lower slowly to the start.
The cable keeps tension throughout, including the bottom. Stay upright and avoid leaning back away from the stack. Stop short of any pinching in the shoulder.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding an EZ-bar with an overhand grip on the angled sections, arms straight and the bar resting against the thighs.
Lead with the elbows to pull the bar up along the body until the elbows are at shoulder height and the bar is at lower-chest level. Pause briefly, then lower under control.
The angled grip reduces strain on the wrists compared with a straight bar. Keep the bar close to the body. Avoid jerking the weight up with the legs or hips.
Stand with feet hip-width holding one kettlebell by the horns with both hands, or a kettlebell in each hand, hanging in front of the thighs.
Pull the kettlebell up the front of the body by driving the elbows up and out to shoulder height, bringing the handle to about chest level. Lower slowly to the thighs.
A single bell held by the horns gives a narrow grip that loads the traps more, so keep the range modest. Keep the bell close to the body. Do not shrug excessively.
Set the Smith machine bar at mid-thigh height. Stand facing it close to the bar and grip overhand at shoulder width or slightly wider, arms straight.
Unhook the bar and pull it up along the fixed track by leading with the elbows until they reach shoulder height and the bar is at lower-chest level. Lower slowly.
The guided path keeps the bar close to the body so you can focus on the delts. Stop at chest height. Rotate the wrists to re-hook the bar at the end of the set.
Set a barbell in a rack at mid-thigh height. Grip it overhand or with a mixed grip at shoulder width, stand tall with feet hip-width and let the arms hang straight.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears as high as possible, pause for a second at the top, then lower slowly until the traps are fully stretched.
Do not roll the shoulders forward or back; straight up and down is enough. Keep the arms straight and avoid bouncing with the knees. Use lifting straps for heavy sets.
Set a barbell in a rack at about mid-thigh height. Stand facing away from it, reach back and grip it overhand at shoulder width, then step forward with the bar against the back of the thighs.
Shrug the shoulders straight up and slightly back toward the ears, pause at the top, then lower slowly to a full stretch.
Holding the bar behind changes the line of pull and brings in more of the middle traps. Keep the chest up and arms straight. Use straps if grip limits the set.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, palms facing the body and arms fully straight.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears as high as possible, hold the top for one to two seconds, then lower slowly to a full stretch at the bottom.
The neutral grip and free path suit most shoulders. Do not roll the shoulders or bend the elbows. Pause at the top instead of bouncing heavy weights.
Sit on the end of a flat bench with feet flat on the floor, back tall and a dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down at the sides.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears, squeeze and hold for a second, then lower slowly until the arms and traps are fully stretched.
Sitting removes any leg drive so the traps do all the work. Keep the head neutral rather than jutting forward. Use moderate loads with a strict pause.
Load a trap bar (hex bar) and stand in the center. Deadlift it to standing using the high or low handles, feet hip-width and arms straight at the sides.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears, pause briefly at the top, then lower slowly to a full stretch before the next rep.
The neutral grip and load centered on the body allow heavy, shoulder-friendly shrugs. Keep the arms straight and knees still. Use straps for heavy sets.
Set the Smith machine bar at mid-thigh height. Stand facing it with feet hip-width and grip overhand just outside the thighs, then unhook the bar.
Shrug the shoulders straight up as high as possible, pause and squeeze, then lower slowly to a full stretch. Rotate the bar to re-hook it after the set.
The fixed path lets you focus purely on the squeeze. Stand close so the bar travels in contact with the thighs. Use straps for heavy loads.
Adjust a dedicated shrug machine or standing calf raise machine so you can reach the handles or fit the shoulders under the pads with the knees slightly soft.
Shrug the shoulders straight up against the resistance as high as possible, pause at the top, then lower slowly to a full stretch.
Machines allow heavy loading with no grip or balance limits. Keep the arms or torso still so only the shoulders move. Control the eccentric rather than dropping.
Attach a straight bar to the lowest pulley, or use D-handles on two low pulleys. Stand close and hold the attachment in front of the thighs with straight arms.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears, pause and squeeze, then lower slowly until the traps are fully stretched.
Cables keep constant tension at the top and bottom. Stand far enough from the stack that the plates never rest. Use straps if grip limits the set.
Set a bench to 30-45 degrees and lie face down with the chest on the pad. Let dumbbells hang straight down from the shoulders, palms facing in.
Shrug the shoulder blades up and back toward the ears along the line of the torso, pause and squeeze, then lower slowly to a full stretch.
The angle shifts emphasis toward the middle and lower traps. Keep the chest on the pad and arms straight. Moderate weight with a strong pause works best.
Press or jerk a barbell overhead and lock it out with a wide, snatch-style grip. Stand with feet hip-width, ribs down and the bar over the back of the neck.
With the elbows locked, shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears, raising the bar a few centimeters, pause, then lower the shoulders slowly without bending the arms.
Strengthens the upper traps in the overhead position used in snatches and jerks. Keep the arms locked and core braced. Use light loads.
Set a barbell in a rack at mid-thigh height. Take a snatch-width grip, wide enough that the bar sits in the hip crease, and stand tall with straight arms.
Shrug the shoulders straight up as high as possible, pause and squeeze, then lower slowly to a full stretch.
The wide grip brings more of the mid traps and rhomboids into play and has a shorter range. Use straps for heavy loads. Keep the arms straight and chest up.

Hold a barbell at mid-thigh with a clean-width overhand grip (hook grip or straps for heavy sets), feet hip-width, knees slightly bent, torso leaning slightly forward and shoulders just in front of the bar.

Explosively extend the hips, knees and ankles and shrug the shoulders up hard in one motion, rising onto the balls of the feet while the arms stay long. Absorb the bar back to mid-thigh with soft knees and reset the position before the next rep.

Trains the finish of the clean and snatch pull. Keep the arms straight; do not pull with the biceps. The feet stay in contact with the floor (leaving it makes it a jump shrug). Loads above your clean are possible.
Stand tall holding a dumbbell at one side with the arm straight. Place the free hand on the hip or hold a rack for balance.
Shrug the working shoulder straight up toward the ear, pause and squeeze, then lower slowly to a full stretch. Finish the set and switch sides.
Lets you correct side-to-side imbalances and feel each trap. Keep the torso upright without leaning away from the weight. Do not tilt the head toward the shoulder.
Stand tall holding a barbell with an overhand grip about shoulder width or slightly narrower, bar against the thighs and arms straight. Use straps for heavy sets.

Shrug the shoulders up while bending the elbows and flaring them out to drag the bar up the body to about the navel or lower ribs, leaning back slightly, like a shortened upright row. Pause at the top, then lower slowly to the thighs.

Named after powerlifter Kirk Karwoski; a hybrid of a shrug and an upright row that hits the upper traps and side delts together. Keep the bar in contact with the body and the elbows high and wide. Use moderate loads and a deliberate pause.
Put on a neck (head) harness and attach a light weight plate to the chain. Stand with feet wide, hinge forward with hands on the knees and let the head hang down toward the chest.
Raise the head up and back against the weight until the face points forward or slightly up, pause briefly, then lower slowly until the chin approaches the chest.
Start very light and add load slowly; the neck adapts well but dislikes sudden jumps. Move smoothly with no jerking. Keep the torso still so only the neck moves.

Lie face up on a flat bench with the shoulders at the end and the head and neck off the bench. Place a folded towel on the forehead and hold a light plate on it with both hands; start with no plate if you are new to neck training.
Let the head lower back slowly until it is level with or slightly below the bench, then curl the chin toward the chest as far as comfortable. Pause, then lower slowly back.
Keep the hands securing the plate and the shoulders on the bench. Start with bodyweight before adding a plate, using 15-25 reps. Move only through a pain-free range and never jerk.
Lie face down on a flat bench with the head and neck off the end. Place a folded towel on the back of the head and hold a light plate on it with both hands.
Lower the head slowly toward the floor, then raise it back up until the head is in line with the torso or just past it, eyes toward the floor. Pause, then lower again under control.
Keep the plate secured on the towel. Avoid cranking into excessive extension. Start light and build reps before load.
Lie on your side on a flat bench with the head off the end. Place a folded towel on the side of the head and hold a light plate on it with the top hand, or use no weight.
Lower the ear toward the floor slowly, then raise the head up toward the top shoulder as far as comfortable. Pause, then lower. Complete the set and switch sides.
Start with bodyweight only; the lateral neck muscles are small. Keep the shoulders stacked and still. Move slowly through a pain-free range.
Sit in a 4-way neck machine facing the pad, adjust the seat so the pad sits on the forehead and grip the handles. Select a light weight.
Push the head forward and down against the pad, bringing the chin toward the chest, pause, then return slowly to an upright position.
Keep the torso still against the seat so only the neck moves. Start very light and use higher reps. Control the eccentric rather than letting the stack pull you back.
Sit in a 4-way neck machine facing away from the pad, adjust it so the pad sits on the back of the head and grip the handles. Select a light weight.
Push the head back against the pad until the face points slightly upward, pause, then return slowly until the chin moves toward the chest.
Keep the shoulders and torso fixed. Start light and progress gradually. The same machine can be turned side-on for lateral flexion.
Sit side-on in a 4-way neck machine with the head pad against the side of the head above the ear. Hold the handles and set a light weight.
Tilt the head sideways toward the shoulder against the pad through a short, comfortable range, then return slowly to the start. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Go light and slow; the neck needs gradual loading. Move only the head and neck, not the torso. Stop at any pain or tingling.
Sit or stand tall with a neutral spine. Place one or both hands on the forehead, the back of the head or one side of the head.
Push the head into the hands while the hands resist equally so the head does not move. Hold 10-20 seconds, release, then repeat in each of the four directions.
No equipment needed, making it ideal for daily neck work or rehab. Build pressure gradually over two to three seconds. Keep breathing throughout the hold.
Lie on your back on a soft mat with knees bent and feet flat. Place the hands beside the head, then lift the hips and roll onto the top of the head.
Rock gently forward and back on the head, keeping the hips high, then lower carefully back to the mat. Hands stay ready to take weight at any time.
An advanced drill; build up with hands bearing most of the weight. Always use a thick mat. Never perform it with any existing neck pain.
Kneel on a thick mat and place the forehead on the mat in front of the knees, with hands on the floor beside the head for support.
Lift the knees and straighten the legs to shift weight onto the forehead, rock gently forward and back, then lower the knees and return to the start.
Keep the movement small and controlled. Use the hands to unload as needed when starting. Do not use it with any existing neck injury.
Sit or stand tall with shoulders relaxed and eyes forward, or lie on your back with the head resting on the floor and knees bent.
Draw the chin straight back as if making a double chin, without tilting the head up or down. Hold for 5-10 seconds, then release and repeat.
The movement is small; think of sliding the head back on a shelf. Do not nod or drop the chin. Excellent for posture and deep neck flexor endurance.
Anchor a light loop band at head height. Wrap it around the head, stand side-on to the anchor and step out until there is light tension, shoulders square.
Rotate the head away from the anchor against the band through a comfortable range, pause, then return slowly to face forward. Complete the set and switch sides.
Keep the shoulders facing forward so only the head turns. Use very light bands and slow tempo. A harness device can replace the band.

Lie on the side opposite the working arm, head supported. Bend the top elbow to 90 degrees and place a rolled towel between the elbow and ribs. Hold a light dumbbell with the forearm resting across the stomach.
Keeping the elbow pinned to the towel, rotate the forearm up until it points toward the ceiling or as far as comfortable. Pause, then lower slowly.
Targets the infraspinatus and teres minor. Use very light weight, often 1-5 kg. Do not let the torso roll back to help the lift.

Set a pulley at elbow height with a D-handle. Stand side-on with the stack on the side opposite the working arm, so you hold the handle with the far hand, elbow bent 90 degrees and tucked against a rolled towel at the side.
Rotate the forearm outward away from the stomach while the elbow stays fixed at the side, pause, then return slowly to the start across the body.
Keep the elbow pinned and wrist straight. Use a light load and smooth reps. Squeezing the towel prevents the elbow drifting away from the body.

Set a pulley at elbow height with a D-handle. Stand side-on with the stack on the side of the working arm, holding the handle with the near hand, elbow bent 90 degrees and pinned to the side with a rolled towel.
Rotate the forearm inward across the stomach while keeping the elbow fixed, pause, then return slowly out to the start.
Trains the subscapularis. Keep the elbow tight and the torso still; do not turn the body to help. Use light to moderate loads and a slow return.
Anchor a light resistance band at elbow height. Stand side-on with the anchor beside the non-working arm and hold the band with the working hand, elbow bent 90 degrees at the side.
Rotate the forearm outward away from the stomach against the band, keeping the elbow pinned, pause, then return slowly.
A rolled towel under the elbow keeps it in place. Use light bands and high reps. Common in warm-ups and shoulder prehab.
Anchor a light band at elbow height. Stand side-on with the anchor beside the working arm, elbow bent 90 degrees and pinned to the side with a rolled towel, forearm pointing out and holding the band.
Rotate the forearm inward across the stomach against the band while keeping the elbow fixed, pause, then return slowly out to the start.
Trains the subscapularis. Keep the elbow pinned and the torso still; do not turn the body to help. Control the outward return and use light bands and higher reps.

Set a pulley between chest and shoulder height with a D-handle. Face the stack and raise the working upper arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent 90 degrees and forearm pointing forward, holding the handle with the cable taut.
Keeping the upper arm level and the elbow in place, rotate the forearm up and back until it points toward the ceiling. Pause, then lower slowly back to forward.
Important for throwers and overhead athletes. Keep the elbow at shoulder height and the shoulder blade set. Use light loads; a band works too.
Sit on a bench with one foot on the bench, or seated with feet down. Rest the working elbow on the knee at shoulder height, forearm pointing forward, light dumbbell in hand.
Rotate the forearm up until it points toward the ceiling, keeping the elbow resting on the knee. Pause, then lower slowly back to forward.
The knee support isolates the cuff in an abducted position. Keep the wrist straight. Use very light loads.

Lie face down on a flat bench with the working arm off the side, upper arm out at shoulder height and supported on the bench edge, elbow bent 90 degrees and forearm hanging toward the floor holding a light dumbbell.
Keeping the upper arm still, rotate the forearm forward toward the head and up until it is parallel with the floor. Pause, then lower slowly back to hanging.
Very demanding on the cuff, so 1-3 kg is plenty. Keep the shoulder blade set back. Do not lift the elbow to cheat.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding light dumbbells or an empty barbell in front of the thighs with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width.

Upright row until the upper arms are parallel to the floor with elbows bent 90 degrees, externally rotate so the forearms point up and the hands are above the elbows, then press overhead to lockout. Reverse each step to lower.
Combines an upright row, external rotation and press for cuff strength and overhead readiness. Use very light loads and move smoothly. Keep the elbows level at shoulder height during the rotation.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding light dumbbells with the upper arms out to the sides at shoulder height, elbows bent 90 degrees and forearms pointing down (the top of an upright row).
Rotate the forearms up and back until they point toward the ceiling, keeping the elbows at shoulder level and the upper arms still. Pause, then lower slowly back to pointing down.
Keep the upper arms still and level; do not let the elbows drop as you rotate. Use very light loads or no weight. A useful warm-up before pressing or snatching.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a light band overhead with straight arms, an overhand grip and hands about 1.5 times shoulder width so the band is slightly tensioned.
Pull the band apart as you lower it behind the head to around shoulder or upper-back level, squeezing the shoulder blades down and together, then return slowly overhead with arms still straight.
Keep the arms straight and ribs down; do not push the head forward to make room. Use light bands and widen the grip if it pinches. Good for lower traps, scapular depression and overhead mobility.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a light band, PVC pipe or dowel with a wide overhand grip, about 1.5-2 times shoulder width, in front of the hips with arms straight.
Raise the band overhead and continue behind the body in one slow arc until it reaches the lower back, then reverse the path to return to the front. Keep the arms straight throughout.
Use a grip wide enough to keep the elbows locked and move without pain. Narrow it gradually as mobility improves. Keep ribs down and do not arch the lower back to get the band past the head.
Start in a high plank with hands under the shoulders, fingers spread, arms straight and the body in a straight line from heels to head, glutes and abs braced.

Keeping the elbows locked, let the chest sink a few centimetres between the shoulder blades as they squeeze together (retraction), then push the floor away to spread them apart and round the upper back slightly (protraction). Repeat slowly.
Arms stay straight; only the shoulder blades move. Trains the serratus anterior and scapular control. Perform on the knees or against a wall to scale down, or add a pause at full protraction.
Stand facing a wall in a split stance. Place the pinky sides of both forearms on a foam roller pressed against the wall at chest height, elbows about shoulder-width apart.

Roll the foam roller up the wall by reaching the arms overhead while pushing the forearms into it and letting the shoulder blades wrap forward and up. Lift slightly off at the top, then return slowly.
Trains the serratus and lower traps, which turn the shoulder blades upward as the arms rise. Keep the ribs down and do not shrug. Add a mini band around the wrists for extra cuff work.
Stand tall with feet hip-width holding light dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip, thumbs pointing up, arms straight with a slight elbow bend.
Raise the arms in the scapular plane, about 30 degrees forward of straight out to the side, up to shoulder height with thumbs leading. Pause, then lower slowly over 2-3 seconds.
The thumbs-up full-can position is safer for the supraspinatus than the old empty-can version. Keep the shoulders down away from the ears. Use light loads and stop at shoulder height.
Lie on your back and press a light kettlebell to lockout over the shoulder. Bend the knee on the same side with the foot flat; the other leg and arm stay straight on the floor.
Keeping eyes on the bell and the arm vertical, push through the bent leg to roll onto the opposite side, letting the top hip drop toward the floor. Hold for a few breaths, then roll back and lower.
Keep the wrist straight and the arm locked and perpendicular to the floor. Pull the shoulder blade down into its socket. Start light and move slowly.
Stand tall or half-kneel holding a light kettlebell upside down by the horns at chest height, bell pointing up, glutes and abs braced.
Circle the kettlebell around the head, passing it beside one ear, behind the head at the base of the skull and beside the other ear back to the front. Alternate directions each rep.
Keep the bell close to the head and the ribs down so the lower back does not arch. Move slowly through the full circle. A plate or dumbbell works the same way.
Anchor a light band low on the side opposite the working arm. Stand tall and hold the band with the working hand in front of the opposite hip, palm facing the body.
Pull the band up and across the body in a diagonal, like drawing a sword, finishing with the arm overhead and out to the side, thumb pointing back. Return slowly along the same path.
Move in one smooth diagonal arc with the thumb rotating outward. Keep the torso still. Common in rehab and for throwing athletes.
Lie on your side on the shoulder to be stretched, with that upper arm out in front at shoulder height and the elbow bent to 90 degrees so the fingers point toward the ceiling.
Use the top hand to gently press the bottom forearm down toward the floor until a stretch is felt in the back of the shoulder. Hold 30 seconds, release and repeat 2-3 times.
Use gentle pressure only and stop short of pain. Rolling the body back slightly reduces pinching at the front. Useful for throwers with internal rotation deficit.
Stand or sit tall with shoulders relaxed. Bring one straight arm across the front of the chest at shoulder height.
Hook the other hand or forearm just above the elbow and gently pull the arm closer to the chest until a stretch is felt in the back of the shoulder. Hold 30 seconds per side.
Keep the stretched shoulder down and back rather than letting it hike up. Do not rotate the torso to fake range. Breathe slowly and relax into it.
Sit or stand tall. Reach one hand down and hold the side of a chair or tuck it behind the back, then place the other hand on the opposite side of the head.
Gently tilt the ear toward the shoulder of the free hand, using the hand on the head for light assistance, until a stretch is felt along the side of the neck. Hold 30 seconds per side.
Keep the anchored shoulder pulled down. Use only light hand pressure. Avoid rotating the face toward the floor, which shifts the stretch.
Sit or stand tall. Turn the head about 45 degrees to one side, then drop the chin as if looking toward that armpit. Place the same-side hand on the back of the head.
Gently pull the head further down and forward along that diagonal until a stretch is felt at the back and side of the neck toward the shoulder blade. Hold 30 seconds per side.
Hold the opposite arm down or behind the back to anchor the shoulder blade. Keep pressure light. Breathe and relax the shoulders.

Set a pulley at chest to shoulder height with a rope or two D-handles. Sit or stand facing the stack, take an overhand grip and step back until the arms are straight at shoulder height and the stack lifts. Brace with the torso upright.

Row toward the upper chest or neck with the elbows flared out at about 75-90 degrees from the torso until the upper arms are in line with the shoulders, separating the rope ends. Pause for a second, then return slowly to straight arms.

Unlike a face pull there is no external rotation at the end; the wide elbows and short pull bias the rear delts. Do not lean back or squeeze the shoulder blades hard. Use moderate loads for 10-20 reps.

Stand tall with feet hip-width holding a light weight plate (5-15 kg) at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions with a neutral grip. Raise it in front so the arms are straight and parallel to the floor, elbows soft. Brace the abs.

Keeping the arms at shoulder height, rotate the plate as far as possible one way like turning a steering wheel, then all the way the other way. Continue alternating for 20-40 seconds or a set number of turns, then lower the plate.
The isometric hold loads the front delts while the turns challenge the cuff and forearms. Do not let the arms drop or the torso twist. Use a lighter plate if the shoulders rise toward the ears.
Lie on your back holding a light dumbbell with the arm straight up over the shoulder, elbow locked.
Without bending the elbow, reach the hand toward the ceiling so the shoulder blade lifts off the floor and wraps around the ribs. Pause, then let the shoulder blade sink back down slowly.
A small movement that comes only from the shoulder blade. Keep the elbow straight and the neck relaxed. Light weight, slow reps.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, knees soft, glutes and abs braced. Hold a straight barbell with an underhand (palms-up), full thumbs-around grip at shoulder width, hands just outside the thighs. Arms hang straight, elbows at the sides of the ribs, shoulder blades set down and back.

Exhale and flex the elbows to sweep the bar up in an arc, keeping the upper arms near vertical, until the forearms are just short of vertical and the bar is at upper-chest height (elbows may drift 2-3 inches forward at the very top). Squeeze one second, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full elbow extension without relaxing at the bottom.

Elbows stay by the ribs; the torso does not rock back and the hips do not drive the bar. Wrists stay straight, not curled or bent back. If the lower back arches or the shoulders roll forward, the load is too heavy.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Take an underhand, thumbs-around grip about 4-6 inches wider than shoulder width on each side, so the forearms angle outward from the elbows. Elbows sit at the sides, arms straight, chest up.

Curl the bar toward the upper chest by flexing only the elbows, keeping the elbows tucked at the ribs rather than flaring with the hands. Squeeze at the top with forearms just short of vertical, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

The wide grip puts the shoulder in slight external rotation and is commonly used to bias the short (inner) head. Use 10-20 percent less load than a shoulder-width curl. Keep the wrists neutral; stop if the inside of the elbow or wrist feels strained and switch to an EZ-bar.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a straight barbell with an underhand (palms-up) grip, hands about 6-8 inches apart (well inside shoulder width), arms straight and elbows at the sides so the forearms angle slightly inward.
Flex the elbows to curl the bar to upper-chest height, keeping the elbows at the ribs and the upper arms still. Pause one second at the top, then lower in 2-3 seconds to a full stretch at the bottom.

The narrow grip is commonly used to bias the long (outer) head. A straight bar at this width forces strong supination and can stress the wrists and elbows; switch to the EZ-bar inner grips if it does. No hip drive and no leaning back.

Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width, knees soft. Hold a barbell 10-20 percent heavier than your strict curl with an underhand shoulder-width grip, bar resting at the thighs. Brace the abs hard and keep a neutral spine.

Make a small, controlled hip extension (a few degrees of forward-and-back lean, not a swing) to get the bar past the weakest early range, then finish the curl with the biceps to upper-chest height. Stand tall at the top, then lower strictly over 3-4 seconds to full extension with no lean.

The cheat only gets the bar moving; the slow strict eccentric is the point. Keep the spine neutral and never yank from a rounded back. Limit to the last 1-3 sets for experienced lifters; drop the load if the lowering cannot be controlled.

Stand with heels about 6-12 inches from a wall or post and press glutes, upper back and the back of the head against it. Hold a barbell with an underhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight, backs of the elbows lightly touching the wall.

Curl the bar to upper-chest height while the back and elbows stay in contact with the wall so no swing or forward elbow drift is possible. Squeeze briefly, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension, keeping contact the whole time.

The wall removes momentum: expect 20-30 percent less load than a normal curl. Keep the shoulders down rather than shrugging as the bar rises. In strict curl competition the elbows and back must stay on the board, so train the full range.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a barbell with an underhand shoulder-width grip, bar resting against the front of the thighs, elbows at the sides.

Curl by pulling the elbows straight back behind the torso so the bar drags up the front of the body in light contact, finishing at the lower chest with the elbows well behind the ribs. Lower along the same path back to the thighs over 2-3 seconds.

The elbows travel back, never forward, which shortens the long head at the shoulder and removes front-delt help. Keep the bar touching the body and the shoulders down, not shrugged or rolled forward. Use 20-30 percent less than a regular curl.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a barbell with an overhand (palms-down), thumbs-around grip at shoulder width, arms straight in front of the thighs, elbows at the sides.

Flex the elbows to curl the bar up while the palms stay facing down and the wrists stay straight, until the forearms are near vertical and the bar is at upper-chest height. Lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

The overhand forearm puts the biceps at a mechanical disadvantage, shifting work to the brachioradialis and brachialis, so use roughly 60-70 percent of your curl load. Keep the knuckles in line with the forearm; do not let the wrists drop. An EZ-bar eases wrist strain.

Set the preacher seat so the armpits sit snugly over the top of the angled (about 45 deg) pad with the backs of the upper arms flat on it. Sit with feet flat. Take an underhand, shoulder-width grip on a straight bar handed to you or lifted from the hooks.

From elbows almost straight (about 10-15 deg short of lockout), curl the bar up until the forearms are near vertical, keeping the upper arms on the pad. Lower in 3 seconds back to just short of full extension.

The stretched bottom is the hardest and most vulnerable range: never bounce or drop into a hyperextended elbow. Keep the triceps glued to the pad and the hips on the seat. Straight-bar preacher work stresses the wrists; use the EZ-bar version if needed.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Grip an EZ-bar on the angled sections with palms semi-underhand (turned slightly inward): the inner bends are about shoulder width or narrower, the outer bends slightly wider. Arms straight, elbows at the sides.
Flex the elbows to curl the bar to upper-chest height, upper arms staying close to vertical. Squeeze one second, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full elbow extension.

The camber reduces forced supination, so it is easier on wrists and elbows than a straight bar, with slightly less supination demand on the biceps. Narrow grip is commonly used for long-head bias, wide for short head. No swinging or leaning back.

Adjust the preacher seat so the armpits rest on the top edge of the pad and the backs of the upper arms lie flat on it. Hold an EZ-bar on the inner or outer angled grips, palms semi-underhand, arms nearly straight.
Curl the bar toward the shoulders keeping the upper arms on the pad until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to about 10-15 deg short of a locked elbow.

The most common preacher variation because the camber spares the wrists. Control the stretched bottom with no bounce. Lighten the load if the elbows lift off the pad, the shoulders roll forward or the hips rise from the seat.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold an EZ-bar with an overhand grip on the outer angled sections (palms facing down and slightly in), arms straight in front of the thighs, elbows at the sides.
Flex the elbows to curl the bar up with the palms staying down until the forearms are near vertical. Lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

The camber lets the forearms sit slightly toward neutral, reducing wrist strain compared with a straight-bar reverse curl. Keep the knuckles in line with the forearms and the elbows still. Trains the brachioradialis and brachialis; use about 60-70 percent of your curl load.

Set the preacher seat so the armpits rest on the top of the pad and the backs of the upper arms lie flat. Hold an EZ-bar (or straight bar) with an overhand shoulder-width grip, palms down, elbows almost straight.
Curl the bar up with the palms staying down and the upper arms on the pad until the forearms approach vertical. Lower in 3 seconds to just short of lockout.

Fixing the upper arm and pronating the hand shifts work to the brachialis and brachioradialis. Use light loads: the stretched bottom position is demanding on the elbow. Keep the wrists straight and the elbows on the pad.

Lie chest-down on an incline bench set to about 45 deg (or the vertical side of a preacher bench), chin just over the top, feet on the floor. Let the arms hang straight down, perpendicular to the floor, holding an EZ-bar with an underhand (palms-up) grip on the angled sections.

Curl the bar up by flexing only the elbows, upper arms staying vertical, until the biceps are fully shortened and the bar is near the forehead. Squeeze one to two seconds, then lower to full extension.

With the upper arms vertical, the bar is hardest to move when the forearms are level with the floor and eases near the top; pause at the top for the squeeze, not because it is heaviest there. Keep the chest on the pad and do not let the elbows swing back. Use moderate loads and a strict tempo.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a barbell or EZ-bar with an underhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight, elbows at the sides. Use about 50-60 percent of your normal curl load.

Without resting: 7 partial reps from full extension to halfway (forearms parallel to the floor, elbows at 90 deg), then 7 partials from halfway to the top, then 7 full-range reps. That is 21 reps in one set.

Stop each partial crisply at the 90 deg mark rather than drifting. Keep the elbows pinned and the torso upright throughout; fatigue tempts a swing in the final sevens. Rest 60-90 seconds between sets.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with an underhand (palms-up) grip (palms forward), arms straight at the sides, elbows at the ribs, shoulder blades set down and back.

Curl both dumbbells up together by flexing the elbows until the forearms are just short of vertical and the dumbbells are at shoulder height, keeping the pinky side slightly higher at the top. Squeeze one second and lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Elbows stay by the ribs and the torso stays still. Do not let the dumbbells rest on the shoulders at the top or the arms relax at the bottom. Reduce the weight if the shoulders roll forward or the elbows drift up and forward.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides with a neutral grip (palms facing the thighs) or palms forward, elbows at the ribs.

Curl one dumbbell up, supinating so the palm faces up by the time the forearm passes parallel, and finish at shoulder height. Squeeze, lower over 2-3 seconds to full extension, then curl the other arm. One rep per arm is one rep each.

Finish each rep fully before starting the other arm. Keep the shoulders square: no twisting the torso or rocking toward the working side. The non-working arm stays straight and still, not partly flexed.

Stand or sit tall holding dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip, palms facing the thighs. Grip with the thumb side of the hand touching the inner head so more of the dumbbell sits on the pinky side.

Curl the dumbbells up and actively rotate the palms up as they pass about 45 deg, finishing at the top with the palms up and the pinky turned slightly higher than the thumb. Squeeze, then reverse the rotation while lowering in 2-3 seconds.

Supination is a primary job of the biceps, so this trains both elbow flexion and forearm rotation. The offset grip increases the supination demand. Keep the elbows at the ribs and avoid turning the shoulder out to fake the rotation.
Sit upright on the end of a flat bench or on an upright bench set to 80-90 deg, feet flat and hip-width. Hold dumbbells at the sides, arms straight, palms forward, elbows at the ribs.

Curl the dumbbells up together or alternately by flexing the elbows until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds until the arms are straight with the dumbbells just above the bench.

Sitting removes leg drive and limits torso sway, making the curl stricter than standing. Do not let the dumbbells rest on the bench between reps. Keep the chest up and the shoulders back; no leaning back to finish.

Set a bench to 45-60 deg and sit back with the head and upper back on the pad, feet flat. Let the arms hang straight down from the shoulders so the upper arms are slightly behind the torso, palms forward (underhand).
Curl the dumbbells up while the upper arms stay hanging toward the floor, until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to full elbow extension in the deep stretch.

The shoulder-extended start lengthens the long head, making this a stretch-focused curl. Keep the shoulders pinned to the pad and the elbows pointing at the floor; do not let them swing forward. Use 20-30 percent lighter weights than standing curls.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip (palms facing the thighs, thumbs forward), arms straight, elbows at the ribs.

Flex the elbows to curl the dumbbells up with the palms still facing each other until the forearms are near vertical and the top end of the dumbbell is near the front of the shoulder. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension. Both arms together or alternating.

The neutral grip emphasizes the brachialis and brachioradialis alongside the biceps and usually allows more load. Keep the wrists straight and the elbows by the ribs. No swinging; the upper arm does not drift forward.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip, palms facing the thighs, elbows at the ribs.

Curl one dumbbell up and across the front of the body toward the opposite chest or shoulder, keeping the neutral grip so the thumb end leads. Squeeze, lower along the same diagonal to full extension, then repeat on the other side.

The diagonal path increases brachialis and brachioradialis emphasis. The upper arm stays close to the torso and only the forearm crosses; do not swing the elbow across the chest. Keep the torso from rotating to help the weight up.

Sit on the end of a flat bench, feet wider than shoulder width and flat. Lean forward slightly and brace the back of the working upper arm (just above the elbow) against the inner thigh, arm straight down, palm up. Rest the other hand on the opposite knee.

Curl the dumbbell toward the front of the shoulder, keeping the upper arm fixed against the thigh, until fully flexed. Squeeze hard with the pinky turned slightly up, then lower in 3 seconds to full extension. Finish the set, then switch arms.
Keep the torso still and do not press the arm off the thigh or lift the shoulder to help. Allow full extension at the bottom. Use a moderate weight you can control for 8-15 reps; a strong finisher.

Stand with feet wider than shoulder width and hinge forward until the torso is about 45 deg or lower, back flat. Rest the free hand on a thigh or bench. Let the working arm hang straight down from the shoulder holding a dumbbell, palm forward.

Curl the dumbbell toward the chest or opposite shoulder by flexing only the elbow while the upper arm stays hanging vertically. Squeeze at the top, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension. Switch arms after the set.

Keep the back flat and the upper arm still; it must not swing. Keep the upper arm hanging still; the dumbbell is hardest to move when the forearm is level with the floor. Use a slow tempo and moderate load.

Sit or stand at a preacher bench with one upper arm flat on the angled pad and the armpit snug over the top edge. Hold a dumbbell with an underhand (palms-up) grip, elbow about 10-15 deg short of straight. The free hand can steady the pad.
Curl the dumbbell up keeping the upper arm on the pad until the forearm is near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to just short of lockout. Finish the set and switch arms.

Working one arm at a time evens out side-to-side differences and lets the wrist supinate freely. Control the bottom; do not drop into a hyperextended elbow. Using the steep vertical side of the pad shifts tension toward the top of the curl.

Sit at a preacher bench with the armpit over the top of the pad and the back of the upper arm flat on it. Hold a dumbbell with a neutral grip, thumb pointing up, elbow about 10-15 deg short of straight.

Curl the dumbbell up keeping the neutral grip and the upper arm on the pad until the forearm is near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to near full extension. One arm at a time, or both with two dumbbells.

Combines the fixed preacher arm position with the neutral grip, emphasizing the brachialis and brachioradialis. Keep the wrist straight in line with the forearm and control the stretched bottom position without bouncing.

Lie chest-down on an incline bench set to about 45 deg, chin over the top edge, feet braced on the floor. Let the arms hang straight down perpendicular to the floor, holding dumbbells with palms forward.
Curl the dumbbells up by flexing only the elbows, upper arms staying vertical, until the biceps are fully shortened. Squeeze one to two seconds, then lower to full extension.

The dumbbells are hardest to move when the forearms are level with the floor; pause at the top for the squeeze and lower slowly. Keep the chest on the pad and do not swing the elbows back or shrug. Light to moderate loads, 10-15 reps. Pairs well with an incline curl, which loads the opposite end of the range.

Set a bench to 45-60 deg and sit back with head and upper back on the pad, feet flat. Let the arms hang straight down behind the line of the torso holding dumbbells with a neutral grip, palms facing the body.
Curl the dumbbells up keeping the neutral grip and the upper arms hanging still until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to full extension in the stretch.
Combines the incline stretch with brachialis and brachioradialis emphasis. Keep the head and shoulders on the pad and the elbows pointing at the floor. Use lighter weights than standing hammer curls.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells at the sides with an underhand (palms-up) grip (palms forward), arms straight, elbows at the ribs.

Curl the dumbbells up palms-up to shoulder height. At the top, rotate the forearms so the palms face down, then lower slowly over 3-4 seconds with the overhand grip. At the bottom, rotate back to palms-up and repeat.

The underhand lift trains the biceps; the slow overhand lowering loads the brachioradialis and wrist extensors eccentrically. Choose a weight you can control on the way down, which is the limiting phase. Keep the wrists straight and the elbows still.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells with an underhand (palms-up) grip, palms forward, the dumbbells touching the sides of the thighs and the elbows at the ribs.
Curl while pulling the elbows straight back so the dumbbells travel up close to the torso, finishing at the lower ribs with the elbows behind the body. Lower along the same path in 2-3 seconds.
Elbows go back, never forward, which reduces front-delt help and shifts the curl's peak tension. Keep the shoulders down and the chest up. Use moderate loads; the range is shorter than a normal curl.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold one dumbbell vertically by cupping the underside of the top head with both palms facing up and the fingers interlaced or overlapped, like carrying a tray. Arms hang straight, elbows at the sides.
Curl the dumbbell up toward the chin by flexing the elbows, keeping the palms flat under the head and the dumbbell vertical. Squeeze at the top, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

The flat-palm hold reduces forearm and grip contribution and keeps the biceps working into the top range. Keep the wrists firm and the elbows still. Use a moderate dumbbell you can balance without it tipping toward your face.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells at the sides with an overhand grip, palms facing back toward the thighs, arms straight, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the dumbbells up by flexing the elbows while keeping the palms facing down, until the forearms are near vertical. Lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Emphasizes the brachioradialis and brachialis, with the wrist extensors holding the wrist level. Keep the knuckles in line with the forearm; do not let the wrists droop. Use light weights and a strict tempo with the elbows by the sides.

Lie face-up on a high flat bench with the shoulders near the edges so the arms can hang straight down past the bench toward the floor. Hold dumbbells with an underhand (palms-up) grip, palms facing up toward the ceiling at the bottom.
Curl the dumbbells up toward the shoulders while the upper arms stay hanging in shoulder extension. Squeeze at the top, then lower in 3 seconds into the deep stretch at full extension.

Places the long head in an even longer position than an incline curl, so use light weights and control the bottom carefully. Keep the shoulders on the bench and do not let the elbows travel forward. Skip it if the front of the shoulder feels strained.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold dumbbells with an underhand (palms-up) grip and curl them until the elbows are at 90 deg, forearms parallel to the floor and elbows at the ribs.
Hold the 90 deg position for a set time, usually 20-45 seconds, without letting the dumbbells sink or the elbows drift forward. Breathe steadily throughout, then lower slowly at the end of the hold.

Brace the core and do not lean back as fatigue builds. Useful for time under tension, for training around elbow pain at end ranges, or as a finisher after the last set of curls. Can also be held at other angles to target a sticking point.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a weight plate (10-25 kg) vertically in front of the thighs, gripping the rim with both hands at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions, fingers on the back and thumbs on the front, arms straight and elbows at the sides.

Curl the plate up toward the chest by flexing the elbows, keeping the plate vertical and the elbows close to the body, until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

The rim grip is close to neutral and adds pinch-grip and forearm demand. Keep the wrists straight and the torso still. A practical option when no dumbbells or bars are available; a larger plate diameter makes it harder to hold.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold one kettlebell per hand by the handle with an underhand (palms-up) grip so the bell hangs below the hand, or one kettlebell by the horns with both hands. Arms straight, elbows at the sides.
Curl the kettlebell up by flexing the elbows until the forearms are near vertical, letting the bell stay hanging below the handle. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Because the bell's mass sits below and behind the handle, tension stays higher at the top of the curl than with a dumbbell. Keep the wrists straight against the pull of the bell and the elbows still. Avoid swinging the bell.

Stand tall, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold a light kettlebell by the handle upside down, bell pointing to the ceiling, elbow bent about 30 deg and close to the side, forearm and wrist in a straight line. Crush the handle to balance it.
Curl the bell up toward the shoulder while keeping it balanced bottom-up and the forearm vertical at the top. Pause one second, then lower slowly to the start without letting the bell tip.

Maximal grip tension is what balances the bell, so this trains grip and wrist stability with the curl. Start very light (8-12 kg). If the bell tips, reduce the weight rather than catching it near the face.

Attach a straight bar or EZ-bar to a low pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold the bar with an underhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the bar toward the upper chest by flexing the elbows, keeping the upper arms still. Squeeze one second, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension against the cable.

The cable keeps tension at the bottom of the range, where free weights unload. Do not lean back to move the stack. Standing a half step back so the cable angles slightly forward keeps load on the biceps at the start.

Attach a rope to a low pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, core braced. Hold the rope ends with a neutral grip, thumbs up and knuckles toward the rope stops, arms straight, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the rope toward the chest by flexing the elbows, keeping the neutral grip and pulling the rope ends slightly apart at the top. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.
Constant cable tension with brachialis and brachioradialis emphasis. Keep the elbows pinned and avoid leaning back or shrugging. Keep the wrists neutral rather than curling them.

Attach a D-handle to a low pulley. Stand facing the stack or side-on with the working arm nearer to it, feet hip-width. Hold the handle with an underhand (palms-up) grip, arm straight, elbow at the ribs. Steady yourself on the frame with the free hand.
Curl the handle toward the shoulder, supinating fully at the top. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension. Complete all reps, then switch arms.

Keep the working elbow at the ribs and the torso square. Stepping slightly away from the stack keeps tension at the bottom. One arm at a time allows a stronger focus on each side and evens out imbalances.

Set a D-handle on a low pulley (or at knee height). Face away from the machine and step forward into a staggered stance until the cable pulls the working arm behind the torso. Hold the handle with an underhand (palms-up) grip, arm straight, upper arm about 20-30 deg behind the body.

Curl the handle forward and up by flexing the elbow, keeping the upper arm behind the torso, until fully flexed. Lower in 3 seconds until the arm returns to full extension behind you in a deep stretch.

The shoulder-extended position loads the long head at long muscle lengths, like an incline curl but with constant cable tension. Do not let the elbow drift forward to cheat. Keep the chest up and the torso still.

Set D-handles on both high pulleys of a cable crossover, about shoulder height or slightly above. Stand centered, feet hip-width, and hold a handle in each hand with the arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms up, elbows almost straight.

Curl the handles toward the sides of the head by flexing only the elbows, keeping the upper arms level and parallel to the floor, as in a front double-biceps pose. Squeeze, then extend slowly back out to just short of lockout.

Upper arms stay level and still; only the forearms move. The shoulder-flexed position shortens the long head, so this hits peak contraction. Light loads only. Can be done one arm at a time for better control.

Attach a straight bar to a low pulley. Lie on your back on the floor or a flat bench with the feet toward the stack, knees bent. Hold the bar with an underhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight along the torso and the backs of the upper arms on the floor or bench.

Curl the bar toward the shoulders by flexing the elbows, keeping the upper arms on the support, until the forearms are near vertical or slightly past. Squeeze and lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Lying down removes body swing entirely. Keep the upper arms still against the support. Good for strict, high-rep sets and drop sets. Have a partner hand you the bar or pull it into position before lying back.

Place a preacher bench in front of a low pulley so the cable runs straight toward the bench. Attach an EZ-bar, straight bar or D-handle. Sit with the armpits over the top of the pad and the backs of the upper arms flat, gripping the attachment with an underhand (palms-up) grip.
Curl the handle up keeping the upper arms on the pad until fully flexed. Squeeze, then lower in 3 seconds to about 10-15 deg short of full extension.

The cable keeps tension at the top, where a free-weight preacher curl gets easier. Keep the arms flat on the pad and the hips on the seat. Use controlled reps; do not let the stack pull the elbows into hyperextension.

Attach a straight bar to a low pulley. Stand facing the stack, close enough that the cable runs nearly vertically, feet hip-width. Hold the bar with an underhand shoulder-width grip at the front of the thighs.
Curl while pulling the elbows straight back so the bar drags up the body to the lower chest, finishing with the elbows behind the torso. Lower along the same path to the thighs in 2-3 seconds.
Elbows go back, not forward. Keep the bar close to the body and the shoulders down. The cable adds tension at the bottom compared with the barbell version.
Attach a straight bar or EZ-bar to a low pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width. Hold the bar with an overhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the bar up keeping the palms down until the forearms are near vertical. Lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Builds the brachioradialis and brachialis with constant tension. Keep the knuckles in line with the forearms and the elbows by the sides. Use light to moderate loads; an EZ-bar is easier on the wrists.

Adjust the seat height so the backs of the upper arms lie flat on the pad and the elbows line up with the machine's pivot axis. Sit with the chest against the pad and grip the handles with an underhand (palms-up) grip, elbows nearly straight.
Curl the handles up until the elbows are fully flexed, squeeze, and lower in 3 seconds until the arms are nearly straight without letting the weight stack touch down.

Aligning the elbows with the axis is the key setup point: misalignment causes the arms to slide on the pad and stresses the elbow. Keep the hips on the seat. Machines allow safe drop sets and slow eccentrics close to failure.
Set the seat of the biceps curl machine so the back of the upper arm lies flat on the pad with the elbow in line with the pivot. Hold one handle with the arm nearly straight.
Curl the handle up until the biceps is fully shortened, squeeze, then lower slowly to nearly straight. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Keep the upper arm on the pad and the shoulder down. Control the lowering. Good for evening out arm strength.
Stand on the middle of a loop or tube resistance band with feet hip-width. Hold a band end or handle in each hand with an underhand (palms-up) grip, arms straight at the sides, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the hands toward the shoulders by flexing the elbows, keeping them at the sides. Squeeze at the top where the band is most stretched, then lower in 2-3 seconds against the band.

Band tension rises toward the top, the opposite of a dumbbell. Widen the stance or shorten the band to add resistance. Keep the torso upright and control the lowering phase; check the band for nicks before use.
Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip-width. Hold the ends or handles with a neutral grip, palms facing each other, arms straight at the sides, elbows at the ribs.
Curl the hands up keeping the neutral grip until the forearms are near vertical. Squeeze, then lower in 2-3 seconds to full extension.

Emphasizes the brachialis and brachioradialis with rising tension toward the top. Keep the wrists straight and the elbows by the ribs. Adjust tension by stance width or band thickness. Good for high reps and travel training.

Set a barbell in a rack or a Smith machine bar at about waist height. Lie underneath and grip it with an underhand shoulder-width grip, arms straight, heels on the floor and body in a straight line, with the bar over the chest.
Keeping the upper arms fixed at their starting angle, flex the elbows to pull the body up so the forehead travels toward or under the bar. Lower slowly back to straight arms.

It is not a row: the elbows stay pointing toward the feet and do not drive back to the ribs. Keep the body rigid. Raise the bar or bend the knees to make it easier, elevate the feet to make it harder.

Attach a straight bar to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, knees soft, torso leaning forward 10-15 deg from the hips. Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width or slightly narrower and pin the elbows to the sides, forearms just above parallel.

Extend the elbows to push the bar down until the arms are straight and the triceps fully contracted, bar at the front of the thighs. Let the bar rise in 2 seconds until the forearms are just past parallel to the floor, elbows staying put.

Upper arms stay still at the sides; only the forearms move. Do not lean over the bar and push with body weight, and do not let the elbows flare or drift forward on the way up. Keep the wrists straight, stacked over the bar.

Attach a V-bar to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, slight forward lean. Grip the angled handles with palms facing down and slightly in, thumbs on top, elbows pinned to the sides and forearms just above parallel.
Extend the elbows to press the handle down until the arms are straight. Squeeze one second, then let it rise in 2 seconds until the forearms are just above parallel.

The semi-neutral angle is comfortable for most wrists and usually allows the heaviest pushdown loads. Keep the elbows tucked and the shoulders down, not shrugged or rolled forward. Avoid leaning over the handle to finish reps.
