Attach a rope to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, slight forward lean. Hold the rope ends with a neutral grip, hands just above the stoppers, elbows pinned to the sides and forearms angled up just above parallel.

Extend the elbows to push the rope down and pull the ends apart over the last few inches so the hands finish just outside the thighs with the elbows locked. Squeeze, then return in 2 seconds until the forearms pass parallel.

Spreading the rope at the bottom lets the elbows reach full extension past the thighs for a stronger contraction. Keep the upper arms still and the chest up. Use a load you can fully lock out; a rope typically needs less weight than a bar.

Attach a straight bar or EZ-bar to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack about one foot away, feet hip-width, torso upright. Grip the bar underhand (palms up) at shoulder width and pin the elbows to the sides with the forearms bent to about chest height.
Extend the elbows to push the bar down until the arms are straight. Squeeze, then let the bar rise in 2 seconds to about lower-chest height, elbows staying at the ribs.

Use 30-40 percent less load than an overhand pushdown; the grip, not the triceps, usually limits it. Keep the wrists straight, not bent back. Often more comfortable for sore elbows and gives a strong lockout contraction.

Attach a D-handle to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack, feet hip-width, slight forward lean. Hold the handle overhand (or neutral) in one hand with the elbow tucked against the side and the forearm just above parallel. Brace the free hand on the frame.

Extend the elbow to push the handle down until the arm is straight beside the thigh. Squeeze, then let it rise in 2 seconds until the forearm is just above parallel. Finish all reps, then switch arms.
Training one arm at a time fixes side-to-side differences and lets the hand follow its natural path. Keep the shoulder down and the elbow still at the ribs. Do not rotate the torso to help.

Attach a D-handle to a high pulley. Stand facing the stack, feet hip-width, torso upright. Hold the handle with an underhand (palm-up) grip in one hand, elbow tucked at the side and the forearm raised to about chest height.
Extend the elbow to push the handle down until the arm is straight. Squeeze, then let it rise under control to about chest height. Finish the set, then switch arms.
Keep the wrist straight and the elbow pinned. Use light loads. Allows a strong peak contraction and is often comfortable for cranky elbows; a good finisher after heavier pushdowns.

Set a cable at shoulder height or higher, with no handle (grip the cable ball) or a D-handle. Stand side-on to the stack and reach across the body with the arm farther from the stack, so the hand starts near the opposite shoulder, elbow bent about 90 deg and at shoulder height or slightly below.
Extend the elbow to drive the hand out and away across the body until the arm is straight and slightly behind the shoulder line. Squeeze, then return slowly across the body to the start.

Keep the upper arm steady; only the forearm moves. This angle loads the lateral head and suits people who find pushdowns hard on the elbows. Gripping the cable itself gives the smoothest path. Can be done with both arms using a crossover.

Attach a rope to a pulley set at about head height. Grip the rope ends with a neutral grip, turn to face away from the stack and step forward into a staggered stance, torso leaning 30-45 deg forward. Hands are behind the head, elbows bent fully and pointing forward beside the ears.
Extend the elbows to press the rope forward and up until the arms are straight and in line with the torso. Return in 2-3 seconds into the deep stretch behind the head.

The overhead shoulder position stretches the long head, making this a strong long-head builder. Keep the elbows pointing forward at about head width, not flaring wide. Brace the abs so the lower back does not arch. A low pulley version is pressed straight up instead.

Attach a D-handle to a low pulley. Face away from the stack, feet hip-width or staggered, and hold the handle in one hand behind the head with the elbow fully bent and pointing up, upper arm beside the ear. The free hand can support the working elbow.
Extend the elbow to press the handle straight overhead until the arm is straight. Lower in 2-3 seconds into the stretch behind the head. Finish the set, then switch arms.
Keep the upper arm vertical and close to the head. Brace the core to avoid leaning or arching. Use light loads and focus on a full stretch; good for evening out long-head strength between sides.

Place a flat bench 2-3 feet in front of a low pulley with a straight bar, EZ-bar or rope attached. Lie on the bench with the head toward the stack and hold the bar overhand above the forehead, arms extended and angled back 10-20 deg toward the stack.
Keeping the upper arms fixed at that angle, bend the elbows to lower the bar behind the head. Extend the elbows to press the bar back up to straight arms.

The cable keeps tension on the triceps in the stretched position and at lockout, unlike a free-weight skull crusher. Position the bench far enough from the stack for a full range. Keep the elbows at shoulder width, not flaring.

Set a pulley at about knee to hip height, with no handle or a D-handle. Face the stack and hinge forward until the torso is 45-60 deg from vertical, back flat. Hold the handle in one hand with the upper arm pinned parallel to the torso and the elbow bent about 90 deg.
Extend the elbow to drive the hand back until the arm is straight and in line with the torso. Squeeze one second, then return slowly until the forearm is about vertical.

Keep the upper arm locked in place; the shoulder must not swing. The cable keeps the triceps loaded through the whole range, unlike a dumbbell kickback which is loaded mainly at lockout. Use light loads.

Anchor a resistance band above head height, such as over a pull-up bar or with a door anchor. Stand facing it, feet hip-width, slight forward lean. Hold the ends with an overhand or neutral grip, elbows tucked at the sides and forearms just above parallel.
Extend the elbows to push the hands down until the arms are straight beside the thighs. Squeeze, then let the hands rise slowly to just above parallel.

Band tension is highest at lockout. Step back from the anchor or use a thicker band to add resistance. Keep the upper arms still and the shoulders down. Good for warm-ups, home and high-rep finishers.

Stand on one end of a resistance band with the rear foot of a staggered stance, or anchor it low behind you. Hold the other end with both hands behind the head, elbows fully bent and pointing up beside the ears.
Extend the elbows to press the hands overhead until the arms are straight. Lower in 2 seconds back behind the head into the stretch.
Keep the elbows close to the head and pointing up, and brace the core so the lower back does not arch. Shorten the band for more resistance. Good for warm-ups and home training.

Lie on a flat bench, feet flat, with an EZ-bar held on the inner angled grips with an overhand grip (hands about 6-8 inches apart). Press it up so the arms are straight over the shoulders, then angle the upper arms back about 10-15 deg toward the head.

Keeping the upper arms at that angle, bend only the elbows to lower the bar in 2-3 seconds to just above the forehead or slightly behind the top of the head. Extend the elbows to return to straight arms.

Lowering slightly behind the head keeps tension on the triceps at the top and adds long-head stretch. Keep the elbows pointing at the ceiling about shoulder width apart, not flaring. Use controlled loads; a spotter or a partner hand-off helps with heavier sets.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat. Hold a straight barbell with an overhand grip about shoulder width or slightly narrower, arms straight over the shoulders and angled back about 10 deg toward the head.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar in 2-3 seconds toward the forehead or just behind the head, keeping the upper arms still. Extend back to straight arms.

A straight bar puts the wrists in full pronation and is harder on the wrists and elbows than an EZ-bar; switch if it causes discomfort. Keep the elbows tucked to shoulder width and control the lowering phase. Use a spotter for heavy sets.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat. Hold dumbbells with a neutral grip (palms facing each other), arms straight over the shoulders and angled back slightly toward the head.
Bend the elbows to lower the dumbbells in 2-3 seconds beside the head, ending around the ears with the elbows at about 90 deg or deeper. Extend back to straight arms, keeping the upper arms fixed.

The neutral grip is easy on the wrists and elbows, and each arm works independently. Keep the elbows pointing at the ceiling, not flaring outward. Lower slowly; do not let the dumbbells drop toward the head.

Set a bench to about 30 deg and lie back with the feet flat. Hold an EZ-bar on the inner angled grips with an overhand grip, arms extended up from the shoulders and angled back about 15 deg toward the head.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar in 2-3 seconds behind the head into a deep stretch, keeping the upper arms fixed. Extend to straight arms.

The incline places the arms further overhead, increasing long-head stretch. Keep the elbows pointing up and in at about shoulder width. Use 10-20 percent less load than a flat skull crusher and control the stretch.

Set a decline bench to about 15-30 deg and hook the legs under the pads. Lie back and take an EZ-bar from a partner, holding it on the inner angled grips with an overhand grip, arms straight above the shoulders.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar in 2-3 seconds toward the forehead, keeping the upper arms still. Extend back to straight arms.

The decline shifts the arms' angle so the triceps stay loaded closer to lockout. Keep the elbows in at shoulder width and control the descent. Have a spotter hand you the bar and take it at the end of the set.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat. Hold dumbbells with a neutral grip over the chest, arms straight.

Bend the elbows and let the upper arms roll back so the dumbbells lower to the sides of the head near the ears, or touch the shoulders. Then roll the elbows forward toward the chest and press back to straight arms in one smooth motion.

Blending a press into the extension allows heavier loads than a strict skull crusher while still working the triceps through a big range. Keep the dumbbells close to the head. Control the bottom and keep the shoulders on the bench.

Lie on a flat bench, feet flat. Hold a dumbbell in one hand with the arm straight above the shoulder, palm facing your feet (or neutral). Brace the working upper arm with the free hand just below the elbow.
Keeping the upper arm vertical, bend the elbow to lower the dumbbell across the face toward the opposite shoulder. Extend to straight. Finish all reps and switch arms.
Use the free hand to keep the upper arm vertical. Use a light dumbbell and a slow tempo; the cross-body path is easy on the elbow and gives a strong lateral-head contraction.

Sit on an upright bench set to 80-90 deg with the back supported and feet flat. Hold one dumbbell vertically overhead with both hands cupping the underside of the top head, thumbs around the handle, arms straight.
Bend the elbows to lower the dumbbell behind the head in 2-3 seconds until the forearms are below parallel and the triceps are fully stretched. Extend the elbows to press it back overhead.

Keep the elbows pointing forward, about head width, close to the head. Brace the core and keep the lower back on the pad so it does not arch. Lower slowly into the stretch and never bounce out of the bottom. Done standing, brace harder so the ribs stay down.
Sit or stand tall, core braced. Hold a dumbbell overhead in one hand, arm straight and upper arm beside the ear, with the free hand supporting the working upper arm just below the elbow.
Bend the elbow to lower the dumbbell behind the head, keeping the upper arm vertical, until the forearm is below parallel. Extend back to straight. Finish the set and switch arms.
Keep the upper arm vertical and the elbow pointing up. Use a light dumbbell. Lowering slightly behind the opposite ear rather than straight behind the head is often more comfortable for the elbow.
Sit on an upright bench with back support and feet flat. Hold an EZ-bar overhead on the narrow angled grips with an overhand grip, arms fully extended above the head.
Bend only at the elbows to lower the bar behind the head until the forearms are below parallel and the triceps are stretched. Extend the elbows to press the bar back to straight arms overhead.
Keep the elbows pointing forward and close to the head rather than flaring wide. Brace the abs so the lower back stays on the pad. Control the stretch and never bounce out of the bottom.

Lie on a flat bench with feet flat and shoulder blades retracted, as for a bench press. Unrack a barbell with an overhand grip about shoulder width (thumbs roughly over the outer chest), arms straight over the upper chest.

Lower the bar toward the chin and upper chest by bending the elbows while letting the upper arms drift forward, so the elbows point toward the feet and stay in front of the bar. Stop when the forearms meet the biceps or the bar is about 2-3 inches above the throat, then press back by extending the elbows.

A hybrid of a close-grip bench press and skull crusher, popularized by J.M. Blakley for lockout strength. Keep the elbows tucked, not flared. Start light and always use safeties or a spotter: the bar travels over the neck.

Set a flat bench under a Smith machine so the bar descends over the upper chest and throat. Set the safety stops just above throat height. Lie down and grip the bar overhand at about shoulder width, arms straight.
Unhook the bar and lower it toward the throat by bending the elbows and letting them drift forward toward the feet. Stop when the forearms meet the biceps, then extend the elbows to press back up.
The fixed path makes the JM press easier to learn and safer to push close to failure. Always set the safeties. Keep the elbows tucked and the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat. Press dumbbells up over the chest with an overhand grip, palms facing the feet, and turn them so the inner heads touch, elbows pointing out to the sides.
Keeping the upper arms still and flared, bend the elbows to lower the dumbbells down to the chest with the heads touching. Extend the elbows to press back up to the start.

The elbows point out while the upper arms stay fixed; this is not a press. Use light dumbbells. Control the descent and stop if the elbows feel strained. A lockout-specific triceps builder used by powerlifters.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat and shoulder blades retracted. Unrack a barbell with a close grip, hands about shoulder width or slightly inside, arms straight over the chest.

Lower the bar toward the lower chest by bending the elbows partway, as in a close-grip press, then let the elbows travel forward so the bar finishes over the upper chest or throat. Press back up by extending the elbows.

A press-and-extension hybrid like the JM press, with more pressing at the start. Keep the elbows tucked. Use light to moderate loads and a spotter or safeties. Pick JM press or California press, not both, in a single block.
Lie on the floor inside a power rack with the J-hooks set at arm's length and the bar over the chest. Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width, legs straight or knees bent with feet flat.
Unrack and lower the bar until the backs of the upper arms touch the floor, elbows tucked about 45 deg. Pause briefly with the arms relaxed on the floor, then press back to straight arms.
The floor shortens the range and emphasizes the lockout, removing leg drive. Keep the elbows tucked and do not bounce them off the floor. Set safeties just below chest height.
Lie on a flat bench, feet flat and shoulder blades retracted. Hold dumbbells over the chest with a neutral grip, palms facing each other and the dumbbells pressed together.
Lower the dumbbells in 2 seconds to the lower chest while squeezing them together and keeping the elbows tucked close to the sides. Press back to straight arms, maintaining the squeeze.
The tucked elbows shift work to the triceps; squeezing the dumbbells together adds inner chest tension. Keep the dumbbells touching throughout. Control the descent.

Place one knee and the same-side hand on a flat bench, or stand and hinge forward, so the torso is near parallel to the floor and the back is flat. Hold a dumbbell in the free hand with a neutral grip, upper arm pinned parallel to the torso and elbow bent at 90 deg.
Extend the elbow to drive the dumbbell back until the arm is straight and in line with the torso. Squeeze one second, then return slowly to 90 deg.
Keep the upper arm still; only the forearm moves. The load is greatest at lockout and nearly zero at the bottom, so focus on the squeeze. Use a light dumbbell.

Sit on the edge of a flat bench or sturdy chair with hands beside the hips, shoulder-width, fingers pointing forward. Walk the feet out and slide the hips just off the edge so they are close to the bench. Knees bent at 90 deg (easier) or legs straight (harder).
Bend the elbows to lower the body straight down until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor, elbows at about 90 deg. Press back up to straight arms.

Keep the back close to the bench and the elbows pointing straight back, not flaring. Do not dip past 90 deg; the deep end range stresses the front of the shoulder. Raise the feet on a second bench to add difficulty, or add a plate on the lap.

Grip parallel dip bars with a neutral grip, slightly wider than the shoulders, and press up to straight arms. Keep the torso upright, shoulders down and away from the ears, legs straight or knees bent and crossed behind.
Bend the elbows to lower the body until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor, elbows pointing back and close to the body. Press back up to full lockout.

An upright torso keeps emphasis on the triceps; a forward lean shifts it to the chest. Keep the shoulders depressed and avoid diving deep below parallel. Use an assisted dip machine or band to scale, or a dip belt to add load.

Adjust the seat so the elbows line up with the machine's pivot axis and the backs of the upper arms rest flat on the pad. Grip the handles with a neutral or overhand grip, elbows bent about 90 deg or more.
Extend the elbows to push the handles down and forward until the arms are straight. Squeeze, then return in 2-3 seconds to the start without letting the stack touch down.
Align the elbows with the axis to protect the joint and keep tension even. Keep the upper arms on the pad and the back against the seat. Good for drop sets and slow negatives.

Set a barbell in a rack or a Smith machine bar at about hip height. Grip it overhand at shoulder width and walk the feet back so the body forms a straight plank, arms straight and the bar at forehead level.
Bend only the elbows to lower the head under the bar until the forehead is just below it. Extend the elbows to press the body back to straight arms.
Keep the body rigid with glutes and abs braced. Raise the bar to make it easier, lower it to make it harder. Elbows point down toward the floor and stay about shoulder width.

Sit on the end of a flat bench, feet flat and hip-width. Rest the forearms on the thighs (or kneel and lay them along the bench) with the wrists just past the knees or edge. Hold a barbell with an underhand (palms-up) grip about shoulder width.

Extend the wrists to lower the bar toward the floor and let it roll partway down the fingers. Close the fingers, then flex the wrists to curl the bar up as high as possible. Squeeze one second at the top and lower slowly to the full stretch.
Keep the forearms fixed on the support; only the hands move. Use moderate loads for 12-20 reps rather than heavy, jerky reps. Do not lift the forearms or use the biceps to help the bar up.

Sit on the end of a flat bench, feet flat. Rest the forearms on the thighs, palms down, with the wrists hanging just past the knees. Hold a light barbell or EZ-bar with an overhand shoulder-width grip, thumbs around.
Let the wrists flex so the bar lowers toward the floor, then extend the wrists to lift the knuckles as high as possible. Pause one second at the top, then lower in 2-3 seconds.

The wrist extensors are much weaker than the flexors, so use roughly a third to half of your wrist curl load. Keep the forearms still and the grip secure but not white-knuckled. Balances flexor work and supports elbow health.

Set a barbell in a rack at about hip height. Stand with your back to it, feet hip-width, and take it behind the thighs with a shoulder-width grip, palms facing backward (away from the legs). Step forward, stand tall with arms straight and the bar against the backs of the thighs.
Let the bar roll down toward the fingertips, then close the fingers and flex the wrists to curl the bar up and back as high as possible. Pause, then lower slowly.

Keep the arms straight and the shoulders still; only the wrists and fingers move. This position typically allows heavier loading than the seated version. Keep the bar close to the legs and return it to the rack when done.
Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in one hand. Rest the forearm on the thigh or bench, palm up, with the wrist just past the edge. The free hand can stabilize the working forearm.
Lower the dumbbell by extending the wrist, letting it roll slightly down the fingers. Curl the fingers and wrist up as high as possible, squeeze, then lower slowly. Finish the set and switch arms.
Keep the forearm flat and still. Working one arm at a time evens out imbalances. Use a full range and moderate weight for 12-20 reps rather than heavy, jerky reps.
Sit on a bench with one forearm resting on the thigh, palm facing down and the wrist just past the knee. Hold a light dumbbell with an overhand grip; the free hand can hold the working forearm down.
Let the wrist flex so the dumbbell lowers toward the floor, then extend the wrist to raise the back of the hand as high as possible. Pause and lower in 2-3 seconds. Switch arms after the set.

Use a light dumbbell; the extensors fatigue fast. Keep the forearm still and avoid rotating the wrist or lifting the elbow. A useful prehab exercise for lateral elbow pain (tennis elbow) and grip-heavy athletes.

Attach a straight bar to a low pulley. Kneel or sit facing the stack with the forearms resting on the thighs or a bench, palms up and wrists just past the edge, holding the bar with an underhand (palms-up) grip.

Let the cable pull the wrists back into extension and the bar roll slightly down the fingers, then flex the wrists to curl up as high as possible. Squeeze at the top and lower slowly against the cable.
The cable keeps tension consistent through the range. Keep the forearms fixed on the support. Position yourself so the cable runs roughly perpendicular to the forearms at mid-range.
Attach a straight bar to a low pulley. Kneel or sit facing the stack with forearms on the thighs or a bench, palms down and wrists just past the edge, holding the bar with an overhand grip.
Let the cable pull the wrists down into flexion, then extend the wrists to lift the knuckles as high as possible. Pause one second and lower slowly.
Constant cable tension makes light loads effective. Keep the forearms fixed and avoid using the shoulders. Pairs well with cable wrist curls for balanced forearm work.

Use a wrist roller: a 1-1.5 inch handle with a rope and a small plate (2.5-10 kg) hanging from its center. Stand tall, feet hip-width, and hold the handle with an overhand grip at shoulder width, arms straight in front at shoulder height, plate hanging near the floor.

Turn the handle one hand at a time, alternating short wrist flexion and extension, to wind the rope until the plate reaches the handle. Then unwind slowly with the same alternating action to lower the plate under control. Reverse the winding direction on the next set.

Keep the arms straight and level; the front delts work isometrically, so start light. Rolling the top of the handle toward you mainly trains the flexors, away from you the extensors. Do not let the weight drop on the way down.

Place two smooth-sided weight plates (for example two 10 kg) together, smooth faces out. Stand beside them, squat down with a flat back and pinch them with the four fingers on one face and the thumb on the other, arm straight.
Stand up holding the plates at your side and hold for a set time, usually 15-45 seconds, without letting them slide apart. Squat back down to lower them under control.
The thumb does much of the work, so squeeze it hard into the plates. Progress by time, heavier plates or more plates. Keep the plates close to the leg and the shoulder pulled back; chalk helps.

Use a weight plate with a raised center hub (classic York-style plates) or a loadable hub-lift tool. Stand beside it, squat down with a flat back and grip the hub with the fingertips on one side and the thumb on the other, arm straight.
Stand up and lift the plate off the floor using only the hub pinch. Hold for a few seconds or for time, then lower it under control back to the floor.
A strong test of thumb and pinch strength. Keep the arm straight and the plate close to the body. Progress by plate size or by adding weight to a loadable tool. Lift with the legs, not the back.

Load a pinch block (a wooden or metal block with a loading pin) with plates, or use a blob (the cut-off head of an old hex dumbbell). Stand over it with feet hip-width and grip the block with the fingers on one face and the thumb on the other.
Lift by standing up with a straight arm and a flat back. Hold at your side for time or a few seconds, then lower to the floor under control.
Keep the wrist neutral and the grip deep on the block. Progress by adding load in small jumps. Chalk helps. Train both hands evenly and avoid jerking the block off the floor.
Stand a hex dumbbell on one end. Squat beside it with a flat back and grip the top head with the fingertips on one flat face and the thumb on the opposite face, arm straight.
Stand up to lift the dumbbell off the floor, holding it at your side by the head only. Hold for time or a few seconds, then lower it back down with control.
Heavier dumbbells have wider heads and are much harder to pinch, so progress slowly. Keep the arm straight and the shoulder set. Chalk the hands and train both sides equally.

Hold a torsion-spring hand gripper in one hand with one handle against the palm (heel of the hand) and the other across the middle of the fingers. Set the gripper deep in the hand; the free hand can help position it.
Squeeze the handles together until they touch or as far as possible. Hold the close for 1-2 seconds, then open the hand slowly against the spring.
Choose a gripper that allows full closes for the planned reps. For maximal strength, use heavier grippers for low reps or timed holds at the closed position. Train both hands and control the release.
Stand beneath a pull-up bar and grip it with one hand, overhand. Keep the other hand lightly on the bar or a strap at first, then let go so you hang from one arm with feet off the floor.
Hang for a set time, keeping the shoulder slightly engaged and the body from spinning. Lower to the floor or step onto a box with control, then switch arms.
Keep the working shoulder packed down, not shrugged up by the ear. Scale by keeping fingers of the other hand on the bar or toes on a box. Build up from short holds of 5-10 seconds.

Drape two thick towels over a pull-up bar about shoulder width apart. Grip the hanging ends of one towel in each hand, thumbs wrapped, and step off a box so the arms are straight and the feet hang free.
Hang from the towels for a set time, squeezing hard to prevent slipping. Step back onto the box or lower yourself carefully to finish.
The thick, vertical towel grip trains crushing grip much harder than a bar. Start with short holds of 10-20 seconds. Scale by keeping the feet on a box or using one towel with a hand on the bar.

Attach thick rubber grip sleeves (about 2-2.75 inch diameter) to a pair of dumbbells, or use thick-handle dumbbells. Deadlift them from the floor or rack with a flat back, then stand tall holding them at the sides, arms straight.
Hold for a set time, usually 20-45 seconds, keeping the shoulders back and the hand closed as far as possible around the thick handle. Lower the weights under control.

The thick diameter forces the hand open, overloading crushing and thumb strength. Progress by time, then load. Keep the shoulders packed and the chest tall rather than letting the arms pull you forward.
Sit on a bench with the forearms resting on the thighs, palms up and wrists just past the knees. Hold a barbell with an underhand shoulder-width grip.
Open the fingers to let the bar roll down to the fingertips under control. Curl the fingers closed to roll the bar back into the palm, then finish with a small wrist curl.
Keep the forearms still and the wrists neutral during the finger roll. Use light to moderate loads and higher reps. Do not let the bar slip off the fingertips; start very light to learn the range.
Fill a deep bucket with uncooked rice. Stand or sit beside it and push one or both hands into the rice up to the wrists.

Perform a series of movements for time: opening and spreading the fingers, closing into fists, twisting the wrists, flexing and extending the wrists, and pinching rice. Work 20-40 seconds per movement.

The rice resists movement in every direction, training the small hand muscles and the forearm flexors and extensors. Move with intent and keep good wrist alignment. A good warm-up, finisher or rehab tool.

Stand tall with the arm straight at the side. Hold a loading dumbbell handle with plates on one end only (or a sledgehammer or club), gripping the empty end so the weighted end points forward, thumb side up.
Keeping the arm still, tilt the wrist toward the thumb side to raise the weighted end. Lift as high as possible, then lower slowly back down to just below horizontal.
Only the wrist moves; keep the elbow straight and the shoulder still. Choke up toward the weight to make it easier, slide the hand away from it to make it harder. Use a slow tempo.
Stand tall with the arm straight at the side. Hold the empty end of a single-end-loaded dumbbell handle (or a sledgehammer or club) with the weighted end behind the body, pinky side toward it.
Keeping the arm still, tilt the wrist backward toward the pinky side to raise the weighted end behind you. Lift as high as possible, then lower slowly back down.
Keep the elbow straight and the shoulder from moving. The range is small, so focus on control. Move the hand along the handle to adjust difficulty. Use light loads and higher reps.

Sit on a bench with one forearm resting on the thigh or bench, wrist just past the edge. Hold a single-end-loaded dumbbell handle or a sledgehammer by the empty end, weight pointing up and thumb toward the ceiling.
Slowly rotate the forearm to turn the palm down until the weight points out to the side, return to vertical, then rotate the other way to turn the palm up. Continue alternating with control.
Keep the forearm flat and still; the rotation comes from the forearm, not the shoulder. Slide the hand away from the weight to make it harder. Use light loads and a slow tempo.
Place two heavy dumbbells, kettlebells or farmer's handles at your sides. Deadlift them up with a neutral spine, then stand tall with arms straight, shoulders back and the core braced.
Hold the weights in place for a set time, usually 20-60 seconds, without letting them drift or the shoulders round forward. Lower them by hinging at the hips with control.
Crush the handles and keep the shoulders packed down and back. Breathe behind a braced core. Progress by time, then by load. Lift and lower with the legs and a flat back.
Set a barbell in a rack at mid-thigh height. Grip it double-overhand at shoulder width, step back and stand tall with arms straight, shoulders back and core braced.
Hold the bar for a set time, usually 10-30 seconds, without letting it roll toward the fingers. Return it to the rack or safety pins with control.
Train with a double-overhand grip, no straps, to build deadlift grip. Squeeze the bar hard and keep it close to the thighs. Progress by heavier loads or longer holds; use chalk.
Set a thick axle bar (about 2 inches / 5 cm in diameter, usually non-revolving) in a rack at mid-thigh height. Grip it double-overhand at shoulder width, step back and stand tall with arms straight.
Hold the axle for a set time, keeping the bar from rolling out of the hands. Return it to the rack or pins under control.

The thick, non-rotating bar forces an open hand, building crushing and thumb strength for axle deadlifts and cleans. Chalk up. Progress by time or load, and keep the shoulders packed and the core braced.
Attach a Rolling Thunder handle (a thick, freely rotating handle) to a loading pin with plates. Stand over it with feet hip-width and grip the handle with one hand, fingers around and thumb over.

Squat down and stand up to lift the weight off the floor with one hand, hold briefly or for time, then lower it with control. The handle rotates, so the grip must stop it from spinning out of the hand.
A grip-sport and strongman event lift. Keep the wrist neutral and the arm straight. Lift with the legs, not the back. Chalk well and progress in small increments.
Place a rubber band or finger-extension band around all five fingertips with the fingers held together in a cone shape.
Spread the fingers and thumb apart against the band as wide as possible, hold briefly, then return slowly to the closed position. Repeat for high reps.
Trains the finger extensors, which balance heavy gripping work and help prevent elbow pain. Use 20-30 slow reps. Add a second band or a thicker band to increase resistance.
Hold a light kettlebell by the handle with the bell pointing straight up, upside down, elbow bent at 90 deg and forearm vertical in front of the shoulder.
Hold the bell balanced in the bottoms-up position for time, or walk with it as a carry. Lower it under control at the end of the set.
Crush the handle as hard as possible; a loose grip makes the bell tip. Keep the wrist straight and the forearm vertical. Start light and progress by time, then weight. Train both arms.
Stand or sit tall and extend one arm straight in front at shoulder height with the palm facing up or forward and the elbow straight.
Use the other hand to gently pull the fingers and palm back toward you until a stretch is felt along the inside of the forearm. Hold, then release slowly and switch arms.
Hold for 20-30 seconds, one to three times per side. Keep the elbow straight and the shoulder relaxed. Stretch to mild tension only; never force the wrist into pain.
Stand or sit tall and extend one arm straight in front at shoulder height with the palm facing down and the elbow straight.
Use the other hand to gently press the back of the hand down toward you, bending the wrist until a stretch is felt along the top of the forearm. Hold, then release and switch arms.
Hold for 20-30 seconds per side. Curl the fingers into a loose fist for a stronger stretch. Keep the elbow straight and shoulders relaxed. Useful for desk workers and tennis elbow.
Place two pairs of smooth plates together, smooth sides out. Squat and pinch one pair in each hand with fingers on one side and thumb on the other, then stand tall.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps for a set distance or time, keeping the plates at the sides. Squat down to set them down when finished.
Squeeze the thumbs hard and keep the shoulders packed. Walk smoothly so the plates do not swing and slip. Progress by distance, then heavier plates; chalk helps.
Hold a stress ball, grip ball or therapy putty in one hand with the fingers wrapped around it. Sit or stand comfortably with the forearm supported.
Squeeze the ball as hard as possible, hold for 3-5 seconds, then relax the hand slowly. Repeat for 10-20 reps, then switch hands.
A low-intensity option for rehab, desk breaks and beginners. Choose a firmer ball or putty to progress. Pair with finger extension work so the hand stays balanced.
Stand or sit tall with the arms extended in front or the elbows bent and close to the body. Make loose fists or interlace the fingers.
Slowly rotate the wrists in large circles in one direction for 10-15 reps, then reverse direction. Move through the full available range each circle.
Use as a warm-up before pressing, curling or grip work. Move smoothly and slowly, not fast and jerky. Keep the forearms still so the motion comes from the wrists.
Stand or sit tall and press the palms together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, elbows out to the sides.

Slowly lower the hands toward the waist while keeping the palms pressed together until a stretch is felt in the wrist flexors. Hold. For the reverse version, press the backs of the hands together, fingers pointing down.
Hold for 20-30 seconds. Keep the shoulders relaxed and the palms fully in contact. Stretch to mild tension only and ease off if there is tingling or sharp pain.
Sit on the end of a flat bench with feet flat. Hold a barbell with an underhand shoulder-width grip, resting it on the thighs with the elbows bent and by the sides.
Curl the bar up from the thighs to the top position by flexing the elbows, squeeze, then lower slowly back to the thighs. The range covers roughly the top half of a full curl.
Seated removes leg drive and lets you overload the strongest part of the curl. Keep the torso upright and the elbows pinned. Lower to the thighs gently rather than dropping.
Place a bench beside a low pulley with a D-handle attached. Sit and brace the back of the working upper arm against the inner thigh, arm straight, palm up, holding the handle.
Curl the handle toward the shoulder while keeping the upper arm against the thigh, squeeze hard, then lower slowly to full extension. Finish the set and switch arms.
The cable keeps tension at the bottom where the dumbbell version goes slack. Keep the torso still and do not push the arm with the thigh. Supinate fully at the top.
Fit thick grip sleeves over the handles of two dumbbells. Stand tall holding them at the sides with palms forward, arms straight and elbows by the ribs.
Curl the dumbbells up by bending the elbows until the forearms are near vertical, squeeze, then lower slowly to full extension, keeping the thick handles fully gripped.
The thick handle adds grip and forearm demand and is often easier on the elbows. Expect to use less weight. Keep the wrists straight and do not let the hands open at the bottom.
Stand on the middle of a sturdy towel with feet hip-width apart. Hold one end in each hand with palms up, elbows bent to about 90 deg and close to the sides.
Pull up on the towel as hard as possible as though curling, while the feet keep it from moving. Hold the maximal effort for 6-10 seconds, rest, and repeat at different elbow angles.
Build effort over the first second rather than yanking. Keep breathing; do not hold the breath. Useful for equipment-free training and for strengthening a specific sticking point.
Stand facing the edge of a sturdy door frame with feet close to its base. Grip the frame with one hand at about chest height, palm facing up or inward, and lean back until the arm is straight.
Curl the body toward the frame by bending the elbow, keeping the upper arm level and the body straight. Lower back slowly until the arm is straight. Switch arms after the set.
Move the feet closer to the frame to make it harder. Keep the body rigid and the shoulder down. Use a frame you can grip securely and test it before loading it fully.
Attach a straight or EZ-bar to a low or mid pulley. Face away from the stack in a staggered stance, holding the bar overhand behind the head with elbows bent and pointing forward.
Extend the elbows to press the bar forward and up until the arms are straight overhead. Return slowly behind the head into the deep stretch.
The bar allows heavier loads than a rope. Keep the elbows at shoulder width and pointing forward, not flaring. Brace the core to avoid arching the lower back.
Sit or stand tall holding one kettlebell by the horns with both hands, bell hanging down, arms extended overhead.
Bend the elbows to lower the bell behind the head into a full stretch, then extend the elbows to press it back overhead.
Holding the horns keeps the wrists neutral. Keep the elbows pointed forward and close to the head. Brace the abs and lower slowly; the bell can swing if rushed.

Set the bar in a rack at mid-chest height. Grip just outside shoulder width with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped, step under and seat the bar on the upper traps above the spine of the scapula. Unrack and step back to stand with heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees.

Take a big breath into the belly and brace. Break at the hips and knees together, knees travelling forward and out over the toes, torso fairly upright (around 30 to 45 degrees of forward lean). Descend until the hip crease is below the top of the knee, then drive up through the whole foot, bar travelling in a vertical line over mid-foot, and exhale at or near lockout.
Bar stays over mid-foot; heels stay down. Knees track in line with the second or third toe, never caving in. If the pelvis tucks at the bottom, reduce depth or load.

Seat the bar about 5 to 7 cm lower than a high-bar squat, across the rear delts just below the spine of the scapula. Grip as narrow as shoulder mobility allows and lift the elbows up and back to form a shelf. Unrack and set heels slightly wider than shoulder width, toes out 20 to 30 degrees.

Brace hard, push the hips back and down while the knees travel forward less than in a high-bar squat; the torso leans further forward to keep the bar over mid-foot. Descend until the hip crease is just below the top of the knee (competition depth), then drive the hips and upper back up together to lockout.

Do not let the hips rise faster than the chest and turn it into a good morning. Keep the wrists straight and in line with the forearms; the back carries the bar, not the hands or elbows. Knees out over the toes.

Set the bar at upper-chest height. Take a clean grip just outside shoulder width, step in so the bar sits on the front delts touching the throat, then drive the elbows forward and up until the upper arms are near parallel to the floor; fingertips stay under the bar. Unrack, step back and stand with heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees.

Brace, then sit straight down between the heels, knees travelling well forward over the toes and the torso staying close to vertical. Descend to full depth with the hip crease below the knee, then drive up leading with the elbows and chest, bar travelling vertically over mid-foot, to full lockout.

Elbows high out of the hole; if they drop, the bar rolls forward and the upper back rounds. Use a straps or cross-arm grip if wrist or lat mobility limits the rack. Weight stays over mid-foot, never on the toes.

Set the bar at upper-chest height. Step in so the bar sits on the front delts against the throat, then cross the forearms so each hand rests on top of the bar over the opposite shoulder, upper arms parallel to the floor. Unrack, step back and stand with heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out.

Brace and squat straight down with the torso upright and knees travelling forward, keeping the elbows level with the shoulders. Reach full depth, then drive up through mid-foot without letting the elbows sink, finishing with hips and knees locked.

Differs from the clean-grip front squat only in arm position; it needs less wrist and lat mobility but holds the bar less securely, so loads are usually lighter. Press the hands down on the bar to pin it. End the set when the elbows start to drop.

Place a box behind you at a height that puts the hip crease at or just below the top of the knee when seated. Back squat the bar off the rack and set a stance wider than shoulder width, toes out 20 to 30 degrees, heels about one foot-length in front of the box.

Brace, push the hips back and down while keeping the shins near vertical, and sit under control onto the box. Stay braced and keep the bar on the back; release the hip flexors slightly for a split second without rocking or relaxing the trunk. Then drive the hips and upper back up together explosively to lockout.

Do not crash onto the box or rock back and forward off it. Wide stance and vertical shins is the classic powerlifting version; a narrower stance with knees forward makes it more quad-biased. Raise or lower the box to set depth.

Load the bar to about 50 to 60 percent of a one rep max, often with bands or chains adding roughly 25 percent at lockout. Set a parallel-height box behind you and take your wide box squat stance, toes out, shins near vertical.

Descend quickly but under control, sit onto the box, keep tension and then explode up as fast as possible to lockout. Rerack or reset and repeat. Typical programming is 8 to 12 sets of 2 reps with 45 to 60 seconds rest, rotating stance width each set.
Every rep must be fast; stop the set if bar speed visibly slows. Stay tight on the box and drive the upper back into the bar first. Treat it as power and technique practice, not a grinder.

Set up exactly as for your competition or training back squat: bar on the upper back (high or low bar), heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees, a full breath and brace before unracking and again before each rep.

Descend at a normal controlled speed to your normal depth, then hold the bottom position motionless for 1 to 3 seconds (2 is standard) with the trunk braced, knees out and hips not sinking. Drive straight up from the dead stop, with no bounce, to full lockout.

The pause removes the stretch reflex, so it builds strength out of the hole and fixes position. Do not relax or sink deeper during the pause; chest and hips stay where they were. Use about 10 to 20 percent less load than a touch-and-go squat.
Take a clean-grip front rack with the bar on the front delts against the throat and elbows high, heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out. Breathe and brace before each rep.

Squat straight down to full depth with an upright torso and knees forward, then hold motionless for 2 to 3 seconds without letting the elbows drop or the upper back round. Drive up from the dead stop, elbows leading, to lockout.

The pause exposes any collapse of the upper back, so it is excellent for Olympic lifters and quad strength out of the hole. Do not breathe out during the pause. Use roughly 10 to 15 percent less than your normal front squat.

Set the safety pins in a power rack so the bar rests on them at your target depth, usually parallel or a sticking point. Unrack the bar from the J-hooks above, step into your normal squat stance centred over the pins.

Squat down under control until the bar settles on the pins and comes to a dead stop. Pause for about 1 second, keeping your position and most of the tension but letting the pins take the bar, then rebrace and drive up to lockout. Each rep returns to the pins.

Do not slam the bar into the pins or relax into a round back. Because there is no stretch reflex, the start of the drive must come from a deliberate rebrace. Unlike the Anderson squat, the rep starts at the top with an eccentric.

Set the pins of a power rack at the bottom or sticking-point height of your squat and rest the loaded bar on them. Squat down underneath, set the bar on the upper back, take your normal stance and pull the upper back tight into the bar.

From the dead stop, brace hard and drive the bar off the pins to full lockout. Lower it back down under control until it rests on the pins, then reset your breath, brace and position before the next rep.

Starts with the concentric, which is the difference from the pin squat. Take the slack out by pushing up into the bar before driving, or the bar jerks and position breaks. Heavy singles to triples work best.

Set the bar in a rack around lower-chest to belly height, or deadlift it and set it on the thighs. Hold it in the crook of the elbows with forearms vertical and hands clasped or fists together under the chin, bar pulled tight to the body. Unrack and stand with heels shoulder width or slightly wider, toes out.
Brace and squat down between the legs with an upright torso, elbows passing inside the knees. Reach full depth, keeping the bar tight to the stomach, then drive up through mid-foot to standing.

Use a bar pad or towel if the elbows hurt. Keep the upper back from rounding as the bar pulls forward; it is an excellent trunk-bracing builder. Start light; the elbows, not the legs, often limit the load.

Use a safety squat bar (yoke bar with padded collar and forward handles) set at mid-chest height. Place the yoke on the upper traps, hold the handles lightly with both hands in front of the chest and elbows down, unrack and set heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees.

Brace and squat to full depth while the cambered bar tries to pitch the torso forward. Keep the chest up and drive the upper back into the pads out of the hole, pushing through the whole foot to lockout.

Rounding of the upper back is the main fault; think push the yoke up toward the ceiling. Friendly on shoulders, elbows and wrists. Expect about 5 to 10 percent less load than a straight bar back squat.

Set a safety squat bar in a power rack with the safety pins or a pair of handles at about chest height in front of you. Put the yoke on the upper traps, let go of the bar handles and hold the rack uprights or safety arms with both hands. Heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out.

Squat to full depth with a very upright torso, knees travelling forward. Use the hands only for balance and, at most, slight assistance through the sticking point. Drive up mainly through the legs to lockout.

Named after Dr. Fred Hatfield. Removing the balance and trunk demand lets you load the quads heavily. Do not pull yourself up with the arms; if you must, the load is too heavy. Keep knees tracking over the toes.

Use a cambered squat bar, whose sleeves drop 30 to 40 cm below the bar line so the plates hang low. Seat it on the upper traps like a high-bar squat, hold the handles or the bar just outside the shoulders, unrack and set heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out.

Brace and squat to depth, keeping the descent slow enough that the hanging plates do not swing. Stand up keeping the bar balanced over mid-foot. A Buffalo bar is a milder bend that simply reduces shoulder strain.

The low, swinging load increases trunk and upper-back stabilization demand. Move deliberately and pause briefly at the top so the plates settle. A shoulder-friendly alternative when external rotation is limited.

Set up for a normal back squat. Choose a four-digit tempo (eccentric, bottom pause, concentric, top pause) such as 3-1-1-0 or 4-2-1-0 and set the load to roughly 60 to 75 percent of your normal working weight.

Brace, then lower for the full counted eccentric while keeping the bar over mid-foot and the knees tracking over the toes. Hold any prescribed bottom pause motionless, then stand up at the prescribed speed (usually as fast as possible with a 1 count) to lockout before starting the next rep.

Count honestly; the controlled lowering and position are the point. Breathe and rebrace at the top of each rep. Great for grooving technique, building positional strength and limiting load during rehab or lighter (deload) weeks.
One and a Half Rep Squat
Back squat setup with a moderate load, around 60 to 70 percent of your normal working weight, on the upper back. Heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out, breath and brace before the rep.

Squat to full depth, rise only to about halfway (thighs about 45 degrees above parallel), lower back to full depth, then stand all the way up to lockout. That whole sequence counts as one rep. A 1 1/4 rep variant rises only a quarter of the way before going back down.
Keep the brace and tension at the half point; do not hurry the second descent. The extra time in the bottom range builds quad strength and depth. Drop the weight compared with straight sets.
Set safety pins in a power rack just below the target depth. Back squat setup with the bar on the upper traps, heels about shoulder width and toes slightly out.

Brace, then bend hips and knees to the set depth: about 90 degrees of knee bend (thighs roughly 45 degrees above parallel) for a half squat, or about 45 to 60 degrees of knee bend for a quarter squat. Drive back up to full lockout without pausing.

Used for overload, partial-range strength and sport-specific jumping or sprint power. Heavier loads tempt the hips to shoot back and the torso to fold; keep the bar over mid-foot. Pair with full-range squats rather than replacing them.

Place a loaded barbell on the floor directly behind your heels. Stand with feet hip width, squat down with the chest up and grip the bar behind the legs with an overhand, shoulder-width grip, arms straight, shins and calves near the bar.

Keeping the torso as upright as possible and the knees forward, drive through the feet and stand up, sliding the bar up the backs of the calves and thighs until hips and knees are locked. Lower it back to the floor along the same path under control.

This is the original free-weight hack squat, not the machine. Keep the bar touching the legs and the chest up for quad emphasis. Raise the plates on blocks if the bar hits the calves early. Use straps if grip limits the set.
Place the heels on a slant board, wedge or 2.5 to 5 cm plates. Take a clean-grip or cross-arm front rack, elbows high, with a narrow stance, feet about hip width and toes forward or slightly out.

Brace and squat straight down, letting the knees travel far past the toes while the torso stays nearly vertical. Reach full depth with the hamstrings near the calves, then stand up through the whole foot without the heels leaving the wedge.
The heel lift and narrow stance increase knee flexion, making this one of the most quad-dominant barbell squats; expect lighter loads. Control the bottom instead of bouncing. Keep elbows high.

Loop resistance bands over the barbell sleeves and anchor them to the rack base, band pegs or heavy dumbbells so they are slightly taut at the bottom. Typical band tension is 20 to 35 percent of the total load at lockout. Back squat setup as normal.
Squat to depth as the band tension decreases, controlling the bands as they pull you down faster than gravity. Drive up and keep accelerating as the bands stretch and add load toward lockout.

Bands overspeed the eccentric; stay braced and in control. Check that both bands are the same strength and length so the bar stays level. Used for speed, rate of force development and lockout strength.

Hang chains from each barbell sleeve using a lead chain so that at the bottom of the squat most links pile on the floor and at lockout most are off the floor. Back squat setup with normal stance and grip.
Squat to depth as chain links unload onto the floor and the load lightens, then drive up as links lift off and the load increases toward lockout. Finish each rep fully locked out.

Set chains evenly so the bar stays level. Accelerate through the top half where the load increases. Keep the descent controlled so the chains do not swing. Chains add less overspeed eccentric than bands.

Hang bands from the top of a power rack and loop them around the barbell sleeves so they are stretched most at the bottom of the squat. The bands take roughly 20 to 30 percent of the weight off at the bottom while you hold the full weight at lockout.
Unrack and squat to depth while the bands increasingly assist you, then drive up as the assistance decreases until you carry the full load at lockout.
Builds confidence and nervous system adaptation to loads heavier than your max. Stay as tight as on a normal heavy squat. Ensure both bands are equal so the bar stays level, and set safeties.

Rest a light barbell or PVC pipe on the front delts against the throat, then extend both arms straight forward at shoulder height, palms down, hands not touching the bar. Heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Squat to full depth keeping the torso upright and the shoulders elevated so the bar does not roll forward, then stand back up to full lockout with arms still extended.
A front squat posture drill: if the bar slides, the chest is falling or the upper back is rounding. Start with an empty bar or PVC. Keep the shoulders pushing up into the bar the whole time.

Stand straddling a loaded barbell so it runs front to back between your legs. Take a wide stance, about 1.5 times shoulder width, with feet slightly staggered and toes turned out. Squat down and grip the bar with one hand in front of the body and one behind, both overhand, arms straight.
Brace, keep the chest up and drive through both feet to stand up to full lockout, the bar rising vertically between the legs. Squat back down under control until the plates touch the floor.

Alternate which hand is in front, and which foot is forward, between sets to balance the rotational load. Keep the bar under the hips and the torso tall; do not twist. Use moderate loads; it is a squat pattern, not a max deadlift.

Wedge one end of a barbell in a landmine unit or a corner and load the other end. Face the anchor, lift the loaded end and hold the sleeve at chest height with both hands cupped over it, elbows tucked. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out, leaning slightly into the bar.
Squat down between the legs, keeping the bar against the chest and the torso upright, until the hips are below the knees. Drive up through mid-foot to stand tall, keeping the bar on the chest.

The angled bar path pushes you upright, which makes it a great teaching squat for beginners. Keep the elbows inside the knees at the bottom. Step the feet further from the anchor to increase forward lean.
Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the free end. Face the anchor and hold the sleeve with both hands at the chest, or with one hand at the shoulder. Stand tall with feet hip width.

Step one foot straight back about 60 to 90 cm and lower the back knee toward the floor until the front thigh is about parallel and the front knee is over the mid-foot. Drive through the front foot to return to standing. Complete all reps on one side.

Holding the bar on the side opposite the working leg is most common; same-side holding increases lateral trunk demand. Keep the torso tall and the hips square. Stop the back knee just above the floor.

Unrack a barbell onto the upper back. Stand about 60 to 90 cm in front of a knee-height bench and place the top of the rear foot (laces down) on it. Front foot flat and pointing forward, feet hip width apart laterally.

Brace and lower straight down until the back knee is just above the floor and the front thigh is near parallel, front knee travelling forward over the toes. Drive through the whole front foot to stand back up. Finish all reps then switch legs.

Balance is the limiter, so learn it with dumbbells first and set safety pins. A shorter stance and upright torso bias the quads; a longer stance and forward lean bias the glutes. Do not push off the rear foot.
Unrack a barbell onto the upper back. Take a split stance about one leg length long, front foot flat, back heel raised and on the ball of the foot, feet hip width apart laterally.

Without moving the feet, drop the back knee straight down until it is just above the floor and the front thigh is about parallel, then press up through the front foot. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
Keep the feet on separate tracks for balance. Torso tall, weight over the front mid-foot. Letting the front knee travel forward biases the quads; keep the back leg relaxed rather than pushing.

Load a safety squat bar on the upper traps in a power rack. Hold the bar handles, or let go and hold the rack uprights for balance, and take a split stance about one leg length long, feet hip width apart laterally.
Lower the back knee straight down toward the floor with the torso upright and front knee moving forward, then drive through the front foot to the top. Finish one side and switch.
Holding the rack lets you load heavier with less balance demand, making it a great quad builder. Keep the front heel planted. Control the eccentric and do not push off the back foot.
Unrack a barbell onto the upper back and stand tall with feet hip width, braced.

Step one leg forward about 60 to 90 cm, land heel first and lower until both knees are about 90 degrees, back knee just above the floor and front knee over the mid-foot. Push hard through the front foot to step back to the start. Alternate legs or complete one side.

Decelerating the forward step is the hardest part, so start light. Keep the front heel down and the torso upright. Step long enough to keep balance and keep the feet hip width apart, not on a tightrope.
Unrack a barbell onto the upper back and stand tall with feet hip width apart, braced.

Step one foot straight back about 60 to 90 cm onto the ball of the foot and lower the rear knee until it is just above the floor and the front thigh is near parallel. Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to bring the back foot forward to the start.
More knee-friendly and easier to balance than forward lunges because the front leg stays planted. Keep hips square and the torso tall. Leave hip-width between the feet to avoid a tightrope stance.
Unrack a barbell in a clean-grip front rack, bar on the front delts against the throat and elbows high. Stand tall with feet hip width.

Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm and lower the back knee to just above the floor while keeping the torso vertical and the front knee over the mid-foot. Drive through the front foot to return to the start.
The front load keeps the torso upright and emphasizes the quads more than a back-loaded lunge. Keep the elbows up so the bar does not roll. Expect lighter loads than with the bar on the back.
With a barbell on the upper back, stand at one end of a clear lane of at least 10 to 15 metres, feet hip width.

Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee to just above the floor with the front knee over the mid-foot. Drive up through the front foot and bring the back leg straight through into the next stride without pausing with the feet together. Continue for distance or reps.
Need a clear lane and safe way to dump the bar. Shorter strides with an upright torso bias the quads; longer strides bias the glutes. Do not let the torso fold forward under fatigue.
Press or jerk a barbell overhead from behind the neck with a snatch grip and lock the arms, bar over the back of the neck. Stand tall with ribs down, feet hip width.

Keeping the bar stacked over the shoulders and hips, step forward into a lunge and lower the back knee to just above the floor, then drive through the front foot into the next step. Continue alternating for distance.
Ribs down to avoid arching the lower back. Keep the bar from drifting forward and the arms locked. Scale with a single dumbbell, a plate or a PVC pipe; dump the bar forward if balance is lost.
Unrack a barbell onto the upper back and stand with feet together or hip width, toes pointing forward.

Take a wide step out to one side, about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, plant the foot and sit the hips back over that leg until the thigh is near parallel, keeping the trailing leg straight and both feet flat. Push off the bent leg to return to the start.
Chest up, bent knee tracking over the toes, trailing leg feeling a stretch in the inner thigh (adductors). Learn the range with bodyweight or a goblet weight before using the bar.
Place a sturdy box or bench, about knee height or so the working thigh is near parallel, in front of a rack. Unrack a barbell onto the upper back and stand facing the box.

Place one whole foot on the box and drive through it to stand fully on top, bringing the trailing foot up. Step down with the trailing leg under control, keeping the working foot on the box, and repeat on the same side.
Minimize push-off from the bottom leg; the top leg does the work. Keep the knee aligned over the foot. A lower box allows heavier loads; a taller box increases hip demand.

Set the Smith bar at upper-chest height and the safety stops just below your bottom position. Step under and place the bar on the upper traps, grip just outside the shoulders, and position the feet shoulder width, about 15 to 30 cm in front of the bar line, toes slightly out. Rotate the bar to unhook.

Brace and squat down along the fixed vertical path until the thighs reach parallel or below, keeping the back flat. Drive up through the whole foot to just short of hard lockout, then rotate the bar back onto the hooks.
Feet slightly forward lets the torso stay more upright and the knees travel naturally; feet further forward shifts toward the hack squat. Set the safeties every time. Keep heels down.

Set the Smith bar at shoulder height and safeties just below your bottom position. Rest it on the front delts against the throat with a clean grip or crossed arms, elbows high, feet hip to shoulder width directly under or slightly ahead of the bar.
Rotate to unhook, brace and squat straight down with an upright torso and knees forward to full depth, then drive straight up to just short of lockout.
Keep elbows high so the bar stays on the shoulders. The fixed path removes balance demands and lets you focus on the quads. Use the stops for safety.

Place the Smith bar on the upper traps and walk the feet 30 to 45 cm in front of the bar line, hip width or closer, so you lean back slightly into the bar. Set the safety stops just below your bottom position.
Unhook and squat down, letting the knees travel forward until the thighs pass parallel, with the torso staying upright along the bar line. Press up through the whole foot to just short of lockout.
Mimics a hack squat machine. Keep heels down and the lower back from rounding at the bottom. Constant-tension reps without locking out increase the quad stimulus.

Place the Smith bar on the upper traps and take a split stance about one leg length long, front foot flat and slightly in front of the bar line, back heel raised. Set the safeties just above the bottom position.
Unhook and lower the back knee straight down to just above the floor, front knee travelling slightly forward, then press through the front foot to rise. Complete all reps then switch legs.
The fixed bar removes most of the balance demand so you can load the quads. Find the front foot position where the front heel stays down at the bottom. Keep the torso tall.

Place a knee-height bench behind a Smith machine. Put the bar on the upper traps, rest the top of one foot on the bench and set the front foot slightly in front of the bar line so the shin can travel forward. Set safeties.
Unhook and lower straight down until the front thigh is near parallel and the back knee nears the floor, then drive back up through the front foot. Finish all reps on one side.
Adjust the front foot until the movement feels smooth and the heel stays down. Stay tall for quad focus. Do not push off the rear foot.
Place the Smith bar on the upper traps and stand with feet hip width directly under the bar. Set the safeties just above your bottom position.

Unhook and step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm, lowering the back knee toward the floor while the bar travels straight down, until the front thigh is about parallel. Drive through the front foot and step back to the start.
The bar path is vertical, so the front foot must stay under the bar for the knee to move naturally. Keep the step length consistent rep to rep. Stay tall.

Hold one dumbbell vertically with both palms cupped under the top head, or a kettlebell by the horns, against the sternum with elbows pointing down. Stand with heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees.

Brace and squat down between the legs, letting the elbows track inside the knees and the knees travel forward over the toes, until the thighs are below parallel. Drive through the mid-foot back to standing, keeping the weight tight to the chest.
Keep the weight touching the chest and the torso tall; the front load acts as a counterbalance. Use the elbows to gently push the knees out at the bottom. The best teaching squat for beginners.

Place the heels on a slant board, wedge or 2.5 to 5 cm plates, feet about hip width and toes forward or slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at the chest with both hands cupped under the top head.
Squat straight down with the knees travelling far past the toes and the torso upright until the hamstrings approach the calves. Pause briefly, then press back up through the whole foot to standing.

The heel lift reduces how far the ankles must bend (knees travelling over the toes), making this very quad dominant and kind to tight ankles. Use a 2 to 3 second lowering and a controlled bottom. Do not let the heels slip off the wedge.

Stand with the heels on a high wedge or slant board (about 5 to 10 cm), feet together or a few centimetres apart, toes forward. Hold dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip, or one goblet-style at the chest.

Lower slowly, about 3 seconds, with the knees driving straight forward well past the toes and the torso nearly vertical, until the hamstrings meet the calves. Stand back up while keeping tension on the quads, stopping just short of lockout for constant tension.

Very narrow stance plus heel elevation gives maximal knee flexion and quad loading with light weights. Keep the knees together and tracking over the toes. Use a slow eccentric rather than heavy loads.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip, arms long. Stand with heels hip to shoulder width, toes slightly out, shoulders back and down.

Brace and squat down, keeping the torso upright and the dumbbells hanging beside the outside of the feet, until the thighs reach parallel or the dumbbells approach the floor. Drive up through the whole foot to standing.
Grip can limit the load, so use straps for heavy sets. Keep the shoulders back and the chest up; do not let the dumbbells swing. Elevate the heels slightly for more depth and quad focus.

Clean or lift two dumbbells to the shoulders so one head of each rests on the front of the shoulder, neutral grip, elbows high and pointing forward. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace and squat down with an upright torso and knees travelling forward to full depth, then drive up through mid-foot to lockout, keeping the dumbbells on the shoulders throughout.
Keep elbows up and forward so the dumbbells do not slide off. Breathe and brace before each rep. A good front squat alternative when no barbell or rack is available.

Stand with a wide stance, about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, toes turned out about 30 to 45 degrees. Hold one dumbbell vertically by the top head with both hands, hanging at arm's length between the legs.

Keeping the torso upright, lower straight down, pushing the knees out in line with the toes, until the thighs are parallel or the dumbbell nears the floor. Drive back up through the whole foot and squeeze the glutes at the top.

Knees must follow the toes. Stand on two plates or low boxes to increase range without the dumbbell touching the floor. Wider stance increases inner-thigh (adductor) and glute involvement relative to a goblet squat.
Press or snatch one dumbbell overhead and lock the arm, biceps by the ear, wrist stacked over the shoulder. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out, free arm out to the side for balance.

Brace and squat to as deep as you can keep the weight stacked over the shoulder and mid-foot, torso upright. Stand back up without the arm bending or drifting forward. Complete all reps, then switch arms.
Keep eyes forward, ribs down and the shoulder actively pushing up. Start with a light weight; shoulder and thoracic mobility set the limit. Do equal reps per arm.

Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip. Stand about 60 to 90 cm in front of a knee-height bench and place the top of the rear foot on it, laces down. Front foot flat and pointing forward, feet hip width apart laterally.

Lower straight down until the front thigh is about parallel and the back knee is just above the floor, front knee travelling forward over the toes. Drive through the whole front foot back to the top. Finish one leg and switch.
A shorter stance and upright torso hit the quads; a longer stance and forward lean hit the glutes. Keep the front heel down. Do not push off the back foot; it is only for balance.
Hold dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip and take a split stance about one leg length long, front foot flat, back heel raised on the ball of the foot, feet hip width apart laterally.

Without moving the feet, lower the back knee straight down until it is just above the floor and the front thigh is about parallel, then press through the front foot to rise. Complete all reps on one side.
Torso tall, weight over the front mid-foot. Let the front knee move forward for quad focus. The natural first progression before Bulgarian split squats.
Place the front foot on a step, block or plates 5 to 10 cm high. Hold dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip and take a split stance about one leg length long, back heel raised.

Lower the back knee toward the floor, below the level of the front foot, letting the front knee move forward over the toes for a deep range. Drive back up through the whole front foot to the top. Finish one side and switch.
The elevation increases range of motion for both the front quad and glute and the rear hip flexor. Keep the torso upright. Start with bodyweight if hip flexors are tight.
Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, neutral grip, feet hip width.

Step one leg forward about 60 to 90 cm and lower until both knees are about 90 degrees, back knee just above the floor and front knee over the mid-foot. Push back powerfully off the front foot to return to standing. Alternate legs or complete one side.
The front knee may travel past the toes as long as the heel stays down. Keep the torso upright. Shorten the step if balance fails, and slow the landing.
Hold dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip and stand with feet hip width apart.

Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm onto the ball of the foot and lower until the rear knee is just above the floor and the front thigh is near parallel. Drive through the front foot to bring the rear foot back beside it. Alternate or complete one side.
Easier on the knees and to balance than forward lunges. Keep most of the weight on the front foot. Avoid a narrow tightrope stance; keep hips square.
Hold dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip and stand at one end of a clear lane of 10 to 20 metres.

Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee to just above the floor with the front knee over the mid-foot. Drive up and bring the back leg straight through into the next lunge without stopping with feet together. Continue for distance or reps.
Flow from rep to rep while keeping the chest up and the dumbbells still. Shorter strides target quads; longer strides target glutes. Use straps if grip fails first.
Hold one dumbbell at the chest goblet style, or one in each hand at the sides. Stand with feet together or hip width, toes pointing forward.

Step wide to one side, about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, sit the hips back and bend the stepping knee while the other leg stays straight. Lower until the thigh is near parallel, then push off the bent leg back to the start.
Keep both feet pointing forward and flat. Do not let the bent knee collapse inward. Builds side-to-side strength and inner-thigh (adductor) flexibility.
Hold dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip, or one goblet-style at the chest. Stand with feet hip width.

Step one leg back and diagonally behind the other, about 45 degrees, landing on the ball of the foot, and lower the back knee toward the floor until the front thigh is near parallel. Drive through the front foot to return.
Keep hips mostly square and the front knee in line with the toes; the crossing angle increases glute medius demand. Do not twist the spine. Reduce the crossing distance if the knee feels strained.
Stand on a 5 to 15 cm step or stacked plates holding dumbbells at your sides, feet hip width.

Step one foot back off the platform and lower the back knee toward the floor, which is below the front foot, gaining extra range for the front leg. Drive through the front foot to return to the platform.
Keep the front foot fully on the platform. The added depth increases stretch on the quads and glutes, so start light. Stay tall for more quad emphasis; lean forward slightly for more glutes.
Hold light dumbbells at the sides, or use no weight. Stand tall with feet hip width, imagining you are at the centre of a clock face.

With one leg, lunge forward to 12 o'clock and return, lunge laterally to 3 (or 9) o'clock and return, then reverse lunge to 6 o'clock and return. Complete the pattern, then repeat with the other leg. Each lunge lowers until the working thigh is near parallel.
Keep each lunge controlled and return fully before the next direction. Knee tracks over toes in every direction. Excellent as a warm-up and for field-sport movement prep.
Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, about knee height or lower so the working thigh is at or slightly above parallel when the foot is on it. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip.

Place one whole foot on the box and drive through the heel and mid-foot to stand fully on top, bringing the trailing foot up. Step back down slowly with the trailing leg, keeping the working foot on the box. Complete all reps on one side.
Do not bounce off the floor leg. Lower the box if the knee rises above the hip. Stay upright for quads; lean the torso slightly forward for more glutes.
Stand side-on to a box or step about mid-shin to knee height, with the near foot flat on top. Hold dumbbells at your sides with a neutral grip.
Drive through the top foot to stand on the box, bringing the outside foot up beside it or keeping it hovering. Lower slowly, about 3 seconds, back down to a light toe tap on the floor.
Keep the knee aligned over the second toe and avoid hip hiking. The slow eccentric builds knee control. Start with a lower box.
Stand side-on to a box about knee height or lower, holding dumbbells at your sides. Cross the far leg in front of the near leg and place that whole foot on the box.
Drive through the crossed-over foot to stand on top of the box, bringing the other foot up. Step back down with the trailing leg under control to the start position, crossing again for each rep.
Challenges hip stability in the frontal and transverse planes and loads the glute medius. Keep the trunk tall and avoid twisting. Start without load.
Hold a dumbbell vertically or a kettlebell by the horns at the chest. Stand in a very wide stance, about twice shoulder width, toes turned out 15 to 30 degrees.
Shift onto one leg and squat deep over it, heel down, while the other leg straightens with the heel on the floor and toes pointing up. Push back through the centre and lower to the other side.
