The weight acts as a counterbalance, helping depth and an upright torso. Keep the working heel down and the knee tracking over the toes. Go only as deep as you can control.

Clean two kettlebells into the rack position, bells resting on the outside of the forearms, handles at about collarbone height, wrists straight and elbows tucked against the ribs. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace and squat to full depth with an upright torso, elbows inside the knees, then drive back up to standing with the bells staying tight in the rack.
Keep wrists straight and elbows tucked. The front load punishes rounding. Breathe behind the brace, taking short breaths at the top only.
Clean one or two kettlebells into the rack position, wrists straight and elbows tucked. Stand tall with feet hip width.
Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm into a reverse lunge, lowering the rear knee to just above the floor with the front knee over the mid-foot, then drive through the front foot to return.
A single bell adds anti-lateral flexion work for the trunk. Keep the rack tight and the torso tall to focus on the quads.
Hold a kettlebell by the horns at the chest, elbows tucked. Take a split stance about one leg length long, front foot flat, back heel raised, feet hip width apart laterally.
Drop the back knee straight toward the floor until it is just above it and the front thigh is about parallel, then drive up through the front foot. Complete all reps then switch.
Keep elbows close and chest proud. A good option when grip limits dumbbell split squats. Drive through the front heel and mid-foot.
Stand with heels about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees, arms at the sides or extended forward.

Break at the hips and knees together, raising the arms forward for balance and keeping the chest up, until the hip crease is below the knees. Drive through the whole foot to stand tall, squeezing the glutes at the top.
Knees track over the toes and heels stay down. Use a box or bench as a depth target while learning. Speed up reps or add a pause or jump to progress.
Stand with heels about shoulder width, toes slightly out. Interlace the fingers lightly behind the head and pull the elbows back in line with the ears.
Keeping the elbows back and chest high, squat to full depth with knees tracking over the toes, then drive back up to standing.
The hand position removes arm counterbalance and trains upper back extension. Do not pull on the neck. Add a 2 to 3 second pause at the bottom to progress.

Stand in front of a box or bench with the backs of the heels about 15 cm from it, at a height that allows a controlled sit (start around knee height). Heels shoulder width, toes slightly out, arms forward.
Sit back and down slowly until you lightly touch or briefly sit on the box, then stand back up through the whole foot without rocking or using momentum.
Great for beginners, older adults and rehab. Lower the box over time. Avoid plopping down. Keep the knees tracking over the toes.
Stand with feet hip width, holding a post or rack upright with one hand for balance. Rise onto the balls of the feet.

Push the knees forward and lean back so the body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders, hips staying extended. Lower until the knees are well in front of the toes and the thighs are close to parallel to the floor, then extend the knees to return to standing.
Hips stay extended; do not sit back into a normal squat. Start with a partial range to build knee tolerance. Hold a plate on the chest to progress.
Stand on one leg with the other leg extended straight out in front, heel off the floor, arms reaching forward for balance.
Squat down on the standing leg to full depth, hamstring against calf, keeping the heel planted and the free leg off the floor. Drive up to standing without touching down.
Hold a TRX strap or post, or squat to a box, to build up. Knee tracks over the toes. The hip flexors and abdominals must hold the free leg up; a light counterweight helps.
Stand on one leg with the back of the heel about 15 cm in front of a box or bench, the other leg extended forward, arms out in front.
Lower under control on one leg until you lightly touch the box, then stand back up without rocking or letting the free foot touch the floor.
Lower the box as strength improves. Keep the knee in line with the toes. Hold a light weight forward as a counterbalance if balance is the limiter.
Stand on one leg holding a light plate or dumbbell, about 2.5 to 10 kg, at arm's length in front of the chest, the free leg extended forward.
Reach the weight forward as you squat down on one leg to full depth, then stand back up keeping the arms extended.
The weight shifts the centre of mass forward and makes balance easier. Keep the heel down. Reduce the weight as strength improves.
Stand on one leg and bend the other knee, holding that foot behind you with the same-side hand. Free arm forward. Place a pad where the back knee will land.
Lower on the standing leg, leaning slightly forward, until the back knee lightly touches the pad, then drive back up to standing.
Easier progressions let go of the foot or touch the back knee to a raised pad. Harder versions hold the foot with both hands. Knee tracks over the toes.
Stand on one leg with the other knee bent about 90 degrees so that foot is behind you, arms forward. Place a pad or folded mat where the back knee will land.
Hinge slightly at the hips and lower until the back knee lightly touches the pad, keeping the free foot off the floor, then drive up through the standing leg.
Differs from a shrimp squat because the back foot is not held. Hold small dumbbells forward as a counterbalance. Control the descent and keep the knee over the toes.
Stand in a very wide stance, about twice shoulder width, toes turned out slightly, hands clasped in front of the chest.

Shift the weight onto one leg and squat deeply over it, heel down, while the other leg straightens with the heel on the floor and toes pointing to the ceiling. Return through the centre and repeat on the other side.
Keep the working heel down and the chest up. Hold a support for balance initially. Builds hip and inner-thigh mobility as well as single-leg strength.
Stand about 60 to 90 cm in front of a knee-height bench and rest the top of one foot on it behind you, laces down. Front foot flat and forward. Hands on hips or in front.
Lower straight down until the back knee is just above the floor and the front thigh is about parallel, then drive up through the front foot.
Shift the weight onto the front leg. Find a stance where the front heel stays down. Add a pause, tempo or dumbbells to progress.
Take a split stance about one leg length long, feet hip width apart laterally, back heel raised, hands on hips.
Lower the back knee straight down until it nearly touches the floor and the front thigh is about parallel, then press through the front foot to the top, keeping the feet in place.
Upright torso and a vertical drop. Do not push from the back toes. The best entry-level single-leg exercise.
Take a split squat stance about one leg length long and lower until the back knee is about 2 to 5 cm off the floor and the front knee is around 90 degrees.
Hold the bottom position motionless for 20 to 60 seconds while breathing steadily, then stand and switch legs.
Used for knee rehab and tendon loading. Keep the front knee over the mid-foot. Add dumbbells or longer holds to progress.
Stand tall with feet hip width, hands on hips or by the sides, shoulders over hips and core braced.

Step one leg forward about 60 to 90 cm, land heel first and lower until both knees are around 90 degrees, front knee over the mid-foot and back knee hovering just above the floor. Push back off the front foot to return to the start. Alternate legs.

The front heel stays planted; the knee may travel slightly past the toes. Keep the torso upright and the feet hip width apart, not on a tightrope. Shorten the step if the back knee hits the floor hard.
Stand tall with feet hip width, hands on hips, core braced and weight centred over the mid-foot.

Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm onto the ball of the foot and lower the rear knee to just above the floor until the front thigh is about parallel and the front knee is over the mid-foot. Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to bring the feet back together. Alternate legs or finish one side.
Most of the weight stays on the front leg. Easier on the knees and easier to balance than forward lunges. Keep the hips square and the torso tall.
Stand at the start of a clear lane of 10 to 20 metres with feet hip width and hands on hips.

Step forward about 60 to 90 cm into a lunge, lowering the back knee to just above the floor with the front knee over the mid-foot. Drive up through the front foot and bring the back leg straight through into the next lunge without stopping with the feet together. Continue alternating for distance or reps.
Keep strides consistent and feet hip width apart. Maintain an upright posture; shorter strides bias the quads, longer strides the glutes. Add dumbbells or distance to progress.
Stand with feet together or hip width, toes pointing forward, hands clasped in front of the chest.

Take a big step to one side, about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, plant the foot and sit the hips back over it, bending that knee until the thigh is near parallel while the other leg stays straight. Push off the bent leg to return to the centre. Alternate sides or finish one side.
Both feet stay flat and pointing forward. Chest up and the bent knee over the toes; the straight leg should feel an inner-thigh (adductor) stretch. Go only as deep as the hips allow.
Stand with feet hip width, hands on hips or clasped at the chest, torso tall.

Step one leg diagonally back behind the other, about 45 degrees, landing on the ball of the foot, and lower the back knee toward the floor until the front thigh is near parallel. Drive through the front foot to return to the start. Alternate or finish one side.

Keep the front knee aligned with the toes and the hips mostly square; the angle increases glute medius demand. Avoid twisting through the lower back. Reduce the cross-behind distance if the knee hurts; hold dumbbells to progress.
Stand facing a stable box or bench of mid-shin to knee height, so the working thigh is at or just above parallel when the foot is on it. Hands on hips or arms relaxed.

Place one whole foot on the box and drive through the heel and mid-foot to stand fully on top, bringing the trailing foot up. Step down slowly with the trailing leg, keeping the working foot on the box. Alternate or finish one side.
Use the top leg, not a bounce off the bottom leg. Keep the knee over the foot and the torso tall for quad focus. Raise the box or add dumbbells to progress.
Stand on one leg on a step or box 10 to 20 cm high, facing forward, toes at the front edge. The free leg hovers straight off the front edge. Hands on hips.

Slowly bend the standing knee over 2 to 3 seconds, knee travelling forward over the toes, and lower until the free heel lightly touches the floor in front. Press back up to a straight leg without pushing off the heel.
Keep the pelvis level and the knee from caving inward over the second toe. A common knee rehab exercise and movement screen. Raise the step height or hold dumbbells to progress.
Stand side-on on one leg on a step or box 10 to 20 cm high, the other leg hanging straight off the side. Hands on hips.
Bend the standing knee and lower slowly, about 2 to 3 seconds, until the free heel taps the floor beside the step, then straighten the standing leg to return to the top.
Knee stays over the second toe and the hips stay level. Touch the heel lightly rather than resting weight on it. Raise the step or hold dumbbells to progress.

Stand side-on on a low step of 10 to 20 cm with the working foot flat on the step near its edge and the other foot hanging off the side. Hold a rail lightly for balance if needed; hands on hips otherwise.

Raise the heel of the working foot so you balance on the forefoot, then bend the knee forward well past the toes to lower the free heel toward the floor. Straighten the knee fully, then lower the working heel back to the step. Complete all reps, then switch sides.

The range is small and the heel-raised, knee-forward position biases the lower quad and the inner quad above the knee (vastus medialis) around the knee. Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the second toe. Named after physiotherapist Lennart Peterson; add a light dumbbell to progress.

Place a slant board or a small wedge (about 5 cm heel lift) on a low step of 10 to 20 cm. Stand side-on with the working foot on the wedge, heel raised, and the other leg hanging off the side. Hold a rail lightly or a dumbbell on the working side.

Bend the working knee so it travels forward over the toes and lower the free heel toward the floor, about a 2 to 3 second descent. Then extend the knee fully to return to the top without pushing off the floor with the free foot.

Lock the knee fully at the top; the last degrees of extension are the point. Move slowly and keep the hips level and the knee over the second toe. Popularized by Charles Poliquin for knee health and lower quad development.

Stand facing forward on one foot on a low step of 5 to 15 cm, ideally with the working heel raised on a small slant board. The free leg hangs straight just in front of the step. Hold a rail or wall lightly for balance.

Push the working knee forward far past the toes, keeping that heel raised, and lower the free leg until its heel lightly touches the floor in front of the step. Straighten the working knee to return to the top. Complete all reps, then switch legs.

Named after Ben Patrick (Knees Over Toes); it trains the quad and patellar tendon in deep forward knee travel. Start with a very low step and increase height gradually. Keep the pelvis level and control both directions.

Take a long split stance, front foot flat and pointing forward, rear leg nearly straight on the ball of the foot. Beginners elevate the front foot on a box or bench (15 to 45 cm) and hold a rail or dumbbells for support.

Shift forward and down so the front knee travels well past the toes until the hamstring covers the calf, keeping the front heel down, while the rear hip extends into a hip flexor stretch with the back knee off the floor. Drive back up through the whole front foot to the top.

Build range with an elevated front foot and hand support before adding load; lower the elevation over time. Full depth is the goal, but never force it into pain. Keep the torso tall and the back knee off the floor.
Kneel on a padded surface with knees hip width, shins flat and toes tucked or pointed. Keep a straight line from knees to shoulders with glutes squeezed, arms crossed or at the sides.
Lean back slowly as one unit, hips staying fully extended, as far as you can control (often 30 to 60 degrees). Then use the quads to pull back to upright.

Do not bend at the hips; that turns it into a stretch and offloads the quads. Anchor a band in front at chest height for assistance, or hold a plate on the chest to progress. A powerful eccentric builder for the quads, especially rectus femoris.
Loop a heavy resistance band or non-stretch strap around a fixed post or rack at knee height and behind both knees. Step back until the band is taut, feet hip width and toes forward.

Sit back into a squat with shins vertical, the band pulling the knees back, and the torso upright, lowering to about 70 to 90 degrees of knee flexion. Hold for 30 to 45 seconds or perform slow reps, then return to standing.

A classic patellar tendinopathy and anterior knee pain exercise, since the band lets you load the quads with vertical shins. Keep the weight through the heels and the torso upright. Five holds of 45 seconds is a common prescription.
Stand with the back flat against a wall and walk the feet out about 45 to 60 cm, feet hip width, toes forward.

Slide down until the knees and hips are both at about 90 degrees, thighs parallel to the floor and knees directly over the ankles. Hold for the prescribed time while breathing steadily, then slide back up.

Keep the back and head on the wall and the weight through the heels. Hold higher (about 45 to 60 degrees of knee bend) to scale. Hold a plate on the thighs or squeeze a ball between the knees to progress.
Set up in a wall sit with the back flat on the wall, thighs parallel to the floor, knees over the ankles and feet hip width.
Shift the weight onto one leg, then lift the other foot and extend that leg straight in front. Hold for the target time on the standing leg, then lower the foot and switch.
Keep the hips level and the knee of the working leg tracking over the second toe. Shorten the hold before compromising position. An advanced progression of the wall sit.
Place a swiss ball between the lower back and a wall. Walk the feet about 30 to 45 cm forward, hip to shoulder width, toes forward or slightly out.
Squat down while the ball rolls up the back until the thighs are about parallel, then press back to standing.
A great beginner or rehab squat. Find the foot position where the shins stay roughly vertical and the knees stay over the ankles at the bottom. Hold dumbbells at the sides to progress.
Place a BOSU dome side up (easier) or flat side up (harder). Step onto it with feet about shoulder width, centred over the middle, toes forward or slightly out.
Squat to about parallel while keeping the platform level and balanced, then stand back up.
Move slowly and keep the core tight. Use a spotter or nearby support. Not a heavy strength builder. Keep the knees tracking over the toes.

Use a furniture slider, Valslide or towel on a smooth floor (a paper plate on carpet). Stand with the ball of one foot on the slider and the other foot flat, feet hip width, hands on hips or holding dumbbells.

Slide the slider foot straight back while bending the planted knee, lowering until the front thigh is about parallel and the back knee is just above the floor. Pull the slider back under you by driving through the front foot to stand.

Keep most of the weight, about 80 to 90 percent, on the front leg so it does the work. The slide keeps constant tension and is gentler on the knees than a stepping lunge. Add dumbbells or a goblet weight to progress.
Use a slider or towel on a smooth floor. Stand with feet hip width, one foot on the slider and the other flat, toes forward, hands clasped at the chest or holding a goblet weight.

Slide the slider foot straight out to the side, keeping that leg straight, while sitting the hips back and bending the planted knee until the thigh is near parallel. Drive through the planted foot and pull the slider back in to stand.
The pull-in phase heavily loads the inner thigh (adductors) of the sliding leg. Keep the planted knee tracking over the toes and the heel down. Chest up; start with a short slide and increase range.
Pick up a sandbag and hug it tight against the chest, arms wrapped around it and hands gripping the opposite forearms or the fabric. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace and squat to full depth with the torso upright, squeezing the bag against the body so it does not slide, then drive through mid-foot to stand.

The front-loaded, shifting bag trains upper back, biceps and trunk bracing. Take short breaths at the top and keep the brace during the rep. The bag often lets you squat deeper and more upright than a barbell.
Lift a sandbag into the crook of the elbows, palms up or hands clasped, forearms vertical and the bag pulled tight to the stomach. Stand with heels shoulder width or slightly wider, toes out.
Brace and squat between the legs to full depth with the chest up and elbows passing inside the knees, then drive back up through mid-foot to standing.

Keep elbows tucked and squeeze the bag so it does not slide down the forearms. A forgiving way to learn the Zercher pattern and good for higher reps. Keep the heels planted and the upper back from rounding.
Clean and shoulder a sandbag onto one shoulder, holding it in place with both hands. Stand tall with feet hip width, ribs down.

Step back into a reverse lunge about 60 to 90 cm, lowering the rear knee to just above the floor with the front knee over the mid-foot. Drive through the front foot to return. Complete a set, then switch the bag to the other shoulder.
The offset load challenges lateral trunk stability; resist the bag pulling you sideways and keep hips square. Use both shoulder sides equally. A great asymmetric trunk and leg combination.

Attach straps or a rope to a loaded sled. Face the sled and hold the handles at arm's length, arms straight, and lean back slightly until the straps are taut. Sit into a quarter squat with the knees bent about 30 to 45 degrees.

Walk backward with short, quick steps, landing on the forefoot and pushing through the front of the foot while the knees extend from the bent position. Keep the knees bent and the chest up throughout. Continue for distance or time.

A low-stress, concentric-only quad exercise popular for knee health and rehab because there is no eccentric loading. Stay on the balls of the feet and keep the arms straight. Increase load or distance gradually.
Load a prowler or push sled and grip the upright poles, either high with arms extended or low with arms straight and the body leaned forward at about 45 degrees. Feet staggered, hips below shoulders.

Drive the sled forward with short, powerful steps through the balls of the feet, extending each knee fully while keeping the hips low and the back flat. Continue for the set distance, usually 10 to 40 metres.

Drive the knees forward and keep the arms locked so the legs do the work. Heavy loads build leg strength; light loads build conditioning. Like the backward drag, it has no eccentric, so soreness is low.

Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place the feet shoulder width in the middle of the platform, toes slightly out. Press the platform up and release the safety handles.

Lower the platform under control until the knees reach about 90 degrees or as deep as possible while the lower back stays flat on the pad. Press back up through the whole foot to just short of locking the knees.

Never let the hips curl off the seat at the bottom; that rounds the lower back under load. Keep knees tracking in line with the toes. Do not lock the knees hard, and re-engage the safeties at the end of the set.
Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place the feet low on the platform, about hip width, so the heels are near the bottom edge. Release the safety handles.
Lower the platform through a full range, letting the knees travel well forward over the toes, until the knees are deeply bent. Press back up through the whole foot to just short of lockout.
Low foot placement increases knee flexion and quad loading. Keep the heels on the platform; if they lift, move the feet up slightly. Expect less load than a standard placement.

Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place the feet high on the platform, shoulder width, toes slightly out, so the shins are closer to vertical at the bottom. Release the safety handles.
Lower the platform until the hips flex deeply while the lower back stays on the pad, then press through the heels and mid-foot to extend.
Biases the glutes and hamstrings over the quads by increasing hip flexion and reducing knee flexion. Do not let the pelvis tuck under at the bottom. Control the bottom position.

Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place the feet close together, about 10 to 15 cm apart, in the middle of the platform with the toes pointing forward. Release the safety handles.
Lower the platform keeping the knees tracking straight over the toes until they are about 90 degrees or the pelvis begins to tuck, then press back up to just short of lockout.
Narrow stance increases knee flexion and quad demand overall; it does not isolate the outer quad. Range is often limited by the hips meeting the torso; stop before the pelvis lifts off the pad.

Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place the feet wider than shoulder width, mid to high on the platform, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Release the safety handles.
Lower the sled with the knees tracking out over the toes until the knees reach about 90 degrees, then press back up through the heels and mid-foot.
Increases inner-thigh (adductor) and glute involvement. Keep knees in line with the toes and the hips and lower back flat on the pad. Avoid hard knee lockout.

Sit in a 45-degree leg press with the back and hips flat on the pad. Place one foot in the centre of the platform in line with the hip, toes slightly out, and rest the other foot on the frame or floor. Release the safety handles with both feet, then remove one.
Lower the sled with one leg to about 90 degrees of knee bend, then press back up to just short of lockout. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
Use well under half of the bilateral load. Keep the knee tracking over the toes and the hips flat on the seat; the pelvis tends to rotate. Great for correcting side to side imbalances.

Sit in a horizontal (selectorized) leg press with the back against the pad and the feet shoulder width in the middle of the platform. Adjust the seat so the knees start bent around 90 degrees or slightly more. Hold the side handles.
Press the platform away until the legs are nearly straight, then return slowly to the starting position without letting the weight stack touch down between reps.
Do not lock the knees. Keep the hips and lower back pressed into the seat. A simple, safe beginner machine.
Lie on your back in a vertical leg press with the hips directly under the platform and the feet shoulder width on it. Press up and unlock the safeties.
Lower the platform under control toward the chest until the knees are about 90 degrees or the tailbone starts to lift, then press it straight up to just short of lockout.
Range is limited by hip mobility; keep the tailbone on the pad. Always use the safety stops. Expect lighter loads than a 45-degree press.

Stand in a hack squat machine with the back flat against the pad and shoulders under the pads. Place the feet shoulder width in the middle of the platform, toes slightly out. Stand up to release the safety handles.
Lower under control until the thighs pass parallel, letting the knees travel forward over the toes, then press through the whole foot back to the top without hard lockout.
Keep the hips and back flat on the pad. A lower foot placement increases quad emphasis; a higher one shifts toward the glutes. Re-engage the safeties when finished.

Stand in the hack squat with the shoulders under the pads and the back on the pad. Place the feet wider than shoulder width on the platform with the toes turned out about 20 to 30 degrees. Release the safeties.
Squat down with the knees tracking over the toes until the thighs reach parallel or below, then drive up to standing.
The wide stance adds inner thighs and glutes. Push the knees out in line with the toes. Keep the heels and the back flat on the pad.
Set up in a hack squat machine with the back and shoulders against the pads. Place the feet about 10 to 15 cm apart, low to mid on the platform, toes forward. Release the safety handles.
Lower deeply with the knees travelling forward together over the toes, then press back up to just short of lockout.
Narrow stance increases knee flexion and quad demand; it does not isolate the outer quad. Heels stay down. Use moderate loads and a slow eccentric.
Face the hack squat machine with the chest against the back pad and the shoulders under the pads. Feet hip width on the platform, toes slightly out. Release the safety handles.
Push the hips back and squat down until the thighs are about parallel, then drive up through the heels to stand.
Shifts the emphasis toward the glutes and hamstrings compared with the normal hack squat. Keep the spine neutral; do not round the lower back at the bottom. Avoid excessive load.
Step into a pendulum squat machine with the back against the pad and the shoulders under the yokes. Place the feet on the angled platform about hip width, slightly forward. Release the safety.
Squat down as the pad swings through its arc until you reach maximal depth with the knees well forward, then drive up to just short of lockout.
Provides a deep quad stretch with low spinal load and a resistance curve that is hardest at the bottom. Keep tension on at the top. Control the bottom position.
Stand in a V-squat or leverage squat machine with the shoulders under the pads and the back against the pad. Feet shoulder width on the platform. Release the safety.
Squat down until the thighs reach parallel or below, keeping the back against the pad, then drive up to standing.
Foot placement changes emphasis: forward for glutes, under the hips for quads. Keep the heels down. Use the safeties.
Stand in the V-squat machine facing the back pad, chest against it, with the shoulder pads on the shoulders and the feet hip width on the platform. Release the safety.
Squat down, letting the knees travel forward, until the thighs reach parallel or below. Drive up to standing.
Facing the pad keeps the torso upright like a front squat, so the quads do most of the work. Keep the heels down and the chest on the pad. Use the safety stops.
Stand in the V-squat machine with the shoulders under the pads, legs straight, and the balls of the feet on the lower edge of the platform with the heels hanging off.
Lower the heels slowly for a full stretch, then rise onto the toes as high as possible and pause. Repeat.
Keep the knees straight but not locked. Pause in the stretch to stop bouncing. Push through the big toe.

Attach a hip belt to a belt squat machine, or hang plates from a dip belt while standing on two boxes or benches. The belt sits low on the hips. Stand with heels shoulder width, toes slightly out, holding the machine handles lightly for balance.
Squat down as deep as you can with an upright torso and knees tracking over the toes, then drive up through the whole foot to standing.
Loads the legs heavily without compressing the spine, so it suits athletes with back issues. Keep the belt low on the hips and the torso tall. Excellent for high-volume quad work.
Set up in a belt squat machine with the belt low on the hips and the knees bent about 20 to 30 degrees, holding the handles. Feet hip width.
March in place for time or steps, lifting alternate feet a few centimetres off the platform while keeping the hips level and the knee bend constant.
Builds leg endurance and hip stability with no spinal load. Stay tall and breathe steadily. Use moderate loads for 30 to 60 second sets.
Attach the belt around the hips and stand on the platform with the feet hip width and a soft bend in the knees.
Push the hips back, letting the torso tip forward with a flat back until the hamstrings are stretched. Drive the hips forward to stand tall.
Load comes from the hips, so the lower back is spared. Keep the shins nearly vertical and the spine neutral. Squeeze the glutes at the top.
Sit in a leg extension machine and adjust the back pad so the knees line up with the machine pivot. Set the ankle pad just above the feet, on the lower shins. Hold the handles and keep the hips down.
Extend the knees until the legs are straight and squeeze the quads for a moment, then lower under control back to the start, about 90 degrees of knee bend.
Avoid swinging or lifting the hips off the seat. A slow lowering increases effectiveness. Adjust the back pad so the knees line up with the pivot every time.
Set up in the leg extension machine with the knee aligned to the pivot and one ankle behind the pad, the other leg relaxed beside it. Hold the handles.
Extend the working knee to full straightness, squeeze for one second, then lower slowly. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
Fixes side to side imbalances. Keep the hips down. Use about half of the bilateral load or less.

Attach an ankle strap to the low pulley of a cable station and fasten it around the working ankle. Face away from the stack, holding a support with both hands. Lift the working thigh until it is roughly level with the hip or slightly lower, letting the knee bend about 90 degrees so the foot hangs behind and below the knee.

Keeping the thigh still, extend the knee against the cable until the leg is straight out in front, squeeze the quad for a second, then bend the knee slowly back to the start. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
The thigh must stay fixed so the knee does the work; if the hip swings, lighten the load. Use light to moderate loads and 12 to 20 reps. Useful when no leg extension machine is available.

Stand on a sissy squat bench or machine with the lower calves behind the rear pad and the front of the ankles or shins locked under the front pad, feet hip width. Hold the handle in front, or a plate on the chest for load.

Keeping the hips extended, push the knees forward and lean back so the body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Lower until the thighs are near parallel to the floor or the hamstrings approach the calves, then extend the knees to return.
The pads anchor the lower leg so you can go deeper and more safely than the freestanding sissy squat. Do not bend at the hips. Progress with a plate, a slower tempo or a pause at the bottom.
Hold a kettlebell by the horns at the chest, elbows tucked, or upside down by the bell. Stand tall with feet hip width, ribs down and trunk braced.

Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm onto the ball of the foot and lower the rear knee to just above the floor, front thigh near parallel and front knee over the mid-foot. Drive through the front foot to return to standing. Alternate legs or finish one side.
The front load keeps the torso upright and the quads working. Keep the elbows tight and most of the weight on the front foot. Progress with a heavier bell or a slower lowering.
Stand facing a stable box or bench about knee height, so the working thigh is near parallel with the foot on top. Place one whole foot on the box. Bodyweight, or hold dumbbells at the sides.

Drive through the top foot to stand fully on the box, and as you reach the top drive the trailing knee up to hip height with the toes pulled up, opposite arm swinging forward. Hold the single-leg balance for a moment, then step the trailing foot back down under control. Complete all reps on one side.
Finish the hip and knee extension of the stance leg before the knee drive. Do not push off the floor leg. Keep the pelvis level at the top; add dumbbells for strength or move faster for power.

Anchor a barbell in a landmine unit and load the free end. Face away from the anchor and rest the sleeve on one shoulder, or behind the neck on a pad or landmine handle, holding it with both hands. Walk the feet forward so you lean back into the bar, feet hip to shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Squat down with the torso leaning back along the bar and the knees travelling forward over the toes until the thighs pass parallel. Drive through the whole foot back to just short of lockout.

Mimics a hack squat machine using only a barbell and landmine; the lean-back position biases the quads. Keep heels down and the bar secure on the shoulder. Swap shoulders between sets if racking on one side.

Place a box or bench behind you at a height that puts the hip crease at or just below the knee when seated. Hold a dumbbell vertically or a kettlebell by the horns at the chest, heels shoulder width about 15 cm in front of the box, toes slightly out.

Brace and squat down under control until you lightly touch or sit on the box for a one-second pause without relaxing the trunk. Drive up through the mid-foot to standing, keeping the weight tight to the chest.
The box teaches consistent depth and controlled lowering, ideal for beginners and rehab. Do not crash or rock off the box. Lower the box over time to increase range.
Sit or lie on your back with the leg straight. A small rolled towel under the knee is optional.
Tighten the front of the thigh to press the back of the knee down into the floor or towel; the kneecap slides up toward the hip. Hold 5 to 10 seconds, then relax fully.
Pull the toes up toward you to help the squeeze. Keep breathing. A common first exercise after knee surgery or injury; follow your clinician's plan.
Lie on your back with both legs straight. A towel or strap around the foot can help pull, and a plastic bag or sock under the heel helps it glide.
Slide the heel toward the buttocks, bending the knee as far as is comfortable. Hold 2 to 5 seconds, then slide the heel back out until the leg is straight.
Keep the heel on the floor and the knee pointing at the ceiling. Move slowly; aim for a little more range over time, not pain.
Lie on your back with a foam roller or rolled towel (about 15 cm high) under the knee, so the knee is bent and the heel rests on the floor.
Keeping the back of the knee on the roll, straighten the knee fully to lift the heel. Hold 3 to 5 seconds with the thigh tight, then lower slowly.
Lock the knee out fully at the top. Pull the toes toward you. Add a light ankle weight once 3 sets of 10 to 15 are easy.
Sit tall on a chair or bench with the thighs supported and the knees bent about 90 degrees, feet off or just touching the floor. Hold the seat edge.
Straighten one knee until the leg is level with the floor, squeeze the thigh for 2 to 3 seconds, then lower slowly. Complete the reps, then switch legs.
Keep the thigh on the seat and sit upright, not leaning back. Pull the toes toward you. Add an ankle weight to progress.

Feet hip-width, toes out 10 to 15 degrees, bar over the midfoot. Grip just outside the shins, arms vertical (double overhand, hook or mixed). Bend the knees until the shins touch the bar; hips above knees and below shoulders, shoulders just ahead of the bar, spine neutral.

Breathe into the belly, brace and pull the slack out. Push the floor away so the bar rises vertically over the midfoot along the shins; hips and shoulders rise together until the bar passes the knees, then drive the hips forward to lock out. Lower by pushing the hips back first, then bend the knees once the bar clears them.

Lats tight so the bar never drifts forward. Faults: hips shooting up first, jerking the bar, leaning back at lockout. Scale with a block pull or trap bar if you cannot reach the floor with a neutral spine.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stance about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, toes out 30 to 45 degrees, bar over the midfoot touching the shins. Grip shoulder-width inside the legs, arms vertical. Knees out over the toes so the shins are near vertical; hips close to the bar, torso more upright than conventional.

Brace, pull the slack out and spread the floor so the knees track over the toes. Drive the legs and push the hips toward the bar as it breaks the floor; the bar rises vertically and knees and hips lock out almost together. Lower by sitting the hips back and down between the knees, knees out.
Wedge in: pull yourself down to the bar before it breaks. Do not let the knees cave or the hips rise first. Too wide a stance kills leg drive.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Unrack the bar from mid-thigh height. Overhand grip just outside the thighs (straps for heavy sets), feet hip-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees. Shoulders back, lats tight, ribs down.

Push the hips straight back while keeping the shins near vertical and the knee bend fixed; the bar slides down the thighs on a vertical line over the midfoot. Descend until the hamstrings reach a full stretch, typically mid-shin to just below the knee, with a neutral spine; the bar does not touch the floor between reps. Drive the hips forward to stand tall, finishing with glutes squeezed, without leaning back.
Hips back, not knees forward. The bar stays on the legs. End range is where the pelvis stops tilting or the spine starts to round, not the floor. Lower over 2 to 3 seconds.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Bar on the floor over the midfoot, feet hip-width. Hinge with the knees only slightly bent (about 10 to 15 degrees, less than an RDL) and grip shoulder-width overhand; hips sit higher than a conventional deadlift. If you cannot reach the bar with a neutral spine, raise it on blocks.

Brace and lift the bar from a dead stop mainly by extending the hips while the knees stay nearly straight, keeping the bar close to the legs. Stand tall with glutes squeezed. Lower along the same path by pushing the hips back, setting the bar down on the floor each rep (or just touching) before the next pull.
Unlike the RDL, each rep starts at the floor and the knees stay straighter. Never hyperextend the knees or round the lower back. Use lighter loads than an RDL and a 2 to 3 second lowering.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a trap (hex) bar. Step inside, feet hip-width, ankles in line with the handles. Bend hips and knees to grip the centre of each handle with a neutral grip, arms straight. Hips sit lower than a conventional pull, chest up, spine neutral. High handles shorten the range.

Brace and push the floor away, extending knees and hips together so the torso angle stays constant off the floor. Stand tall with glutes squeezed and shoulders down, not shrugged. Lower by pushing the hips back and bending the knees until the plates touch the floor, keeping the bar level.
Grip the handles in the middle or the bar tilts. Push, do not yank. More knee bend and a more upright torso make it more quad-dominant and easier on the lower back than a straight-bar pull.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand on a stable platform or plates 2.5 to 10 cm high (most use 2.5 to 5 cm) with the bar over the midfoot. Take your normal conventional or sumo stance and grip. The extra range means the hips start lower and the knees more bent; keep the shins against the bar and spine neutral.

Brace, pull the slack out and push the floor away, keeping the bar against the shins as it breaks from the lower start position. Keep the back angle constant until the bar passes the knees, then drive the hips through to lockout. Lower under control to the floor; reset each rep.

Builds strength and speed off the floor for lifters who are slow at the start. Use 10 to 20 percent less than your normal deadlift. Choose a deficit you can reach with a flat back; if the lower back rounds, reduce the height.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand on a 5 to 10 cm plate, block or low step holding a barbell (small-diameter plates, or 5 kg plates with blocks, let it travel lower) at the hips with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Feet hip-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulders back.

Push the hips back with fixed knees and slide the bar down the legs past the level of the feet, using the extra range for a deeper hamstring stretch. Reverse by driving the hips forward to stand tall, squeezing the glutes without leaning back.

Only use the added range if the pelvis keeps tilting and the spine stays neutral; most people gain little depth before rounding. Keep the bar touching the legs. Use 10 to 20 percent less load than a standard RDL and a 3 second lowering.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the plates (not the bar) on pulling blocks or stacked mats so the bar starts at the chosen height, commonly 5 to 10 cm, just below or just above the knee. Use your competition stance and grip. Hips start higher than a floor pull; shoulders slightly ahead of the bar, lats tight.

Brace, pull the slack out and drive the bar up the thighs, extending the hips to lockout. Plate-on-block contact keeps the bar flex and feel close to a floor pull. Lower under control and settle the plates on the blocks, rebracing each rep.

Overloads the top half of the pull and lockout. Keep the same back angle you would have at that bar height in a full pull. Do not hitch or ramp the bar up the thighs; finish with the hips, not by leaning back.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the safety pins of a power rack so the bar rests at the chosen height, usually just below or at the knee (above the knee for a lockout bias). Stand with the bar touching the legs, feet hip-width and grip just outside the thighs, overhand or mixed. Hinge to the bar with the hips higher than in a floor pull, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar.

Brace and push the floor away, driving the hips forward to stand tall with the bar dragging up the thighs. Lock out knees and hips together with shoulders back and down. Lower under control to the pins and let the bar settle before the next rep.

Do not bounce the bar off the pins. Squeeze the lats to keep the bar on the legs. Avoid leaning back or shrugging at the top. Unlike a block pull, the bar (not the plates) rests on steel, so it feels stiffer.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Feet hip-width, bar over the midfoot. Take a wide snatch grip, set so the bar would sit in the hip crease when standing with straight arms (roughly collar to collar on many bars), hook grip or straps. The wide grip lowers the hips and increases knee bend; keep the chest up, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar and shins close.

Brace and push through the whole foot, keeping the back angle constant until the bar passes the knees, then extend the hips to stand tall. The bar stays in contact with the legs and finishes in the hip crease. Lower under control along the same path.

Upper back must stay set against the long lever; do not let the shoulders round forward. Use straps if grip limits the set. Expect to use 10 to 20 percent less than a conventional deadlift. Builds the first pull for the snatch and upper-back strength.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Unrack the bar from mid-thigh height with a wide snatch grip so it sits in the hip crease when standing tall (straps help). Feet hip-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulder blades retracted and the upper back set.

Push the hips back with the knee bend fixed and slide the bar down the thighs on a vertical path until the hamstrings are fully stretched, about mid-shin for most. Keep the upper back tight against the long lever arms. Drive the hips through to stand tall.

The wide grip lowers the bar for more range and makes the upper back and traps work hard to hold position. Keep the bar against the legs. Stop where the pelvis stops rotating; do not round to reach lower.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Set up exactly as for your competition deadlift, conventional or sumo: bar over the midfoot, usual grip, shins on the bar, slack pulled out and a full brace.

Break the bar from the floor and stop it at a set point, typically 2 to 5 cm off the floor or just below the knee, holding for 1 to 3 seconds without moving. Keep the hips, shoulders and bar fixed during the pause, then finish the pull to full lockout. Lower under control; each rep starts from a dead stop.

Hold the same back angle and bar position you would have at that point in a normal pull; the bar must not drift away from the legs. Breathe only at the top. Typical loads are 60 to 75 percent of 1RM. Builds positional strength and fixes hips shooting up.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Set up as for a conventional (or clean-grip) deadlift with feet hip-width, bar over the midfoot, shins touching the bar, lats tight and a firm brace.

Push the floor away and raise the bar to just above the knee, keeping the shoulders over or slightly in front of the bar and the back angle constant. Hold this position for 1 to 3 seconds, then lower the bar back to the floor without locking out. Reset each rep.

Hips must not rise faster than the shoulders. Shoulders stay ahead of the bar; the bar stays on the shins and lower thigh. Builds the floor-to-knee position for deadlifts and the first pull of the clean; keep loads moderate (about 60 to 80 percent of deadlift).
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Hang chains from the sleeves (directly or via a lead chain) so most links pile on the floor when the bar is down and lift off as you stand; resistance rises toward lockout. Set the chain weight to roughly 10 to 25 percent of bar weight, equal on both sides. Use your normal deadlift stance and grip.

Brace and pull as fast as possible while staying in position, accelerating through the knee as more chain unloads from the floor. Finish hard at lockout where the load is heaviest. Lower under control to the floor and reset; often programmed as speed singles with 30 to 60 seconds' rest.
Use for speed or lockout work, not grinding maxes. Keep reps crisp and explosive; drop the weight if bar speed fades. Check the chains are hung evenly and do not swing into the shins.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses resistance bands. Anchor a band on each side under a band platform, heavy dumbbells or the bar's own plates when the band is choked over the sleeve, so it pulls the bar down and tension rises as you stand. Use equal bands on both sides; band tension at lockout is typically 15 to 30 percent of bar weight. Take your normal deadlift stance and grip.

Brace and pull as fast as possible, keeping the bar on the legs, and accelerate through the knees into a hard lockout against peak band tension. The bands also pull the bar down, so lower it under control rather than letting it crash, and reset on the floor each rep.

Bands overspeed the eccentric, so stay tight on the way down. Keep the bar path vertical; bands anchored too far forward pull the bar away from you. Best for speed singles and doubles or lockout work.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand beside a lightly loaded barbell with the bar running front to back alongside one foot. Find the exact midpoint of the bar (mark it with chalk) and grip it there with one hand, neutral grip, thumb wrapped. Feet hip-width, hips back, knees bent, chest up and shoulders level.

Brace the trunk and stand up, extending hips and knees together while the bar stays at your side and stays horizontal. Finish tall with shoulders and hips level. Lower the bar back to the floor with the same control, then complete all reps before switching sides.

Do not lean toward or away from the bar; resist side bending. Grip dead centre or the bar will tip front to back. A heavy grip and anti-lateral-flexion challenge; start with an empty or lightly loaded bar.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet hip-width and a dumbbell (or kettlebell) on the floor beside the outside of one foot. Hinge and bend the knees to grip the handle with a neutral grip, arm straight, shoulders level and square, chest up and spine neutral.

Brace and stand up, extending hips and knees together while the weight stays at your side and the torso stays upright with no lean. Pause tall with shoulders and hips level. Lower the weight back to the floor beside the foot along the same path. Complete all reps, then switch sides.

Do not let the loaded side drop or the free side hike; keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis. Pull the working shoulder down and back. A great anti-lateral-flexion core and grip exercise; progress load before range.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet hip-width and parallel, holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs with an overhand grip (or at the sides with a neutral grip). Knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulders back, lats tight.

Push the hips straight back with the knee angle fixed, letting the dumbbells slide down the front of the thighs and shins until the hamstrings are fully stretched, usually about mid-shin. Keep the spine neutral. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes without leaning back.
Dumbbells stay in contact with or very close to the legs. Do not bend the knees further as you descend or it becomes a squat. Lower over 2 to 3 seconds and stop where the back would round.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet hip-width and a dumbbell on the floor just outside each foot (neutral grip) or in front of the shins (overhand). Push the hips back and bend the knees to grip them with straight arms, hips above the knees, chest up and spine neutral.

Brace and push the floor away, extending hips and knees together so the dumbbells travel straight up beside or in front of the legs. Stand tall with glutes squeezed. Lower by pushing the hips back and bending the knees until the dumbbells touch the floor, then repeat.

Arms are hooks: drive with the legs and hips, not the arms. Keep the back flat at the bottom. Dumbbells at the sides make it more upright and easier on the back. A good way to teach the deadlift before using a barbell.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand tall with feet hip-width, holding dumbbells in front of the thighs with an overhand grip. Unlock the knees only slightly, about 10 degrees, and keep that angle throughout.

Hinge from the hips with nearly straight knees, lowering the dumbbells toward the floor or tops of the feet while the spine stays neutral. Pause briefly at the bottom of your range, then drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes.

Straighter knees and greater range than a dumbbell RDL; the dumbbells may travel slightly in front of the shins. Stop before the lower back rounds. Move slowly with lighter loads; never lock or hyperextend the knees.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet about 1.5 times shoulder width, toes out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold one dumbbell vertically by the top head with both hands, arms straight, letting it hang between the legs. Chest up, spine neutral.

Push the hips back and bend the knees out over the toes to lower the dumbbell until it touches the floor or a low step between the feet, keeping the torso upright. Drive through the whole foot and push the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes.
Knees track over the toes; do not let them cave. The dumbbell hangs straight down under the shoulders, close to the body. Stand on two plates to add range if the bell touches too early.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand on one leg with the standing knee unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees. Hold a dumbbell in the hand opposite the standing leg (more side-glute demand) or one in each hand. Hips and shoulders square to the floor, lats tight.

Hinge at the standing hip, pushing it back as the torso tips forward and the free leg extends straight behind in line with the torso, heel driving back. Lower until the torso is near parallel or the standing hamstring is fully stretched, the dumbbell close to the standing shin. Drive the standing hip forward to return upright and set the free foot down only if needed.
Keep the hips level; do not let the free hip open toward the ceiling (toes of the back foot point down). Reach the back heel away. Hold a wall or dowel with the free hand to scale balance.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Place a kettlebell on the floor just inside the standing foot, or hold it in the hand opposite the standing leg. Stand on one leg with the knee unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, hips and shoulders square, lats tight.

Hinge at the standing hip as the free leg extends behind in line with the torso, lowering the bell straight down toward the floor beside the standing foot until the torso is near parallel. If starting from the floor, grip the handle there. Drive the standing hip forward to stand tall, finishing with the glute squeezed.
The bell travels straight down close to the standing leg. Hips and shoulders stay square; back toes point down. Pause briefly at the bottom to own balance; scale by tapping the back toe down.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand on one leg with the knee unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, foot gripping the floor. Arms at the sides or reaching forward, gaze on the floor a couple of metres ahead, spine neutral.

Hinge at the standing hip, reaching the hands toward the floor as the free leg rises behind, until the body forms a straight line from head to raised heel near parallel to the floor. Pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then squeeze the standing glute to drive the hip forward and return upright without setting the free foot down.
Hips stay square; back toes point down. Move slowly and keep the standing knee from collapsing inward. Touch a wall or hold a dowel to scale; close the eyes or add a pause to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with the working foot flat and the other foot placed so its toes are level with the working heel, about 15 cm to the side, heel up. Hold dumbbells (or a barbell) at the hips. Put 80 to 90 percent of your weight on the working leg; the back foot is a kickstand for balance only. Working knee unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees.

Push the hips back over the working leg with the knee angle fixed, lowering the weights along the front of the working thigh and shin until the hamstring is fully stretched. Drive the working hip forward to stand. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Do not push off the back foot. Hips stay square and level. Bridges the gap between bilateral RDLs and single-leg RDLs, allowing heavier unilateral loading with less balance demand.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a landmine-anchored barbell. Stand beside the loaded end of the bar, perpendicular to it, and hold the end of the sleeve in the hand opposite the working leg with a neutral grip. Stand on the leg farther from the bar with the knee unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, hips square.

Hinge at the standing hip as the free leg extends behind you, letting the bar end travel down its arc toward the floor beside the standing foot until the torso is near parallel. Drive the standing hip forward to return upright. Complete all reps, then switch sides and hands.
The fixed arc reduces balance demand, so you can load it more than a dumbbell version. Keep the hips square; do not let the loaded shoulder drop or rotate toward the bar.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width and a kettlebell on the floor between the feet, handle in line with the ankle bones or midfoot. Push the hips back and bend the knees just enough to grip the handle with both hands, arms straight, shoulders slightly in front of the bell, spine neutral.

Brace, pack the lats and push the floor away to stand tall, squeezing the glutes and finishing with the hips fully extended. Return by pushing the hips back first and letting the knees bend until the bell touches the floor softly between the feet.

Arms stay long; pull the shoulders down away from the ears. The bell travels straight up and down between the heels. A foundational hinge before learning swings; progress to single-arm or heavier bells.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet about 1.5 times shoulder width, toes out 30 to 45 degrees, kettlebell centred between the feet under the hips. Push the hips back and down to grip the handle with both hands, arms straight, knees out over the toes, chest up.

Brace and drive through the whole foot, pushing the knees out, to stand tall and squeeze the glutes. Lower by sitting the hips back and down between the knees until the bell touches the floor, keeping the torso upright.
Knees track over the toes; do not let them cave. Torso stays more upright than a hip-width kettlebell deadlift. Stand on two plates or boxes to increase range once the bell touches too early.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand tall with feet hip-width, holding one kettlebell by the horns with both hands, or one in each hand, against the front of the thighs. Knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulders back and lats tight.

Push the hips back with the knee angle fixed and let the bells slide down the front of the legs until the hamstrings are fully stretched, about mid-shin. Keep the spine neutral. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes; the bells do not touch the floor between reps.
Do not let the bells pull the shoulders forward; keep the lats engaged. Lower over 2 to 3 seconds. Stop where the spine would round rather than chasing the floor.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Attach a straight bar or rope to a low pulley set at the lowest position. Face the stack, grip the bar overhand at shoulder width and step back 60 to 90 cm so the cable is taut and angled toward the stack. Feet hip-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, standing tall.

Push the hips back with fixed knees, letting the bar travel down the front of the legs toward the stack until the hamstrings are fully stretched. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes, keeping the arms straight.
The cable pulls forward, so sit back slightly to stay balanced over the midfoot. Constant tension suits lighter, higher-rep work. Keep the spine neutral and do not let the stack drag you forward.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a long loop resistance band. Stand on the middle of the band with feet hip-width and hold the top of the loop in each hand at hip height with arms straight (or loop it around the back of the neck for more tension). Knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, spine neutral.

Push the hips back with fixed knees, lowering the hands down the front of the legs to about mid-shin until the hamstrings are fully stretched. Drive the hips forward to stand tall against the band, squeezing the glutes hard at lockout.

Band tension is lowest at the bottom and highest at lockout, so finish every rep. Keep the back neutral and the band close to the legs. Use a thicker band or a wider foot stance on the band to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the Smith bar at about mid-thigh height and the safety stops just above shin height. Stand with the bar touching the thighs and the feet slightly back under it so the vertical bar path stays against the legs, feet hip-width. Grip overhand at shoulder width and rotate the hooks to unrack.

Push the hips back with the knees unlocked 15 to 20 degrees and fixed, letting the bar slide down the thighs until the hamstrings are fully stretched, about mid-shin. Keep the spine neutral. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes.

Because the bar path is fixed, foot position decides whether the bar stays on the legs; adjust it before loading. Do not round to reach the safeties. Good for high-rep hamstring work without balance demands.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Bar on the floor; stand with feet shoulder-width or wider, toes slightly out. Squat down deeply with the knees outside the elbows and work the bar into the crook of both elbows, forearms vertical and hands clasped or fists up. Torso as upright as possible; this needs good hip and ankle mobility. Lifters who cannot reach the floor start from blocks or low pins.

Brace hard and stand up, driving through the whole foot until hips and knees lock out, holding the bar tight to the body with elbows up. Lower back to the floor or blocks under control by sitting down between the knees.

Keep the upper back tight and the bar tucked into the elbows. Use a pad or sleeves for comfort. Very high trunk demand: some lumbar flexion is common in experienced strongmen, but beginners should build gradually from blocks.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand tall holding a barbell at the hips with a shoulder-width overhand grip, feet hip-width to slightly wider. Use a light load, about 30 to 40 percent of your deadlift. Knees unlocked, chest up and lower back slightly arched.

Push the hips back and lower the bar quickly to just below the knees without changing the knee angle much, then reverse explosively at the bottom, driving the hips forward to lockout and squeezing the glutes. Perform rapid, rhythmic reps with no pause at either end.
Named after Westside lifter Matt Dimel. Speed and the stretch reflex are the point; this is not a slow RDL. Keep the back neutral throughout. Sets of 15 to 20 reps are typical.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a strongman axle (about 5 cm diameter, non-revolving sleeves). Set up like a conventional deadlift: feet hip-width, bar over the midfoot, double overhand grip just outside the shins (mixed or straps if the event allows). Shins close, hips above knees, lats tight.

Brace and push the floor away, keeping the bar close; the axle has little whip, so it breaks the floor immediately. Stand to full lockout with knees and hips extended and shoulders back. Lower under control; in competition, straps may be allowed or forbidden.
Grip is the main limiter: the thick handle and non-rotating sleeves punish an open hand, so squeeze hard and chalk up. Do not jerk the bar. Without straps, it doubles as a grip strength exercise.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand over a sandbag with feet hip- to shoulder-width and the bag between the feet. Hinge and bend the knees to grip the side handles with a neutral grip, or pinch the fabric with both hands at the ends of the bag. Chest up, spine neutral, shoulders slightly in front of the bag.

Brace and stand up, keeping the bag close to the shins and thighs, and finish tall with the glutes squeezed. Lower by pushing the hips back and bending the knees to place the bag down under control rather than dropping it.
The shifting sand challenges the trunk and grip. Keep the back flat at the pick-up. Grip the fabric with full hands, not fingertips. Use the bag lengthways between the feet so it does not swing.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a landmine-anchored barbell. Straddle the bar facing the loaded end, feet hip-width, and hold the sleeve end with both hands interlaced (or use a V-handle) at hip height, arms straight. Knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, shoulders back.
Push the hips back with fixed knees, letting the bar end travel down its arc between the legs until the hamstrings are fully stretched. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes.

The arc keeps the load close to your centre of mass and is easy for beginners. Keep the back flat; do not let the bar pull you forward onto the toes. Facing away from the anchor with the bar between the legs is the alternative setup.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set up as for a clean: feet hip-width, toes out slightly, bar over the balls of the feet, hook grip about a fist-width outside the legs. Hips slightly higher than the knees, shoulders over or slightly in front of the bar, arms straight and rotated so the elbows point to the sides, chest up and back arched.

Push through the whole foot to lift the bar, keeping the back angle constant until the bar passes the knees as the knees move back. Then bring the torso upright and sweep the bar into the upper thighs while extending to standing, staying flat-footed with no explosive extension. Lower under control along the same path.

Shoulders stay over the bar past the knee; do not let the hips rise first. Weight shifts from midfoot toward the heel as the bar rises. Rehearses the first pull of the clean at 90 to 120 percent of clean max.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Unrack the bar onto the upper back in a high- or low-bar back squat position, hands just outside the shoulders. Feet hip- to shoulder-width, toes slightly out, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees. Upper back tight, big breath and brace.

Push the hips straight back and tip the torso forward with a neutral spine and fixed knee angle until the torso is near parallel to the floor or the hamstrings reach a full stretch, whichever comes first. Drive the hips forward to return to standing, keeping the bar over the midfoot.
Keep the knee angle fixed; bending the knees turns it into a squat. Stop before the lower back rounds. Start light, around 30 to 50 percent of squat; the long lever makes small loads heavy.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit on the end of a flat bench (or straddle it) with a barbell on the upper back, set from a rack placed at seated shoulder height. Feet planted wide and flat, knees bent about 90 degrees, toes out. Brace and set a neutral spine.

Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back, letting the torso travel between the thighs until the chest nears the bench or the hips stop flexing. Raise the torso back to upright by extending the hips and back.

With the knees bent the hamstrings are slack, so the lower back and glutes do more work than in a standing good morning. Move from the hips, not by rounding the spine. Keep loads light to moderate; spread the knees to allow depth.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a safety squat bar. Unrack it with the yoke pad on the upper back and hands on the front handles, elbows down. Feet hip- to shoulder-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, brace hard.

Push the hips back with a flat spine and fixed knee angle until the torso is near parallel or the hamstrings are fully stretched, resisting the cambered bar as it tries to pull you forward and round the upper back. Drive the hips through to stand tall.

Push the handles down and forward to keep the bar seated. The forward-cambered load makes the upper back work harder than with a straight bar. Useful when shoulder mobility limits a straight-bar back position.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a long loop resistance band. Stand on the band with feet hip-width, then loop the other end behind the neck so it rests across the upper back (traps), holding it in place with the hands at the shoulders. Knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, spine neutral.

Push the hips back and hinge until the torso is near parallel or the hamstrings are fully stretched; band tension is lowest here. Drive the hips forward to stand tall against the band, squeezing the glutes at lockout.

Tension peaks at lockout, so finish every rep with the glutes. Keep the back flat and the neck neutral; do not let the band pull the head forward. Ideal for warm-ups and high-rep posterior chain work.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Unrack a barbell from pins set at about hip height, holding it in the crook of the elbows with forearms vertical and hands clasped. Feet hip- to shoulder-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees, bar pulled tight to the torso, brace hard.

Push the hips back and tip the torso forward with a flat spine and fixed knee angle, lowering as far as the hamstrings allow while the bar stays tight to the body. Drive the hips through to stand tall.

The load sits in front, so the trunk resists flexion harder than in a back-loaded good morning, and the range is usually shorter. Keep the elbows up and bar tight. Use a pad or sleeves for the elbows.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the Smith bar at upper-chest height and the safety stops at about the height the bar reaches with the torso near parallel. Step under the bar, place it on the upper back as for a back squat and unrack with the feet slightly in front of the bar line, hip-width, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees.
Push the hips back and lower the torso toward parallel with a flat back; the vertical bar path means the hips travel back while the bar stays over the midfoot. Drive the hips forward to stand tall.

Set the safety stops before loading. The fixed path may not match your natural groove, so go light and find a foot position that lets you hinge without the knees bending further. Keep the knee bend constant.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet hip-width, toes forward, knees unlocked about 15 to 20 degrees. Place the hands lightly behind the head (prisoner position) with elbows wide, or cross the arms on the chest. Ribs down, spine neutral.

Push the hips straight back and hinge forward with a flat back until the torso is near parallel or the hamstrings reach a full stretch. Squeeze the glutes and drive the hips forward to return to standing.
Hold a dowel along the spine touching the head, upper back and sacrum to learn a neutral hinge. Do not pull on the neck. Move slowly; an ideal warm-up for deadlift days.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the pad of a 45-degree hyperextension bench so its top edge sits just below the hip crease, letting the hips flex freely. Lock the heels under the ankle rollers, feet hip-width and parallel. Body in a straight line from head to heels; cross the arms over the chest or hold a plate against it.

Lower the torso by flexing at the hips (and allowing the spine to move only as programmed) until a hamstring stretch is felt or the torso is near vertical. Raise back up by extending the hips and back until the body is again a straight line from head to heels, then pause.

Do not hyperextend past a straight line at the top. A neutral spine works hips and back extensors; a rounded upper back with toes out biases the glutes. Add load by holding a plate or dumbbell at the chest once 15 to 20 reps are easy.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

On a 45-degree hyperextension bench, set the pad lower so its top edge sits just below the hip crease and the hips can flex freely. Feet turned out about 30 to 45 degrees and pressed into the footplate. Tuck the chin and round the upper back slightly, arms crossed or holding a weight.

Hinge down until the hips are fully flexed, keeping the spine rounded and still. Drive the hips into the pad by squeezing the glutes to rise until the body is straight, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly.
The fixed rounded spine and turned-out feet keep the lower back out of it so the hips do the work. Push the feet out against the footplate. Hold a plate or dumbbell to load.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set up on a 45-degree back extension bench with the pad just below the hip crease and only one foot anchored under the roller. The free leg hangs bent or rests behind. Body straight, arms crossed on the chest.
Hinge down over the pad, flexing the hip of the anchored leg, then extend that hip to lift the torso back to a straight line. Pause at the top. Complete reps and switch legs.
Doubles the load per side without adding weight. Keep the pelvis square; do not twist toward the free leg. Lower slowly to own the stretch; add a light dumbbell once bodyweight is easy.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down with the hips and lower belly on a stability ball (55 to 65 cm for most), legs straight, feet wider than hip-width with the toes on the floor or braced against a wall. Hands by the temples or crossed on the chest.
Round forward over the ball, then lift the chest by extending the back and hips until the body forms a straight line from head to heels. Pause, then lower with control.
Do not overextend past straight. Wider feet or bracing against a wall make balance easier. Squeeze the glutes at the top; hold a plate at the chest to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit on the floor with the bottom edge of the shoulder blades against a bench 35 to 45 cm high, placed so it cannot slide. Roll a padded barbell over the legs into the hip crease. Feet flat, hip- to shoulder-width, toes slightly out, positioned so the shins are vertical at the top. Hold the bar just outside the hips.

Brace, tuck the chin and drive through the heels and midfoot to lift the hips; the bench acts as a pivot under the shoulder blades. Finish with the torso parallel to the floor, hips fully extended and knees at about 90 degrees. Squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower until the bar is a few centimetres from the floor.

Keep the ribs down and the pelvis tucked slightly at the top; do not finish by arching the lower back. Eyes look forward, not at the ceiling. Feet too far out bias the hamstrings, too close bias the quads.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit with the bottom edge of the shoulder blades against a stable bench and lay one dumbbell horizontally across the hip crease, holding each end. Feet flat, hip- to shoulder-width, set so the shins are vertical at the top.

Tuck the chin and drive through the heels to raise the hips until the torso is parallel to the floor and the hips are fully extended. Squeeze the glutes for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower until the hips are just above the floor.
Hold the dumbbell firmly so it does not roll toward the ribs; a pad or folded mat helps. Ribs down, no lumbar arch at the top. Dumbbell loads are limited, so use pauses, slow lowering or higher reps.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit with the bottom of the shoulder blades against a stable bench. Plant one foot flat under the knee, about mid-line of the body, and lift the other leg with the knee pulled toward the chest (or held straight). Arms out along the bench for balance.

Tuck the chin and drive through the heel of the planted foot to raise the hips until the torso is parallel to the floor and the pelvis is level. Squeeze the glute for 1 second, then lower under control until the hip is just above the floor. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Keep the pelvis level; do not let the free hip drop or rotate. Push through the heel, not the toes. Load with a dumbbell held on the working hip once 15 to 20 reps are easy.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in a hip thrust (glute drive) machine with the back pad just below the shoulder blades and the hip pad or belt across the hip crease. Feet flat on the platform, hip- to shoulder-width, set so the shins are vertical at the top. Hold the handles.

Tuck the chin and drive through the heels to lift the pad until the hips are fully extended and the torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower until the weight nearly touches, keeping tension.
Same cues as a barbell thrust: chin tucked, ribs down, no lumbar arch at the top. Adjust foot position for glute focus. Faster setup than a barbell and comfortable for heavy, high-rep sets.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Sit in the hip thrust machine with the upper back on the pad and the belt or pad across the hips. Plant one foot under the knee and lift the other foot off the platform.
Drive through the heel to lift the hips until the body is straight from shoulders to knee, squeeze the glute, then lower under control. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Tuck the chin and keep the ribs down. Keep the hips level; do not let the free side drop. Use lighter weight than on two legs.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Place a bench perpendicular to the Smith machine so your shoulder blades rest on its edge with the hips under the bar. Set the bar at hip height and the safeties just below the bottom position. Pad the bar, roll under it into the hip crease and rotate the hooks to unrack. Feet flat, shins vertical at the top.

Tuck the chin and drive through the heels to lift the bar until the torso is parallel to the floor and the hips are fully extended. Squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower under control to just above the safeties.

The vertical bar path stabilises heavy sets, but the bench must sit so the hips rise straight under the bar. Keep the chin tucked and ribs down. Re-rack with a twist of the wrists before sitting down.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
