Uses a long loop resistance band. Sit with the shoulder blades against a bench, stretch the band across the hip crease and anchor its ends under heavy dumbbells on each side, under the bench legs, or on the pegs of a hip thrust platform. Feet flat, hip-width, shins vertical at the top.
Tuck the chin and drive through the heels to lift the hips to full extension against the band. Hold the top for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower with control until the hips nearly touch the floor.
Band tension peaks at lockout, so squeeze hard there. Add a band over a barbell for accommodating resistance. Ribs stay down; do not finish by arching the lower back.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set up as for a barbell hip thrust with the shoulder blades on a bench and the padded bar in the hip crease. Keep the working foot flat under the knee and move the other foot forward about one foot-length so only its heel touches the floor, toes up.

Drive mostly through the working heel to raise the hips to full extension, torso parallel to the floor and pelvis level. Squeeze the working glute for 1 second and lower under control. Complete all reps, then switch.

Keep about 70 to 80 percent of the effort on the working leg; the front heel only stabilises. Pelvis stays level. A bridge between bilateral and single-leg thrusts that allows heavier unilateral loading.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set up like a barbell hip thrust but with the shoulder blades on the bench at about mid-scapula, so the torso stays fixed on the bench throughout. Padded bar in the hip crease, feet flat and positioned so the shins are vertical at the top, knees at about 90 degrees.

Starting at the top, lower the hips only a short distance, about 10 to 15 cm, keeping the torso and head still rather than rocking on the bench. Drive back up to full hip extension and squeeze for 1 second. Repeat in the top half of the range only.
Named after coach Kassem Hanson. Constant tension on the glutes with no rest at the bottom. Chin tucked, ribs down, torso still. Use slightly less load than a full hip thrust.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with the knees bent about 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor hip-width apart, heels 20 to 30 cm from the glutes. Arms on the floor by the sides, palms down. Flatten the lower back gently by tilting the pelvis back.

Press through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift the hips until the knees, hips and shoulders form a straight line, with weight on the upper back, not the neck. Pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower slowly to just above the floor.

Keep the slight pelvic tuck so the lower back does not arch. Push the knees slightly out so they do not cave. Feet farther away bias the hamstrings; closer biases the quads. Progress with a pause, band or single leg.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back on the floor with a padded barbell over the hip crease, using full-size (45 cm) plates so the bar rolls over the hips. Knees bent, feet flat about hip- to shoulder-width, heels 20 to 30 cm from the glutes. Hold the bar just outside the hips.

Drive through the heels to lift the hips until they are fully extended and the knees, hips and shoulders are in a straight line. Squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower until the glutes lightly touch the floor.
Shorter range than a hip thrust, so heavy loads are possible and setup needs no bench. Ribs down and chin tucked; do not arch the back to finish. Keep the bar steady with both hands.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with one foot flat on the floor, knee bent about 90 degrees and heel 20 to 30 cm from the glute. Extend the other leg straight in line with the bent thigh, or hug its knee to the chest to block lumbar arching. Arms on the floor.

Drive through the planted heel to lift the hips until the shoulders, hip and knee form a straight line and the pelvis is level. Pause for 1 to 2 seconds and lower under control. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Keep the pelvis from tilting or rotating toward the free leg. Push through the heel, not the toes. Hold the top for 2 seconds or elevate the shoulders on a bench to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your back with the heels on a bench, step or box about 30 to 45 cm high, knees bent about 90 degrees and feet hip-width. Arms on the floor by the sides.
Press the heels down into the bench and lift the hips until the body is straight from shoulders to knees. Squeeze for 1 second, then lower slowly until the hips nearly touch the floor.

The elevation increases range and hamstring demand. Keep the ribs down and do not arch the lower back. Straighter knees shift more of the work to the hamstrings; a single leg or a weight on the hips progresses it.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat hip-width, arms on the floor. Lift into a glute bridge with the hips fully extended and the shoulders, hips and knees in a straight line.

Keeping the hips high and level, lift one foot a few centimetres and bring the knee toward the chest to about 90 degrees of hip flexion, then return the foot to the floor and repeat with the other side. Continue alternating slowly for reps or time.
The hips must not drop or rotate as each foot lifts; press hard through the standing heel. Place a dowel across the hips to check they stay level. Cross the arms on the chest to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your back with the heels or lower calves on top of a stability ball, legs straight, arms out on the floor at about 45 degrees, palms down.
Press down into the ball and lift the hips until the body is straight from shoulders to feet, keeping the ball still. Pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower slowly to just above the floor.

Use the arms for balance; bring them closer to the body or cross them on the chest to progress. Ribs down; do not arch. Do not let the ball roll side to side. Heels on the ball bias the hamstrings more than calves on the ball.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Place it just above the knees and lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet flat, hip-width. Push the knees out so the band is under tension before you start.

Keep pushing the knees out against the band and drive through the heels to lift the hips to full extension, shoulders, hips and knees in a straight line. Pause for 1 to 2 seconds and lower slowly, keeping tension on the band.
Do not let the knees collapse inward at any point; the band adds glute medius work. Squeeze the glutes at the top and keep the ribs down. Higher-rep sets work well as an activation drill.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your back with the heels on the floor 50 to 70 cm from the hips so the knees are only bent about 20 to 30 degrees, toes up. Arms on the floor by the sides.
Dig the heels into the floor and pull them toward you without moving them, lifting the hips until the body is straight from shoulders to heels. Pause for 1 second, then lower slowly.

The long lever makes the hamstrings work much harder than a normal bridge; expect cramping at first. Keep the pelvis slightly tucked so the lower back does not take over. Elevate the heels on a step or go single-leg to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a landmine-anchored barbell. Sit with the shoulder blades against a bench placed beside or in front of the anchor so the loaded sleeve can rest across the hip crease. Pad the sleeve and hold it with both hands. Feet flat, hip-width, shins vertical at the top.
Tuck the chin and drive through the heels to lift the hips to full extension, torso parallel to the floor. Squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower the hips under control.
Quick to set up and the bar end stays stable on the hips. Chin tucked, ribs down. Load is limited by how the sleeve sits; use pauses or slow lowering to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with the soles of the feet pressed together and the knees falling out to the sides, heels 15 to 25 cm from the glutes. Prop up on the elbows or lay the arms on the floor, chin tucked.
Tuck the pelvis, squeeze the glutes and drive the hips up through the outside edges of the feet to full extension. Lower quickly to just above the floor and repeat in a steady rhythm.

The externally rotated position reduces hamstring involvement and biases the glutes. Keep the pelvis tucked so the lower back stays out of it. Keep the feet pressed together. Sets of 20 to 50 are common.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with the soles of the feet together, knees out and heels 15 to 25 cm from the glutes. Hold a dumbbell or plate horizontally over the hip crease with both hands; propping the shoulders on a pad adds range.
Tuck the pelvis and drive the hips up through the outside edges of the feet, squeezing the glutes hard at full extension. Lower under control to just above the floor, keeping the weight steady.
Hold the weight still with both hands. Do not arch the lower back. Moderate load, high reps (15 to 30). Progress load only while the glutes, not the back, finish each rep.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat hip-width near the glutes, and lift into a glute bridge with the hips fully extended. Arms on the floor.

Keeping the hips high, take small alternating steps with the heels away from the body, 3 to 5 steps until the knees are nearly straight, then walk the heels back in to the start. Lower the hips only at the end of the set or each rep.
Hips stay up the whole time. Use short heel steps with toes up. Walk out only as far as you can hold hip height. Heavy hamstring eccentric demand, so build volume gradually.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Set up for a hip thrust with the bottom of the shoulder blades on a bench, feet flat and shins vertical at the top, optionally with a band or barbell over the hips.
Drive the hips up to full extension so the torso is parallel to the floor and hold the top position for 20 to 60 seconds, glutes fully contracted and breathing steadily. Lower slowly and rest.
Ribs down and chin tucked for the whole hold. Keep the shins vertical. End the set if the lower back or hamstrings start to take over or the hips sag below parallel.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Kneel on a pad with the ankles anchored under a Nordic bench, padded bar, heavy object or a partner's hands, knees hip-width. Hips fully extended so the body is straight from knees to head, arms ready in front of the chest.

Lower the body forward as slowly as possible, keeping the hips extended and resisting with the hamstrings until you can no longer control the descent. Catch yourself with the hands in a push-up position at the bottom and push back up just enough to let the hamstrings curl the body back to upright.

Do not bend at the hips; the movement is all knee. Focus on a slow 3 to 5 second eccentric; full concentric reps are an advanced goal. Scale with band assistance, a reduced range or lowering onto a box.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a resistance band. Anchor a heavy band high behind you (a rack upright at about head height) and loop it around the chest under the armpits. Kneel on a pad with the ankles secured, body straight from knees to head.

Lower forward slowly with the hips extended, letting the band take more of the load as you descend, then curl back up with the hamstrings as far as you can, using the band and a light hand push if needed.
Hips stay extended; do not pike. Progress to lighter bands over time. Control the descent through the full range rather than dropping at the end.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Adjust a glute-ham developer so the knees sit just behind (below) the thigh pad and the balls of the feet press firmly into the footplate with the ankles locked under the rollers. Start with the torso parallel to the floor, hips extended so the body is straight from knees to head, arms crossed on the chest.
Push the toes into the plate and contract the hamstrings to curl the body up by flexing the knees, keeping the hips extended, until the torso is upright. Lower under control back to parallel.
Keep a straight line from knees to head; bending at the hips turns it into a back extension. Use the arms to push off the pad early on, or use a band. Hold a plate at the chest to load.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Set up on a glute-ham developer, or kneel on a pad with the ankles anchored. Start upright on the knees, body straight from knees to head, arms across the chest or ready in front.

Lower forward as in a Nordic curl until about halfway, then flex the hips so the torso folds down into a hinged position with the hips bent about 90 degrees, shortening the lever. Return by curling the knees and extending the hips together in one smooth motion back to upright kneeling.
The hip bend shortens the lever, so it is easier than a full Nordic or glute-ham raise and is a progression toward them. Keep the motion smooth and control the lowering. Do not drop into the hinge.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down on the leg curl machine with the knees just off the bench edge so the knee joint lines up with the machine pivot. Set the roller pad on the lower calves just above the heels, feet hip-width. Grip the handles and press the hips into the pad.

Curl the heels toward the glutes as far as possible, ideally past 90 degrees of knee flexion, squeeze for 1 second, then lower over 2 to 3 seconds to almost full knee extension without letting the stack touch.
Keep the hips pressed down; lifting them shortens the hamstrings and cheats the rep. Do not swing. Pointing the toes (plantarflexion) reduces calf help; pulling them up (dorsiflexion) increases it.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in the machine with the back against the pad and the knee joint aligned with the machine pivot. Set the lower roller just above the heels and lock the thigh pad firmly onto the lower thighs above the knees. Grip the handles.
Curl the legs down and back as far as possible, squeezing for 1 second at full knee flexion, then return over 2 to 3 seconds to near full extension without letting the stack touch.

The flexed hip lengthens the hamstrings, which tends to give a stronger hypertrophy stimulus than lying curls. Leaning the torso forward adds stretch. Keep the thigh pad tight so the hips do not lift.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand in the standing leg curl machine with the working thigh against the knee pad, knee joint aligned with the pivot, and the roller just above the back of the ankle. Hold the handles; the standing leg is slightly bent.
Curl the heel toward the glute as far as possible, pause for 1 second, then lower over 3 seconds to near full extension. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
Keep the hips still and the torso upright; avoid kicking the hip back or arching. The unilateral setup exposes left-right differences. Pause at the top and lower slowly.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down on a lying leg curl machine with the knees just off the bench and aligned with the pivot. Place the roller above one heel and rest the other leg beside or under the pad without pushing. Grip the handles.
Curl the working heel toward the glute, pause for 1 second, then lower over 2 to 3 seconds to near full extension. Complete the set, then switch legs.
Fixes side-to-side imbalances. Keep the hips flat; do not twist the pelvis. Use roughly half the bilateral load or less. Start each set with the weaker leg and match its reps on the other side.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in a seated leg curl with the knee aligned to the machine pivot and the thigh pad locked snugly over both thighs. Place only the working ankle in front of (above) the lower roller; rest the free foot on the frame.
Curl the working leg down and back as far as possible, squeeze for 1 second, then return over 2 to 3 seconds without letting the stack touch. Switch sides after the set.
Keep the torso still and the hips down. Match reps between legs, starting with the weaker side. Slow eccentrics work well here.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley and secure it around one ankle. Face the machine, hold the frame with both hands and step back until the cable is taut. Stand on the other leg with a slight knee bend; the working thigh stays vertical beside the standing thigh.
Keeping the thigh still, curl the heel toward the glute until the knee reaches at least 90 degrees, squeeze for 1 second, then lower slowly to near full extension. Complete all reps, then switch.
Do not let the hip extend or flex; the knee points straight down the whole time. Use a light load and strict reps. Lean slightly into the frame for stability.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down on a flat bench with the knees just off the end. Have a partner place a dumbbell vertically between your feet so the top plate rests on the soles and the handle is gripped between the arches, or pick it up with the feet carefully. Grip the bench.
Squeeze the dumbbell with the feet and curl it toward the glutes until the shins are vertical, then lower slowly until the knees are nearly straight.
Use a light dumbbell and a secure foot grip; past vertical the dumbbell can slide. Keep the hips pressed down. Stop just short of full extension to keep control and tension.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a resistance band. Anchor a band low (at ankle height) to a rack or heavy object in front of you and loop it around both ankles or one ankle. Lie face down far enough from the anchor that the band is taut with the legs straight.
Curl the heels toward the glutes against the band, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly to straight legs while keeping band tension.
Keep the hips on the floor. Pick a band that allows smooth, full-range reps; tension rises as the knees bend. Good for home workouts and rehab. Move farther from the anchor to add tension.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses gliding discs (sliders) on carpet or towels on a smooth floor. Lie on your back with the heels on the sliders, knees bent about 90 degrees, and lift the hips into a bridge so the shoulders, hips and knees are in line. Arms on the floor.
Keeping the hips up, slowly slide the heels away over 3 seconds until the legs are nearly straight, then dig the heels in and curl them back toward the glutes while holding the bridge.
Hips stay high throughout; dropping them shortens the work. Scale by doing only the eccentric and lowering the hips to reset. Squeeze the glutes to protect the lower back.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a slider or towel. Lie on your back with one heel on a slider, knee bent about 90 degrees, and the other leg raised straight or bent above the hip. Lift the hips into a bridge.
Slide the working heel away slowly while holding the hips up and level, until the knee is nearly straight, then curl it back in under the hips. Complete all reps, then switch.
Keep the pelvis level; the free side must not drop. Slow is harder and safer. Progression from the two-leg version; scale by doing eccentrics only.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with the heels on top of a stability ball (55 to 65 cm), legs straight and hip-width, arms out on the floor at about 45 degrees. Lift the hips so the body is straight from shoulders to heels.

Keeping the hips up, curl the ball toward the glutes by bending the knees, letting the hips rise further until the shoulders, hips and knees are in line. Roll the ball back out slowly to straight legs without lowering the hips.
Do not let the hips sag on the way out. Arms closer to the body or crossed on the chest increase difficulty. Keep the ball centred under the heels.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your back with one heel centred on top of a stability ball and the other leg lifted straight toward the ceiling. Arms wide on the floor. Lift the hips into a straight line from shoulders to heel.
Curl the ball toward the glute with the working leg, keeping the hips high and level, then roll it back out slowly to a straight leg. Complete all reps, then switch.
Very demanding on balance and the hamstring; use the arms wide for stability. Hips must stay level. Master the two-leg version for 3 sets of 12 first.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down on a reverse hyper machine with the hip bones at the edge of the pad and the legs hanging vertically. Place the strap around the lower legs just above the ankles (or the roller behind the calves). Grip the handles, chest and stomach flat on the pad.

Extend the hips to swing the legs up until they are in line with the torso, squeezing the glutes. Let the legs swing back down under control and past vertical under the pad, allowing the pendulum to flex the hips and gently traction the lower back, then go straight into the next rep.

Lift with the glutes and hamstrings, not momentum alone. Do not hyperextend beyond a straight line at the top. Use light to moderate loads for 10 to 20 reps; many lifters use it to decompress after heavy pulls.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down on a high flat bench, plyo box or incline bench with the hip bones at the edge and the legs hanging toward the floor. Grip the sides or the end of the bench firmly to hold the torso in place.
Lift the legs straight back by extending the hips until the legs are in line with the torso, squeeze the glutes for 1 second, then lower slowly until the feet are near the floor.
Keep the legs straight and together. Avoid arching beyond neutral at the top. Add ankle weights or hold a dumbbell between the feet to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down over a stability ball with the hips and lower belly on top, legs straight and toes touching the floor behind. Walk the hands out until they are planted on the floor under the shoulders, arms straight.
Lift both legs together until they are in line with the torso, squeezing the glutes, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly until the toes lightly touch the floor.
Keep the arms locked and the shoulders over the hands for stability. Lift with the glutes, not a lumbar crank, and keep the legs together and straight. Slow tempo helps keep the ball still.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Attach a rope to a low pulley at the lowest setting. Face away from the stack, straddle the cable and grab the rope ends between the legs with a neutral grip. Walk forward 1 to 1.5 m until the weight lifts, feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes slightly out, knees unlocked.

Push the hips back and hinge with a neutral spine, letting the rope draw the hands back between the legs until the hamstrings are stretched and the torso is about 45 degrees or lower. Drive the hips forward to stand tall and squeeze the glutes, arms long the whole time.

Arms are hooks, not pullers. Hinge, do not squat; the knees bend only slightly. Finish tall with the glutes, without leaning back against the cable. Good for teaching the hinge and high-rep glute work.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a long loop resistance band. Anchor it low (about shin height) to a rack or post behind you. Face away, reach between the legs to grab the band, and walk forward until it is taut. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, knees unlocked.
Hinge the hips back with a neutral spine as the band draws your hands back between the legs, then thrust the hips forward to stand tall against the band, squeezing the glutes.
Band tension is highest at lockout, so finish every rep. Keep the back flat and the arms long. Great as a warm-up or high-rep finisher; step farther away for more tension.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width and a kettlebell on the floor about 30 cm behind the heels, centred between the feet. Push the hips back and bend the knees slightly to reach between the legs and grip the handle with both hands, spine neutral.

Drive the hips forward to stand up, dragging the bell forward between the legs and past the front of the feet until you stand tall with glutes squeezed. Then hinge back down and drag or place the bell behind you again, alternating the bell between front and back positions.
The hips do the work, not the arms. Keep the back flat and the bell low; it slides or is set down rather than swung. A controlled drill that teaches the hike and hip snap before learning swings.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley and secure it to one ankle. Face the stack about 60 cm away, hold the frame and hinge forward 20 to 45 degrees at the hips, standing on the other leg with a soft knee. The working leg starts slightly in front of the body with tension on the cable.

Drive the strapped leg back and slightly up by extending the hip, keeping a slight knee bend, until the glute is fully contracted, about in line with the torso. Squeeze for 1 second, then return the leg forward under control.
Do not arch the lower back or rotate the pelvis to get more range; the motion stops when the hip stops. Keep the torso still. Toes slightly turned out can increase glute feel.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set up in the glute kickback machine with the forearms or chest on the support pad and the hips square. Place one foot on the footplate (or the pad behind the knee, depending on the model), knee bent about 90 degrees, standing knee soft.

Push the plate back and up by extending the hip until the thigh is in line with the torso, squeeze the glute for 1 second, then return slowly until the hip is flexed about 90 degrees. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
Keep the hips square and the lower back neutral; do not arch to finish. No swinging. Use a controlled tempo and adjust the pad so the start position allows a full hip stretch.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a resistance band. Either loop a long band around the arch of one foot and anchor it low in front of you, standing and holding a support, or kneel on all fours with a mini band looped around both feet or the arches, hands under shoulders and knees under hips.

Kick the working leg straight back against the band by extending the hip until the leg is in line with the torso, squeeze the glute for 1 second, then return under control. Complete all reps, then switch.
Keep the spine neutral and the pelvis square; move from the hip, not the lower back. Good for activation work and high-rep finishers.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Get on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips, back flat and core braced, neck neutral.

Keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees and the foot flexed, lift one leg so the sole of the foot drives toward the ceiling until the thigh is parallel to the floor. Squeeze the glute for 1 second, then lower until the knee nearly touches the floor. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Stop when the thigh is level; going higher only arches the lower back. Do not rotate the hips. Add ankle weights or a band to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the Smith bar low, at about the height of your foot when kneeling with the thigh parallel to the floor, and set the safeties just below. Kneel on all fours (or lean forearms on a bench) under the bar and place the arch of one foot, shoe on, under the bar, then rotate the hooks to unrack.

Press the bar upward by extending the hip, knee bent about 90 degrees, until the thigh is in line with the torso. Squeeze for 1 second, then lower under control until the hip is flexed about 90 degrees.
Keep the hips square and the core tight; do not arch to lift higher. Use light loads and set the safeties before starting.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your side with hips stacked, hips bent about 45 degrees and knees bent about 90 degrees, heels in line with the glutes and feet together. Rest the head on the lower arm and place the top hand on the top hip to check it stays still.
Keeping the feet together, rotate the top knee upward as high as possible without rolling the pelvis back, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly.
The knee turns out and up (hip external rotation), working the side glute and deep hip rotators. Stack the hips and keep them still; rolling the pelvis slightly forward helps. Move slowly.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a mini loop band. Place it just above the knees and lie on your side with hips stacked, hips bent about 45 degrees and knees about 90 degrees, feet together. Head on the lower arm, top hand on the hip.
Open the top knee against the band while keeping the feet touching and the pelvis still, pause for 1 second at the top, then return slowly, keeping some band tension.
Do not rock the hips backward to gain range. Squeeze the side of the glute. Progress band thickness gradually.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your side with the bottom knee slightly bent for stability and the top leg straight in line with the torso (or slightly behind it), hips stacked vertically. Rest the head on the lower arm and the top hand on the floor in front.
Lift the top leg upward about 30 to 45 degrees, leading slightly with the heel and keeping the toes pointing forward, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly without resting it.
If the toes turn up, the hip flexors take over; keep them forward or slightly down. Avoid rolling backward or hiking the hip. Add ankle weights to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Get on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips, back flat and core braced.

Keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, lift one leg out to the side by abducting the hip until the thigh is near parallel to the floor or the pelvis would start to tilt, pause for 1 second, then lower. Complete all reps, then switch.
Do not shift the weight onto the other side or rotate the torso; keep both hands loaded equally. Keep the movement slow. Use a mini band above the knees or an ankle weight to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Get on all fours with the band just above both knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips, elbows straight, back flat and neck neutral.

Lift one knee out to the side against the band, keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, until the thigh is near parallel or the pelvis would tilt. Pause for 1 second, then lower slowly. Complete all reps, then switch.
Stay square through the hips and shoulders; do not lean away. Keep tension on the band at the bottom. Short pauses at the top add difficulty.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in the hip abduction machine with the back against the pad and the pads on the outside of the knees or lower thighs. Set the start position so the knees are together or slightly apart. Feet on the footrests, hands on the handles.
Push the knees outward as far as possible, pause for 1 second, then return slowly without letting the stack touch.
Sitting upright biases the outer hip (glute medius, tensor fasciae latae); leaning the torso forward biases the upper glute max. Control the return and avoid bouncing at end range.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Sit in the hip abduction machine with the pads on the outside of the knees. Lean the torso forward off the back pad about 30 to 45 degrees and hold the handles or the seat.
Push the knees out as far as they go, pause, then return slowly without letting the weight stack touch.
Leaning forward brings in more of the upper glutes. Keep the back flat while leaning. Control the return.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in the hip adduction machine with the back against the pad and the pads on the inside of the knees or lower thighs. Set the start lever to a comfortable stretch, not your maximum range. Feet on the footrests, hands on the handles.
Squeeze the knees together until the pads meet, pause for 1 second, then return slowly to the stretched position.
Do not start in an excessive stretch, especially when cold. Keep the back against the pad. Slow eccentrics protect the groin; progress range before load.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley and secure it to the ankle farther from the stack. Stand side-on to the machine with the inside leg nearest the stack and hold the frame with the near hand. The working leg starts slightly crossed in front of the standing leg with the cable taut.
Lift the strapped leg out to the side, away from the stack, to about 30 to 45 degrees, toes forward and knee straight, pause for 1 second, then return under control.
Keep the torso upright; do not lean away or hike the hip. Toes point forward. Use light loads and strict reps.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley and secure it to the ankle nearest the stack. Stand side-on, holding the frame, with the working leg out toward the stack about 30 degrees and the cable taut.
Pull the strapped leg across the body, past the standing leg and slightly in front of it, keeping the knee straight. Pause for 1 second, then return under control to the start.
Keep the torso still and upright. Do not swing. Light loads and smooth reps; good for groin strength.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Stand with the band around the ankles or just above the knees, feet hip-width, hands on the hips or a support. Standing knee soft.
Lift one leg out to the side against the band, about 20 to 30 cm, keeping the toes forward and the leg straight, pause for 1 second, then return slowly. Complete all reps, then switch.
Stand tall without leaning; the standing hip works too, holding the pelvis level. Keep the movement controlled.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Sit on the edge of a bench with the band just above the knees, feet flat and hip-width or slightly wider, knees bent about 90 degrees.
Push the knees out against the band as far as possible, keeping the feet planted, pause for 1 second at the widest point, then return slowly while keeping tension.
Lean forward to bias the upper glutes or sit tall for the outer hip. Push both knees out evenly. High reps (20 to 30) work well.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Place it around the ankles, above the knees or around the forefoot (hardest), and assume a quarter-squat with feet hip-width, chest up and hands on the hips.

Step sideways about 30 cm with the lead foot, then follow with the trailing foot only half as far, so the feet never come together and the band stays taut. Continue for 10 to 15 steps, then return the other way.
Keep tension on the band throughout. Stay low and level; do not bob or lean. Do not let the knees cave; keep the toes pointing forward.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Uses a mini loop band. Place it around the ankles or above the knees and assume a half-squat with feet slightly wider than hip-width, chest up.
Step forward and out diagonally about 45 degrees with one foot, then the other, keeping the band taut and the half-squat height constant. Walk forward for 10 to 15 steps, then backward.
Keep the knees tracking over the toes. Do not bob up and down or let the feet come together. Short, deliberate steps.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Get into a side plank on the forearm with the elbow directly under the shoulder, legs straight and stacked, body in a straight line from head to feet, hips lifted.

Holding the plank, lift the top leg upward about 30 to 45 degrees with the knee straight and toes facing forward, pause for 1 second, then lower it slowly without dropping. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Both hips work: the bottom glute medius holds the plank, the top one lifts the leg. Keep the hips high and do not rotate the torso. Drop to the bottom knee to scale.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your side next to a flat bench with the elbow on the floor under the shoulder. Rest the inside of the top leg's ankle and lower shin on the bench, knee straight; the bottom leg rests on the floor underneath.

Press the top leg down into the bench to lift the hips until the body is straight from head to feet, bringing the bottom leg up to touch the underside of the bench. Hold for time (10 to 30 seconds), or lower and raise the hips for reps. Switch sides.
Body stays straight from head to feet; do not pike or let the hips sag. Squeeze the top leg down into the bench. Scale with the short-lever version on the knee.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your side next to a flat bench with the elbow on the floor under the shoulder. Rest the inside of the top knee on the bench, knee bent about 90 degrees; the bottom leg rests on the floor.
Press the top knee into the bench to lift the hips until the body is straight from head to knee, lifting the bottom leg toward the bench. Hold for time or perform reps, then switch sides.
The shorter lever reduces load on the groin, so it suits beginners and rehab. Keep the hips stacked. Build to 3 sets of 30 seconds before the long-lever version.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie on your side with the bottom leg straight in line with the torso. Bend the top leg and plant its foot flat on the floor in front of the bottom knee (or rest the top knee on a bench). Head on the lower arm.
Lift the straight bottom leg upward off the floor as high as possible using the inner thigh, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly without resting it.
Keep the toes pointing forward and the leg straight. Do not roll backward. Add an ankle weight to progress.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a soft ball, foam roller or folded pillow. Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees (or 45 degrees for more groin stretch), feet flat, and the ball between the knees. Lower back neutral.
Squeeze the knees together into the ball, building to a firm effort over 2 seconds, and hold for 5 to 10 seconds while breathing steadily. Relax and repeat for 5 to 10 reps.
Build intensity gradually; this is a common groin rehab and prehab test. Keep the feet flat. Progress by holding longer, squeezing harder or straightening the legs.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand on one leg with the knee unlocked and hinge into a single-leg RDL position with the torso near parallel and the free leg extended behind. Hold a support with one hand if needed.

Keeping the standing knee still, rotate the pelvis and torso open toward the free leg side (hip external rotation), then close back past square so the pelvis faces the standing leg (internal rotation). Move only through the stance hip for 5 to 8 slow reps per side.
Move slowly and stay balanced. Keep the standing knee stable over the foot. Use a support to scale.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie face down on the floor or a mat with the forehead on the stacked hands and legs straight. Press the front of the hips into the floor.
Squeeze one glute and lift that leg off the floor 5 to 10 cm without rotating the pelvis or lifting the hip, hold for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower. Alternate legs.
Lift from the glute, not the lower back; the range is small. Bend the knee to 90 degrees to reduce hamstring help and target the glutes more.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the shoulder pads so you must bend the knees slightly to get under them. Stand with the balls of the feet on the platform edge, feet hip-width, toes forward, heels hanging. Stand up to lift the stack, knees straight but not locked.
Lower the heels slowly over 2 seconds to a full stretch below the platform, pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then rise onto the toes as high as possible. Squeeze for 1 second at the top and repeat.
Straight knees target the gastrocnemius. Pause at the bottom to remove the Achilles bounce. Full range beats heavy partials. Push through the big toe so the ankles do not roll out.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Set the standing calf raise machine so you get under the shoulder pads with the knees slightly bent. Stand on one foot with the ball of the foot on the edge of the platform and the heel hanging.
Lower the heel slowly for a full stretch, then rise as high as possible onto the toes and pause. Finish all reps, then switch sides.
Keep the knee straight but not locked. Pause in the stretch. Use about half the two-leg weight.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set a barbell in a rack at shoulder height with safeties just below the shoulders. Unrack it onto the upper back as for a back squat and stand with the balls of the feet on a 5 to 10 cm plate or block, heels free, feet hip-width.
Lower the heels for a full stretch, pause, then rise onto the toes as high as possible, straight up without leaning forward. Pause for 1 second at the top and lower slowly.
Balance is the limiter, so work inside a rack with safeties. Keep the body tall and the knees straight. Slow eccentrics; no bouncing.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Set the Smith bar at shoulder height and place a 5 to 10 cm block or step under it. Place the bar on the upper back, stand with the balls of the feet on the block, heels hanging, feet hip-width, and rotate the hooks to unrack.
Lower the heels to a deep stretch, pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then rise onto the toes as high as possible. Pause at the top and lower slowly.
The fixed path removes balance demands. Keep the knees straight and the ankles from rolling out. Set the safeties before starting.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in the seated calf raise machine with the knee pad snug on the lower thighs just above the knees, knees bent about 90 degrees. Place the balls of the feet on the platform, hip-width, heels hanging.

Push up slightly and release the safety lever. Lower the heels to a deep stretch, pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then push up onto the toes as high as possible and squeeze. Re-engage the lever after the last rep.
The bent knee slackens the gastrocnemius, so the soleus does most of the work. Use a full range with a bottom pause and avoid bouncing. Higher reps (12 to 20) suit the slow-twitch soleus.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit on a bench with the knees bent about 90 degrees and the balls of the feet on a plate or step 5 to 10 cm high, heels hanging. Rest a dumbbell vertically on each lower thigh just above the knee, with a folded towel underneath for comfort.
Lower the heels for a full stretch, then lift them as high as possible, pushing through the big toe, and squeeze for 1 second. Lower slowly.
Bent knees target the soleus. Hold the dumbbells steady with the hands. Higher reps work well; add a pause at the bottom.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Use a donkey calf machine with the hip pad over the lower back and hips, or bend forward about 90 degrees at the hips with forearms on a support and the balls of the feet on a step, with a partner sitting on the hips or a dip belt loaded on the hips. Knees straight but not locked.
Lower the heels for a deep stretch, pause for 1 second, then rise onto the toes as high as possible. Squeeze and repeat.
Straight knees keep the gastrocnemius (the big calf muscle) working; the stretch comes from letting the heels drop below the step. Keep the knees straight throughout. Control the bottom; no bouncing.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand on one foot on the edge of a step, ball of the foot on the edge and heel hanging, knee straight but not locked. Hook the free foot behind the working ankle and hold a rail or wall for balance; hold a dumbbell in the same-side hand to add load.
Lower the heel below the step for a full stretch over 2 seconds, then rise as high as possible onto the toes. Pause at the top. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
Use the support for balance only, not to pull yourself up. Full range each rep. Max reps per leg (about 25 or more is a common benchmark) is a standard calf endurance test.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand with the balls of the feet on a step or plate 5 to 10 cm high, heels hanging, feet hip-width and toes forward. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides with a neutral grip, or one dumbbell and a rail with the other hand.
Lower the heels for a full stretch, pause, then rise onto the toes as high as possible. Squeeze for 1 second and lower slowly.
Keep the body tall and still; do not bounce out of the bottom. Use straps if grip fails before the calves. Pause at both ends.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand with feet hip-width, toes forward, on the floor or with the balls of the feet on a step, lightly holding a wall for balance. Knees straight but not locked.
Rise onto the balls of the feet as high as possible, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly over 2 to 3 seconds to the floor or below the step edge.
Keep the weight over the big and second toes so the ankles do not roll out. Progress with a step for range, a single leg or added weight.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Sit in a leg press with the balls of the feet on the lower edge of the platform, hip-width, heels off. Press the platform up until the legs are straight but not locked, and keep the safety stops engaged if the machine allows it at this position.

Let the platform push the toes back toward you for a full stretch, pause, then press through the balls of the feet to extend the ankles as far as possible. Pause and repeat, moving only at the ankles.
Never let the feet slip off the platform; wear shoes with grip. Keep the knees straight but soft throughout. Use controlled, full-range reps.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand in the hack squat machine with the shoulder pads on and the balls of the feet on the lower edge of the platform, hip-width, heels hanging. Stand up and release the safety handles with the knees straight but not locked. Some lifters face the pads instead, chest against them.
Lower the heels for a full stretch, pause, then rise onto the toes as high as possible, squeezing the calves. Repeat, moving only at the ankles.
Keep the knees straight throughout. Re-engage the safeties before stepping off. Facing the pads changes the angle and is often easier on the lower back.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Stand facing a wall with the hands on it for balance. Bend the knees about 30 to 45 degrees (more bend shifts more work to the soleus), on one or both feet, on the floor or with the balls of the feet on a step.
Keeping the knee bend fixed, rise onto the balls of the feet as high as possible, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly over 3 seconds.
Do not straighten the knees as you rise. Hold a dumbbell or use a single leg to load. Common in Achilles and running rehab.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand on the edge of a step on the balls of both feet, heels hanging, holding a rail. Rise onto the toes using both legs.

Shift onto the working leg and lower the heel slowly below the step over 3 to 5 seconds. Return to the top using both legs (or the uninjured leg) and repeat. Perform with straight knees and with knees bent about 20 to 30 degrees.

The Alfredson protocol uses 3 sets of 15 per knee position, twice a day, for 12 weeks; follow a clinician's plan. Some discomfort is acceptable; sharp pain is not. Add load in a backpack when bodyweight is easy.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Trains the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin. Stand with the back and glutes against a wall and the heels about one foot-length out in front, legs straight.
Lift the toes and front of the feet toward the shins as high as possible, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly without letting the toes slap the floor.
Walk the feet farther out to increase difficulty. High reps (15 to 25) work well. Balances calf work and helps shin-splint prevention in runners.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a tib bar. Trains the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin. Sit on a bench or box high enough that the feet hang, with a lightly loaded tib bar strapped over the tops of the feet and the heels resting on the bench edge or floor.
Pull the toes up toward the shins against the load as far as possible, pause for 1 second, then lower slowly over 2 to 3 seconds into full plantar flexion.
Start light; the tibialis is small. Keep the heels planted. Full range each rep. Pairs well with calf work.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Uses a resistance band. Trains the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin. Sit on the floor with the leg straight and a band looped over the top of the forefoot, anchored low to a post or rack in front of you.
Pull the toes back toward the shin against the band, pause for 1 second, then return slowly over 2 to 3 seconds.
Keep the heel fixed on the floor and the knee straight. Use smooth, full-range reps. A common rehab exercise for shins and ankles; progress with a thicker band.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Pick up heavy dumbbells or farmer's handles with a neutral grip and stand tall with the weights at the sides, shoulders down and back. Rise onto the balls of the feet as high as possible.
Walk forward with short, quick steps while staying high on the toes for 20 to 40 m or 20 to 40 seconds. At the end, lower the heels and set the weights down with a flat back.
Heels must not touch during the walk; stop the set when they start to drop. Stay tall and brace. Use moderately heavy weights over short distances.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand tall with feet hip-width, knees nearly straight and arms relaxed at the sides.

Bounce rapidly on the balls of the feet with stiff ankles and minimal knee bend, spending as little time on the ground as possible; heels do not touch the floor. Arms can swing lightly for rhythm. Perform 10 to 30 contacts per set.
Think 'stiff spring': the ankle does the work. Build volume gradually to protect the Achilles. Stop if landings become loud or heavy or ground contact slows.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Lie on your side with the hips stacked, hips bent about 45 degrees and knees bent about 90 degrees, knees together. Rest the head on the lower arm.
Keeping the knees touching, lift the top foot toward the ceiling (the top hip turns inward), pause for 1 second, then lower slowly.
Keep the pelvis still; do not roll back. The knees stay together the whole time. Works the front part of the side glute.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves
Stand sideways on a step on one foot, the other foot hanging just off the edge. Stand tall and hold a rail or wall lightly.
Keeping both knees straight, let the hip of the hanging leg drop a few centimetres, then lift it back up above level using the side glute of the standing leg. Complete the reps, then switch sides.
The working side is the standing leg. Move only at the pelvis; do not lean the trunk or bend the knees. Small, slow movement.
Legs: hinges, glutes, hamstrings and calves

Lie face down and prop up on the forearms, elbows directly under the shoulders, forearms parallel (or hands lightly clasped). Legs straight, feet hip-width, toes tucked. Neck neutral, eyes on the floor just ahead of the hands.

Brace the abs, squeeze the glutes and quads, and lift the hips so the body is one straight line from ears to heels, hips level with the shoulders. Hold for time, breathing in short breaths behind the brace. Lower the knees to finish.

Tilt the pelvis slightly under and keep the ribs down so the low back does not sag. Push the forearms into the floor so the shoulder blades stay spread. End the set when the hips sag or pike. Scale from the knees; progress to RKC or long-lever planks rather than holds beyond 60 to 90 seconds.

Start at the top of a push-up: hands flat directly under the shoulders, fingers spread, elbows straight but not hyperextended. Feet hip-width on the balls of the feet. Neck neutral, gaze just ahead of the hands.

Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes so the body is a straight line from head to heels. Hold for time, breathing behind the brace, then lower the knees. Compared with the forearm plank, the straight arms load the shoulders, chest and serratus more and the trunk slightly less.

Push the floor away so the upper back is broad, not sunken between the shoulder blades. Screw the hands into the floor (elbow pits forward) to stabilize the shoulders. Keep the pelvis tucked so the hips do not sag. Wider feet or hands on a bench make it easier.

Set up in a forearm plank with elbows under or slightly ahead of the shoulders, hands in fists. Feet together, legs straight. Before lifting, tuck the pelvis under (posterior tilt) and pull the ribs toward the hips.

Lift and create maximal full-body tension: pull the elbows toward the toes and the toes toward the elbows without moving, squeeze the glutes, quads and fists as hard as possible. Hold 10 to 20 seconds of all-out tension, relax down, and repeat for 3 to 5 sets.

Tension, not duration: if you can hold it for a minute you are not contracting hard enough. Breathe in short sips behind the brace. Keep the pelvis tucked and glutes locked; end the rep the moment the low back arches. Produces far higher abdominal activation than a standard plank.

Start in a forearm plank, then walk the elbows forward so they sit several inches in front of the shoulders, roughly under the eyes or forehead. Feet together, legs straight, glutes squeezed, pelvis tucked and ribs down.

Hold the lengthened position, resisting the increased pull into spinal extension, shoulders pushing away from the floor and hips in line with shoulders and heels. Hold for time, then walk the elbows back under the shoulders before lowering the knees.

The farther the elbows are ahead of the shoulders, the harder the anti-extension demand; progress an inch or two at a time. End the set when the low back starts to arch. Keep the neck long. Sits between the RKC plank and the ab wheel rollout in difficulty.

Lie on one side with the bottom elbow directly under the shoulder, forearm on the floor pointing forward. Legs straight and stacked, or top foot just in front of the bottom foot for an easier base. Top hand on the hip.

Brace and lift the hips until the body is a straight line from head to feet, supported on the forearm and the side of the bottom foot. Hold for time, lower and switch sides. McGill-style practice uses repeated 8 to 10 second holds instead of one long hold.

Do not let the hips sag or drift back into a pike; push them slightly forward so shoulders, hips and ankles stack in one plane. Keep the shoulder away from the ear. Trains the bottom-side obliques, quadratus lumborum and glute medius. Scale from the knees; progress with a top-leg raise or load on the hip.
Lie on your side and place the bottom hand flat under the shoulder, fingers pointing forward or away from the feet, arm straight. Legs straight and stacked, or top foot staggered in front.

Press through the hand and lift the hips into a straight line from head to heels. Reach the top arm to the ceiling so both arms form one vertical line, or rest it on the hip. Hold for time, lower with control and switch sides.

Stack wrist, elbow and shoulder vertically and push the floor away so the shoulder does not sink. Drive the bottom hip up and slightly forward. Harder on the shoulder and wrist and slightly easier on the obliques than the forearm version; use the forearm version if the wrist or shoulder complains.

Lie on your side with the bottom elbow directly under the shoulder, forearm on the floor. Bend both knees about 90 degrees so the feet are behind you, keeping the knees, hips and shoulders in one line when viewed from above. Top hand on the hip.
Brace and lift the hips off the floor so the body is straight from the head to the knees, supported on the forearm and the side of the bottom knee. Hold for time, lower the hip and switch sides.

This short-lever regression of the full side plank roughly halves the load, making it ideal for beginners, rehab or pregnancy (with clearance). Push the hips forward so they do not pike back behind the line of the shoulders and knees. Keep the shoulder away from the ear. Progress by extending the top leg straight with the foot on the floor, then moving to the full side plank.

Set up in a forearm side plank with the elbow under the shoulder, forearm perpendicular to the body, legs stacked or top foot staggered in front, hips lifted in line with the body. Top hand on the hip.

Keeping the upper body still, lower the bottom hip a few inches until it almost touches the floor, then contract the bottom-side obliques to drive it back to the straight line or slightly above. Take 1 to 2 seconds each way. Finish all reps, then switch sides.

Trains lateral flexion through range, unlike the static side plank. Move only at the hips and keep the shoulder stacked over the elbow. Do not bounce off the floor or roll the hips forward or back. Bend the knees to scale; add a top pause or a plate on the hip to progress.
Set up in a forearm or straight-arm side plank with the feet staggered (top foot in front) for a stable base and the hips lifted. Reach the top arm straight up toward the ceiling.

Keeping the hips high, rotate the chest toward the floor and thread the top arm under the body, reaching behind you through the gap between the hip and the floor. Then rotate back open and reach to the ceiling again. Move slowly for the prescribed reps, then switch sides.

The hips stay lifted throughout; rotate through the thoracic spine and rib cage rather than dropping or twisting the pelvis. Keep the supporting shoulder stacked over the elbow or hand. Follow the hand with your eyes. Holding a light dumbbell in the top hand progresses it; dropping to a kneeling base regresses it.

Set a cable pulley low, roughly at the height your top shoulder will be in the plank (about knee height). Lie in a forearm side plank facing the stack, supporting elbow under the shoulder, feet staggered. Grab a single D-handle with the top hand, arm extended toward the pulley with a neutral grip.

Hold the side plank rigidly and row the handle toward the lower ribs, drawing the shoulder blade back and keeping the elbow close to the side. Pause briefly, then extend the arm under control. Complete the reps and switch sides.

Primarily an anti-rotation and lateral stability drill; the pull tries to rotate the trunk toward the stack and drop the hips. Keep the hips high and the chest square to the stack. Use a light to moderate load. A resistance band anchored low works the same way at home. Regress with a kneeling side plank base.
Start in a high plank with hands under the shoulders, arms straight, body in a straight line and feet together on the balls of the feet.

Jump both feet out to slightly wider than shoulder-width, then jump them back together, like a horizontal jumping jack, while the upper body stays fixed over the hands. Continue at a steady rhythm for reps or time (commonly 20 to 40 seconds).

Keep the hips level with the shoulders; do not let them bounce up into a pike or sag on each landing. Land softly on the balls of the feet. Keep the shoulders stacked over the wrists. A conditioning drill as much as a core drill. Scale by stepping one foot out and in at a time, or with hands on a bench; perform from forearms to make it harder for the trunk.
Start in a high plank with hands directly under the shoulders and feet wider than hip-width (about shoulder-width or wider) for a stable base. Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.
Shift weight slightly onto one hand, lift the other hand and tap the opposite shoulder, then replace it on the floor. Alternate sides slowly for reps or time, keeping the body still.

The goal is anti-rotation: the hips should barely move or rock side to side. Move slowly, about one second per tap, and keep the shoulders level. Squeeze the glutes and push the floor away with the supporting hand. Bring the feet closer together to make it harder; widen the feet, elevate the hands or work from the knees to scale.
Start in a forearm plank with elbows under the shoulders and feet slightly wider than hip-width for stability. Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.

Place one hand on the floor where the elbow was and press up, then do the same with the other hand to reach a high plank. Lower back down to the forearms one arm at a time, leading with the same arm. Alternate the leading arm each rep or each set.

Minimize hip sway and rotation as you shift weight from side to side. Put each hand directly under its shoulder in the top position rather than reaching forward. Keep the hips level with the shoulders. Widen the feet or work from the knees to scale; bring the feet together or wear a vest to progress. Also trains the triceps and shoulders.
Start in a forearm or high plank with the feet together or hip-width apart and the body in one straight line from head to heels. Brace the trunk.

Squeeze one glute and lift that leg straight up a few inches (about 15 to 30 cm) off the floor, keeping the knee straight and the toes pointing down. Hold for 2 to 3 seconds, lower and alternate legs for reps or time.

Only lift as high as you can without the low back arching or the pelvis rotating; the hip extension comes from the glute, not the lumbar spine. Keep both hip bones facing the floor. Removing a point of contact adds an anti-rotation challenge. Longer pauses or a forearm base increase difficulty; widen the feet to scale.
Start in a forearm or high plank with the feet wider than hip-width for a stable base and the body in a straight line.
Shift weight slightly to one side and reach the free arm straight forward in line with the ear, thumb up, at head height. Hold for 2 to 3 seconds, return the hand to the floor and alternate arms.

Resist rotation: hips and shoulders stay square to the floor and level. Do not shift the hips to the side to make room for the reach. Keep the supporting shoulder stacked over the elbow or hand. Bring the feet closer together to progress, or combine with the opposite leg lift (two-point plank). Widen the feet further to scale.

Get into a forearm plank with elbows under the shoulders. Have a partner place a weight plate (or plates) flat across the upper back between the shoulder blades, never on the lower back. A weighted vest is a convenient alternative.

Brace hard and hold the straight body line for the prescribed time, breathing in short breaths behind the brace. When finished, have the partner remove the plate before lowering the knees so it does not slide onto the neck or low back.

Only add load once you can hold a perfect unloaded plank for about 60 seconds. Load in small increments (5 to 10 kg). Never let the low back sag under the plate; end the set as soon as the hips drop. Keep the plate centred so it does not create rotation. Shorter, heavier holds (20 to 40 seconds) are the point of loading a plank.

Get into a forearm plank on the floor with the elbows under the shoulders, forearms parallel, feet together on the balls of the feet (no sliders; the toes stay planted). Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.

Rock the whole body forward by flexing the ankles so the shoulders move a few inches past the elbows, then rock backward by pushing through the forearms so the shoulders move behind the elbows. Keep sawing back and forth in a small range for reps or time.

Rocking back is the hard part because it lengthens the lever and increases the anti-extension demand. Keep the body rigid from head to heels throughout; only the ankles and shoulders move. Shorten the range if the low back starts to sag. Differs from the Body Saw, which uses sliders or straps for a much larger range.

Place the feet on sliders (or a towel) on a smooth floor, or in the foot cradles of a suspension trainer set about mid-calf height. Set up in a forearm plank with elbows under the shoulders, pelvis tucked, ribs down.

Push through the forearms to slide the body backward until the elbows are well in front of the head, keeping the body straight. Then pull the body forward again with the abs and lats until the shoulders are back over the elbows. Repeat for reps.

A strong anti-extension drill, comparable to an ab wheel rollout. Keep the pelvis tucked and ribs down throughout; only go as far back as you can without the low back arching. Move slowly, about 2 seconds each way. Shorten the range to scale. Requires sliders or a suspension trainer.

Kneel in front of an exercise ball (55 or 65 cm), place the forearms on top of it with elbows under the shoulders and hands clasped. Extend the legs behind you, feet hip-width or wider on the balls of the feet.
Lift the knees and hold a straight-line plank with the ball as an unstable base, keeping the ball still. Hold for time, then lower the knees.

The unstable surface increases abdominal demand compared with a floor plank. Keep the hips in line with the shoulders and the pelvis tucked. Push the forearms down into the ball to keep the shoulders active. Widen the stance to make it easier; bring the feet together or move the elbows forward on the ball to progress, then move on to stir the pot.
Kneel in front of an exercise ball and set up in a forearm plank with the forearms on top of the ball, elbows under the shoulders, hands clasped. Feet wider than hip-width on the toes, body straight.

Keeping the trunk perfectly still, move the forearms in small circles as if stirring a pot, so the ball traces a circle under the elbows. Do the prescribed number of circles clockwise, then counterclockwise.

A McGill favourite: the trunk resists extension and rotation while the shoulders move. Start with small circles and enlarge them as control improves. The hips must not sway, rotate or sag. Breathe steadily. Widen the feet to scale; bring the feet together or make bigger circles to progress.
Get into a forearm plank with feet together, elbows under the shoulders and forearms parallel or hands clasped.
Rotate the hips to lower one hip toward the floor (without touching), return through the centre, and rotate to lower the other hip. Continue alternating in a controlled rhythm for reps or time.

Keep the shoulders fixed over the elbows and let the rotation happen through the trunk and pelvis. Do not slam the hip into the floor. Keep the hips at plank height as you rotate rather than piking up. Slow down to maximize oblique work; widen the feet slightly if the movement wobbles.
Start on all fours with hands directly under the shoulders, knees under the hips about hip-width apart, toes tucked under, back flat and neck neutral.

Brace the core and lift the knees one to two inches (3 to 5 cm) off the floor so the shins are parallel to the floor and the knees are bent about 90 degrees. Hold the hover for time while keeping the back flat, then lower the knees.

Keep the hips level with the shoulders, not piked up, and the back flat enough to balance a plate on it. Breathe without letting the belly drop. Push the floor away so the upper back stays broad. Progress with alternating shoulder taps, a single opposite arm and leg lift, or by moving into a bear crawl.
Set up in a high plank with hands under the shoulders and feet wider than hip-width. Place a kettlebell or dumbbell on the floor just outside one hand, roughly level with the chest.

Shift weight onto the hand nearest the bell, reach under the body with the opposite hand, grab the bell and drag it across to the other side. Replace the hand on the floor, then repeat with the other hand, dragging it back. Alternate sides for reps.

Do not let the hips rotate or rise as one hand leaves the floor; the hips should stay square and level. Drag the bell along the floor rather than lifting it. Keep the supporting shoulder stacked over the wrist. Widen the feet or use a lighter bell to scale; bring the feet together or use a heavier bell to progress.
Start in a high plank with hands under the shoulders and feet together or hip-width apart. Brace the trunk.
Lift one foot and bring the knee out to the side and up toward the same-side elbow, keeping the foot off the floor and the hips low. Pause, return the leg to plank and alternate sides.

Keep the hips low and level as the knee comes up; side-bend the trunk to bring knee and elbow together rather than piking the hips. Move slowly for more time under tension. Can also be done from a forearm plank. Combine with a push-up for the Spider-Man push-up variation.
Start in a high plank with hands directly under the shoulders, arms straight, body in one line and weight on the balls of the feet, feet hip-width apart.

Drive one knee toward the chest, then switch legs in a running motion so one foot returns as the other knee drives in. Alternate rapidly for reps or time while keeping the hands planted and the hips level.

Keep the shoulders over the hands and the hips at plank height; do not pike or bounce. Land each foot lightly on the ball of the foot. Mostly a conditioning drill at speed; for more core work slow it down (see Slow Mountain Climber). Elevate the hands on a bench or box to scale.
Start in a high plank with hands under the shoulders, arms straight and feet hip-width apart.
Drive one knee across the body toward the opposite elbow, return it to plank and drive the other knee across. Alternate in a controlled or quick rhythm for reps or time.

Rotate through the trunk and pelvis while keeping the shoulders stable over the hands. Avoid bouncing the hips up. Fast tempo makes it a conditioning drill; slowing down and pausing each knee near the opposite elbow makes it an oblique drill. Elevate the hands to scale.
Start in a high plank with hands under the shoulders, arms straight, feet hip-width and the trunk braced.

Slowly draw one knee toward the chest over 2 seconds, rounding the upper back slightly and crunching the abs, pause for 1 to 2 seconds with the knee as close to the chest as possible, then return the foot to the floor over 2 seconds. Alternate legs for reps.

This tempo version prioritizes control and spinal flexion over speed, making it a core exercise rather than a conditioning drill. Exhale as the knee comes in. Keep the hips level with the shoulders and do not let them sag on the return. Elevate the hands to scale; place the feet on sliders to progress.

Kneel in front of an exercise ball, lie over it and walk the hands forward until you are in a high plank with the shins or the tops of the feet on the ball. Hands under the shoulders, arms straight, body straight.

Pull the knees toward the chest, rolling the ball forward onto the toes, while lifting the hips slightly and rounding the low back. Pause, then roll the ball back until the body is straight again. Repeat for reps.

Keep the arms locked and the shoulders stacked over the hands. Do not let the low back sag at the end of each rep. Exhale as you tuck. Start with the ball under the thighs to shorten the lever; progress to the Swiss Ball Pike or single-leg tucks.
Set up in a high plank with the tops of the feet or toes on an exercise ball and the hands planted under the shoulders, arms straight.

Keeping the legs straight, lift the hips high into an inverted V, rolling the ball toward the hands until the hips are roughly over the shoulders. Lower slowly back to a straight plank. Repeat for reps.

Lead with the hips and keep the knees locked. Press through the hands so the shoulders stay strong and stacked over the wrists. Control the lowering so the hips do not dip below the plank line. Harder than the knee tuck; master that first. Tight hamstrings will limit the range.
Place the toes on sliders (or a towel) on a smooth floor and set up in a high plank with hands under the shoulders and arms straight.
Keeping the legs straight, drag the feet toward the hands as the hips lift into a pike until the hips are roughly over the shoulders. Slide back out to a straight plank. Repeat for reps.

Requires sliders or a towel. Keep the arms straight and shoulders over the hands. Control the return so the hips do not dip below the plank line. Squeeze the quads to keep the knees straight. Regress to slider knee tucks if the range is limited.
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Place the fingertips lightly behind the ears or at the temples, or cross the arms on the chest.

Exhale and curl the head, shoulders and shoulder blades off the floor by contracting the abs, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis. The low back stays on the floor. Pause for a second at the top, then lower slowly until the shoulder blades touch down.

Do not pull on the neck or yank the head forward; keep about a fist of space between chin and chest. The range is short; the goal is spinal flexion, not sitting up. Keep the feet relaxed so the hip flexors stay out of it. Slow the lowering or hold a plate on the chest to make it harder.
Lie on your back with arms by your sides, palms down. Lift the legs so the hips and knees are bent about 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor.

Exhale and contract the abs to curl the pelvis toward the ribs, rolling the hips and low back off the floor and bringing the knees toward the chest. Pause, then lower the hips slowly until the tailbone touches down, keeping the knee angle constant.

Think of rolling the spine up from the bottom rather than swinging the legs. Do not use momentum or push hard with the arms. Keep the knees bent at about 90 degrees so the abs, not the hip flexors, do the work. Progress on a decline bench or with a cable.

Lie face up on a decline bench set at about 15 to 30 degrees, with the head at the high end, and grip the bench or handles behind the head. Lift the knees so the hips and knees are bent about 90 degrees.
Exhale and curl the hips up off the bench, drawing the knees toward the chest and the pelvis toward the ribs. Pause, then lower the hips slowly back to the bench, keeping the knee angle constant.

The steeper the decline, the harder it gets because you curl against more gravity. Control the lowering and avoid swinging. Keep the knees bent to focus on the abs rather than the hip flexors. Keep the upper back flat on the bench.

Attach ankle straps to a low pulley, or loop a single strap around both feet. Lie on your back on a mat with the feet toward the stack, far enough away that the cable is taut. Bend the hips and knees to about 90 degrees, arms by your sides or gripping a fixed object behind the head.

Curl the hips off the floor, pulling the knees toward the chest against the cable resistance and rolling the low back up. Pause, then lower the hips back under control without letting the legs straighten.
Shuffle far enough from the stack that there is tension at the bottom. Do not let the cable yank the legs back; control the return. Keep the knee angle fixed. A band anchored low works similarly.

Lie on your back with fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide, and the low back pressed into the floor. Lift the shoulder blades slightly off the floor and raise the legs with the hips and knees bent about 90 degrees.

Rotate the trunk to bring one shoulder (and elbow) toward the opposite knee as that knee draws in, while the other leg extends straight out at about 45 degrees. Switch sides in a slow pedaling motion, alternating continuously for reps or time.

Rotate the rib cage, not just the elbow; the shoulder should travel toward the knee. Move slowly and fully extend the straight leg. Keep the low back on the floor; extend the leg higher if it arches. Shown in EMG studies to be one of the most effective rectus abdominis and oblique exercises.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Place one hand behind the head and the other arm on the floor out to the side. Cross the opposite ankle over the knee, or keep both feet down.
Exhale, curl up and rotate the trunk to bring the elbow toward the opposite knee. Pause, then lower slowly. Complete all reps on one side and switch.
Lead with the shoulder and rib cage, not the elbow. Do not yank the head forward. Keep the hips still and the low back on the floor. Pause at the top for a stronger contraction.
Lie on your back with knees bent and let both knees fall to one side so the hips are turned and the shoulders stay flat. Place both hands lightly behind the head.
Exhale and curl the shoulders straight up toward the ceiling, bringing the ribs toward the top hip. Pause, then lower slowly. Complete reps and switch the knees to the other side.

The range is short; focus on squeezing the side waist. Do not pull on the neck. Keep the hips and knees still on the floor. A side-lying version (lying fully on one side and side-bending up) works the obliques with even less range.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart. Extend the arms straight overhead in line with the ears, one hand on top of the other.
Keeping the arms beside the ears, exhale and curl the head and shoulders off the floor. Pause, then lower slowly with control.
Arms overhead lengthen the lever and make the crunch harder than with hands at the head. Do not swing the arms forward to help. Keep the neck neutral between the arms. Hold a light plate to progress.
Lie on your back and raise both legs straight up toward the ceiling, feet together, so the hips are bent about 90 degrees. Reach the arms straight up toward the toes.
Exhale and curl the shoulders off the floor, reaching the fingertips toward the toes. Lower the shoulders slowly and repeat without lowering the legs.
Keep the legs vertical and still. Reach up, not forward. Bend the knees slightly if the hamstrings are tight. Keep the chin slightly tucked. Hold a light plate or ball to progress.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell on the chest with the arms crossed over it, or hold it with straight arms above the chest.
Exhale and curl the shoulders off the floor, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis. Pause briefly at the top and lower slowly.

Choose a load that allows full, controlled reps. Holding the weight with straight arms or overhead increases difficulty. Do not jerk the weight up. Keep the low back on the floor and the neck neutral.
Sit on a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees and hook the feet under the pads. Lie back with hands across the chest or lightly behind the head.
Exhale and curl the upper back off the bench, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis. Pause, then lower slowly to just short of the bench.
This is a crunch, not a sit-up, so stop when the shoulder blades clear the bench. The decline adds resistance. Increase the decline or hold a plate to progress. Keep the neck neutral.
Sit on an exercise ball and walk the feet forward until the low back and mid back rest on the ball, feet flat and wider than hip-width. Hands behind the head or across the chest.
Let the upper back extend over the ball to stretch the abs, then exhale and curl up until the abs are fully shortened. Lower slowly back over the ball.
The ball allows a bigger range of motion than a floor crunch, including slight spinal extension. Keep the feet wide for balance. Keep the ball still. Hold a plate on the chest to add load.
