Attach a rope to a high pulley. Kneel facing the stack about an arm's length away and hold the rope ends beside the head or forehead, hips slightly back so the cable pulls upward.
Keeping the hips still, exhale and curl the trunk down, bringing the elbows toward the mid-thighs by flexing the spine. Pause, then return slowly to the start without letting the stack touch down.

Flex the spine; do not just hinge at the hips or pull with the arms. Keep the hands fixed at the head. Use a weight that allows a full squeeze. Round the back fully at the bottom and avoid sitting back onto the heels.
Attach a rope (or two D-handles) to a high pulley. Stand facing away from the stack, feet shoulder-width, knees soft, holding the rope ends beside the head with the cable running over the shoulders.
Keeping the hips still, exhale and crunch the rib cage down toward the pelvis by flexing the spine. Pause, then return slowly to upright without arching back.
Avoid sitting back or pulling with the arms; the hands stay fixed by the head. Exhale fully at the bottom. A good option when kneeling is uncomfortable. Use a lighter load than the kneeling version.
Attach a rope to a high pulley and kneel facing the stack, holding the rope ends beside the head as for a cable crunch.
Exhale and crunch down while rotating, bringing one elbow toward the opposite knee. Return slowly to upright. Alternate sides or complete all reps on one side.
Rotate the rib cage, do not just drop one arm. Keep the hips fixed. Use less weight than a standard cable crunch.
Adjust the seat so the chest pad or handles sit at the upper chest or shoulders when seated. Sit tall with the feet secured under the rollers and grip the handles.
Exhale and curl the trunk forward, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis against the resistance. Pause, then return slowly without letting the stack slam.
Drive with the abs, not by pulling with the arms or pushing with the legs. Exhale as you crunch. Control the return for full tension. Start light to learn the movement.

Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, slightly wider than hip-width and about 30 cm from the hips. Lift the head and shoulders slightly with arms reaching along the floor toward the feet.
Side-bend at the waist to reach one hand toward the same-side heel, then the other, alternating while keeping the shoulders off the floor. Continue for reps or time.
Keep the shoulders lifted the whole set. Move from the side waist, not by swinging the arms. Feet farther away make it harder.
Lie on your back with fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide, and the hips and knees bent about 90 degrees with the feet off the floor.
Exhale and simultaneously curl the shoulders up and draw the knees toward the chest, curling the pelvis off the floor so the elbows and knees meet over the trunk. Lower both ends slowly to the start.
Coordinate both ends of the spine; it combines a crunch and a reverse crunch. Do not let the feet slam down. Keep the movement smooth and controlled. Do not pull on the neck.
Sit on the floor or on the edge of a flat bench, lean back about 45 degrees and support yourself on the hands behind the hips. Lift the feet with the knees bent.
Extend the legs out straight while leaning back slightly, then pull the knees in toward the chest while bringing the chest toward the knees. Repeat for reps.
Keep the feet off the floor throughout. Avoid rounding the low back excessively. Move the hands closer to the hips or cross the arms to increase difficulty.
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet flat, hip-width apart, anchored under a pad or held by a partner if needed. Arms across the chest or fingertips at the temples.
Exhale and curl the head and shoulders up, then continue to sit all the way up until the chest is close to the thighs. Lower slowly, rolling the spine back down one segment at a time.

Curl up segment by segment rather than jerking up with a flat back. Do not pull on the neck. Anchoring the feet increases hip flexor involvement in the second half of the rep. Slow the lowering to add difficulty.
Sit with the soles of the feet together and the knees falling out to the sides (butterfly position). Place an AbMat or folded towel behind the low back to support the lumbar curve.
Lie back over the mat until the hands touch the floor behind the head, then swing the arms forward and sit up until the hands touch the floor beyond the feet. Repeat for reps.

The AbMat increases range of motion and supports the low back. The butterfly position reduces hip flexor involvement compared with a bent-knee sit-up. Use the arm swing for rhythm in conditioning workouts; keep the feet together.
Sit on a decline bench at about 15 to 30 degrees with the feet hooked under the pads. Arms across the chest or fingertips beside the head.
Lower the trunk back with control until the back nearly touches the bench, then exhale and curl up through the spine to upright. Repeat for reps.
Steeper decline equals harder reps. Hold a plate on the chest to add load. Avoid bouncing off the bench. Curl up rather than jerking up with a flat back.
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet anchored under a pad or by a partner. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell on the chest with both hands, or with straight arms above the chest.
Exhale and curl up to a full sit-up, keeping the weight in position. Roll back down slowly, one segment at a time.
Keep the weight on the chest before progressing to straight arms or overhead. Do not bounce off the floor. Use moderate loads for 8 to 15 reps.

Adjust the glute-ham developer so the hips sit just off the back of the pad and the feet are locked under the rollers with the knees slightly bent. Sit upright with the arms crossed or reaching forward.
Lean back with control until the torso is parallel to the floor or the hands touch the floor behind, then kick the knees straight and sit up explosively to touch the footplate. Repeat for reps.

Very demanding on the hip flexors and abs; start with partial range above parallel and build volume slowly over weeks to avoid rhabdomyolysis. Avoid hyperextending at the bottom. Keep the movement controlled.

Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet flat. Have a partner hold behind the calves, or loop a band around the back of the calves anchored in front, so you can pull the heels down and back into the floor.
Actively pull the heels down and back to engage the hamstrings and glutes, then exhale and slowly curl the trunk up as far as possible while maintaining the heel pull. Lower slowly.
Engaging the hamstrings reduces hip flexor involvement through reciprocal inhibition, keeping the work on the abs. Expect a smaller range than a normal sit-up. Move slowly; do not jerk.
Lie on your back with legs straight and together, feet anchored if needed. Arms extended overhead or crossed on the chest.
Exhale and curl the head and shoulders up, then continue to sit up to vertical, reaching toward the toes. Roll back down slowly, one segment at a time.
The hip flexors work hard here; curl the spine rather than jerking up with a flat back. Anchor the feet if needed. Slow the lowering. Bend the knees if the low back is uncomfortable.
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet anchored under a pad or by a partner. Fingertips behind the head or arms crossed on the chest.
Exhale and sit up, rotating at the top to bring one elbow toward the opposite knee. Lower slowly, then alternate sides on the next rep.
Twist through the rib cage at the top, not by yanking the neck or elbow. Keep the movement controlled. Hold a light plate on the chest to progress.
Lie on your back with legs straight and together and arms extended overhead in line with the ears. Lift the arms and legs slightly off the floor to engage the abs.
In one movement, raise the straight legs and torso so the hands reach the toes at the top, balancing on the sit bones in a V. Lower both ends together to the start without resting.
Keep the legs straight and lift the legs and chest at the same speed. Lower with control rather than crashing back. Use tuck-ups or the alternating V-up to scale.
Lie on your back with legs straight and together and arms extended overhead.
Lift one straight leg and the torso together, reaching both hands or the opposite hand to the raised foot. Lower both, then repeat with the other leg.
An easier progression toward full V-ups. Keep the non-working leg hovering just above the floor for extra difficulty. Avoid jerking up. Exhale as you reach.
Lie on your back with legs extended and arms overhead, both hovering slightly off the floor if possible.
Exhale and sit up while drawing the knees to the chest, reaching the arms around or beside the shins at the top while balancing on the sit bones. Extend back out to the start.
A regression of the V-up with a shorter lever. Keep the feet hovering between reps if possible. Control the descent. Squeeze the abs at the top.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, facing a partner or a solid wall about 1.5 to 3 m away, holding a medicine ball at the chest.
Sit up explosively and throw the ball (chest pass or overhead) to the partner or wall at the top. Catch the return and lower slowly with the ball at the chest. Repeat for reps.
Explosive on the way up, controlled on the way down. Use a light ball (2 to 5 kg) you can catch safely. Keep the feet planted. A rebound or wall ball is safest.

Lie on your back with one knee bent (foot flat) and the other leg straight on the floor. Slide the hands, palms down, under the lumbar spine to preserve its natural curve. Elbows can rest on the floor.

Brace the abs without flattening the back and lift the head and shoulders a few centimetres off the floor as one unit, without flexing the neck or the lumbar spine. Hold 8 to 10 seconds, lower, and repeat. Switch the bent leg halfway through.

Part of the McGill Big 3 for low-back health; spinal flexion is minimal. Imagine the head resting on a scale and lift just enough to lighten it. Progress by lifting the elbows off the floor or adding deep breaths during the hold, not by curling higher.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in one hand at the side with a neutral grip, arm straight. Place the other hand on the hip or behind the head.

Lean sideways toward the weight, sliding it down the outside of the leg, then contract the opposite-side obliques and quadratus lumborum to pull the trunk back to upright and slightly past. Complete reps and switch sides.
Bend straight sideways; do not lean forward or rotate. Hold only one weight, as two dumbbells counterbalance each other. Use moderate loads and controlled tempo.
Stand side-on to a low pulley, holding a single D-handle in the near hand, feet hip-width.
Allow the cable to pull you into a side bend, then contract the far-side obliques to pull upright and slightly past center. Complete reps and switch sides.
Keep the hips over the feet; move only at the waist. Keep the arm straight. Provides constant tension unlike the dumbbell version.
Lie sideways on a 45-degree back extension bench with the side of the hip on the pad and the feet secured, top foot in front of the bottom foot. Hands across the chest or behind the head.
Lower the torso sideways toward the floor, then side-bend back up past horizontal using the upper obliques. Complete reps and switch sides.
Move in a pure side bend, not twisting. Hold a plate to the chest to progress. Control the stretch at the bottom.
Lie on your back with legs straight and together, arms by the sides or hands under the hips. Press the low back into the floor.
Keeping the legs straight, raise them until they are vertical, then lower slowly until the heels hover just above the floor. Repeat without resting.
Stop the lowering before the low back arches off the floor. Bend the knees to shorten the lever if needed. Avoid swinging.
Lie on your back with knees bent about 90 degrees and feet just off the floor, arms by the sides, palms down.
Draw the knees toward the chest, then lower until the heels lightly tap the floor, keeping the low back down.
A regression of the straight-leg raise. Exhale as the knees come in. Keep a slow tempo. Curl the tailbone slightly off the floor at the top for a stronger ab contraction.
Lying Leg Raise to Hip Raise
Lie on your back with arms by the sides and legs straight and raised to vertical.
Press the arms into the floor and lift the hips straight up toward the ceiling, keeping the legs vertical. Lower the hips, then lower the legs to just above the floor and raise them back up.
Lift the hips by curling the pelvis, not by swinging. Keep the legs straight throughout. Do the hip lift alone if the full combo is too hard.
Lie on a flat bench with the hips near the end, gripping the bench behind the head. Legs straight out from the bench.
Raise the legs to vertical, curling the hips slightly off the bench at the top, then lower until the legs are just below bench level.
The bench allows a larger range than the floor. Keep the low back pressed down during lowering. Bend the knees to scale.
Lie face up on a decline bench set at about 15 to 30 degrees with the head at the high end, gripping the handles or the bench behind the head. Legs straight and together, extended down the bench.

Exhale and raise the straight legs to vertical, then curl the hips and low back off the bench at the top by tilting the pelvis toward the ribs. Lower slowly, uncurling the hips first, until the legs are just above bench level. Repeat without resting the feet.

The decline adds range and resistance; a steeper angle is harder. Control the lowering and avoid swinging the legs. Keep the upper back flat on the bench and hold the handles firmly. Bend the knees to scale.

Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder-width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Pull the shoulders slightly down away from the ears (active hang) and keep the legs together and still.

Exhale and draw the knees up toward the chest, then keep going by curling the pelvis up and back so the low back rounds and the knees rise above hip height. Pause for a second, then lower slowly over 2 to 3 seconds to a full, still hang.

Curl the pelvis rather than just lifting the thighs; lifting only to 90 degrees of hip flexion is mostly hip flexor work. Kill any swing before the next rep, using the lats to press the bar slightly down. Use ab straps if grip fails first. Progress to straight-leg hanging leg raises.

Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder-width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight, shoulders actively pulled down. Legs straight and together, slightly in front of the body to remove swing.

Keeping the knees locked, exhale and raise the legs until they are at least parallel to the floor, ideally higher, curling the pelvis up at the top so the low back rounds. Lower slowly over 2 to 3 seconds to a still hang.

The ab work comes from posteriorly tilting the pelvis; raising straight legs only to parallel with a flat back is largely a hip flexor exercise. Avoid swinging; press the bar slightly down with straight arms to stabilize. Master hanging knee raises first; tight hamstrings will limit how high you go.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder-width, arms straight and shoulders active. Legs together.
Exhale and raise the knees up and toward one side, rotating and side-bending the pelvis so the knees travel toward one armpit. Pause, lower slowly to a still hang and alternate sides.

Twist and curl the pelvis rather than just swinging the knees sideways. Control the descent to avoid swinging; bend the elbows slightly and engage the lats if the body starts to swing. Use ab straps if grip limits the set. Progress toward hanging windshield wipers.

Attach two padded ab straps to a pull-up bar about shoulder-width apart and place the upper arms in the slings so the body hangs from the elbows, forearms holding the straps. Shoulders pulled down, legs together.
Exhale and draw the knees up toward the chest, curling the pelvis up so the low back rounds at the top. Pause, then lower slowly to a straight, still hang.

Removing grip as a limiting factor lets the abs reach fatigue. Do not swing or kick. Keep the shoulders depressed rather than sinking into the straps. Progress to straight legs or hold a dumbbell between the feet once knee raises are easy.

Stand on the steps of a captain's chair (vertical knee raise station), back flat against the pad, forearms on the arm pads with elbows under the shoulders, gripping the handles. Step off and let the legs hang straight.
Exhale and bring the knees up toward the chest, curling the pelvis up so the hips lift slightly off the back pad at the top. Pause, then lower slowly to a full hang.

Keep the back against the pad and avoid swinging the legs. Press down through the forearms so the shoulders do not shrug. Lifting only to 90 degrees of hip flexion is mostly hip flexors; the curl at the top trains the abs. Hold a dumbbell between the feet to progress.
Position yourself on a captain's chair with forearms on the arm pads, elbows under the shoulders, gripping the handles, back flat against the pad and legs hanging straight.
Keeping the legs straight, exhale and raise them to at least parallel to the floor, curling the pelvis at the top. Lower slowly to a full hang.

Harder than the knee raise version because of the longer lever. Control the lowering. Do not lean the torso back away from the pad to cheat. Bend the knees slightly if tight hamstrings limit the range.
Set up on a captain's chair with forearms on the arm pads, elbows under the shoulders, gripping the handles, back against the pad, legs hanging together.
Exhale and raise the knees up and toward one shoulder, rotating the pelvis. Pause, lower slowly and alternate sides.

Rotate the pelvis rather than leaning the upper body. Keep a controlled tempo and pause at the top for a strong contraction. Keep the shoulders down away from the ears and press firmly into the arm pads.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight and shoulders active. Legs together.

Press down on the bar with straight arms (engaging the lats), tilt the pelvis under and raise the legs until the toes touch the bar between the hands. Lower with control to a hang. In CrossFit-style workouts a kip from the shoulders links reps; strict reps start from a dead hang.

Strict versions demand strong abs and good hamstring flexibility. Pushing the bar down with the lats shortens the distance and adds control. Keep the legs as straight as possible. Use knees-to-elbows or hanging knee raises to scale.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder-width or slightly wider, arms straight and shoulders active.
Press the bar down with straight arms, curl the pelvis up and raise the knees up and in until they touch the elbows. Lower slowly, or cycle reps with a controlled kip in conditioning work.
Pulling down on the bar with the lats shortens the distance. Control the swing. A stepping stone to toes-to-bar. Start with strict, controlled reps before adding a kip.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder-width and raise the straight legs up toward the bar so the body is in an inverted pike (toes near the bar).
Keeping the legs together and straight, rotate them side to side like a windshield wiper to about 45 to 90 degrees each way. Return to centre between sides and continue alternating.
Highly advanced; master toes-to-bar first. Keep the arms straight and shoulders engaged. Use bent knees or a smaller arc to scale. Move slowly and control the momentum at each end.
Lie on your back with arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms down, and legs raised straight up to vertical with the feet together.
Lower the legs slowly to one side, stopping a few inches before they touch the floor, then use the obliques to bring them back to centre and lower to the other side. Continue alternating.
Keep both shoulders pinned to the floor; the opposite shoulder lifting means the range is too big. Bend the knees to 90 degrees to scale. Control the range to keep tension on the obliques.
Lie on your back with legs straight and together, hands under the hips or by the sides. Press the low back into the floor and lift the heels about 15 cm off the floor.
Kick the legs up and down in small, quick, alternating movements of about 15 to 20 cm, keeping the knees straight and the toes pointed. Continue for reps or time.
Keep the low back pressed into the floor; raise the legs higher if it arches. Smaller, controlled kicks are better than big swings. Lift the head and shoulders slightly to engage the upper abs.
Lie on your back with hands under the hips or by the sides. Press the low back into the floor and lift both straight legs about 15 cm off the floor.
Open the legs slightly, then cross one leg over the other, open again and cross with the other leg on top, alternating in a horizontal scissoring motion. Continue for reps or time.

Keep the low back flat; raise the legs higher if the back arches. Keep the legs straight and toes pointed. Differs from flutter kicks in that the legs move side to side rather than up and down, adding inner-thigh work.

Lie face up on a flat bench and grip the bench edges or a fixed post behind the head. Roll up so only the upper back and shoulders rest on the bench, with the body straight and vertical above you, legs together.

Keeping the body rigid and straight from shoulders to toes, lower the legs and hips slowly toward the bench, pivoting only at the shoulders, stopping just above the bench. Raise the straight body back to vertical with control.

Very advanced; the hips must stay extended. If they bend, regress. Keep the weight on the upper back, never on the neck. Progress via the negative and tuck versions. The lats and abs hold the body rigid against a long lever.
Lie on a flat bench and grip it behind the head. Swing or tuck up to the vertical top position with the body straight and supported on the upper back.
Lower the straight body as slowly as possible, 3 to 5 seconds, toward the bench, then tuck the knees and roll back up to the top to repeat.
Focus on a slow, controlled eccentric. Keep the hips extended and body straight. Stop the rep if the hips pike. Builds strength for the full dragon flag.
Lie on a flat bench and grip it behind the head. Lift into the top position with the knees bent and tucked, supported on the upper back.
Lower the bent-knee body toward the bench with control, keeping the hips in line with the torso. Return to the top.
Keeping the knees bent shortens the lever. Do not let the hips bend. Progress to extending one leg. Keep the weight on the upper back, never on the neck, and grip the bench firmly.

Kneel on a mat with knees hip-width, holding the handles of an ab wheel on the floor under the shoulders, arms straight. Tuck the pelvis slightly and pull the ribs down so the back is neutral to slightly rounded.

Brace and roll the wheel forward slowly, letting the hips and shoulders open together until the body is almost parallel to the floor, arms overhead. Pull back to the start by contracting the abs and lats, keeping the arms straight.

Keep the pelvis tucked and ribs down; stop the rollout before the low back sags. Exhale on the way back. Roll toward a wall to limit range when starting out. One of the highest rectus abdominis activation exercises available.
Stand with feet hip-width, bend forward and place the ab wheel on the floor in front of the feet, arms straight.
Roll the wheel forward until the body is nearly parallel to the floor, then pull it back to the feet without bending the knees.
Extremely advanced; only attempt after full kneeling rollouts are easy. Keep the hips and spine neutral to slightly flexed. Use a wall to limit range when progressing.
Kneel on a mat with knees hip-width, holding an ab wheel on the floor under the shoulders with straight arms.
Roll the wheel out diagonally toward one side, about 30 to 45 degrees from centre, then pull back to centre. Alternate sides each rep.
Keep the hips square and the rib cage down. Shorten the range to keep control. Master the straight kneeling rollout before adding the diagonal path, and exhale as you pull back.
Load a barbell with round plates of the same size (smaller plates give more range) and kneel behind it, gripping it shoulder-width with an overhand grip and straight arms, shoulders over the bar.
Roll the barbell forward, extending the body until it is nearly parallel to the floor, then pull back to the start using the abs and lats, arms straight.
Works like an ab wheel with a wider, more stable base. Keep the pelvis tucked to protect the low back. Smaller plates allow a greater range. Use a collar to stop plates rolling off.
Kneel on a mat in front of an exercise ball (55 to 65 cm) with knees hip-width, and place the forearms (easier) or fists (harder) on top of the ball. Tuck the pelvis slightly.
Roll the ball forward, extending the hips and arms together until the body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Pull the ball back with the abs and lats to the start.
An easier rollout because the ball is high. Keep the low back from sagging. Progress from forearms to fists, then to an ab wheel. Exhale as you roll back.

Lie on your back with arms reaching straight up over the shoulders and the hips and knees bent 90 degrees, knees stacked over the hips (tabletop). Exhale fully to press the low back gently into the floor and keep the ribs down.

Slowly extend one arm overhead toward the floor and the opposite leg out straight until the heel hovers just above the floor, stopping before the low back lifts. Return to the start and alternate sides. Move at about 2 to 3 seconds each way.

Keep the low back in contact with the floor throughout; shorten the range if it arches. Exhale as you extend. Move slowly and pause at the end of each rep. Scale by moving only the legs or only the arms.

Lie on your back holding a dumbbell or kettlebell with both hands straight above the chest, or a dumbbell in each hand. Hips and knees bent 90 degrees over the hips. Press the low back into the floor.

Keep the weight still and extend one leg toward the floor until the heel hovers, then return and extend the other. Alternatively, with a dumbbell in each hand, lower the opposite arm and leg together.
The weight adds an anti-extension challenge. Keep the low back pressed down. Start light and progress slowly.
Anchor a resistance band low behind the head. Lie on your back and hold the band with both hands, arms straight over the chest. Hips and knees bent 90 degrees, low back flat.
Pull the band down toward the hips with straight arms and hold that tension, then extend one leg toward the floor and return, alternating legs.
Pulling the band engages the lats and increases core tension. Keep the low back flat. Use a band that lets you hold the arms still.
Quadruped Opposite Arm and Leg Raise
Start on all fours with hands directly under the shoulders and knees under the hips, hip-width apart. Back flat (neutral), neck in line with the spine, eyes on the floor.

Brace lightly and extend one arm forward and the opposite leg back until both are parallel to the floor, arm at head height with the thumb up and the heel pushing back. Hold 8 to 10 seconds (McGill) or 2 to 3 seconds for reps, return the knee and hand without touching down and repeat, then switch sides.

Part of the McGill Big 3; trains the spinal erectors and multifidus with low spinal load. Keep the hips level; do not rotate or arch the back to lift the leg higher. Make a fist and squeeze the glute to increase tension. Scale by moving only a leg or only an arm.

Set a cable at chest height with a single D-handle. Stand side-on to the stack, feet shoulder-width, knees soft, holding the handle at the sternum with both hands interlocked. Step away until there is tension in the cable.

Brace and press the handle straight out from the chest until the arms are fully extended, resisting the cable's pull to rotate you toward the stack. Hold for 2 to 3 seconds, then bring it back to the sternum. Complete reps and switch sides.

The hips and shoulders stay square to the front throughout; the challenge is anti-rotation. Step farther from the stack for more resistance. Keep the hands in line with the sternum. Exhale as you press.

Set a cable at chest height. Kneel side-on to the stack with the inside knee (closest to the stack) down and the outside foot forward, front shin vertical, down knee directly under the hip. Hold the handle at the sternum with both hands.
Brace and press the handle straight out, hold for 2 to 3 seconds resisting rotation, then return to the sternum. Complete reps and switch sides.
The kneeling stance reduces help from the hips. Squeeze the down-leg glute. Keep the torso tall and the hips square.
Set a cable at chest height. Kneel on both knees (pad underneath) side-on to the stack, knees hip-width, hips extended so they are stacked under the shoulders. Hold the handle at the sternum.
Brace and press the handle straight out, hold for 2 to 3 seconds resisting rotation, then return to the sternum. Complete reps and switch sides.
The narrow base makes rotation harder to resist. Squeeze both glutes. Keep the hips stacked under the shoulders. Use a lighter load than the standing version.

Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack in a split stance, feet hip-width apart laterally and one foot about a stride ahead of the other, weight even, front knee over mid-foot. Hold the handle at the sternum.

Press the handle out slowly, hold for 2 seconds at full extension resisting rotation, then return under control. Complete reps, switch sides, and train both the inside-leg-forward and outside-leg-forward stances.
Keep weight evenly distributed between both feet. Do not let the front knee cave. Keep the hips and shoulders square.
Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack, feet shoulder-width, holding the handle at the sternum with both hands.
Press the handle straight out, then raise it overhead with straight arms and hold briefly. Lower to chest height and return to the sternum. Complete reps and switch sides.
The overhead position adds an anti-extension challenge. Keep the ribs down. Use a light load. Return the handle along the same path rather than letting it drift toward the stack.
Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack, feet shoulder-width, and press the handle out to arm's length in line with the sternum.
Hold the extended position for time, resisting rotation, then return the handle to the chest and switch sides.
Keep the hands in line with the sternum. Breathe behind the brace. Start with 10 to 20 second holds per side and build to 30 to 45 seconds before adding load.
Anchor a resistance band at chest height to a rack or sturdy post. Stand side-on to the anchor, feet shoulder-width, holding the band at the sternum with both hands, stepping away until it is taut.
Brace and press the band straight out, hold for 2 to 3 seconds resisting rotation, then bring it back to the sternum. Complete reps and switch sides.
Step away from the anchor to increase tension. Keep the hips and shoulders square. A great home or warm-up alternative to the cable version; use a thicker band to progress.
Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack, feet hip-width, and press the handle out to arm's length in line with the sternum.
Side-step away from the stack with short, deliberate steps while keeping the arms extended and the trunk square, hold briefly at the farthest point, then side-step back. Switch sides.
Resistance increases as you step farther. Keep the arms straight and centred. Do not let the feet cross.
Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack, feet shoulder-width, and press the handle out to arm's length.
Rotate the trunk away from the stack with straight arms, then return to centre with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Rotate from the trunk, not just the arms. Keep the hips stable. Control the return. Use a light load and keep the eyes following the hands.

Set a cable pulley at its highest position with a single D-handle or rope. Stand side-on to the stack, feet a little wider than shoulder-width, knees soft, and grip the handle with both hands above the near shoulder, arms extended.

Pull the handle diagonally down across the body toward the outside of the opposite hip or knee, rotating the trunk and pivoting the back (inside) foot. Return slowly along the same path. Complete reps and switch sides.
Rotate through the trunk and hips together and pivot the back foot. Keep the arms long. Control the return.
Set a cable pulley at its lowest position. Stand side-on to the stack, feet a little wider than shoulder-width, and grip the handle with both hands near the outside of the inside knee.
Drive through the legs and pull the handle diagonally up across the body to above the opposite shoulder, rotating the trunk. Return slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.
Drive with the legs and rotate through the trunk. Keep the arms straight. Avoid rounding the back at the bottom.
Set a cable at chest height. Stand side-on to the stack, feet shoulder-width, gripping the handle with both hands at arm's length in front of the chest.
Rotate the trunk away from the stack, pulling the handle horizontally across the body. Return slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.
Keep the arms straight and the hips stable. Rotate from the trunk. Use a moderate load.
Set a cable high with a rope or chop bar. Kneel side-on to the stack, inside knee up and outside knee down. Grip the rope with both hands above the inside shoulder.
Pull the rope to the chest first, then press it down and across the body toward the outside hip. Return slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.
The kneeling stance removes leg drive. Keep the torso tall. Control the return.
Set a cable low with a rope or chop bar. Kneel side-on to the stack, inside knee down and outside knee up. Grip the rope with both hands near the inside hip.
Pull the rope to the chest first, then press it up and across the body to above the outside shoulder. Return slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.
Keep the hips square. Avoid leaning back. Control the descent. Keep the head neutral.
Stand with feet a little wider than shoulder-width, holding one dumbbell by its ends with both hands. Start with the dumbbell above one shoulder, arms nearly straight, trunk rotated toward that side.

Squat slightly and rotate the trunk, bringing the dumbbell diagonally down across the body to outside the opposite knee, pivoting the back foot. Reverse the path under control to the start. Complete reps and switch sides.

Pivot the back foot so the knee and hip turn together and the knee is not twisted. Keep the arms long and the back flat at the bottom. Use a light to moderate dumbbell; the free weight has no resistance at the top of the arc, unlike a cable.
Stand with feet a little wider than shoulder-width, holding a medicine ball with both hands above one shoulder, arms nearly straight.

Rotate the trunk and bend the knees, bringing the ball diagonally down across the body to outside the opposite knee. Stand tall as you return the ball along the same path. Complete reps and switch sides.
Keep the arms long and rotate through the trunk and hips together, pivoting the back foot. Keep the back flat at the bottom. A light ball allows faster, more athletic reps.
Sit on the floor with knees bent about 90 degrees, heels on the floor or lifted. Lean back to about 45 degrees with a long, neutral spine and clasp the hands in front of the chest.
Rotate the trunk to one side, bringing the hands beside the hip, then rotate to the other side. Continue alternating for reps or time.
Rotate from the rib cage, moving the shoulders with the hands, not just swinging the arms. Keep the chest lifted rather than slumping. Keep the feet on the floor to scale; lift them to progress.

Sit on the floor with knees bent about 90 degrees, lean back to about 45 degrees with a long spine, and hold a medicine ball (or plate or dumbbell) at the chest with both hands. Feet on the floor or lifted.
Rotate the trunk to one side, touching the ball to the floor beside the hip, then rotate through centre to the other side. Continue alternating for reps or time.
Keep the spine long. Rotate the shoulders with the ball. Use a lighter ball if form breaks or the low back rounds.

Load one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or wedge it in a corner. Stand facing the anchor, feet shoulder-width or slightly wider, holding the free end of the bar with both hands interlaced, arms extended in front of the face.
Keeping the arms straight, rotate the bar in an arc down to one hip, pivoting the opposite foot, then drive it back up over centre and down to the other hip. Continue alternating for reps.

Brace the abs and move the bar smoothly rather than swinging it. Pivot the back foot to protect the knee and spine. Keep the arms straight. Start light; the load increases with the distance from the anchor.

Load one end of a barbell in a landmine. Kneel facing the anchor in a half-kneeling stance (one knee down, the other foot forward, front shin vertical), holding the end of the bar with both hands, arms extended in front of the face.
Rotate the bar in an arc from one hip to the other while keeping the hips square. Continue alternating for reps.
Kneeling removes lower body assistance. Keep the arms straight. Stop the arc at the hip and squeeze the glute of the down leg throughout. Start light.
Sit or kneel in a rotary torso machine with the chest against the pad, knees or legs secured by the pads, and grip the handles. Set the start angle to a comfortable range.
Rotate the torso against the resistance through a comfortable range, then return slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.
Control the range and avoid using momentum. Keep the chest in contact with the pad. Exhale as you rotate. Start light to find a pain-free range.
Stand side-on to a solid wall about 1 to 2 m away, feet a little wider than shoulder-width, knees soft. Hold a medicine ball (2 to 6 kg) with both hands at the hip farthest from the wall.

Load the back hip, then rotate explosively, driving from the back foot and hip through the trunk, and throw the ball against the wall at about chest height. Catch the rebound and reset before the next rep. Complete reps and switch sides.
Power comes from the hips and legs, not the arms. Use a soft or rebound-safe ball. Reset between reps for maximal power.
Set up on a 45-degree or horizontal back extension bench with the top of the pad just below the hip crease and the heels secured under the rollers. Cross the arms over the chest.
Raise the torso until the body is in a straight line from head to heels and hold for time. Lower slowly when finished.
Avoid overarching past straight. Squeeze the glutes. Hold a plate to progress. Keep the neck neutral and gaze at the floor.
Lie face down on a mat with arms extended overhead, palms down, and legs straight and hip-width apart. Rest the forehead on the mat with the neck neutral.

Squeeze the glutes and lift the arms, chest and legs a few inches off the floor at the same time. Hold for two to five seconds or for the prescribed time, then lower slowly back to the mat and repeat.
Lift by squeezing the glutes and back muscles, not by craning the neck; gaze at the floor. Do not overarch; a few inches is enough. Scale by lifting only the arms or only the legs.
Lie face down on a mat with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Lift the arms, chest and legs slightly off the floor into a superman position.

While holding the lifted position, flutter the arms and legs by raising the right arm and left leg higher, then switching to the left arm and right leg in a swimming rhythm. Continue for reps or time and lower to rest.
Keep the neck neutral and eyes down. Keep the movements small and controlled rather than flailing. Rest the torso on the floor between sets if the low back fatigues.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart holding a heavy kettlebell or dumbbell in one hand at the side, arm straight. The other arm hangs free or rests on the hip.
Brace the trunk and hold the weight for the prescribed time while staying perfectly upright, resisting the pull to lean toward the weight. Set the weight down with a hinge and switch hands.
The obliques on the opposite side work hardest to stop the lean. Keep the shoulders level and packed down. Pick up and set down the weight with a neutral spine.
Deadlift a heavy kettlebell or dumbbell to the side in one hand, standing tall with the shoulders level and the free arm relaxed or out to the side.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps for the prescribed distance or time, keeping the torso vertical and resisting any lean toward the weight. Set it down, switch hands and repeat.
Do not lean away from or toward the weight; stay stacked. Keep the shoulder packed and grip hard. A dumbbell, kettlebell or single trap bar handle all work.
Place the hands on parallettes, dip bars or yoga blocks beside the hips. Press down to straighten the arms and lift the body so it is supported only by the hands.
Raise the straight legs together until they are parallel to the floor, forming an L shape. Hold for the prescribed time, then lower the feet to the floor or the bars to finish.
Lock the elbows and push the shoulders down away from the ears. Point the toes and squeeze the quads. Scale with the tuck L-sit or one leg extended.
Place the hands on parallettes, yoga blocks or the floor beside the hips, fingers forward, and sit with the knees bent.
Press down through straight arms to lift the hips and feet off the floor, drawing the knees tight to the chest. Hold for the prescribed time, then lower with control.
Keep the arms straight and the shoulders depressed. Lean slightly forward to balance. Progress by extending one leg at a time toward a full L-sit.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand, shoulder-width grip, arms straight and shoulders slightly engaged. Legs together.
Raise the straight legs until they are parallel to the floor, forming an L, and hold for the prescribed time. Lower the legs slowly back to a still hang.
Engage the lats to prevent swinging. Keep the legs straight and toes pointed. Bend the knees to 90 degrees to scale, or extend one leg at a time.
Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold the arms out in front at shoulder height or grip the backs of the thighs.
Lean back slightly and lift the feet, straightening the legs so the body forms a V balanced on the sit bones. Hold for the prescribed time, then lower the feet to the floor.
Keep the chest lifted and the spine long, not rounded. Keep the legs straight and together. Scale by bending the knees with the shins parallel to the floor.
Lie on your back with arms extended overhead beside the ears and legs straight together. Press the low back firmly into the floor.

Lift the arms, head, shoulders and legs a few inches off the floor so the body forms a shallow banana shape with only the low back touching. Hold for the prescribed time while breathing steadily, then lower.
The low back must stay glued to the floor; raise the legs higher if it lifts. Point the toes and squeeze the legs together. Scale with bent knees or arms by the sides.
Lie on your back and set up a hollow body hold: low back pressed down, arms overhead, legs straight and lifted a few inches.
Keeping the hollow shape rigid, rock the body back toward the shoulders and forward toward the hips like a rocking chair. Continue for reps or time, then lower.
The shape must not change; the rocking comes from momentum, not from bending at the hips. Keep the ribs down. Scale with bent knees or arms by the sides.

Lie on your back on a mat. Bring the legs to tabletop (hips and knees at 90 degrees) or extend them at about 45 degrees. Curl the head and shoulders up so the eyes look toward the navel, arms straight by the sides and hovering a few inches off the mat.
Pump the straight arms up and down in small, brisk beats of about 15 cm. Breathe in for five pumps and out for five pumps; ten full breath cycles make 100 pumps. Lower the head and legs to finish.
Keep the low back down. Keep the neck relaxed. Bend the knees to scale. Reach the fingertips long and keep the arm pumps small and brisk.
Lie on your back on a mat with legs straight together and arms extended overhead. Flex the feet and draw the abs in.
Bring the arms to the ceiling, curl the head and shoulders up and continue rolling up one vertebra at a time, reaching forward over the legs. Reverse the movement, rolling down slowly to the start.
Move slowly and articulate through the spine instead of jerking up. Keep the legs on the mat. Bend the knees or hold a band around the feet to scale.
Lie on your back on a mat with the legs extended at about 45 degrees and arms reaching overhead.
Reach the arms forward and roll up through the spine into a V balance with the arms parallel to the legs. Hold briefly, then roll down slowly with control, keeping the legs lifted.
Avoid jerking up; use the abs to articulate through the spine. Keep the legs still. Scale by bending the knees or keeping one foot on the mat.
Lie on your back on a mat with the head and shoulders lifted. Draw one knee toward the chest and extend the other leg at about 45 degrees.
Place the outside hand on the bent ankle and the inside hand on the knee. Switch legs, pulling the other knee in and extending the first leg, alternating in a steady rhythm.
Keep the trunk still and the low back pressed into the mat as the legs move. Exhale on each switch. Raise the extended leg higher to scale.
Lie on your back on a mat with the knees pulled to the chest, hands on the shins, and the head and shoulders lifted.
Inhale and extend the arms overhead and the legs out at about 45 degrees at the same time. Exhale, circle the arms out and around, and pull the knees back in to the chest.
Keep the low back down and the head lifted throughout. Reach long through the arms and legs. Raise the legs higher to scale.
Lie on your back on a mat with hands behind the head, elbows wide, and knees in tabletop. Lift the head and shoulders.
Rotate the trunk to bring one elbow toward the opposite knee while extending the other leg long. Switch sides, alternating slowly and holding each rotation for a moment.
Rotate from the rib cage, not by pulling the elbow forward. Keep the elbows wide and the pelvis still. Move slower than a bicycle crunch.
Lie on one side on a mat with legs straight and stacked, bottom arm extended along the floor or forearm on the floor for support, top hand lightly behind the head with the elbow pointing up.

Exhale and simultaneously lift the top of the trunk and both legs off the floor by side-bending, bringing the top elbow toward the hip and legs. Pause, then lower both ends slowly. Complete reps and switch sides.

Lift the legs together; do not swing them. Keep the body in one plane rather than rolling forward or back. Keep the head neutral and do not pull on the neck. Scale by lifting only the legs or only the trunk.

Bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, toes out 10 to 15 degrees. Wide overhand hook grip so the bar sits in the hip crease when standing. Hips above the knees, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar, arms long, elbows turned out, back flat, breath held.

Push the floor away with a constant back angle until the bar passes the knees, then sweep it into the thighs. At the hip crease extend hips, knees and ankles explosively, shrug and pull under with high outward elbows. Feet move to squat stance as the arms punch to lockout in a full overhead squat, bar over the back of the neck. Stand, then lower to the hips and floor.
Bar brushes the hip, never bumped forward. Lock out as the feet land; never press out. Scale with hang or power snatches.

Identical start to the full snatch: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip that puts the bar in the hip crease, hips above the knees, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar, back flat and lats tight. Breathe in and brace before the bar leaves the floor.

Lift the bar smoothly past the knees with a constant back angle, then extend explosively at the hip crease and pull under. The feet move slightly outward to the receiving stance and the arms lock out with the bar over the back of the neck, received in a partial squat with the thighs above parallel. Stand to full extension, then lower to the hips and floor.

Same pull as the full snatch, only a higher catch: the extra height must come from a more powerful extension. Land flat-footed and absorb the weight in the legs. Fault: wide 'frog' landing or pressing out the lockout.

Deadlift the bar to standing with a wide overhand hook grip (bar in the hip crease). Push the hips back with a slight knee bend until the bar sits just above the knees (mid-hang): shins about vertical, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar, weight over the mid-foot, back flat, lats pressing the bar into the thighs.

From a brief pause or a smooth countermovement, drive through the legs and extend the hips so the bar slides up the thighs to the hip crease. Finish the extension, then pull under with high outward elbows into a full overhead squat, feet landing in squat stance. Stand up and return the bar to the hang for the next rep.

Keep contact with the thighs; do not swing the bar away with the hips or lean back to finish. A pause in the hang removes the stretch reflex and builds position. Teaches the second pull and turnover speed.

Stand tall with a wide overhand hook grip so the bar sits in the hip crease. Hinge with soft knees until the bar is just above the knees: shins vertical, shoulders slightly in front of the bar, back flat, lats engaged and arms long with the elbows turned out.

Drive the legs and extend the hips explosively, bringing the bar into the hip crease. Shrug and pull the elbows high and outside, turning the bar over, then punch under and lock the arms out in a partial squat with thighs above parallel. Stand fully with the bar over the back of the neck, return it to the hips and reset.

Bar contacts the hip crease, not the mid-thigh. Feet move from pulling to receiving stance quickly and land flat. Popular power exercise for athletes; reduce load as soon as the arms start pressing out.

Wide overhand hook grip. Stand tall, then unlock the knees and slide the bar to the upper thigh or hip crease (the power position): torso nearly vertical, shoulders over the bar, knees bent about 20 to 30 degrees, weight balanced over the mid-foot, arms straight.

Make a short dip of the knees, then drive vertically through the legs and hips to finish the extension, and immediately pull yourself under with high outward elbows into a full overhead squat, feet landing in squat stance. Stand up, lower to the hip position and repeat.

Minimal dip, maximal leg drive; the hips should not swing forward into the bar. Elbows stay over the bar until extension finishes. Use it to train an aggressive, fast pull under with a short pulling distance.

Lift the bar from the floor with a wide overhand hook grip, then lower it to just below the kneecaps: hips high, shoulders in front of the bar, shins slightly angled forward, back flat and lats pressing the bar back. Hold the position for a second to set it.

Push the knees back as the bar rises so it passes them close, then let the knees move forward under the bar as it sweeps into the thighs. Extend explosively at the hip crease and pull under into a full squat catch. Stand, lower back to the low hang and repeat.

Keep the back angle from the hang until the bar clears the knees; do not let the hips shoot up. Bar stays tight to the legs through the transition. Builds positional strength and patience in the scoop.

Set the bar on lifting blocks, typically at one of three heights: below the knee, at the knee or above the knee (mid-thigh). Take a wide overhand hook grip, set the back flat, shoulders slightly in front of the bar and the bar touching the legs where it would be at that point of a normal snatch. Pull the slack out of the bar before it leaves the blocks.

Break the bar from a dead stop with leg drive, keep it close, extend aggressively at the hip crease and pull under into a full overhead squat. Stand up, then lower the bar onto the blocks under control or drop it onto the platform and reset it on the blocks.
No stretch reflex, so build full-body tension first. Lower blocks emphasise the transition, higher blocks speed under the bar. Fault: jerking the bar off the blocks or starting with loose arms.

Bar resting on blocks, most often at or just above the knee. Wide overhand hook grip, shins near vertical, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar, back flat and lats pressing the bar toward the legs. Take the slack out of the bar and brace.

Break the bar from the blocks with the legs, accelerate it into the hip crease and extend fully, then pull under and lock out overhead in a partial squat with the thighs above parallel. Stand fully, then return the bar to the blocks or drop and reset.

Tension first, then speed. Removes the first pull so athletes with poor timing from the floor can focus on the finish. Land flat-footed in the receiving stance; reduce load if the catch drops below parallel.
Wide overhand snatch grip (hook grip optional), bar starting at mid-thigh or the floor. Back flat, shoulders over the bar, arms long with the elbows turned out.

Extend the hips and knees fully, rising onto the balls of the feet. Keep the legs straight (no rebend) and continue pulling with the elbows moving high and outside, then rotate the arms around the bar and press it in a smooth arc to lockout over the back of the neck, without dropping under. Lower to the hips with control.

The feet stay in place (the heels may rise as you extend) and the knees do not rebend to catch. Bar stays close to the body as it turns over; elbows high before rotating. Use light loads to teach the turnover path and strengthen the top of the pull.

Take the bar out of a rack onto the upper traps behind the neck with a snatch-width overhand grip. Feet in the pulling stance, about hip width, weight on the whole foot, torso upright and trunk braced.

Make a short, controlled dip and drive just enough to unweight the bar, then push yourself down under it, moving the feet out to the squat stance and locking the arms at the same moment, sinking into a full-depth overhead squat with the bar over the back of the neck. Stand up and return the bar to the rack.
Speed and commitment downward, not a press out. Feet and lockout land together. Teaches the snatch receiving position under load; scale with the pressing or heaving snatch balance.

Bar on the upper traps behind the neck with a snatch-width overhand grip. Feet already set in the squat (receiving) stance, about shoulder width with toes slightly out, since they will not move. Torso upright and trunk braced.

Dip a few inches and drive the bar upward off the shoulders with the legs, then aggressively punch the body down under the bar into a full overhead squat, locking the arms as you descend. The feet stay planted. Stand up and return the bar to the rack.

Feet stay put, so all speed comes from the drive and the punch under. Drive the bar, do not simply drop. Builds aggressive arm lockout and confidence; it sits between the pressing and full snatch balance in difficulty.
Bar on the upper traps behind the neck with a snatch-width overhand grip. Feet together or in the pulling stance (hip width), standing tall with the trunk braced. No dip will be used.

With no dip or leg drive, pull and push yourself down beneath the bar as fast as possible, moving the feet out to the squat stance and locking the arms at the same moment, catching in a full overhead squat. Stand up and return the bar to the rack.
Purely a speed-under drill: the bar should barely move upward. Feet and lockout land together. Differs from the snatch balance by having no drive at all; keep loads light and technique crisp.
Bar on the upper traps behind the neck with a snatch-width overhand grip. Feet set in the squat stance, toes slightly out. Torso tall, trunk braced, elbows under the bar.

Slowly press yourself down under the bar: the bar stays at roughly the same height while the body sinks, so the arms push up against it until they reach lockout at the bottom of a full overhead squat. Stand up with the bar overhead and return it to the rack.

The bar stays in place while the body moves down; do not press the bar up away from you. Arms push against the bar the whole time. A beginner drill for overhead position, mobility and the feel of pushing under.

Take the bar from a rack, then press or jerk it overhead from behind the neck with a wide snatch grip. Lock the elbows, push up into the bar with the shoulders active (armpits facing forward) and position the bar over the back of the neck and mid-foot. Feet in the squat stance, about shoulder width, toes out 15 to 30 degrees.

Brace and squat straight down with an upright torso, knees tracking over the toes, keeping the bar balanced over the mid-foot, to full depth (hips below knees). Drive up to standing while pushing up into the bar. Return the bar to the back rack or drop it safely forward.
Push the bar up and slightly back. If the bar drifts forward the torso is collapsing. Scale with a PVC pipe, a wider grip or the pressing snatch balance if mobility limits depth.
Take the bar from a rack onto the upper traps behind the neck with a snatch-width overhand grip. Feet hip width, weight on the whole foot, torso upright and trunk braced.

Dip straight down 3 to 4 inches by bending the knees, then drive the legs explosively and press the bar to lockout as it leaves the shoulders, finishing over the back of the neck without rebending the knees. Hold briefly, then lower the bar to the traps by bending the elbows and absorb it with a slight knee bend.

Dip straight down with the torso upright and the whole foot flat; the knees travel forward over the toes while the chest and bar stay over the mid-foot. Finish the drive before the arms take over. Builds lockout strength and overhead stability for the snatch; distinct from the heaving snatch balance because you stay standing.
Set up exactly as for the snatch: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip, hips above the knees, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar, back flat and lats tight.

Pull with the same positions and speed as the snatch: constant back angle to the knees, bar swept into the thighs, then an explosive extension of hips, knees and ankles finishing with a shrug, arms kept straight. Lower the bar back to the floor under control.
Match competition snatch positions exactly; do not bend the arms or lean back. Usually loaded at 90 to 120 percent of the snatch. Straps are fine for higher-volume sets.
Snatch Grip High Pull from Floor
Same start as the snatch: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip, hips above the knees, shoulders slightly in front of the bar and back flat.

Pull as in the snatch through full extension and shrug, then continue upward with the arms, driving the elbows high and outside so the bar rises close to the body to about lower-chest height. Lower under control to the hips and then to the floor.
Extend first, then pull with the arms. Elbows lead and stay above the wrists, bar stays close. Teaches the transition into the pull under; keep loads light enough to finish with height.
Snatch start position: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip, back flat, shoulders slightly in front of the bar and lats tight.

Lift until the bar is just above the knees with the shoulders still over or in front of the bar, shins about vertical, and hold that position for 2 to 3 seconds. Then lower back to the floor, or (common variation) continue to standing after the pause.
Shins near vertical and back angle unchanged at the halt. Weight balanced across the whole foot, not on the toes. Excellent for fixing hips that rise early or a bar that drifts forward.
Stand on a 1 to 4 inch plate or riser so the bar starts lower. Wide overhand hook grip, hips lower than normal, shoulders slightly in front of the bar, back flat and lats tight.

Pull with full snatch speed and positions: constant back angle past the knees, bar swept into the thighs, then full extension and shrug with the arms straight. Lower the bar back to the platform under control.
The longer range makes it harder to hold the back angle; do not let the hips rise first. Builds strength and position off the floor. Use straps only when grip limits the set.
Normal snatch start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip, back flat, shoulders slightly in front of the bar.

Lift the bar to the chosen pause point, usually just below or just above the knee (or mid-thigh), and hold for 2 to 3 seconds with the correct back angle and the bar against the legs. Then accelerate from the pause into a full snatch, catching in the bottom of the overhead squat and standing up.
Hold the correct position, not the comfortable one. Keep full tension in the pause. Loads are lower than the regular snatch, usually 60 to 80 percent.
Set up for a snatch but place the feet in the receiving squat stance (about shoulder width, toes out) from the start. Wide overhand hook grip, bar over the mid-foot, back flat.
Perform the snatch while keeping the feet flat on the platform throughout: lift, extend, and pull under into a full overhead squat without lifting or moving the feet. Stand up and lower the bar.

Teaches vertical extension and staying connected to the platform. Any jump forward or back shows a horizontal bar path. Use moderate weights; the wider stance makes the first pull feel slightly different.
Stand fully extended with flat feet (or up on the balls of the feet) in the pulling stance, holding the bar at the hip crease with a wide snatch grip and long arms.

With no dip or leg drive, pull the elbows high and outside to lift yourself down, turning the bar over and moving the feet out to the receiving stance. Lock the arms as the feet land, in a full overhead squat. Stand and reset at the hips.
A pure pull-under drill: speed comes from the arms and the feet. Keep the bar close and do not hop it up. Keep loads very light; it isolates the third pull.
Standard snatch start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, wide overhand hook grip, back flat, shoulders slightly in front of the bar.

Pull as in the snatch, then receive the bar in a split: front foot forward with the shin roughly vertical, back knee bent with the heel up, feet about hip width apart side to side, arms locked overhead. Recover by stepping the front foot back half way, then the back foot forward, and lower the bar.
The traditional style, useful for lifters lacking overhead squat mobility. Split depth comes from the front leg, not a long stride. Recover front foot first so the bar stays balanced.

Bar locked overhead with a wide snatch grip after a press or jerk from behind the neck, shoulders active and bar over the back of the neck. Feet in the squat stance, about shoulder width, toes out, trunk braced.

Squat under control to full depth and hold the bottom for 2 to 5 seconds, keeping the bar balanced over the mid-foot and the arms pushing up. Drive up to standing without letting the bar drift forward. Return the bar to the back rack.
Stay tight in the pause; do not relax into the bottom. Push up into the bar the whole time. Builds strength and confidence in the snatch receiving position; start with an empty bar.

Bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, toes out 10 to 15 degrees. Pronated hook grip about one thumb length outside the legs. Hips slightly lower than in the snatch, shoulders over or just ahead of the bar, arms long, back flat, chest up, breath held.

Push the floor away with a constant back angle until the bar passes the knees, then sweep it into the upper thighs. Extend hips, knees and ankles explosively, shrug and pull under, whipping the elbows around so the bar lands on the front of the shoulders, elbows high, in a full front squat. Stand up, then lower the bar to the hips and floor.
Fast elbows so the bar does not crash on the chest. Keep the bar close. Fault: early arm bend or reverse curl; scale with hang or power cleans.

Pronated hook grip about one thumb length outside the legs, bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, hips slightly above the knees, shoulders over or just in front of the bar, back flat and lats tight. Breathe in and brace.

Lift the bar past the knees with a constant back angle, sweep it into the upper thighs and extend explosively. Shrug and pull under, turning the elbows forward so the bar lands on the shoulders in a partial squat with thighs above parallel, feet moving slightly out to squat stance. Stand fully, then lower to the hips and floor.
Land flat-footed and absorb the bar; do not catch with straight legs. Elbows high and fingers relaxed in the rack. Never reverse-curl the bar; a staple power exercise for athletes in all sports.

Deadlift the bar to standing with a clean-width overhand hook grip. Push the hips back with a slight knee bend until the bar is just above the knees: shins vertical, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar, back flat, lats pressing the bar into the thighs.

Drive through the legs and extend the hips so the bar slides up to the upper thigh, shrug and pull under into a full front squat, elbows whipping through fast and high. Stand up and return the bar to the hang for the next rep.
Bar stays against the thighs during extension; do not swing it away with the hips. Pause in the hang to remove the stretch reflex. Builds timing, the second pull and turnover speed.

Stand tall with a clean-width overhand hook grip. Hinge with soft knees to bring the bar just above the knees: back flat, shins vertical, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar, arms long and lats engaged.

Extend explosively through the hips and knees, bringing the bar to the upper thighs. Shrug and pull the elbows up and around, catching the bar on the shoulders in a partial squat with thighs above parallel and elbows pointing forward. Stand fully, lower the bar to the hips and repeat.
Elbows point forward and upper arms near parallel to the floor in the catch. Keep the bar close, not looping out. Popular for athletes; reduce the load before technique breaks into a reverse curl.

Clean-width overhand hook grip. Bar at the upper thigh or hip crease (the power position): torso nearly vertical, knees bent about 20 to 30 degrees, shoulders over the bar, weight balanced over the mid-foot, arms straight.

Make a short dip, drive vertically through the legs and hips to finish the extension, then pull yourself under and receive the bar on the shoulders in a full front squat with fast elbows. Stand and lower the bar to the hip position.
Short dip, violent extension; do not swing the hips into the bar. Elbows whip through quickly. Develops speed under the bar with the shortest pulling distance.

Lift the bar from the floor with a clean-width overhand hook grip, then lower it to just below the kneecaps: hips high, shoulders in front of the bar, back flat, lats pressing the bar back. Hold briefly to set the position.

Keep the back angle as the bar rises past the knees, let the knees move forward under the bar as it sweeps into the thighs, then extend and pull under into a full front squat. Stand and return to the low hang.
Maintain the back angle as the bar passes the knees; do not rush to the hip. Bar stays tight to the legs. Strengthens the transition (scoop) and patience in the pull.

Bar resting on blocks at the chosen height (below the knee, at the knee or above the knee). Clean-width overhand hook grip, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar, back tight, bar in the position it would occupy at that point of a normal clean. Pull the slack out of the bar first.
Lift from a dead stop, accelerate through full extension and pull under into a full front squat with fast elbows. Stand up and return the bar to the blocks or drop it and reset.
Build tension before the lift since there is no stretch reflex. Choose block height to target the weakness. Fault: yanking the bar off the blocks with bent arms.

Bar on blocks at or just above the knee. Clean-width overhand hook grip, shins near vertical, shoulders slightly in front of the bar, back flat and lats pushing the bar back toward the legs. Take the slack out of the bar and brace.

Drive with the legs, extend the hips explosively and pull under, receiving the bar on the shoulders in a partial squat above parallel with elbows high. Stand fully and return the bar to the blocks or drop and reset.
Removes the first pull so athletes can focus on explosive extension. Land flat-footed in the receiving stance. Elbows forward and high in the catch; useful for field and court athletes.
Clean-width overhand grip (hook grip optional), bar at mid-thigh or on the floor, arms long, back flat and shoulders over the bar.

Extend the legs and hips completely, rising onto the balls of the feet, with no rebend of the knees. Keep pulling with the elbows moving high and outside, then whip the elbows around and forward to place the bar on the front of the shoulders without dropping under. Lower to the hips with control.

The feet stay in place (the heels may rise as you extend) and the knees stay straight after extension. Bar stays close to the body. Teaches the turnover and strengthens the upper-body pull; use light loads.
Stand fully extended with flat feet in the pulling stance, holding the bar at the hip crease with a clean-width overhand grip and long arms.

With no leg drive, pull the elbows high and outside to pull yourself down, moving the feet to the squat stance and whipping the elbows through so the bar meets the shoulders as you sink into a full front squat. Stand and reset at the hips.
A pull-under speed drill: do not jump or dip first. Elbows come around quickly so the bar lands softly. Use very light weights and focus on foot speed.
Set up exactly as for the clean: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, hips slightly above the knees, shoulders over or just ahead of the bar, back flat.

Pull with clean positions and speed: constant back angle past the knees, bar swept into the upper thighs, then fully extend the hips, knees and ankles and finish with a shrug, arms straight. Lower the bar to the floor under control.
Match clean positions exactly; do not bend the arms early or lean back. Usually loaded at 90 to 120 percent of the clean. Straps allowed when grip limits volume.
Standard clean start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, back flat and shoulders slightly in front of the bar.

Pull through full extension and shrug, then continue with the arms, driving the elbows high and outside so the bar travels close to the body up to about the lower chest or sternum. Lower under control to the hips and floor.
Extend first, arms second; the arms only continue what the hips started. Elbows lead and stay above the wrists. Keep loads light enough to show real height.
Clean start position: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, back flat and shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar.
Lift until the bar is just above the knees and hold for 2 to 3 seconds with the shoulders still over the bar and shins vertical. Lower back to the floor, or finish to standing after the pause.
Shins vertical and back angle unchanged at the halt. Balance over the mid-foot. Fixes hips rising early; lower with the same control as the lift.
Stand on a 1 to 4 inch plate or riser with a clean-width overhand hook grip. Hips lower than normal, shoulders over or just in front of the bar, back flat and lats tight.
Pull with full clean speed and positions through extension and shrug, arms straight. Lower back to the platform under control.
Keep the back angle constant off the floor; do not let the hips shoot up. The extra range builds strength off the floor. Use straps only if grip limits the set.
Normal clean start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, back flat, shoulders over or just in front of the bar.

Lift to the pause point, usually just below or just above the knee, and hold 2 to 3 seconds with the correct back angle and the bar against the legs. Then accelerate into a full clean, receiving in a front squat, stand and lower.
Hold the right position with full tension, then stay close to the legs after the pause. Use lighter loads than the full clean, typically 60 to 80 percent. Count the pause aloud to keep it honest.
Set the feet in the receiving squat stance (about shoulder width, toes out) from the start. Clean-width overhand hook grip, bar over the mid-foot, back flat.
Perform the clean while keeping the feet flat on the platform: lift, extend and pull straight down into a full front squat without lifting or moving the feet. Stand and lower the bar.
Teaches vertical extension and staying connected to the floor; no jumping. Moderate loads. Elbows still need to be fast.
Standard clean start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, back flat.

Pull as normal, then receive the bar on the shoulders in a split: front foot forward with the shin about vertical, back knee bent with the heel up, feet hip width apart laterally, elbows high. Recover by stepping the front foot back half way, then the back foot forward, and lower the bar.
Front shin vertical, back knee soft and under the hip. Useful for lifters with limited squat mobility or as a variety drill. Recover front foot first.
Clean start: bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand hook grip, hips slightly above the knees, shoulders over or just ahead of the bar, back flat and lats tight.

Clean the bar into a full front squat and stand up. Reset: release the hook, adjust to a jerk grip (often slightly wider), feet hip width, breathe and brace. Dip 10 percent of height straight down, drive explosively and punch under, usually into a split, locking the arms. Recover to the feet in line with the bar locked overhead, then lower to the shoulders, hips and floor.
Breathe and reset between the clean and the jerk. Vertical dip and drive with weight balanced, heels down until the drive. Scale with a power clean and push jerk.
Bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, clean-width overhand grip, hips slightly above the knees, back flat and shoulders over the bar.

Power clean the bar to the front of the shoulders, stand tall and reset the grip so the forearms are vertical. Squeeze the glutes, brace, and strictly press the bar overhead with no leg drive, moving the head back then through so the bar finishes over the mid-foot. Lower to the shoulders, then to the hips and floor.
The press is strict: knees stay locked. Do not lean back excessively; ribs stay down. Scale by switching to a push press.
Bar over the mid-foot, feet hip width, double overhand grip just outside the legs (or mixed grip for the first stage), back flat. A belt is usually worn to give the bar a shelf.

Deadlift the bar to the thighs, then bend the knees and lean back so the bar rides up onto the belt or stomach. Re-grip overhand if needed, dip again and drive the hips forward to roll the bar up the torso onto the front of the shoulders, elbows coming through. Lower back to the belt, thighs and floor.
Accepted in strongman axle and log events where a full clean is too heavy or the axle does not rotate. Keep the bar touching the body throughout. Fault: curling with the biceps.
Clean-width overhand grip, bar at mid-thigh to just above the knee in a hang: knees slightly bent, hips back, shoulders just in front of the bar, back flat, arms long.

Explode upward through the legs and hips so the feet leave the floor slightly, shrugging the shoulders hard toward the ears with the arms kept straight. Land softly on the balls of the feet with bent knees, return the bar to the hang and reset.
Arms stay straight: no pulling. Full extension of hips, knees and ankles is the goal. A teaching and power drill for athletes learning the clean; loads typically 40 to 80 percent of the power clean.

Bar in the front rack on the shoulders with a full grip about one fist outside shoulder width, elbows slightly in front of the bar, feet hip width, weight on the whole foot, torso upright and breath held.

Dip straight down about 10 percent of height, drive hard through the legs, and as the bar leaves the shoulders punch under it, splitting the feet: front foot steps forward so the shin is vertical, back foot steps back onto the ball with the knee soft, arms locked overhead with the bar over the back of the neck. Recover front foot back half way, then back foot forward. Lower to the shoulders.

Dip straight down with the torso upright and the whole foot flat; the knees travel forward over the toes while the chest and bar stay over the mid-foot. Lock out at the moment the feet land. Front foot slightly turned in, back foot slightly turned in, hip width apart for balance.
Bar in the front rack with a full or fingertip grip just outside shoulder width, elbows slightly forward, feet hip width, torso upright and braced.

Dip straight down a few inches and drive explosively, then push yourself under the rising bar with the feet staying in place (or barely moving), re-bending the knees to catch with locked arms in a partial squat. Stand fully with the bar over the back of the neck, then lower to the shoulders, absorbing with the legs.

Feet stay planted; that is what distinguishes it from the power jerk. Distinct from the push press because you re-bend the knees and catch under the bar rather than pressing it out. Drive the bar, then punch down.
Bar in the front rack, hands just outside the shoulders, elbows slightly forward, feet in the pulling stance (hip width), torso upright and braced.

Dip and drive, then jump the feet out to the squat stance (about shoulder width) and punch under the bar, locking the arms in a partial squat with thighs above parallel. Stand with the bar over the back of the neck and lower to the shoulders.
Feet land flat and slightly wider at the same time as the lockout. Do not press out. Useful when split stability is poor or as a power variation with a shorter drop than the split jerk.
Bar in the front rack with a jerk-width grip, feet hip width, torso upright and braced.

Dip and drive, then punch under the bar, moving the feet to the squat stance and locking the arms while descending into a full overhead squat with a narrow jerk grip. Stand up with the bar locked overhead and lower to the shoulders.
Demands outstanding shoulder and ankle mobility and an upright overhead squat with a narrow grip. Lock out before descending far. Advanced lifters only; practise narrow-grip overhead squats first.
Take the bar from a rack onto the upper traps behind the neck with a jerk-width (or slightly wider) overhand grip. Feet hip width, torso upright, trunk braced.

Dip straight down and drive the bar off the back, then split the feet and punch under to lock out over the back of the neck. Recover front foot back half way, then back foot forward. Lower the bar to the upper traps under control.
