Removes the front rack so the bar path is straight up and the head does not need to move. Head neutral. Great for teaching the lockout position and split timing.
Take the bar from a rack onto the upper traps behind the neck with a jerk-width or snatch-width overhand grip. Feet hip width, torso upright, trunk braced.

Dip and drive the bar off the back, then push yourself under it into a partial squat with arms locked over the back of the neck, feet staying in place. Stand fully and lower the bar back onto the traps with control.
Easy way to learn the drive and punch without the head getting in the way. Keep the elbows under the bar. Needs good shoulder mobility; start light.

Bar in the front rack with a full grip just outside the shoulders, forearms close to vertical, elbows slightly in front of the bar. Feet hip width, weight on the whole foot, glutes tight, trunk braced.

Dip 3 to 4 inches at the knees with an upright torso, then drive the legs explosively and press the bar to lockout as it leaves the shoulders, moving the head back slightly then forward 'through the window' so the bar finishes over the back of the neck. The knees do not re-bend. Lower back to the shoulders, absorbing with a slight knee bend.

Dip straight down with the torso upright and the whole foot flat; the knees travel forward over the toes while the chest and bar stay over the mid-foot. Leg drive starts the bar, arms finish it. Overloads the press by 20 to 30 percent; the bridge between the strict press and the jerk.
Take the bar from a rack onto the upper traps behind the neck with a jerk-width or slightly wider overhand grip. Feet hip width, torso upright, trunk braced.

Dip straight down a few inches and drive with the legs, then press the bar from behind the neck to lockout over the back of the neck without re-bending the knees. Lower back to the traps under control.
Bar path is shorter and straighter than from the front. Requires good shoulder external rotation. Strong jerk-assistance exercise; lower the bar slowly to protect the neck.
Take the bar from a rack into the front rack with a jerk grip, elbows slightly forward, feet hip width, torso vertical, weight on the whole foot with the heels down.
Dip straight down about 10 percent of height (a quarter squat), pause briefly, then drive back up to standing at controlled or fast speed. The bar does not leave the shoulders. Rack after the set.
Heavy loads (often above the jerk max) build trunk stability and the dip position. Knees push forward and out over the toes while the chest stays up. Fault: hips sliding back and the chest dropping.
Take the bar from a rack into the front rack with a jerk grip, feet hip width, torso upright and trunk braced.

Dip straight down a few inches, then drive explosively to full extension onto the balls of the feet, letting the bar pop slightly off the shoulders, and absorb it back into the rack position with soft knees. Reset and repeat.
Trains the drive in isolation. Keep it vertical and finish with straight legs and the bar travelling straight up. Loads often 90 to 110 percent of the jerk.

Bar in the front rack with a jerk grip. Feet in a short split: back foot already at its split position on the ball of the foot, front foot about one third of the way forward, weight mostly on the front foot.

Dip and drive the bar upward, then step the front foot forward into the full split position while punching the bar to lockout overhead; the back foot stays put. Hold, recover front foot back then back foot forward, and lower to the shoulders.
Teaches an aggressive forward step of the front foot. Torso stays vertical so the bar travels straight up. Light loads; the front foot lands flat with the shin vertical.

Set the bar on high rack pins at about forehead height. Step under it into a split stance and press or push it up a few inches to lockout, so the bar is overhead with the arms locked and the feet split.

Hold the split position with the bar locked overhead for 2 to 5 seconds, then recover by stepping the front foot back half way and the back foot forward. Hold again with feet together, then lower to the pins.
Builds confidence and stability in the split with loads near or above the jerk max. Arms straight, shoulders active, bar over the back of the neck. Use safety pins and progress cautiously.
Bar on jerk blocks or rack pins set just below shoulder height. Step under it into the front rack with a jerk grip, stand up and step back if needed, feet hip width.
Perform a split, push or power jerk, then lower the bar back to the blocks (or drop it onto them if they are built for it) and reset the rack position for the next rep.
Removes the clean so jerks can be trained in volume and at heavier loads. Reset the grip and rack each rep. Saves the shoulders from lowering heavy loads repeatedly.

Dumbbell on the floor between the feet, feet hip to shoulder width. Squat and hinge to grip the handle with one hand in an overhand grip, back flat, chest up, shoulder over the dumbbell, free arm out for balance.

Drive through the legs and hips, keep the dumbbell close to the body, shrug and pull the elbow high, then in one motion punch it overhead to lockout, receiving in a partial squat. Stand fully, then lower to the shoulder and hip and back to the floor, or hinge it back to the start.
Hips and legs do the work, not the arm. Lock the elbow without pressing out. Alternate arms each rep or switch at the floor; keep the back flat on the way down.
Stand holding one dumbbell at arm's length with an overhand grip in front of the thigh. Hinge with soft knees to bring it just above the knee, back flat, shoulders over the dumbbell.

Extend the hips explosively, shrug, pull the elbow high and turn the wrist over, punching the dumbbell to lockout overhead in a partial squat. Stand fully, then lower it to the shoulder and back to the hang.
Keep the dumbbell close to the body. Finish the hip extension before the arm pulls. Scale with the dumbbell high pull.
Two dumbbells on the floor outside the feet (or hanging beside the thighs), neutral grip, feet hip width, hips hinged, back flat and shoulders over the dumbbells.

Extend the hips and knees explosively, shrug and pull with high elbows, then drop slightly and rotate the elbows forward to receive the dumbbells on the front of the shoulders, heads resting on the deltoids, in a partial squat. Stand, then lower back to the start.
Rest the dumbbells on the shoulders, not just in the hands. Avoid curling them up; the hips create the height. Good alternative to the barbell clean.
Stand with dumbbells at the sides in a neutral grip. Hinge with soft knees to bring them just above the knees, back flat and shoulders over the weights.
Extend the hips and knees explosively, shrug and pull, then rotate the elbows forward catching the dumbbells on the shoulders in a quarter squat. Stand fully and lower to the hang.
Fast elbows. Keep the dumbbells close to the thighs. Do not reverse-curl the weight.
Single Arm DB Clean and Jerk
Dumbbell on the floor between the feet or beside one foot, one hand gripping the handle in a neutral grip, back flat, hips hinged, free arm out for balance.

Clean the dumbbell to the shoulder with hip drive, receiving it in a partial squat with one head resting on the shoulder. Stand, then dip and drive and punch under to jerk it to lockout. Stand fully, lower to the shoulder and then to the floor.
Drive with the legs, not the arm. Keep the trunk square to avoid twisting. A common CrossFit competition movement; switch hands at the floor.
Hold the dumbbells at the shoulders with a neutral or overhand grip, elbows slightly forward, feet hip width, torso upright and trunk braced.

Dip a few inches straight down, drive the legs and press the dumbbells to lockout overhead without re-bending the knees, finishing over the shoulders. Lower to the shoulders, absorbing with a slight knee bend.

Dip straight down with the torso upright and the whole foot flat; the knees travel forward over the toes while the chest and bar stay over the mid-foot. Keep the ribs down at lockout. Single-arm versions add an anti-lateral-flexion demand on the obliques.
Dumbbells at the shoulders in a neutral grip, elbows forward, feet hip width, torso upright and braced.
Dip and drive, then re-bend the knees to drop under the dumbbells, catching them with locked arms in a quarter squat. Stand fully and lower to the shoulders.
Punch under the weight, do not press it out. Land with stable, flat feet. Keep the dumbbells stacked over the shoulders and mid-foot.
One or two dumbbells at the shoulders in a neutral grip, elbows forward, feet hip width, upright torso and braced trunk.
Dip and drive, then split the feet front and back while punching the dumbbells to lockout. Recover front foot back half way, then back foot forward, and lower to the shoulders.
Front shin vertical, back knee soft. Lock out as the feet land. A lighter teaching version of the barbell split jerk; single-arm versions add anti-rotation demand.
Dumbbell held at the hang just above the knee or between the feet, overhand grip, back flat, hips hinged and shoulders over the dumbbell.
Extend the hips explosively and shrug, then pull the elbow high and outside so the dumbbell rises close to the body to chest height. Lower under control and repeat.
Hips drive the bell, the arm only finishes. Elbow stays above the wrist. A progression toward the dumbbell snatch; keep the back flat throughout.

Kettlebell on the floor about a foot in front of the feet, feet hip to shoulder width. Hinge with a flat back, shins near vertical, and grip the handle with one hand, thumb pointing back, arm long, shoulder packed.

Hike the bell back high between the thighs, then snap the hips forward so it floats up close to the body. As it passes the chest, pull the elbow back slightly and punch the hand up through the handle so the bell settles softly on the back of the forearm, arm locked by the ear. Pause, then flip it over, let it drop and guide it back between the legs for the next rep.
Punch through early so the bell does not crash on the wrist. Hips drive, the arm only guides. Keep the arc close (no wide swing); use a lighter bell until the lockout is soft.
Kettlebell on the floor a foot ahead of the feet, feet hip to shoulder width. Hinge with a flat back and grip the handle with one hand, arm long.

Hike the bell back and snatch it to lockout overhead, bell resting on the back of the forearm. Instead of dropping it back into the swing, lower it under control to the rack position at the shoulder, then drop it from the rack into the backswing for the next rep.
Saves the grip and shoulder on the descent; a good snatch progression. Lock out with the biceps by the ear. Keep the wrist straight in both lockout and rack.
Kettlebell on the floor a foot ahead of the feet, feet hip to shoulder width. Hinge with a flat back and grip the handle with one hand, thumb pointing back.

Hike the bell back, drive the hips forward and keep the elbow close to the ribs so the bell travels straight up close to the body. Open the hand and slip it around the handle so the bell rolls onto the back of the forearm in the rack: wrist straight, elbow against the ribs, forearm vertical. Drop it back through the legs for the next rep.
Zip the bell up close, like zipping a jacket: no flipping it over the hand. Hand slides around the handle, not over it. Hips finish at the moment the bell lands in the rack.
Two kettlebells on the floor slightly ahead of the feet, feet slightly wider than shoulder width so both bells fit between the legs. Hinge with a flat back and grip both handles, thumbs back.

Hike both bells back, drive the hips forward and clean them to the rack position at the same time, elbows tight to the ribs and bells resting on the outside of the forearms. Drop them back between the legs for the next rep.
The wider stance makes room for both bells and protects the knees. Keep elbows close and wrists straight. Brace the trunk hard in the rack; the double load challenges breathing.
Kettlebell on the floor between the feet, under the mid-foot line. Squat-hinge to grip it with one hand, back flat, shoulder over the bell.

From a dead stop, extend the hips and knees explosively and pull the bell straight up close to the body, slipping the hand around the handle so it rotates onto the forearm in the rack. Lower to the floor under control and repeat without a backswing.
No backswing: all power comes from a dead start. Keep the bell close. A teaching version of the clean and a good option for beginners who struggle with the swing.
One or two kettlebells in the rack position, elbows resting on the hips or ribs, feet hip width, wrists straight, trunk braced.

First dip: bend the knees a few inches and drive explosively onto the toes to bump the bell upward. Second dip: as the bell rises, drop under it again with bent knees and lock the arm out. Then stand fully with the bell overhead and lower it back to the rack.
Two dips: one to drive, one to catch. Arm locks as you land in the second dip, never press out. A core lift of kettlebell sport.
One or two kettlebells on the floor slightly ahead of the feet, feet hip to shoulder width, hinge with a flat back and grip with the thumbs back.

Swing back and clean the bell to the rack, then jerk it overhead with the double dip (drive, second dip under, stand). Fix the lockout, lower back to the rack, then drop into a backswing for the next clean. Repeat continuously for reps or time.
Breathe through each phase: an exhale on every drive. Efficiency over power for long sets. The kettlebell sport competition lift; in competition one bell or two depending on the event.
Kettlebell in the rack at the shoulder, wrist straight, elbow under the bell, feet hip width, torso upright and trunk braced.
Dip a few inches straight down, drive with the legs and press the bell to lockout overhead without re-bending the knees, biceps finishing by the ear. Lower back to the rack under control.
Vertical dip, upright torso. Keep the wrist straight in the rack and at lockout. Pairs well with clean complexes.
Kettlebell on the floor a foot ahead of the feet, hinge with a flat back and grip with one hand (or both hands on one bell).
Hike the bell back, snap the hips and pull the elbow back and up so the bell rises to chest level, elbow above the wrist and close to the body. Let it drop back into the swing and repeat.
Hips do most of the work; the arm finishes the arc. Elbow stays above the wrist. A progression to the snatch; do not shrug the shoulder to the ear.

Atlas stone (spherical concrete stone) between the feet, feet about shoulder width or wider, toes slightly out. Tacky on the forearms and hands, arm sleeves on. Bend over the stone with a rounded upper back, hands reaching under it, fingers spread, forearms hugging the sides.

Pull the stone off the floor and sit back so it rolls into the lap between the thighs. Re-grip higher, squeeze it into the chest, then extend the hips explosively and drive them under the stone, rolling it up the chest onto a platform at chest height (often 48 to 52 inches). Drop the stone back, reset and repeat.
Lap high and squeeze hard before standing. Hips drive through, arms only hold. Keep arms straight off the floor to protect the biceps; learn with a lighter stone.
Atlas stone on the floor between the feet, wide stance, tacky on the forearms, sleeves on, hands spread under the stone with a rounded upper back.
Lap the stone, wrap it into the chest, then extend the hips explosively and roll the stone up the chest and over one shoulder so it drops behind you. Turn, reset and repeat for reps or time.
Throw with the hips, not the arms. Turn the head away to clear the stone. Alternate shoulders to balance the load; keep arms straight off the floor.
Atlas stone on the floor between the feet, wide stance, tacky and sleeves on, hands reaching under and around the stone with a rounded upper back and straight arms.
Pull the stone off the ground and sit back so it rolls into the lap with the knees bent and the stone pinned between the thighs and chest. Hold briefly, then lower it to the floor and repeat.
Trains the first phase of the stone load. Keep the stone tight and the arms long. Biceps tears are a known risk: keep the elbows straight off the floor and build volume slowly.
Natural (irregular) stone on the floor between the feet. Lap the stone with a rounded back and straight arms, re-grip, then stand with it hugged tightly to the chest, arms wrapped under it.

Walk forward with short, quick steps for the set distance or time, keeping the stone pinned high on the chest and leaning back slightly to balance it. Drop or lower the stone under control at the end.
Brace hard and breathe shallow behind the brace. Elbows squeeze in. Build up with sandbags or kegs first.
Triangular Husafell stone (or replica, about 186 kg for the original) on the floor. Lap it, then roll it into the chest with the point down, arms wrapped under and around it, and stand.
Walk forward for distance with short steps, keeping the stone high on the chest and leaning back slightly to balance it. Set it down at the end.
Keep it high to stop the point digging into the abdomen. Lean back just enough to counterbalance. Scale with a sandbag or keg.

Step under the yoke with the crossbar on the upper traps as in a high-bar squat, hands gripping the uprights at about shoulder height, feet under the hips. Breathe in, brace hard and wear a belt for heavy loads.
Stand to lift the yoke a few inches clear of the floor, settle it, then walk forward with short, fast steps for the set distance. Set it down under control by bending the knees.
Keep the uprights still: no swinging side to side. Small quick steps, eyes ahead. Start light and build distance.
Log (about 12 inch diameter with neutral handles inside) on the floor, feet hip width, shins close to the log, neutral grip, back flat. Belt on.

Deadlift the log to the hips, roll it up the torso onto the upper chest with the elbows high and torso leaning back slightly. Re-dip and drive with the legs to push press or jerk it overhead to lockout, head through. Lower it back to the chest, belt and floor.
Lean back at the chest so the log sits over the mid-foot. Drive with the legs on the press. Get the elbows up fast at the end of the clean.
Log on the floor with neutral handles, feet hip width, shins close to the log, back flat and chest up. Wear a belt to give the log a shelf on the stomach.

Deadlift the log to the hips, then squat slightly and roll it up onto the belt. Dip again and drive the hips forward, rolling it up the torso while pulling the elbows up and through so it lands on the upper chest with the elbows high. Lower it back to the stomach, hips and floor.
Use the legs and hips, not the biceps. Keep the log tight to the body. Many lifters re-dip at the belt before the final roll.
Log on rack pins at upper chest height or cleaned to the chest. Neutral grip, elbows high and forward, feet hip width, torso leaning back slightly so the log sits over the mid-foot.
Dip straight down a few inches, drive hard with the legs and press the log to lockout overhead, pushing the head through the window. Lower back to the chest under control and absorb with the legs.
Drive vertically, not forward. Keep elbows high in the dip. Use pins to save energy for the press portion.
Axle bar (2 inch thick, non-rotating) on the floor, feet hip width, double overhand grip just outside the legs, back flat. Belt on.
Clean the axle to the shoulders, usually with a continental clean via the belt, then press, push press or jerk it overhead to lockout. Lower back to the shoulders and the floor.
Thick bar taxes the grip and does not spin, so a full clean is rare. Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows. Use push press timing to move heavy loads.

Farmer handles (loaded steel frames with knurled handles, 1.25 to 2 inch) beside each foot, handles in line with the ankles. Feet hip width. Hinge with a flat back, grip the centre of each handle in a neutral grip, chalk the hands, brace.

Deadlift the handles to lockout, arms straight and shoulders packed down. Walk forward with short, fast heel-to-toe steps for the set distance or time, keeping the handles level and the torso upright. Set them down by hinging, not by dropping the chest.
Grip at the balance point so the front ends do not dip. Short quick steps and steady breathing behind the brace. Scale with dumbbells or kettlebells; straps are allowed in some competitions.

Step inside a carry frame (a rectangular steel frame with long side rails or handles at about mid-thigh height when standing). Stand centred between the handles with feet hip width, hinge with a flat back and grip the handles in a neutral grip at their balance point.
Deadlift the frame to lockout, brace, then walk forward with short, fast steps for the set distance or time, keeping the frame level and still. Lower it under control by hinging back down.
Grip at the balance point so the front does not dip; front-heavy frames demand an upright posture. Do not let the frame swing. Chalk the hands; straps are usually not allowed.

Sandbag on the floor between the feet, stance about shoulder width. Hinge, wrap the arms under and around the bag, lap it onto the thighs, then re-grip and stand with the bag hugged high against the chest, hands clasped or grabbing fabric.
Walk forward for the distance or time with short steps, keeping the bag tight and high on the chest and leaning back slightly to balance it. Drop or lower the bag at the end.
Squeeze the bag high; letting it slide down pulls you into flexion. Breathe shallow behind the brace. Scale with bag weight.
Shoulder the sandbag from the floor onto one shoulder, centred on the top of the shoulder with one or both hands holding it in place. Stand tall, feet hip width, trunk braced.
Walk forward for distance or time with short steps, keeping the torso upright and resisting the pull to side-bend toward the bag. Set the bag down or drop it, and switch shoulders on the next set.
Resist leaning away from or toward the bag. Short steps. Strengthens the obliques and trunk in anti-lateral flexion.
Sandbag on the floor between the feet, stance about shoulder width or wider. Hinge with a rounded or flat back depending on bag size, and wrap the arms under it.

Lap the bag onto the thighs, then extend the hips explosively and pop it up onto one shoulder, turning the head away. Stand fully with the bag balanced on top of the shoulder, then drop it back down in front. Alternate shoulders each rep.
Hips do the work; the arms only guide. Keep the bag close to the body. Alternate sides to keep the work even.
Sandbag on the floor about a step from a platform at hip to chest height, wide stance. Hinge and wrap the arms under the bag.
Lap the bag, hug it to the chest, then extend the hips and roll it onto the platform. Lower or drop it back and repeat, or carry it to the next station in a medley.
Squeeze tight and drive the hips through. Reset each rep. Scale platform height.
Stand facing a bar, yoke crossbar or wall at about chest to shoulder height, with a sandbag on the floor between the feet and a wide stance.
Lap the bag, extend the hips explosively and throw it up and over the bar to the other side, releasing at the top of the drive. Walk around or reach under and repeat for reps or time.
Use the hip snap, not the arms. Release at the top. Choose a bar height you can clear.
Sandbag on the floor between the feet, feet shoulder width. Hinge with a flat back and grip the bag from the sides, underneath, or by its handles.

Extend the hips and knees explosively and pull the bag up close to the body, then drop under and catch it in the front rack or hugged high on the chest. Stand fully, then lower the bag back to the floor.
Keep the bag close. Hip drive over arm pull. Builds power with awkward, shifting loads.
Stand with your back to the bar, keg on the floor between the feet, hands gripping the rims or handles. Feet shoulder width.
Swing the keg between the legs, then extend the hips explosively and swing it up and back over the head, releasing it over the bar behind you. Look up to follow it.
Swing with the hips. Release high, arms straight. Keep clear of the landing zone; start with a light keg and a low bar.
Keg on the floor between the feet. Hinge, wrap the arms around the keg or grip the rims, lift it to the lap and hug it tight to the chest as you stand.
Walk forward for the set distance with short, fast steps, keeping the keg high on the chest. Lower it to the floor or drop it on soft ground at the end.
Squeeze tight and keep the keg high. Brace and breathe shallow behind the brace. Partially fill with water for a sloshing challenge.
Keg on the floor a step away from a platform at hip to chest height. Wide stance, hands gripping the rims or reaching under the keg, back flat.
Lift the keg to the chest, then extend the hips explosively and place or roll it onto the platform. Lower it or retrieve it from the far side, then repeat or move to the next keg in a medley.
Hips do the work, arms only guide. Keep the keg close. Lighter kegs teach timing before adding load.

Large tire flat on the ground. Stand close with feet about shoulder width, toes at or just off the tread. Squat down with the chest pressed into the tire, hips low, back flat, and slide the fingers under the bottom edge with palms up (underhand), hands shoulder width, arms straight.

Drive the legs and hips forward and up into the tire (a forward push, not a vertical deadlift), lifting it to hip height. Drive a knee into it, quickly switch the hands to an overhand position on the tread and push it over with the arms. Walk up and repeat for reps or distance.
Chest into the tire and arms straight; never curl it, as bent-elbow lifts are a common cause of biceps tears. Push forward at about 45 degrees. Scale with a lighter tire.

Stand facing a large tire, about one hammer-length away, with a sledgehammer (equipment: sledgehammer plus tire). Feet shoulder width or in a slight split. Bottom hand at the end of the handle, top hand near the head of the hammer.

Swing the hammer up over the shoulder, sliding the top hand down toward the bottom hand as it comes over the head, then flex the trunk and drive the hammer down to strike the tire. Let the hammer rebound, slide the hand back up and repeat. Switch the hand position and side each set.
Trunk flexion and hips power the strike; the arms guide. Brace hard and keep the feet planted. Use a light hammer first and keep a clear space around the tire.
Sit on a bench or the ground with the feet braced against a block, or stand in a staggered stance. A rope runs from a sled or vehicle, hands overhand on the rope.
Pull the rope hand over hand toward you with powerful, rapid pulls, letting the rope pile behind or beside you until the object reaches the finish line. Reset the rope and repeat.
Short rapid pulls beat long slow ones. Keep the legs braced and the torso still. Gloves protect the hands from rope burn.
Wear a harness attached by a rope to the vehicle, with a driver ready to brake. Lean forward at a low angle, holding a rope or rail for the hands if available.
Drive forward with short, powerful steps until the vehicle starts moving, then keep momentum with fast steps for the set distance. The driver stops the vehicle at the line.
Low body angle and constant leg drive. Do not stop once moving. Always use a driver and a clear, safe course.
Step under the arm of the Conan's wheel and hold it in the crooks of the elbows, Zercher style, with hands clasped. Feet hip width, back flat, trunk braced.
Stand to lift the arm and walk forward in a circle around the pivot, keeping the arm in the elbows, for distance or time. Set it down under control at the end.
Brace the trunk hard and keep the elbows tight to the body. Short, steady steps. Arm pads or sleeves protect the forearms. A Zercher carry can scale it.
Stand between the handles of a car deadlift frame or under a loaded car frame, feet hip width. Grip the neutral handles, back flat, hips slightly higher than a normal deadlift.
Push through the floor and drive the hips forward to lift the frame to full lockout, standing tall. Lower under control. Often performed for reps.
Neutral handles allow heavy loads. Brace hard before each rep. Lower slowly to keep tension for the next rep.
Barbell set at about 18 inches high on blocks or rack pins, usually just above the knees. Feet hip width, double overhand or mixed grip, back flat and lats tight.
Drive the hips forward and pull the bar to full lockout, squeezing the glutes. Lower it back to the blocks under control and reset for the next rep.
Huge loads stress the back, so brace and use a belt. Keep the bar close to the thighs. Builds lockout strength for the deadlift and strongman partials.

Circus dumbbell (oversized, thick-handled dumbbell, handle often 2 to 2.5 inches) on the floor beside or between the feet, or on a low rack. Feet shoulder width, belt on, back flat. One hand on the handle; the free hand may assist on the bell for the clean if the rules allow.

Clean the bell to the shoulder using the hips and, if allowed, both hands, tilting it so the back head rests on the shoulder and the handle points slightly up. Lean the torso slightly away from the bell so the hip on the bell side sits under it, then dip and drive, then push press or jerk it overhead with one arm to a locked elbow, feet planted. Lower to the shoulder and floor under control.

When racked, get the hip under the bell so it sits over your base instead of pulling you sideways. Lock out quickly and stack the bell over the shoulder. The thick, unbalanced bell demands grip and wrist strength; learn with a light bell.

A series of hinged poles of increasing weight and length, each lying on the ground with its base on a hinge. Stand at the free end of the first pole, squat down with a flat back and grip under the end with both hands, palms up.

Deadlift the end to hip height, then drive it up with the legs and press it overhead, walking forward under the pole and pushing hand over hand along it until it passes vertical and falls the other way. Move quickly to the next, heavier pole and repeat.
Hips and legs start the lift, the arms finish it. Keep moving under the pole so it stays over you. Clear the area where the pole will fall and never stand on its far side.

Stand between two heavy pillars that are hinged or set to fall outward. Each pillar has a handle (or chain to a handle) at about hip height. Grip one handle in each hand with a neutral grip, arms extended out to the sides and slightly down, feet hip width, trunk braced.

Once the pillars are released and lean outward, resist their pull with the arms, lats and grip, holding them upright for as long as possible. When grip or shoulders give out, the pillars fall into a catch or onto pads. Release with control.
Keep the shoulders packed down and the elbows straight; the lats do much of the work. Breathe steadily behind the brace. Scale with lighter pillars, cable handles or a farmer-handle hold.

Stand over a duck walk implement (a loaded weight hanging below a single handle) so it sits between the legs. Feet wider than shoulder width, toes out. Hinge with a flat back and grip the handle with both hands, one in front of the other or side by side.

Stand to lift the implement, letting it hang between the legs with arms straight, then walk forward for distance with short, quick, slightly wide steps, keeping it from striking the legs. Set it down under control.
Keep the chest up and the arms long. Small, wide steps prevent the weight swinging into the knees. Wear a belt for heavier implements.

Shield (a large, heavy, flat steel plate, sometimes shaped like a shield) on the floor or a raised platform. Hinge, lift it and hug it vertically against the chest, arms wrapped around the edges or fingers hooked over the top.
Walk forward for distance with short steps, keeping the shield high on the chest and leaning back slightly to balance it. Lower it under control at the end.
Squeeze the shield hard so it cannot slide down. Breathe shallow behind the brace. Keep it high enough to see over. Scale with a heavy sandbag or a stack of plates.

A set of three to five large steps (each about 16 inches high) and implements of 180 to 300 kg with a single handle. Stand on the first step facing up the stairs, with the implement on the ground behind or between the legs, gripping its handle with both hands, arms long, back flat.

Drive the hips forward explosively to lift the implement onto the next step, then step up onto that step and repeat, swinging the implement up step by step until it reaches the top. Lower it back down or repeat with the next implement.
Hips drive the lift; arms stay straight. Keep the rhythm, as stopping wastes momentum. Wear a belt and practise with lighter implements and low steps.
Stand with your back to the bar, holding a weight with a ring or handle (often 56 lb, as in Highland games) in one or both hands. Feet shoulder width, weight hanging between the legs.
Swing the weight between the legs, then extend the hips explosively and swing it up and back over the head, releasing it at the top so it travels over the bar behind you. Look up to follow it.
Hip snap, not arms. Release at the top of the swing. Keep a safe landing area clear. Start with a light weight and a low bar.
Stand between the two Dinnie Stones (or replicas, about 188 kg and 145 kg, roughly 333 kg together) with one ring handle in each hand, overhand grip. Feet hip width, back flat, hips hinged.
Lift both stones off the ground at once, then hold or walk with them for distance. Set them down under control.
Grip strength is key: use chalk. Brace hard before lifting. Build up with heavy farmer handles first. Straps are not allowed in the traditional lift.

Axle bar (2 inch thick, non-rotating) cleaned to the front of the shoulders, usually with a continental clean, or taken from rack pins. Double overhand grip just outside the shoulders, elbows slightly forward, feet hip width, belt on, trunk braced.

Dip straight down 3 to 4 inches, drive the legs explosively and press the axle to lockout, moving the head back then through so the bar finishes over the back of the neck. Knees do not re-bend (re-bending makes it an axle jerk). Lower to the shoulders, absorbing with the legs.

Dip straight down with the torso upright and the whole foot flat; the knees travel forward over the toes while the chest and bar stay over the mid-foot. Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows; the thick bar resists rolling into the fingers. Train push press and strict press with a thick bar or grips to build the event.

Stand tall holding a light implement in each hand (axes, hammers, plates or kettlebells, often 5 to 20 kg) with a neutral grip. Feet hip width, glutes tight, ribs down. On the start command raise both arms straight out to the sides to shoulder height, palms down or thumbs up per the rules.

Hold the arms out at exactly shoulder height, elbows straight, wrists neutral, for as long as possible; a judge or a sensor stops the clock when the arms drop below the line. Lower the implements under control at the end.

Keep the shoulders down and back; do not shrug or lean back to cheat the angle. Breathe slowly behind a light brace. Train with timed lateral-raise holds at shoulder height before using heavy implements.

Log cleaned to the upper chest or taken from rack pins at upper chest height. Neutral grip on the handles, elbows high and forward, feet hip width, glutes squeezed, belt on, torso leaning back slightly so the log sits over the mid-foot.

Without any dip or leg drive, press the log straight up, moving the head back to clear the log and then pushing it forward through the window as the log passes the forehead, to full lockout over the mid-foot. Lower back to the chest under control.

Knees stay locked the entire rep; any dip turns it into a push press. Keep the elbows high under the log so it does not roll forward. Builds pressing strength for log events and is the standard log accessory.

Stand one short step (30 to 45 cm) from a stable plyo box, feet hip-width apart and toes forward, arms relaxed at the sides. Choose a height you can land on with the hips still above the knees (a quarter squat); 20 to 24 in is typical.

Swing the arms back as you dip quickly into a quarter squat with knees over the mid-foot, then reverse at once: drive the arms up and fully extend hips, knees and ankles, tucking the knees to bring the feet onto the box. Land with the whole foot on the box at once, knees tracking over the second toe, then stand tall to finish the rep. Step down one foot at a time and reset.

Land quietly at roughly the same depth you took off from; landing in a deep squat means the box is too high. Step down rather than jump down to limit Achilles and knee load. Keep reps low (3 to 5) and rest so every jump is maximal.

Sit on a bench or low box so the thighs are about parallel to the floor (knees near 90 degrees), feet flat and hip-width under the knees, facing a plyo box set about one step in front. Torso tall, arms hanging at the sides. Use a target box 10 to 20 cm lower than your standing box jump height.

From a dead stop, swing the arms back, lean the chest slightly forward over the knees and explode up off the seat in one movement, without rocking back or bouncing on the bench. Extend hips, knees and ankles, tuck the knees and land with both feet flat on the box in a quarter squat. Stand tall, step down and sit fully back down to reset each rep.

The seated start removes the countermovement, so it trains starting strength and rate of force development from a static position. Do not swing the torso back to build momentum. Reset completely between reps.

Stand on one leg facing a low plyo box (15 to 45 cm, well below your two-leg height), stance foot about 30 cm from the box and pointing forward. The free knee is bent with the foot off the floor, pelvis level, arms ready to swing.

Dip into a quarter single-leg squat with the knee over the middle toes, swing the arms and jump up and forward off the stance leg, landing on the same foot on the box in a balanced quarter squat. Freeze the landing for 1 to 2 seconds with hips level and knee aligned, then step down on both feet. Complete all reps on one side before switching.

No knee caving inward on take-off or landing. Stick every landing before the next rep. Regress to a two-foot take-off with a one-foot landing if you cannot control it. Keep sets short (3 to 5 per leg).

Stand side-on to a plyo box with the near foot about 30 cm from its edge, feet hip-width apart and toes facing forward, in an athletic quarter squat. Use a box 15 to 30 cm lower than your forward box jump height.

Dip and swing the arms, then push off both feet evenly and jump sideways onto the box, landing with both feet flat and hip-width in a quarter squat, knees over the toes and hips square to the front. Stand tall, step down on the far side or back to the start, and alternate the leading side each set.

Take off from both feet, not a step-up with the near leg. Keep the chest and hips facing forward throughout so the hips generate lateral force. Land softly and quietly with knees aligned over the toes.

Face a plyo box (typically 20 in for women, 24 in for men in CrossFit workouts) one short step away, feet hip-width apart. CrossFit standards allow either jumping on and off the far side or clearing it completely; a two-foot take-off is required.

Dip and jump with both feet onto the box, then immediately hop or step off the far side, landing with soft knees. Turn around and repeat in the other direction. In the advanced version, jump over the box without touching it, tucking the knees high and landing on both feet on the far side in a quarter squat.

Use a soft foam box for high-volume work to protect the shins. Land with bent knees, never stiff-legged. Scale by jumping on and stepping down, and only clear the box when the height is easy and you are fresh.
Stand on a box 30 to 60 cm (12 to 24 in) high, toes near the edge, feet hip-width apart, arms at the sides. This is the landing drill to master before depth jumps.

Step off the box with one foot (do not jump up or out) and let both feet land at the same time, hip-width apart. Absorb the impact by hinging the hips back and bending the knees into a quarter-to-half squat, shins angled forward, chest over the knees, arms reaching forward. Freeze in that position for 2 seconds, then stand and reset.

Land forefoot to mid-foot with the heels then lightly touching, quietly. Knees track over the second toe with no valgus collapse, and the trunk stays braced. Lower the box if the heels slam, the knees cave or you cannot freeze the landing.
Stand on a box 30 to 75 cm (12 to 30 in) high with the toes at the edge, feet hip-width apart. Advanced drill: master depth drops, box jumps and pogos first, and keep total contacts low.

Step off the box (no jump up), land on both feet simultaneously on the balls of the feet and rebound immediately into a maximal vertical jump with a fast arm swing, aiming for a ground contact under about 0.25 seconds. Fully straighten the ankles, knees and hips together (triple extension), then land softly from the jump in a quarter squat. Reset and climb back onto the box for each rep.

Treat the floor as hot: minimal time and minimal knee bend on contact. If the heels crash or you sink deep, the box is too high. Use 3 to 5 reps per set with full rest; stop when jump height or contact speed drops.

Set two boxes 60 to 90 cm apart: a drop box 30 to 45 cm high behind you and a target box in front of moderate height. Stand on the drop box with the toes at the edge, facing the target box, feet hip-width.

Step off the drop box, land on both feet between the boxes on the balls of the feet and rebound immediately into a jump onto the target box, swinging the arms forward and up. Land softly with both feet flat in a quarter squat, stand tall, step down and reset on the drop box.
The rebound off the floor is the point, so keep that contact short and stiff. Keep the target box easy so you do not need to sink before jumping. Stop the set when contacts become slow or noisy.
Face a box or step 30 to 45 cm high and place one whole foot on top so the knee is bent to about 90 degrees, the other foot on the floor. Torso upright, arms bent at 90 degrees in a running position.

Drive hard through the top foot and jump up explosively, switching legs in mid-air so the floor foot lands on the box and the box foot lands on the floor. Land softly with the top foot flat and absorb straight into the next drive. Continue alternating rhythmically for reps or time, pumping the arms opposite to the legs.
Push mostly through the top heel and mid-foot, not off the bottom toes. Keep the top knee tracking over the toes and the torso tall. Use a lower box for speed and a higher one for power.
Stand beside a low box or step (15 to 30 cm) with the inside foot flat on top and the outside foot on the floor, hips square to the front, arms bent in an athletic position.

Push off the foot on the box to jump laterally across it, landing with the opposite foot on top and the first foot on the floor on the far side. Absorb and immediately push back the other way. Keep shuffling back and forth quickly for 20 to 30 seconds or a set number of crossings.
Drive through the foot on the box rather than the floor foot. Keep hips level, chest up and the box foot fully on the step. Choose a low box so the movement stays fast and the landings stay soft.
Stand behind a line on a non-slip surface with feet hip-width apart and toes forward, arms relaxed at the sides, with several metres of clear space in front.

Swing the arms back as you hinge the hips and dip into a quarter-to-half squat, then swing the arms forward and up and extend the hips, knees and ankles explosively to jump out at roughly 30 to 45 degrees. Bring the knees forward and land on both feet in a balanced half squat, hips back and shins angled forward. Stick the landing for 2 seconds, then walk back.
The hips drive the jump, so think push back and out, not dive forward. Distance only counts if you stick it without stepping. Rest fully between maximal reps.
Stand at the start of a clear 15 to 20 m runway with feet hip-width apart, toes forward, arms ready to swing. Use grass, turf or a track.

Perform a broad jump, land on both feet in a quarter squat and use the arm swing to rebound immediately into the next jump with no pause or re-set. Link 3 to 5 jumps, staying at a consistent distance each time, then stop, walk back and rest.

Keep each landing short and springy instead of sinking into a deep squat; this is a reactive drill. Distance per jump will be less than a single maximal broad jump. Return to single broad jumps if landings get sloppy or knees cave.
Stand on one leg behind a line, foot pointing forward and under the hip, free knee bent with the foot behind, arms ready to swing. Also used as a return-to-sport single-hop test.

Hinge into a quarter single-leg squat, swing the arms and hop forward as far as possible from one leg, landing on the same leg. Absorb into a bent knee with hip back and knee over the second toe, and stick the landing for 2 seconds with hands free. Reset and repeat, then switch legs.
The knee must not cave inward on landing. Land through the forefoot to full foot. A hop only counts if you control it; compare left and right distances for symmetry.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, toes forward, arms at the sides. Use it for max-height training or testing against a wall, jump mat or Vertec; for a pure leg test keep the hands on the hips.

Swing the arms back as you dip quickly into a quarter-to-half squat (knees around 90 to 120 degrees), then reverse instantly without pausing, swinging the arms up and extending hips, knees and ankles to jump as high as possible. Reach for the ceiling at the top, then land softly on both feet in a quarter squat. Reset between reps.

Make the dip fast and continuous so the muscles stretch and rebound like a spring (stretch-shortening cycle). Fully straighten the ankles, knees and hips together (triple extension). Rest fully between max efforts.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, hands on the hips (testing) or arms ready to swing (training). Sit down into a half squat with knees at about 90 degrees and hold completely still for 2 to 3 seconds.

From the paused squat, jump straight up as high as possible without any further dip or bounce, extending hips, knees and ankles. Land softly back on both feet and settle into the half-squat position, hold the pause again, then repeat.

No countermovement before take-off: this isolates concentric power. Keep the chest up during the pause. Comparing squat jump and countermovement jump heights indicates how well you use elastic energy.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out 10 to 15 degrees, arms extended in front or hands lightly behind the head.

Sit back and down into a squat with thighs about parallel, then drive up explosively and jump, fully extending hips, knees and ankles. Land softly through the balls of the feet, roll to the full foot and absorb straight into the next squat, repeating continuously for reps or time.

Land quietly with knees tracking over the toes and the chest up. Unlike the paused squat jump, reps are continuous and used for power endurance and conditioning. Scale with a shallower squat or by removing the jump (fast bodyweight squats).
Hold a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip, arms long, feet hip-to-shoulder-width apart. Total load is usually 10 to 20 percent of bodyweight.

Dip quickly into a quarter-to-half squat with the chest up, then jump as high as possible, keeping the arms straight and the dumbbells close to the thighs. Land softly on the balls of the feet into a quarter squat, let the dumbbells settle, reset briefly and repeat.
Keep the dumbbells from swinging or pulling the shoulders forward. Prioritise jump height and speed over load; if the jump becomes a grind, go lighter. Brace the trunk on every landing.

Set a light barbell (about 0 to 30 percent of back squat 1RM) on the upper traps as for a high-bar back squat, gripping firmly just outside shoulder-width. Feet hip-width, toes slightly out, in a rack or open platform.

Brace, dip quickly into a quarter squat, then jump as high as possible while pulling the bar down hard into the traps so it stays pinned. Land softly through the balls of the feet into a quarter squat, absorbing with hips and knees, let the bar settle, reset and repeat.
Pull the bar into the back so it never separates and slams down on landing. Load must allow a fast, clearly airborne jump. Stop if landings become stiff or the trunk folds.

Stand inside a hexagonal trap bar loaded light to moderate (about 10 to 40 percent of trap bar deadlift 1RM). Grip the handles with a neutral grip, arms straight, chest up, hips slightly hinged. Lift the bar to standing first.

From standing, dip into a quarter squat with a slight hip hinge and jump vertically, keeping the arms long as hooks and the bar level. Land softly back on the balls of the feet in the quarter squat, let the load settle, reset and repeat.
Keep the spine neutral; the arms only hold the bar. A safer loaded jump than the barbell version because the load hangs at the hips. Pause to reset if the bar swings or tilts.

Stand in a split stance about one leg-length long, feet hip-width apart on separate tracks, front foot flat and back heel up. Lower so the front knee is about 90 degrees and the back knee hovers just above the floor, torso upright, arms bent.

Drive up explosively through both legs, switch the legs in mid-air with opposite arm swing, and land in the opposite split stance, lowering softly back into the lunge until the back knee nears the floor. Continue alternating for reps or time.

Land with the front foot flat and knee over the mid-foot, not collapsing inward. Keep the torso tall and the feet on separate tracks for balance. Scale with step-back switches or static split squat jumps without switching.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, arms bent with hands at chest height, palms down, elbows slightly out.

Dip quickly and jump straight up, then pull both knees up toward the chest to touch the palms at the top of the jump. Extend the legs back underneath before landing, land softly on the balls of the feet with knees bent and rebound straight into the next jump.
Bring the knees up to the hands; do not fold the trunk down to the knees. Keep ground contacts quick and the landing spot consistent. Scale to single tuck jumps with a reset between reps.
Stand tall with feet together or hip-width apart, arms raised overhead. Requires good hamstring flexibility; warm up first.

Dip and jump straight up, then at the top lift both straight legs forward to hip height (or out to the sides in a straddle) and reach the hands toward the toes, folding at the hips. Return the legs beneath you before landing, land softly on the balls of the feet with knees bent and reset.
Get height first, then pike. Keep the legs straight and the chest up as you reach. Land with bent knees, never stiff-legged. Scale with a tuck jump until you have the height and flexibility.
Stand with feet together and drop into a quarter-to-half squat, arms crossed or hands together in front of the knees.

Explode upward and spread the arms and legs wide into an X shape at the top of the jump, arms overhead in a V and legs wider than shoulder-width. Bring the limbs back together before landing, land softly on both feet into the crouch and go straight into the next jump.
Fully extend hips and knees at the top. Return the feet under the hips before touchdown so you do not land wide. Scale to a stepping star or jumping jacks.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes forward or slightly out, and sit into a quarter-to-half squat with the arms back, ready to swing.

Swing the arms and jump, turning the head, shoulders and hips together to rotate 180 degrees in the air, and land facing the opposite direction in a soft squat with knees over the toes. Pause briefly to stabilise, then jump and rotate back the other way so both directions are trained.
Lead the turn with the head and shoulders and keep the trunk braced. Stick each landing with knees aligned; no twisting on a planted foot. Progress to 360-degree jumps only with full control.
Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 20 to 30 degrees, and squat deep so the fingertips touch the floor between the feet, chest up and back flat.

Swing the arms forward and jump forward and up explosively from the deep squat, extending fully. Land softly on both feet back in the wide stance and sink straight into the deep squat with fingertips touching down, then jump again. Travel 5 to 10 jumps for distance or reps.
Keep the chest proud rather than collapsing over the knees. Knees follow the line of the toes. Use shorter jumps if the hips or knees are uncomfortable at full depth.
Kneel on a mat or pad with knees hip-width apart, toes flat (pointed) or tucked, torso upright and arms raised overhead.

Swing the arms down and back while sitting the hips toward the heels, then whip the arms forward and snap the hips forward to pop up off the knees and land on both feet in a squat, feet hip-to-shoulder-width. Stand up, kneel back down and repeat. Advanced athletes jump to the feet and immediately into a vertical or broad jump.
The hips do the work, so snap them through hard. Land with feet flat and knees aligned over the toes. Use a pad under the knees.
Stand on the right leg in a quarter squat, hips back, torso inclined about 30 degrees, left foot lifted behind the right ankle, arms ready to swing across the body.

Push off the right leg and leap sideways to the left, landing softly on the ball of the left foot and sinking into the hip, with the right foot sweeping behind the left ankle and the right arm swinging across. Immediately push back to the right. Continue rhythmically for reps or time.

Land soft and absorb into the hip with the knee over the toes. Make it bigger and slower for power or smaller and faster for conditioning. Unlike the lateral bound, the skater is continuous with only a brief pause.
Stand on one leg in an athletic quarter squat, hips back, torso slightly forward, the other foot off the floor. Clear 2 to 3 m of lateral space on a non-slip surface.

Load the stance hip and push hard off the whole foot to bound sideways as far as possible, landing on the opposite leg. Stick the landing for 2 seconds with knee over the second toe, hips back and the free foot off the ground, then bound back the other way.
Hold every landing; this distinguishes it from rhythmic skater jumps. Push the ground away laterally with the outside leg. Progress distance only when landings are stable and the knee stays aligned.
Use a straight 20 to 40 m runway on grass, turf or a track. Start from a standing stagger or a 3 to 5 step jog-in.

Exaggerate a running stride: push off one leg to full extension while driving the opposite knee up and forward to hip height, with the opposite arm swinging forward. Hang in the air, then land on the lead foot under or just ahead of the hips and immediately push off it into the next bound, alternating legs for 6 to 10 contacts.
Strike down and back with an active, dorsiflexed foot, not reaching out in front. Aim for distance and hang time per bound, not turnover speed. Walk back for full recovery.
Stand on one leg at the start of a straight 15 to 20 m runway, the free leg relaxed behind, arms ready.

Hop forward on the same leg repeatedly, cycling the stance leg forward under the body between contacts like a running stride and driving the arms, covering as much distance per contact as possible. Complete 3 to 6 hops, stop with control, walk back and switch legs.
Very high intensity; build up from two-leg and alternate-leg bounds first. Keep contacts quick and the knee stable over the foot. Stop the set if landings become heavy or the knee caves.
Stand at the start of a 20 to 30 m lane with tall posture, arms bent at 90 degrees.

Skip forward: as one knee drives up to hip height, the stance leg explodes off the ground with full ankle, knee and hip extension, and the opposite arm swings high. Land on the same stance foot under the hips, step through and repeat on the other side, aiming for maximal height on each skip.
Push the ground away hard with the stance leg; arm drive adds height. Forward travel is small; vertical height is the goal. A skip for distance is a variation that shifts the emphasis horizontally.
Stand on one leg with the foot directly under the hip, knee nearly straight, the free leg bent, hands on hips and pelvis level.
Hop in place with quick, springy ankle contacts, staying on the ball of the foot and keeping the knee nearly straight. Perform 10 to 20 contacts, then switch legs.
Contacts should be short and quiet with no heel slam. Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the foot. Lower volume than two-leg pogos; use it to build Achilles and calf stiffness for running.
Stand beside a line on the floor with feet together, knees slightly bent and weight on the balls of the feet, arms bent at the sides.

Hop sideways over the line and back as quickly as possible, keeping the feet together, the hops low (a few centimetres) and the head and torso steady over the line. Continue for 10 to 20 seconds or a set number of contacts.
Short, quick contacts with the feet together. Keep the shoulders level and the eyes forward. Progress to single-leg line hops or a line-hop test (count contacts in 10 seconds).
Stand behind a line with feet together, knees soft, weight on the balls of the feet, arms bent.

Hop forward over the line and immediately back, keeping contacts quick and hops low. Keep the torso tall with a slight forward lean so the hips stay over the feet. Continue for 10 to 20 seconds or a set number of contacts.
Spend minimal time on the ground. Do not lean back on the backward hop. Progress to single-leg versions for more challenge.
Stand on one leg beside a line or low hurdle, knee slightly bent and over the toes, hands on hips or arms ready.
Hop sideways over the line on the same leg and back again, either rhythmically for speed or sticking each landing for 1 to 2 seconds for stability. Complete the set and switch legs.
Do not let the knee collapse inward or the hip drop. Keep hips level and trunk quiet. Start with stick-and-hold reps before going continuous.
Set a row of 4 to 6 mini hurdles (15 to 30 cm, taller for advanced athletes) about 1 m apart. Stand behind the first hurdle, feet hip-width, arms ready.

Jump over each hurdle with both feet, tucking the knees up to clear it, and land on the balls of the feet. Rebound off each landing quickly into the next hurdle with a fast arm swing. Walk back and repeat.
Use collapsible hurdles to avoid trips. Keep contacts between hurdles quick and stiff; if you need to pause, lower the hurdles. Lift the knees, not the heels to the bum.
Stand side-on to a row of 3 to 5 mini hurdles (15 to 30 cm) spaced about 60 cm apart, feet together or hip-width in an athletic stance.

Jump sideways over each hurdle with both feet, lifting the knees to clear it, and rebound quickly off each landing while staying square to the front. At the end, return in the other direction leading with the other side.
Lift the knees rather than tilting the hips sideways. Keep the shoulders level and the trunk upright. Start with low hurdles.
Set 3 to 5 very low hurdles (about 15 cm) close together, roughly 60 to 75 cm apart. Stand on one leg behind the first hurdle.

Hop over each hurdle on one leg, either sticking each landing for a second or rebounding continuously when advanced. Land on the ball of the foot with the knee over the toes. Walk back and switch legs.
High stress on the stance leg; master two-leg hurdle hops and single-leg pogos first. Keep the knee aligned and the pelvis level. Stop if contacts become heavy.
Stand at the bottom of a flight of stadium bleachers or stairs with dry, non-slip steps, feet hip-width apart.

Jump up one or two steps at a time with both feet, landing on the balls of the feet with the whole forefoot on the step, and immediately jump again. Use an arm swing on each jump. Walk down carefully and repeat.
Always walk, never jump, down. Watch your footing on every landing. Single-leg hops up the steps are an advanced progression.
Stand with feet together and arms extended straight out in front at shoulder height, palms facing each other.

Jump the feet out wider than the shoulders while opening the arms wide to the sides at shoulder height (horizontal abduction). Jump the feet back together while bringing the arms back in front to clap. Repeat at a steady fast pace for 30 to 60 seconds.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together as the arms open. Stay light on the balls of the feet with soft knees. Step side to side for a low-impact option.
Stand with feet together, hands clasped at the chest or on the hips.

Jump the feet out to wider than shoulder-width with toes slightly out and drop straight into a squat with thighs near parallel. Jump the feet back together, rising toward standing as they land. Continue rhythmically for 20 to 40 second intervals.
Keep the chest up and weight over the mid-foot at the bottom, knees tracking over the toes. Land softly each time. Reduce squat depth or step out to scale.
Stand tall on the balls of the feet, feet hip-width apart, arms raised straight overhead. Used as the first landing drill before jumps and depth drops.

Snap the arms down and back while quickly dropping the hips into an athletic quarter-to-half squat, landing flat on both feet as if you had just landed from a jump. Freeze for 1 to 2 seconds with hips back, shins angled forward, knees over the toes and chest over the knees. Stand up and repeat.
Make the drop fast and the stop instant. Feet land flat and quietly, knees never cave. Progress to a small hop into the snap down, then to depth drops.
Stand with feet hip-to-shoulder-width apart, arms at the sides, on a non-slip surface.

Squat down and place the hands flat on the floor just outside the feet, shoulder-width apart. Jump or step the feet back to a high plank, then lower the chest and thighs to the floor (chest-to-floor standard). Push back up to the plank, jump the feet in to land flat just outside the hands, stand up and finish with a small jump, hands clapping overhead. Land softly and go straight into the next rep.
Keep the body in line in the plank; do not let the hips sag first on the way up. Step back and in instead of jumping to scale, or use a hands-on-bench version. Pace sets so form holds.
Stand with feet hip-to-shoulder-width apart, arms at the sides.

Squat down and place the hands flat on the floor under the shoulders, just in front of the feet. Jump the feet back to a high plank with the body straight and arms locked, then jump the feet back in under the hips and stand up. There is no push-up and no jump at the top, which separates it from the full burpee.
Land the plank with hips level and abs braced, not sagging. Keep the hands planted under the shoulders. Speed up as conditioning improves; step the feet back and in to scale.
Stand facing a plyo box (typically 20 or 24 in) about one step away, feet hip-width apart.

Perform a chest-to-floor burpee close to the box, jump the feet in and stand up, then immediately jump onto the box with a two-foot take-off. Land with both feet on the box, stand tall (or jump straight over), then step or jump down the far side. Turn around and repeat.
Drop into the burpee close to the box to save steps. Step down rather than rebounding off the floor to protect the Achilles. Use a lower box or step-ups when fatigued.
Stand at the start of a clear lane 20 to 50 m long, feet hip-width apart.

Perform a chest-to-floor burpee, jump the feet in and, instead of jumping vertically, swing the arms back then forward and broad jump forward. Land softly on both feet in a quarter squat, then drop straight into the next burpee where you landed and continue down the lane.
Jump a sustainable distance, not a maximal one. Land with knees bent and aligned over the toes. Keep the plank solid through every burpee.
Stand facing a loaded barbell on the floor, toes about 15 cm from the bar, feet hip-width apart.

Drop into a chest-to-floor burpee with the body perpendicular to the bar, head toward it. Jump the feet in, then jump forward over the bar with both feet taking off and landing together. Turn around to face the bar and go straight into the next burpee.
Two-foot take-off and landing are required for standard reps. Keep the hands and feet close to the bar to cut distance. Step over the bar to scale.
Stand side-on to a line, low hurdle or dumbbell on the floor, feet together or hip-width.

Perform a chest-to-floor burpee beside the object, jump the feet in and stand, then jump sideways over the line or object with a two-foot take-off, landing softly on both feet. Immediately drop into the next burpee on that side and jump back over.
Push off both feet together and keep the hips square to the front. Keep each plank tight. Make the lateral jump lower when fatigued.
Stand under a pull-up bar that you can reach with a small jump (hands about 15 to 30 cm above the reach height).

Perform a chest-to-floor burpee directly under the bar, jump the feet in and stand, then jump to grab the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders. Perform a pull-up (strict or kipping) until the chin clears the bar, then drop down under control and go straight into the next burpee.
Use the jump to start the pull but avoid a wild swing. Land with bent knees when dropping off. Scale with a jumping pull-up or a lower bar.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, arms at the sides.

Complete a full burpee: hands down, feet back to plank, chest to floor, push up and jump the feet in. Then replace the small jump at the top with a tuck jump, driving both knees up toward the chest. Extend the legs before landing, land softly on the balls of the feet and go straight into the next rep.
Get full knee drive on every tuck. Land softly with knees aligned. Swap the tuck for a normal jump when form slips.
Stand with feet hip-to-shoulder-width apart, arms at the sides.

Drop the hands to the floor and jump back to a plank. Do a push-up, then drive the left knee to the outside of the left elbow and return it. Do a second push-up, then drive the right knee to the right elbow and return it. Do a third push-up, jump the feet in, stand and jump. That is one rep.
Keep the plank square and hips low through the knee drives. Quality push-ups beat fast sloppy ones. Remove the jump or one push-up to scale.
Stand on one leg, the free leg slightly bent and lifted behind you, arms at the sides.

Hinge and squat on the stance leg to place the hands on the floor, kick the stance foot back to a single-leg plank with the free leg held up, and do a push-up. Hop the foot back in under you, stand on the same leg and finish with a small single-leg hop. Complete the reps, then switch sides.
Keep the hips square with only one foot down. Control the single-leg landing with the knee over the toes. Remove the hop or the push-up to scale.
Start in an athletic fighting stance: feet shoulder-width and staggered, knees bent, hands up in front of the chest.

Drop the hands to the floor and shoot the legs back and slightly wide, driving the hips down to the floor with the chest up and the head up, as if defending a takedown. Do not perform a push-up. Snap the feet back under the hips and return to the fighting stance immediately.
Hips go down and back to the floor fast; the chest stays off the ground. Keep the head up throughout. Recovering to the stance quickly is what makes it conditioning.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand at the near end in an athletic stance, knees soft, on the balls of the feet, arms bent at 90 degrees.

Run forward through the ladder placing one foot in each square, alternating feet with quick, light steps under the hips and a strong opposite-arm action. Keep the knees lifting slightly. Exit the end, decelerate and jog back to the start.
Land on the balls of the feet. Eyes forward once the pattern is learned, not down at the rungs. Gain speed only once the pattern is clean.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand at the near end in an athletic stance, knees soft, on the balls of the feet, arms bent at 90 degrees.

Run forward placing both feet in each square one after the other (right then left) before moving to the next square, keeping the same lead foot or alternating it each square. Keep a quick rhythm with short steps to the end, then jog back.
Short, quick steps under the hips with a slight forward lean. Pump the arms in rhythm. Do not clip or kick the rungs.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand side-on at one end in an athletic stance, feet hip-width, knees bent and hips low.
Move sideways down the ladder, stepping the lead foot then the trail foot into each square, then continue to the next square. Return leading with the other foot.
Stay low and level; do not bob up and down. Do not cross the feet. Keep the shoulders square to the front with quick, light contacts.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand to the left side of the first square, facing down the ladder in an athletic stance.

Step the right foot into the first square, then the left foot, then step the right foot out to the right side of the ladder beside the second square. Next step the left foot into the second square, then the right, then the left out to the left side. Continue the in-in-out rhythm down the ladder, moving diagonally forward each time.
Say it in rhythm: in, in, out. Stay on the balls of the feet. Keep the eyes up once the pattern is learned.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand facing the ladder at the first square, feet together, arms ready.

Step the right foot then the left foot into the first square, then step the right foot out to the right and the left foot out to the left beside the next square. Step both back in to the following square and repeat in-in-out-out down the ladder.
Keep the hips facing forward. Small, quick steps with a slight forward lean. Keep the arm action going.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand at the start of the ladder on one foot, ready to hop.

Hop on one foot into the first square, then jump out so both feet land either side of the next square, then hop back onto one foot into the following square, alternating the hopping foot. Continue the one-in, two-out pattern down the ladder.
Stay light and springy with low, fast hops. Land on the balls of the feet. The arms help the rhythm.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand on one leg at the start of the ladder, knee soft, the free leg bent.
Hop forward on one leg into each square, keeping contacts quick and controlled with the knee over the toes. Walk back and repeat on the other leg. Lateral and zigzag single-leg versions can follow.
Knee stays aligned over the toes, hips level. Contacts are quick but stable. Use two-foot hops first if balance is poor.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand side-on at one end in an athletic stance.

Move laterally down the ladder: cross the trail foot in front into the next square, step the lead foot into the following square, then cross the trail foot behind into the next and step out again. Let the hips rotate while the shoulders stay square to the front.
Let the hips rotate and keep the shoulders quiet. Stay on the balls of the feet. Slow down to learn the pattern, then speed up.
Lay an agility ladder flat on firm ground (rungs about 45 cm apart). Stand beside the ladder at one end with feet together.
Jump diagonally forward into the first square with both feet, then diagonally forward and out to the far side, then into the next square, zigzagging down the ladder with the feet together.
Small, quick jumps rather than big ones. Keep the torso facing forward. Land softly each time.
Place three cones or lines in a straight line 5 yards apart. Straddle the middle line in a three-point stance (testing) or two-point athletic stance, feet just wider than the hips.

Push off and sprint 5 yards to one side, plant the outside foot and touch the line with that hand, change direction and sprint 10 yards to the far line, touch it with the other hand, then turn and sprint 5 yards back through the middle line.
Lower the hips and plant the outside foot beside the line to change direction; do not turn wide. Drive out of each cut low with a strong arm swing. Test both starting directions.
Set four cones in a T: a start cone, a middle cone 10 yards straight ahead, and cones 5 yards to the left and right of the middle cone. Start behind the start cone.

Sprint forward to the middle cone and touch its base with the right hand. Shuffle 5 yards left and touch with the left hand, shuffle 10 yards right and touch with the right hand, shuffle 5 yards back left to the middle cone and touch with the left hand, then backpedal to the start.
Shuffle without crossing the feet. Stay low through the transitions. Keep the hips facing forward throughout.
Set three cones in an L, each 5 yards apart: start cone A, cone B 5 yards ahead, cone C 5 yards to the side of B. Start in a three-point stance beside A.

Sprint to B and touch the line, return to A and touch it, then sprint back toward B, round it on the inside, sprint to C and run around the outside of C in a tight loop, then come back around the inside of B and sprint through A to finish.
Lean into the turns and stay tight to the cones with short steps on the bends. Keep the hips low when touching the lines. Learn the pattern before timing it.
Place four cones in a square 5 to 10 yards apart. Start at one corner facing forward.

Sprint forward to the next cone, shuffle laterally to the third, backpedal to the fourth, then shuffle or carioca back to the start, staying square to the same direction throughout. Repeat in the opposite direction.
Stay facing the front throughout. Plant and redirect hard at each cone with hips low. Keep the shuffles low with no crossed feet.
Set 6 to 8 cones in a zigzag, each 3 to 5 yards apart diagonally. Start at the first cone in a two-point stance.
Sprint to each cone, plant the outside foot just past it, sink the hips and cut sharply toward the next cone, continuing the zigzag to the end. Walk back for recovery.
Sink the hips before each cut and keep the eyes on the next cone. Use the arms to drive out of the cut. Tighter spacing gives sharper cuts; wider spacing gives more speed between cuts.

Mark a 10 m long by 5 m wide area with cones at the start, finish and two turning points, plus four cones down the centre line 3.3 m apart. Lie face down at the start, hands by the shoulders, head at the start line.

On the signal, get up and sprint 10 m to the first turn cone, turn and run back to the bottom centre cone, weave up through the four centre cones and back down, then sprint 10 m to the last turn cone and turn to sprint to the finish.
Get up off the floor quickly. Run tight lines around the weave cones. Record time for testing; it has published norms for comparison.
Tape a hexagon on the floor with 24-inch (61 cm) sides and 120-degree angles. Stand in the middle facing one side, feet together, on the balls of the feet.

Jump with both feet out over one side and back into the centre, then over the next side and back, working around all six sides clockwise while always facing the same direction. Complete three full laps, rest, then repeat counterclockwise.
Always face the starting direction. Small, quick jumps with the feet together. In testing, restart the lap if you land on a line.
Place a centre cone with four cones around it, 5 yards away in a cross or X pattern. Start at the centre facing forward.

Sprint to the front cone and backpedal to the centre, shuffle to the right cone and back, backpedal to the rear cone and sprint back, shuffle to the left cone and back. Change the movements and order between reps.
Face forward through all patterns. Decelerate under control before each cone with the hips low. Rest fully between reps.
Two partners face each other 1 to 2 m apart within a small zone marked by cones about 5 yards wide, both in an athletic stance.
The leader shuffles, sprints, stops or backpedals unpredictably within the zone while the follower mirrors every move as fast as possible. Work 10 to 20 seconds, rest, then swap roles.
React to the hips of the leader, do not guess. Stay in an athletic stance with weight on the balls of the feet. Keep the feet apart when shuffling.
Stand in an athletic stance facing a coach or partner who will give a visual or audio cue, with cones 5 to 10 yards away marking two or more directions.
On the cue (point, colour, whistle or dropped ball), turn and sprint in the indicated direction for 5 to 10 yards, then decelerate. Walk back and reset for the next cue.
Stay ready but relaxed. Make the first step toward the target with no false step backward. Vary the cues and timing so the drill stays reactive.
Stand in an athletic stance facing a wall or partner a few metres away, holding a six-sided rubber reaction ball.
Drop the ball or throw it against the floor or wall so it bounces unpredictably, then react, move and catch it before it bounces again. Reset and repeat for 30 to 60 seconds.
Stay low with eyes on the ball. Use small adjustment steps rather than lunging. Begin with gentle drops and progress to harder throws.
Stand in an athletic stance facing a coach, feet just wider than the hips, hips low, weight on the balls of the feet.
Shuffle, backpedal or sprint in whichever direction the coach signals, changing direction immediately each time the signal changes. Work bouts of 10 to 20 seconds with full rest.
Keep the hips low and square to the coach. React quickly and do not cross the feet when shuffling. Watch the coach's hand, not your feet.
Mark two lines 10 to 25 yards apart with cones. Start behind one line in a two-point stance.
Sprint to the far line, plant the outside foot on or beside it, touch it with the hand or foot, turn and sprint back. Continue for the set number of lengths or time.
Lower the hips and shorten steps to decelerate before the line. Turn with a strong plant and accelerate hard out of the turn. Alternate turning direction to train both sides.
Use a court or field with lines (for example free-throw line, half court, far free-throw line and far baseline). Start on the baseline.
Sprint to the first line, touch it and sprint back to the baseline. Then sprint to the second line and back, then the third and back, and finally the full length and back. That is one rep.
Touch every line and decelerate under control at each turn. Pace so the last leg is still fast. Rest 1 to 3 minutes between reps.
Mark two lines 25 yards apart. Start behind one line.

Sprint 25 yards and back six times (12 lengths, 300 yards) as fast as possible. As a test it is run twice with 5 minutes rest and the two times averaged; as training, perform the prescribed number of reps.
