Even pacing beats a fast start. Turn efficiently with a foot plant on the line. Track the time of each rep.
Mark two lines 20 m apart and play the recorded beep audio. Stand behind one line.

Run to the opposite line, reaching it by the beep, then turn and run back with the next beep. The interval shortens each level (about every minute). Continue until you fail to reach the line before the beep twice in a row.
Do not start too fast in the early levels. Pivot on the line rather than running a wide loop. Record the final level and shuttle reached.
Start in a two-point stance (one foot forward, front knee bent, slight forward lean, opposite arm forward) or a three-point stance at a line. Mark 10 to 30 m.

Drive out explosively, pushing the ground back with a forward body lean of about 45 degrees on the first steps, then rise gradually to upright over the distance. Decelerate gradually after the line and walk back with full rest.
Push, do not reach; feet land under or behind the hips. Strong arm drive from the shoulders. Rest 1 to 3 minutes so every rep is maximal.
Stand tall at the start line on the balls of the feet, feet together or hip-width, arms relaxed at the sides or in a sprint position.
Lean forward from the ankles with the body in one straight line until you are about to fall, then drive the first step under the hips with an aggressive arm swing and sprint 10 to 20 m.
Keep the body rigid as you lean, no bending at the waist. React the moment balance is lost. Short, rapid first steps.
Mark a build-up zone of 20 to 30 m followed by a 10 to 30 m fly zone on a track or field.
Accelerate progressively through the build-up zone so you reach top speed as you enter the fly zone, sprint through it at maximum velocity, then decelerate gradually over 20 to 30 m.
Tall posture with relaxed face and shoulders. Strike the ground under the hips with a stiff ankle. Rest fully, 3 minutes or more.
Find a hill with a moderate gradient (about 5 to 10 percent) and good footing. Start at the bottom in a two-point stance.

Sprint up the hill for 8 to 30 seconds with a strong forward lean from the ankles, high knee drive and aggressive arm drive. Walk back down for recovery. Short 8 to 10 second efforts build acceleration power; longer repeats build anaerobic conditioning.
Lean from the ankles, not the waist. Push the ground behind you. Walk down carefully; the recovery is part of the drill.
Attach a sled to a waist belt or harness with a 3 to 5 m strap. Load it so sprint speed drops about 10 to 30 percent (heavier for acceleration work). Stand in a sprint stance with the strap taut.
Sprint forward, pulling the sled, holding a forward lean of about 45 degrees and powerful leg drive for 10 to 30 m. Walk back and rest fully between reps.
Keep the sled light enough to sprint, not grind. Drive the knees forward and push the ground back. Keep the same mechanics as an unloaded sprint.
Wear a waist belt or loop a heavy resistance band around the hips, with a partner holding the other end behind you. Get into a sprint stance.

Sprint forward against the partner's resistance for 10 to 20 m while the partner walks or jogs behind, keeping steady tension. For a release sprint, use a purpose-made quick-release harness operated by a coach; never simply let go of a stretched band.
Lean forward and drive the knees. The partner provides steady, not jerky, resistance. Keep the arm drive aggressive.
Place the hands on a wall at shoulder height, arms straight, and walk the feet back until the body forms a straight line at about 45 degrees, on the balls of the feet.

Drive one knee up under the hips with the foot dorsiflexed (toe up), then switch legs, punching the foot down and back under the hips. Do single exchanges, doubles, or rapid triples while holding the body line.
Keep a straight line from head to heel with no bend at the hips. Strike down and back under the hips. Ankles stay locked.
Start in an athletic stance with the hips low, chest slightly over the knees, arms bent at 90 degrees.
Run backward with quick, short steps, reaching back with the feet and pushing off the balls of the feet while staying low, for 10 to 20 yards. Progress by transitioning to a forward sprint at a cue.
Do not raise the hips or lean back; keep the weight forward over the toes. Pump the arms in a running action. Keep the feet under the hips.
Stand in an athletic stance with feet wider than the hips, hips back, knees bent, chest up, arms ready.
Push off the trail leg and step laterally with the lead leg, bringing the trail foot in without the feet touching. Shuffle a set distance (5 to 15 m) and back, or react to a cue.
Stay low with no bobbing. Do not click the heels together. Push with the trail leg; do not reach with the lead.
Stand side-on to the direction of travel, feet hip-width, arms out to the sides at shoulder height.

Move laterally by crossing the trail leg in front of the lead leg, stepping the lead leg out, crossing the trail leg behind and stepping out again, rotating the hips while the shoulders stay facing forward. Travel 15 to 20 m, then return leading with the other side.
Turn the hips quickly and stay light on the balls of the feet. Keep the shoulders square. Drive the knee up on the front cross for a high-knee carioca.
Stand at the start of a 60 to 100 m straight on a track or field, usually after an easy run.
Run with smooth progressive acceleration to about 85 to 95 percent of top speed by the middle, hold it briefly, then ease off. Walk back and repeat 4 to 8 times.
Relax; this is fast but not strained. Focus on tall posture and quick turnover. Take full recovery between strides.
Plan a run of 20 to 45 minutes on varied terrain after a warm-up of easy running.

Run continuously while mixing in unstructured surges of faster running, for example to the next lamp post or for 30 seconds to 2 minutes, followed by easy running until recovered. Repeat surges throughout the run.
Do not stop between surges. Let the terrain and feel dictate efforts. Keep the easy parts truly easy.
Warm up with 10 to 15 minutes of easy running. Choose a flat route or track where you can hold a steady pace.

Run for 15 to 40 minutes at a comfortably hard pace you could hold for about an hour (roughly 7 to 8 out of 10 effort), then cool down easy. On a heart-rate monitor this sits at roughly 85 to 90 percent of max heart rate.
You should speak only a few words at a time. Hold an even pace and shorten the duration if pace drops off. Finish feeling you could have gone a little longer.
Warm up with easy running and a few strides. Choose a set distance or time, such as 400 metres or 2 minutes. Use a track or a measured flat route.

Run each repeat at a hard but controlled pace, then recover with an easy jog or walk for the set rest, repeating for the prescribed number of intervals. Typical sessions: 6 to 10 x 400 m with 60 to 90 seconds rest, or 4 to 6 x 2 to 3 minutes with equal jog recovery.
Aim for even splits across repeats. Do not race the first one. Respect the rest.
Wear running shoes and choose a road, trail or track route. Start with a few minutes of brisk walking.

Run at a relaxed conversational pace with a short stride, landing under the hips, for the planned time or distance. Finish with a walk. Keep breathing relaxed enough to hold a conversation (about 60 to 70 percent of max heart rate).
Keep cadence quick and steps light. Relax the shoulders. Build weekly volume gradually, by no more than about 10 percent.
Use a flight of stadium or building stairs with good grip and a handrail. Warm up first.
Run up the stairs one or two at a time, driving the knees and pumping the arms. Walk down carefully for recovery and repeat.
Land with the whole forefoot on each step. Lean slightly forward. Walk down to protect the knees. Progress from single to double steps only once rhythm and footing are confident.
Load a rucksack or weight vest, usually 10 to 20 percent of bodyweight at first, packed high and tight on the back. Wear supportive boots or trail shoes.
Walk briskly for distance or time with good posture, short strides and a steady pace. Gradually add weight or distance. Aim for a pace of about 5 to 6.5 km/h (3 to 4 mph).
Stay tall and avoid leaning far forward. Tighten straps so the load does not bounce. Increase only load or distance at a time. Never run with the ruck.
Stand tall, arms bent at 90 degrees, wearing supportive shoes. Choose a flat route.

Walk quickly with short, fast steps, landing on the heel and rolling through to the toe, swinging the arms forward and back. Maintain the pace for the planned time. Aim for about 6 to 8 km/h (4 to 5 mph), with the elbows driving straight back rather than across the body.
Quicken the step rate rather than over-striding. Keep the torso upright. You should be noticeably breathy.
Stand tall on the balls of the feet, arms bent at 90 degrees. Use a 15 to 20 m lane.

March forward, driving one knee up to hip height with the toe pulled up, then drive the foot down under the hip as the other knee lifts. Opposite arm drives with each knee. Keep the stance leg straight and the hips tall throughout.
Tall posture with no backward lean. Strike under the hips. Rhythm before speed; master the march before the A-skip.
Stand tall at the start of a 20 to 30 m lane, arms bent.

Skip forward, driving one knee up with the ankle dorsiflexed while the stance leg gives a small hop, then snap the foot down under the hips. Alternate legs with opposite-arm drive. Travel 15 to 20 m per rep, 2 to 3 reps in a sprint warm-up.
Pop off the ground with the stance foot. The foot lands under the hip, not in front. Keep the torso upright. Elbows stay at about 90 degrees.
Stand tall at the start of a 20 to 30 m lane, arms bent.

Perform an A-skip, but after the knee lifts, extend the lower leg forward and then sweep it down and back in a pawing action, striking under the hips. Alternate legs. Travel 15 to 20 m per rep and perform after A-skips in the warm-up.
The paw back matters more than the kick out. Stay tall. Make sure the hamstrings are warm first. Keep the stance hip high; do not sit down.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and arms bent. Weight on the balls of the feet.

Run in place or travel forward, driving each knee up to hip height with quick contacts on the balls of the feet and an active arm swing. Keep the stance leg nearly straight and the hips tall, foot landing under the hip.
Stay tall without leaning back. Quick feet. March in place to scale; work in 15 to 30 second bursts. Keep the arms pumping in time with the legs.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, arms bent. Weight on the balls of the feet.

Jog in place or forward, flicking each heel up toward the glutes with quick, light contacts while the thighs stay roughly vertical. Use 15 to 30 m runs or 20 to 30 second sets as part of a dynamic warm-up before running.
Knees point down; heels come up beneath. Stay on the balls of the feet. Keep it rhythmic, not forced. Do not lean forward at the waist.
Stand tall with nearly straight legs and arms bent, on the balls of the feet. Use a 15 to 20 m lane.

Take tiny quick steps forward, rolling over the ball of each foot with the ankle stiff and the heel lifting only slightly. Travel 15 to 20 m. The swing foot passes just above the ankle of the stance leg, and the feet strike slightly in front of the stance foot with a stiff ankle.
Small steps, quick contacts. Feet land under the hips. Shoulders relaxed. Use it in warm-ups to build stiff, reactive ankles before faster sprint drills.
Stand tall on a runway with legs straight, arms bent at the sides. Use a 15 to 20 m lane.
Move forward by swinging one straight leg forward and pawing it down and back under the hips, pulling the body forward as the other leg swings through. Keep a quick rhythm. Travel 15 to 20 m per rep.
Keep the legs mostly straight but not locked. Strike under the hips with a pawing action. Stay tall. The hamstrings and glutes pull the body forward; warm up the hamstrings first.
Choose a flat, clear path or track lane. Stand with a slight forward lean.

Run backward by pushing off the balls of the feet and reaching back with each leg, keeping steps short and quick. Glance over the shoulder to check the path. Run 20 to 50 m bouts or a few minutes on a quiet track; it loads the quadriceps and calves with less knee compression than forward running.
Short, controlled steps. Stay on the forefeet. Use a partner if needed for safety. Keep the hips under the shoulders.
Sit tall on the floor with legs straight, arms bent at about 90 degrees. Shoulders relaxed and down, hands loose.
Swing the arms forward and back as in sprinting, hands to cheek height in front and past the hip behind, increasing speed until the hips lift slightly off the floor. Perform 10 to 20 second bouts.
Keep the elbows at 90 degrees. Swing from the shoulders. Stay relaxed in the face and hands. Keep the arm swing front to back, not across the body.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Use a smooth surface such as wood, rubber or a mat.

Turn the rope with small circles of the wrists, not the arms, and jump just high enough to clear it (2 to 3 cm), landing softly on the balls of both feet with the knees slightly bent. Keep one jump per rope turn at a steady 100 to 140 turns per minute, for time or reps.
Small, quiet jumps; heels stay just off the floor. Turn from the wrists and keep the elbows in. Stay tall and look ahead, not down at the feet.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Stand with feet hip-width apart.

Shift the weight from one foot to the other in rhythm with the rope: one foot takes most of the weight for two turns while the other lightly taps, then switch, with a small bounce on every turn. The rope turns at a steady speed throughout.
Stay relaxed and light on the balls of the feet. Keep the rope speed steady and the jumps low. Use it as a sustainable pace for long rounds or as recovery between harder skipping.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Stand with feet hip-width apart.

Jog in place over the rope, stepping over it with one foot at a time as it passes, alternating feet each turn of the rope, so each foot lands every other turn. Keep the knees lifting slightly and the contacts on the balls of the feet.
Keep the rope moving at a consistent rhythm. Stay tall and avoid kicking the heels back. Lift the knees higher or speed the turns to make it harder.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.

Run in place over the rope, driving each knee up to hip height on alternating turns while the stance foot lands on the ball of the foot. Speed up the rope to match the faster leg action and keep the torso upright.
Keep the torso tall with no backward lean. Speed the rope to match the knees. Drop back to the alternate foot step if you start tripping.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Stand on one foot, the other knee bent with the foot lifted behind.

Jump the rope on one foot for a set number of turns (for example 10 to 20), then switch to the other foot, keeping each contact short on the ball of the foot with the knee soft and aligned over the toes.
Keep the pelvis level and the knee from caving inward. Short sets at first. Switch feet before form fades.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Stand with feet together.
Jump the rope with the feet together while moving them 15 to 30 cm to the left and right on alternating turns, like a slalom skier, keeping the upper body centred over the start position.
Small lateral movements; the head and torso stay still. Stay light on the balls of the feet. Use a line on the floor as a guide.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Start with a basic bounce.

On one turn, cross the arms in front at the waist, elbows crossing so the hands reach the opposite hips, forming a loop in the rope that you jump through. On the next turn uncross the arms to a normal jump. Alternate open and crossed jumps.
Cross the arms deeply so the loop is big enough to clear. Keep the hands low at hip level. Practise the arm motion slowly first.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. A light speed rope with bearings helps.

Jump slightly higher than for a single bounce (about 10 to 15 cm) with legs nearly straight and spin the rope fast with the wrists so it passes under the feet twice per jump. Land on the balls of the feet and link reps continuously.
Stay tall with legs nearly straight; avoid piking or kicking the heels back (donkey kicks). Speed comes from the wrists, not the arms. Learn with single-single-double rhythms.

Hold the jump rope handles lightly at hip height, elbows close to the ribs and hands about 20 to 30 cm out from the hips. Size the rope so the handles reach the armpits (beginners) or lower chest (advanced) when you stand on its middle. Use a light speed rope.

Jump higher than for doubles (about 20 to 25 cm), tucking the knees slightly if needed, and spin the rope three times under the feet before landing. Land softly on the balls of the feet and reset or link reps.
Get the jump height first, then the wrist speed. Keep the hands close to the hips. Master unbroken double unders before attempting.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Use a neutral grip, thumbs on top.

Raise one arm to about shoulder height while lowering the other to the hip in a rapid alternating motion, creating continuous waves that travel the length of the rope to the anchor. Work for 20 to 40 seconds.
Keep the knees bent and the core braced; do not stand up as you tire. Waves should reach the anchor. Move from the shoulders with soft elbows.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Use a neutral grip, thumbs on top.
Raise and lower both arms together rapidly from hip to shoulder height, sending matching waves down both ropes. Keep a steady rhythm for 20 to 40 seconds.
Move from the shoulders with a small knee bend on each wave. Keep the back neutral. Smaller and faster waves are fine.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Use a neutral or overhand grip.
Lift both ropes overhead, rising onto the toes and extending the hips, then slam them down forcefully into the floor while dropping into a quarter-to-half squat. Repeat explosively for reps or time.
Full extension up, then slam hard with the whole body. Brace the core on every slam. Reset posture between reps.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Hold the ropes low, near the hips.
Swing both arms together from side to side horizontally, creating snake-like waves along the floor. Continue rhythmically for 20 to 40 seconds.
Rotate through the hips and trunk with a firm stance. Keep the ropes low and the movement controlled.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Use a neutral grip, thumbs on top.
Move both arms in circles, either outward or inward, creating spiralling waves in the ropes. Switch direction halfway through the 20 to 40 second set.
Circles come from the shoulders; keep the core tight. Switch direction to balance the shoulders.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Start with the feet together.
Perform a jumping jack while lifting both ropes out to the sides and up, then bringing them down as the feet come together. Continue for 20 to 40 seconds.
Arms and feet move together. Land softly on the balls of the feet. Use lighter ropes to start.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Hold the ropes low with a neutral grip.
Squat with the ropes low, then jump explosively while lifting the ropes overhead, and slam them down as you land back in the squat. Repeat for reps or time.
Coordinate the jump and the arm lift. Land softly with knees over the toes. Rest when power drops.

Loop a 9 to 15 m battle rope (38 or 50 mm) around a solid anchor post so both ends are equal, and hold one end in each hand. Stand 30 to 60 cm back from the point where the rope is just slack, feet shoulder-width, in a half-squat athletic stance with chest up and core braced. Hold both rope ends together in front of the hips.
Pivot the feet and rotate the hips to sling the ropes across to one side and down, then reverse to throw them to the other side, alternating explosively.
Power comes from the hips and pivoting feet. Keep the arms long. Protect the lower back by bracing.

Clip the safety key cord to your clothing, straddle the belt on the side rails and start the belt at a slow walk before stepping on. Set a 1 percent incline to roughly match the effort of outdoor running.

Increase the speed to your target pace and run with a natural stride, landing with the foot under the hips and a cadence of about 160 to 180 steps per minute. Run for the planned time or distance, then slow to a walk for 3 to 5 minutes to cool down before stopping the belt and stepping off.
Do not hold the handrails or console; it shortens the stride and reduces the work. Stay in the middle of the belt, close enough to reach the stop button. Look ahead, not down at the feet.

Clip the safety key cord to your clothing, straddle the belt on the side rails and start the belt at a slow walk before stepping on. Raise the incline to 8 to 15 percent (the popular 12-3-30 workout uses 12 percent, 3 mph, 30 minutes).

Walk at a brisk pace of about 4 to 5.5 km/h (2.5 to 3.5 mph) for the planned time, staying upright with a slight lean from the ankles and a full heel-to-toe step that drives the hip into extension. Lower the incline and speed gradually to finish.
Do not hang onto the handrails; holding on can halve the effort and strains the shoulders and lower back. Increase incline before speed. Shorten the stride if the calves or Achilles feel tight.

Clip the safety key cord to your clothing, straddle the belt on the side rails and start the belt at a slow walk before stepping on. Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes and use a 1 to 3 percent incline for traction.

Stay on the belt the whole time. For each sprint, raise the speed over a few seconds from a jog to sprint pace, sprint for 15 to 30 seconds, then lower the speed back to a walk for 30 to 90 seconds of recovery. Repeat 6 to 10 times. Never step on or off a belt moving at sprint speed.
Keep the safety clip attached and stay near the front of the belt. Keep fast but relaxed form with knees driving forward. Stop the set if mechanics break down or you drift to the back of the belt.
Step onto a curved, non-motorized treadmill holding the handrails, standing at the lowest point of the curve. The belt is powered only by you, so there is no safety key.

Let go of the rails and start walking or running; the further forward up the curve you move, the faster the belt turns. Hold your position on the curve to hold a pace, move forward to sprint, and drift back toward the bottom of the curve to slow down. Sprints of 10 to 30 seconds with walking recovery are common.
Run on the balls of the feet with a forward lean and strong hip extension; it rewards good sprint mechanics. Stay tall. Drift back gently to slow before stopping or stepping off.

Sit on the seat, fasten the foot straps across the widest part of the feet and set the damper to 3 to 5. Hold the handle with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width, arms straight. At the catch, shins are near vertical, the torso leans slightly forward from the hips and the back is flat.

Drive with the legs first, keeping the arms straight; once the legs are nearly straight, swing the torso back to about 11 o'clock and then pull the handle to the lower ribs, elbows passing close to the body. Recover in reverse: arms extend, torso hinges forward, then the knees bend to slide forward to the catch. Rate is usually 18 to 30.

Sequence is legs, body, arms on the drive and arms, body, legs on the recovery. About 60 percent of the power comes from the legs. A high damper is not harder fitness work; it just feels heavier and tires the back.

Set the seat height so the knee keeps a 25 to 35 degree bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (about level with the hip bone when standing beside the bike). Sit upright with hands lightly on the bars and strap or clip the feet in with the ball of the foot over the pedal axle.

Pedal smoothly at the chosen resistance and cadence (typically 70 to 100 rpm) for the planned time or intervals, pushing down through the front of the stroke and drawing the foot back and up through the bottom and back of the circle.

Keep the hips steady on the saddle with no rocking; rocking means the seat is too high. Raise resistance to build strength, cadence to build speed. Adjust the seat if the front or back of the knee aches.

Sit in the reclined seat with the back and hips against the backrest and hands on the side grips. Slide the seat so the knee keeps a slight bend (about 15 to 25 degrees) when the pedal is at its furthest point. Strap the feet in with the ball of the foot over the pedal.

Pedal steadily at a set resistance and cadence for the planned time, pressing through the whole foot and keeping the back supported. Low-impact with minimal balance demand, so it suits beginners, rehab and those with back issues.
Do not lock the knees at full extension. Keep a steady rhythm and avoid sliding forward in the seat. Increase resistance gradually.

Set saddle height so the knee keeps a 25 to 35 degree bend at the bottom, saddle fore-aft so the front of the knee is over the pedal axle when the cranks are level, and handlebars at or slightly above saddle height. Clip in or tighten the toe cages.

Pedal seated or out of the saddle at a set resistance and cadence (60 to 80 rpm for climbs, 80 to 110 rpm for flats and sprints), varying climbs, sprints and steady efforts. Stand up only with enough resistance to support your weight. Always keep some resistance on the weighted flywheel.
Never pedal at zero resistance; the fixed flywheel can drive the legs. Press the emergency brake to stop. Add resistance if you bounce in the saddle at high cadence.

Adjust the seat so the knee keeps a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke and the handles can be reached without leaning forward. Grip the moving handles with a neutral grip, feet on the pedals.

Push and pull the handles alternately while pedalling, pushing one handle as the same-side leg drives down. The fan resistance rises steeply with effort, so going harder makes it heavier. Use it for steady aerobic work or all-out sprints of 10 to 30 seconds.
Use the arms and legs together, pushing and pulling. Sprints are extremely demanding, so pace long efforts. Keep the hips planted on the seat.
Stand facing the ski erg about 30 cm back with feet hip-width apart. Grasp a handle in each hand with the arms extended overhead and slightly in front, damper 3 to 5.

Initiate the pull by driving the hands down with straight-ish arms while hinging at the hips and bending the knees slightly, crunching the trunk so the hands finish past the thighs. Return by straightening the hips, standing tall on the balls of the feet and reaching the hands back up. Stroke rate usually 30 to 50 per minute.
The lats and trunk flexion drive the stroke, not just the arms. Hinge, do not squat deeply. Keep the elbows slightly bent and the hands close to the body.
Step onto the revolving staircase, holding the handrails lightly for balance, and choose a starting speed (steps per minute).

Climb the revolving stairs with the whole foot on each step, driving through the heel and mid-foot to straighten the hip and knee, upright posture with a slight forward lean from the hips. Continue for the planned time, increasing speed or using intervals to progress.
Do not lean or hang on the rails; it shifts the load off the legs. Push through the whole foot. Start at a lower step rate and progress speed or duration gradually.
Stand on the two independent foot pedals with the whole foot on each, holding the handrails lightly, torso upright with a slight forward lean.
Push down alternately on each pedal through a full range while the other rises, at a steady rhythm. Increase resistance or pace to intensify, or use harder and easier intervals.
Use full-range steps, not short choppy ones. Keep the weight off the arms and stay upright. Let the pace slow gradually before stepping off.
Step onto the pedals while holding the static grips, then take the moving handles and stand upright with the feet flat and the hips over the feet.

Push and pull the handles while driving the pedals in a smooth elliptical path, keeping the whole foot in contact. Adjust resistance and incline for intensity, and pedal backward to shift emphasis toward the hamstrings and glutes.
Keep the feet flat on the pedals; lifting the heels causes numb toes. Stand tall without hunching or leaning on the console. Low impact, so it suits joint issues.
Sit or stand facing the arm crank with the axle at shoulder height and close enough that the elbows stay slightly bent at the furthest point. Grasp the handles with a neutral or overhand grip.
Crank the handles in a circular motion at a steady cadence, forward or backward, for time or intervals (for example 30 seconds hard and 30 seconds easy). Keep the torso still and the feet planted.
Keep the trunk quiet and avoid shrugging. Work both forward and reverse to balance the shoulders. Useful conditioning when the legs are injured.
Strap the feet into the pedals and grasp the handles in front of you at about eye level, standing tall with the hips close to the machine.

Climb by driving one leg down while pulling the opposite handle down, opposite arm and leg together, like climbing a ladder. Use short fast strokes for speed or long full strokes for strength and range.
Keep the hips close to the machine and the back neutral. Push and pull in sync. Very intense, so start with short intervals.
Step onto the angled rungs (about 40 degrees), fasten the waist belt, and hold the rungs with the hands.
Climb the self-paced ladder moving opposite hand and foot together. Climbing faster moves the rungs faster, so you set the pace. Work intervals of 30 to 60 seconds or longer steady climbs.
Keep a steady rhythm and stay close to the ladder. The belt tether stops the rungs when you drift back. Slow down gradually before stepping off.

Clip the safety key cord to your clothing, straddle the belt on the side rails and start the belt at a slow walk before stepping on. Stand facing away from the console, hands lightly on the side rails, with the belt at a very slow speed (1 to 2 km/h).

Walk backward, reaching back with each foot and rolling from the toes to the heel, keeping the knees slightly bent so the quadriceps work throughout. Increase speed or incline gradually as confidence builds.
Start very slowly and keep a light grip at first. Short steps on the forefoot. A knee-friendly way to load the quadriceps.
Stand with feet together and arms by your sides, knees soft.

Jump the feet out to a bit wider than shoulder-width while swinging straight arms out to the sides and overhead, then jump back to the start with the arms returning to the sides. Repeat at a brisk pace, for example 30 to 60 second intervals or as a warm-up.
Stay light on the balls of the feet with soft knees. Keep the arms straight as they rise. Step out instead of jumping for a low-impact option.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, arms extended straight out to the sides at shoulder height.
Jump and cross the feet and arms in front of the body, then jump them back out. Alternate which foot and arm crosses in front each rep so both sides work evenly.
Light, quick contacts on the balls of the feet. Keep the arms at shoulder height and the core braced. Low-impact version: step the cross.
Start in a high plank with each foot on a slider (or a towel on a smooth floor), hands under the shoulders.
Slide one knee toward the chest and back while the other slides forward, alternating in a continuous running motion without lifting the feet. Work in 20 to 40 second intervals.
Keep constant tension in the core. Hips stay level. Move smoothly, not jerkily. Hands stay under the shoulders.
Start on hands and knees, hands under the shoulders, knees under the hips, then lift the knees 3 to 5 cm off the ground. Back flat and head neutral.
Crawl forward by moving the opposite hand and foot together in small steps, keeping the knees low and the back flat. Crawl backward for the return. Travel 10 to 20 m per set.
Back stays flat enough to balance a cup on it. Small steps. Do not let the hips rise high.
Start in the bear position with the knees hovering 3 to 5 cm off the floor, hands under the shoulders.
Crawl sideways, moving the hand and foot on one side out, then bringing the other hand and foot in, travelling a set distance, then return. Travel the same distance in both directions.
Hips stay level and low. Hands stay under the shoulders. Small steps to keep control.
Sit on the floor with knees bent, feet flat, hands behind the hips with fingers pointing toward the feet. Lift the hips off the floor.
Walk forward or backward using opposite hand and foot together, keeping the hips up. Travel the set distance.
Keep the hips high and the chest open. Turn the hands to a comfortable angle. Use shorter distances if the wrists are sore.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.

Hinge at the hips and place the hands on the floor, keeping the legs as straight as you can. Walk the hands out to a high plank, then walk the feet toward the hands with small steps and stand. Reverse the walk-in to return, or step the feet in until a hamstring stretch is felt. Do 5 to 8 reps as a warm-up.
Bend the knees as needed to reach the floor. Keep the hips stable in the plank. Add a push-up for difficulty.
Start in a bear crawl position but lower the hips and chest so they are just above the floor. Hands under the shoulders.
Crawl forward with opposite hand and foot together, bringing each knee out to the side, staying very low throughout. Travel 10 to 20 m at a time.
Stay low and controlled. Keep the trunk braced and the head in line with the spine. Move slowly to begin. Keep the knees off the floor.
Lie face down on the forearms with the legs extended and elbows under the shoulders.

Pull yourself forward using alternating forearms and push with the opposite knee drawn to the side, keeping the body flat to the floor. Travel 10 to 20 m at a time. Keep the head low and avoid lifting the hips as you tire.
Keep the hips low. Coordinate opposite arm and leg. Use a mat or grass. Wear long sleeves on rough ground.
Stand in a boxing stance: lead foot forward, feet staggered and shoulder-width apart, knees soft, hands up guarding the chin, elbows in.
Throw combinations of jabs, crosses, hooks and uppercuts at an imaginary opponent while moving the feet, slipping and returning the hands to guard after every punch. Work in rounds.
Rotate from the hips and pivot the back foot on crosses. Do not lock the elbows. Hands back to the face every time.
Wrap the hands and wear boxing gloves. Stand in a boxing stance an arm's length from the heavy bag. Feet staggered and shoulder-width, hands guarding the chin.

Throw punches and combinations at the bag, moving around it and returning to guard. Work timed rounds, often 2 to 3 minutes, with 30 to 60 seconds rest. Push the bag away with the jab, pivot the back foot on crosses and keep the feet moving between combinations.
Punch through the bag, not at it. Stay balanced. Always use wraps and gloves to protect the wrists.
Adjust the speed bag so its bottom is level with your chin. Stand square to it, hands up near the face. Fists loosely closed.

Strike the bag with the side of the fist in a circular rhythm so it rebounds three times between hits, alternating hands. The bag strikes the platform front, back, front between each hit; move the hands in small forward circles at about face height.
Keep the hands moving in small circles. Hit lightly. Learn the rhythm with one hand before alternating. Stay relaxed in the shoulders.
Stand in an athletic stance, feet shoulder-width, hips low, on the balls of the feet. Arms bent at 90 degrees.

Rapidly patter the feet in place with tiny steps, as fast as possible, for 5 to 15 seconds. React to a cue to sprint or change direction for progression. Feet stay under the hips and barely leave the ground.
Stay low with the chest over the knees. Short, fast contacts. Keep the arms moving. Keep the heels off the floor.
Place an aerobic step 10 to 20 cm (4 to 8 in) high in front of you. Stand facing it. Use a stable non-slip step.

Step up with one foot, follow with the other, then step down in order, continuing basic steps and patterns such as knee lifts and over-the-top to music or a timer. Step onto the centre of the step and down close to it, heel lowering gently on the floor. Sessions usually run 20 to 45 minutes.
Place the whole foot on the step. Stay close to the platform. Lower the step to scale.
In a pool, push off the wall face down in a streamline, arms extended overhead and body horizontal.
Alternate the arms in a continuous overhead stroke, pulling under the body to the hips while kicking from the hips with a flutter kick. Rotate the body to breathe to the side every 2 to 3 strokes.
Keep the head neutral, looking at the pool floor. Rotate the hips and shoulders together. Exhale fully underwater.
In a pool, float on your back with arms by your sides and body horizontal.

Alternate the arms in a straight-arm overhead recovery, entering little finger first, then pull under the water to the hip. Flutter kick continuously. Rotate the body 30 to 45 degrees toward the pulling arm on each stroke and bend the elbow to about 90 degrees under water.
Keep the hips high and the ears in the water. Kick from the hips with relaxed ankles. Eyes look straight up.
In a pool, push off the wall in a streamline face down.

Sweep the hands outward and back, then in under the chest while lifting the head to breathe, and recover the hands forward. Bend the knees to bring the heels toward the hips, then whip the feet out and together. Glide before the next stroke.
Pull, breathe, kick, glide. Keep the knees fairly narrow. Do not skip the glide.
In a pool, push off the wall face down in a streamline.

Move both arms together over the water, enter in front, then pull under the body to the hips, using a dolphin kick (two per stroke) with an undulating body. Breathe by lifting the chin forward during the pull, every one or two strokes, and enter the hands shoulder-width apart.
The rhythm comes from the chest and hips. Breathe forward and low. Very demanding; start with short distances.
In a pool, lie on one side with the lower arm extended past the head and the upper arm along the side. Head rests on the lower arm, face clear of the water.

Pull the lower arm down while the upper arm pushes back, and use a scissor kick. Glide on the side, keeping the face out of the water to breathe. Bring the knees up, then open the legs into a scissor (top leg forward, bottom leg back) and snap them together as the arms push.
Efficient and restful. Time the kick with the arm pull. Change sides to balance.
In deep water, keep the body vertical with the head above the surface. Hands near the surface in front of the chest.

Scull the hands back and forth and use an eggbeater, flutter or scissor kick to stay afloat. Hold for the planned time, or raise the hands out of the water for difficulty. In the eggbeater, each lower leg circles alternately (one clockwise, one anticlockwise) with the knees apart and hips flexed.
Relax and breathe steadily. Keep movements small and constant. Stay near the wall at first.
In the pool, hold a kickboard at arm's length, face down or with the head up. Elbows resting lightly on the board or arms straight holding its end.

Kick from the hips with straight, relaxed legs and pointed toes, propelling across the pool with the board. This is the flutter-kick drill; breaststroke and dolphin kicks use different technique. Swim lengths of 25 to 50 m, resting as needed. Keep the kick narrow, within the width of the body, with the heels just breaking the surface.
Kick from the hips, not the knees. Keep the ankles loose and the body flat.
In deep water, wear a flotation belt so you float upright, head above the water. Use the deep end so the feet do not touch.

Run in the water with a normal running motion, driving the knees and pumping the arms, without touching the bottom. Use steady or interval efforts. Keep cadence close to land running and use an interval of, for example, 30 seconds hard and 30 seconds easy.
Stay upright, not leaning forward. Use the full running action. Excellent for injury rehab.
Mark a start line and a stop line 10 to 15 m apart with cones. Start in a two-point stance.

Accelerate hard to about 80 to 100 percent effort and, at the stop line, brake within 2 to 3 short, choppy steps into an athletic stance: feet wider than the hips, hips back and low, chest over the knees, shins angled back. Freeze for 2 seconds, then walk back.
Lower the centre of mass and shorten the steps before the line; do not stop on a single stiff leg. Knees stay over the toes. Progress to stopping on a cue or into a cut.
Ride a properly fitted road, gravel or hybrid bicycle and wear a helmet. Set saddle height so the knee keeps a 25 to 35 degree bend at the bottom of the stroke.

Ride at the planned intensity for time or distance, using the gears to keep a cadence of about 80 to 95 rpm on flats. Climb seated with a slightly lower cadence or stand briefly on steep sections, and use steady, interval or hill efforts.
Shift early before hills rather than grinding. Keep the upper body relaxed with soft elbows. Ride predictably and follow traffic rules.

Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs over the top or a slight false grip so the wrist can roll over the bar. Arms straight, shoulders depressed, legs together in a slight hollow.

Without kipping, pull explosively and high, driving the elbows back so the bar travels to the lower chest or upper abs. As the bar reaches the sternum, lean the chest over it, bring the elbows up behind the bar and roll the wrists on top, landing in the bottom of a straight bar dip. Press to locked-out support. Lower slowly through the dip, back through the transition and the pull to a dead hang.

Pull to the belly button, not the chin; keep the bar close. Lean the shoulders well forward at the transition so the elbows can come over. Prerequisites: about 10 strict pull-ups, strict chest-to-bar reps and 10 straight bar dips.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width or slightly wider, arms straight, legs together. A thumbless grip eases the turnover but is less secure.

Build a kip swing between arch (chest through, heels behind) and hollow. From the back of the arch, press down on the bar with straight arms and snap into a hollow, then open the hips hard toward the bar like a hip thrust. As the body floats up, pull the bar to the hips, sit the chest over it with elbows coming back and up, and press to lockout. Push slightly away, drop back through the hollow to the arch and re-kip.

Hips to the bar first, pull second; early arm bend kills the swing. Turn the wrists over fast and keep the bar close. Fix chicken-winging (one elbow over first) with low-bar transition drills. Earn it with strict pull-ups, kipping chest-to-bar and straight bar dips.

Uses gymnastic rings set high enough to hang with straight arms and feet clear of the floor. Take a false grip: the heel of each palm over the ring so the wrist is flexed on top and the ring sits in the crease of the hand. Hang with shoulders engaged, legs together.

Pull with elbows tight to the ribs, bringing the rings to the lower chest. At the top of the pull, lean the chest forward through the rings and bring the elbows up and back behind them so the shoulders pass over the hands, landing in a deep ring dip with rings against the ribs. Press to a locked support and turn the rings out. Reverse slowly through dip, transition and pull to the hang.
Keep the false grip all the way; losing it makes the transition near impossible. Rings stay close to the body, never wide. Drill low-ring transitions, false grip pull-ups and deep ring dips first.
Uses gymnastic rings set high, with a regular grip or a light false grip, arms straight. Start from a still hang, body slightly hollow and legs together.

Swing from a front arch (chest pushed through the rings, legs behind) back into a hollow, then open the hips hard toward the rings while pulling the rings down toward the hips with nearly straight arms, so the body travels up and close to the rings. As the hips peak, do a fast sit-up, snapping the chest over the hands with the elbows driving back, and catch in the bottom of a ring dip. Press to lockout. Lower in control to the hang and re-swing.

Hips to the rings, then the fast sit-up; pulling with bent arms early is the common fault. Keep the rings close and elbows in at the catch. Do not crash into the bottom dip; build strict ring dips and the strict transition before high volume.

Use a pull-up bar (or rings with a false grip) with a box underneath. Step or jump to a straight-arm support on top of the bar, hands about shoulder width, body slightly forward of the bar and legs together.

Lower slowly into the bottom of a straight bar dip, keeping the bar close to the chest. Continue down through the transition: lift the elbows back behind and then under the bar as the wrists roll back under, keeping the bar against the sternum. Keep resisting through the pull-up phase to a full dead hang. Total descent about 5-10 seconds. Step back to the box and repeat.

Control the transition hardest, it is the weak link you are training. Keep the body close to the bar. End the set when you can no longer control the speed. Use a low bar or band-assisted transitions if the descent drops fast.

Uses gymnastic rings lowered so they hang at about chest height when seated or kneeling on the floor. Sit or kneel beneath them, take a false grip, and set the rings beside the lower chest with elbows bent and tight to the ribs. Legs extended in front (seated) or knees down give foot support.

Keeping the rings against the ribs, lean the chest forward and roll the shoulders over the hands while the elbows travel up and back behind the rings, using the legs to take some bodyweight. Arrive in the bottom of a ring dip, then press to straight-arm support. Reverse back through the transition to the starting position under control.

Keep the false grip and elbows tight to the body. Lead with the chest, not the head. Reduce leg assistance as you get stronger. This drill teaches the exact shoulder rotation used in the full ring muscle-up.

Uses gymnastic rings at a height where the feet can rest on the floor or just clear it. Place the heel of each palm on the ring so the wrist is flexed over the top and the ring sits in the crease between palm and fingers, thumbs wrapped.

Bend the knees or lift the feet to take bodyweight into the false grip and hang with straight arms or with the elbows bent about 90 degrees (false grip lock-off). Keep the wrists flexed hard and hold for time, typically 10-30 seconds. Put the feet down, reset the grip and repeat. Progress to false grip rows and pull-ups.

Keep the wrist cranked over the ring so the grip does not slide into a normal hang. Start with foot support to manage wrist and forearm load. Chalk helps; expect the forearm flexors to fatigue quickly and build volume gradually.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width, arms straight and body still, legs together.

Push the chest through the arms into an arch: head through, chest forward, heels behind the bar. Then press down on the bar with straight arms (lats) and pull the body into a hollow: chest behind the bar, ribs down, feet slightly in front. Swing rhythmically between arch and hollow, moving from the shoulders and trunk, keeping the arms straight throughout. Stop by shortening the swing.

The swing comes from shoulder press-down and trunk shape, not bending the knees or piking. Keep the legs squeezed and toes pointed. A tight, controlled kip swing is the foundation for kipping pull-ups, toes-to-bar and bar muscle-ups.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width or slightly wider, arms straight.

Build a kip swing between arch and hollow. From the hollow, open the hips hard and pull aggressively, driving the elbows back and down so the chest at or below the collarbone touches the bar. At contact, push the bar away and let the body fall back into the arch to load the next rep.

Pull the elbows back to the ribs rather than just up. Open the hips and lean the head back slightly at the top so the chest, not the chin, reaches the bar. Strict chest-to-bar reps and kipping pull-ups build the range and timing first.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped slightly wider than shoulder width, body slightly hollow and legs together.

Cycle the hips in a continuous oval: drive them forward and up as you pull, opening the hips and arching slightly at the top so the chest at or below the collarbone contacts the bar. Then swing the body back beneath the bar through the arch on the way down and loop straight into the next rep with no pause.

Aim the sternum at the bar with the elbows driving back. Keep the loop tight and smooth so the body does not drift away from the bar. Master butterfly pull-ups to the chin and kipping chest-to-bar first.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped about shoulder width, arms straight and legs together.

Start a kip by pushing into a slight arch with the feet behind. As the body swings back, press the bar down with straight arms (lats) to lean the shoulders back, and flex hard at the hips to snap the toes up to touch the bar between the hands. Let the legs drop and kick them back behind the body to swing the chest through into the arch, loading the next rep.

Lats pressing the bar down drive the lift as much as the hip flexors and abs. Keep the arms mostly straight and the legs together. Scale to kipping knees-to-elbows or hanging knee raises; touch both feet at once for the rep to count.

Stand behind a bar set about chest to shoulder height with an overhand grip shoulder width. Jump lightly from both feet so the hips move back and up, then glide forward with straight arms and a slight pike, feet skimming just above the floor.

At full extension of the glide, with the body nearly straight, quickly pike to bring the ankles to the bar. As the body swings back, pull the bar up the front of the legs to the hips while pressing down with straight arms (like closing a pike), ending in front support on top of the bar with arms locked and hips against the bar. Drop back down to the floor to repeat.

Time the pike at full glide extension, not before. Arms stay straight; press the bar down with the lats rather than pulling with the biceps. Drill glide swings and ankles-to-bar first; a spotter can lift under the hips and back.
Start in front support on a bar at about hip height: overhand grip shoulder width, arms straight, hips against the bar, body straight and slightly hollow.

Cast: pike slightly, then swing the legs back and up so the hips leave the bar while the arms stay straight. As the hips swing back in to the bar, lean the shoulders back and keep a slight pike so the body rotates backward around the bar with the hips in contact. Keep the arms straight and the wrists turning over the top, finishing in the same front support.
Keep the hips glued to the bar through the circle. Lean back with the shoulders as the hips arrive, not before. Learn on a low bar with a spotter guiding the legs; a small cast is enough to start.
Stand between parallel dip bars (or parallettes) and grip them with a neutral grip, hands just outside the hips. Jump or press up so the arms are straight.
Hold with locked elbows, shoulders depressed away from the ears, chest tall and body straight or slightly hollow, legs together. Hold for time, then step down.
Push the bars down so the shoulders stay low; do not let them shrug up. Squeeze the glutes and point the toes. The first support skill, before ring support, dips and L-sits; build to 60 seconds.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about hip height. Grip the rings in neutral, jump up and lock the arms straight with the rings pressed against the sides of the hips and thighs.

Hold the support with locked elbows, shoulders depressed away from the ears, chest tall and body straight or slightly hollow, legs together and toes pointed. Squeeze the rings toward the body to stop them drifting. Hold for time, then step down to the floor.

Keep the rings in contact with the body; drift outward is the main fault and stresses the shoulders. Actively push down to depress the shoulders. Build to 30-60 seconds before moving to the turned-out support.
Uses gymnastic rings set at hip height. Jump into a straight-arm support with the rings pressed against the sides of the hips.

Externally rotate the arms to turn the rings out so the palms face forward or slightly out and the elbow pits face forward. Hold with locked elbows, shoulders depressed and body slightly hollow, legs together. Return the rings to neutral and step down.

Turn out only as far as the elbows stay fully locked. Do not let the shoulders shrug up or the rings drift. It prepares the elbows, biceps tendon and shoulders for straight-arm ring skills like planche, cross and ring handstand; build from 10-15 to 30-60 seconds.
Uses gymnastic rings set at hip height or just higher. Step from a box or jump into a straight-arm support with the rings against the sides of the body.

Lower slowly over 3-6 seconds, rings close to the ribs and elbows tracking back, until the shoulders are below the elbows. At the bottom, put the feet down, stand or step up and return to the top of the support for the next rep instead of pressing.

Fight the rings drifting wide. Keep the shoulders down away from the ears. Use this once you can hold a solid 30 second support but cannot yet press a full ring dip; stop when you cannot control the speed.
Uses gymnastic rings set at hip height. Start in a straight-arm support with the rings close to the body.

Lower to the bottom of a dip while piking the hips and lifting the knees slightly in front. From the bottom, kick the legs down and back hard to drive the hips up while pressing the rings to lockout, finishing in support. Lower and repeat in rhythm.

The leg drive helps through the sticking point; the arms still finish the press. Only kip once strict ring dips are solid. Keep the rings close at the bottom to avoid loading the shoulders in a wide, deep position.
Uses gymnastic rings set at hip height. Start in a straight-arm support with the rings against the hips.

As you lower, let the rings travel out wide and away from the body, turning the palms forward so the elbows flare, bringing the chest down between the hands into a deep pec stretch. Press back up, drawing the rings back in to the hips and finishing in support.

Unlike a standard ring dip, the rings deliberately leave the body, which shifts load to the chest and increases range. Lower slowly and keep the shoulders depressed. Build depth gradually; this is an advanced shoulder and pec move.
Uses gymnastic rings set just above the floor. Take a push-up plank with straight arms, rings under the shoulders, body tight.

Lower the chest between the rings with elbows close to the body. Press up and, as the elbows reach lockout, actively turn the rings out so the palms face forward and the elbow pits face forward, then protract the shoulders. Hold the turnout for 1-2 seconds, return to neutral and lower again.
Lock the elbows fully at the top before turning out. Keep the body hollow throughout. Good preparation for turned-out supports and planche work.
Uses gymnastic rings set just above the floor. Take a push-up plank with the rings wider than the shoulders and arms straight.

Lower toward one ring, bending that elbow, while the other arm slides out to the side and stays nearly straight. Press back up to the middle and repeat to the other side, or complete all reps on one side.

Most of the load goes to the bent arm. Keep the straight arm long but not hyperextended and the hips square. Rings make the straight arm work harder to stabilize than the floor version. A strong step toward one-arm push-ups.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about knee to hip height. Grip them in neutral and lean into an incline push-up position, arms straight in front of the chest, body straight.

Keeping a slight, fixed bend in the elbows, let the arms open out wide so the chest lowers between the rings until you feel a stretch across the chest. Squeeze the chest to draw the rings back together in front of you.
Do not let the elbows bend more as you go down, which turns it into a push-up. A more horizontal body is harder. Stop short of pain at the bottom; the shoulder is in a long, loaded position.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about waist height. Hold the rings wider than the shoulders and lean back underneath with straight arms and the body straight.
Row the chest toward one ring while the other arm stays straight and slides out to the side. Lower and repeat to the other side.
Keep the body rigid and hips level. The straight arm assists only. A step toward the one-arm row and the one-arm pull-up.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about chest height. Hold them with an overhand grip and lean back with straight arms, feet in front of the anchor point.

Pull the rings toward the face with high elbows at about shoulder height, separating the hands and externally rotating the shoulders so the hands finish beside the ears. Return to straight arms with control.
Keep the elbows high and squeeze the shoulder blades back without shrugging. Do not let the hips sag. Adjust the lean to scale; light, high-rep sets suit this rear-delt and rotator cuff exercise.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about chest height. Hold them with palms up and lean back with straight arms, body straight and feet in front.
Curl the rings toward the forehead by bending only the elbows, keeping the upper arms fixed at shoulder height. Lower back to straight arms with control.
Keep the elbows high and still. Brace the core so the hips stay in line. Walk the feet forward to make it harder.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about hip height. Hold them in front of the forehead with an overhand grip, arms straight, and lean forward into an incline plank.
Bend only the elbows to lower the head beneath and between the rings, keeping the upper arms pointed forward. Extend the elbows to press back to straight arms.
Keep the elbows narrow and the body rigid. Lower the rings or step back to make it harder. Control the bottom to protect the elbows.
Uses gymnastic rings set high, or a pull-up bar. Hang with straight arms and a neutral or overhand grip, body still.

Tuck the knees and pull the hips up and back until they rise above the head, then straighten the body to point the feet at the ceiling, hanging upside down between the rings. Hold, then pike and lower back to the start with control.
Keep the arms straight and the rings close to the body. Engage the lats to stay stable. The entry point for skin the cat and back lever work.

Hang from a pull-up bar (or rings) with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms fully straight. Depress the shoulders (pull them away from the ears) and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Pull the knees tight to the chest and, keeping the elbows locked, press the bar down toward the hips with the lats so the body rotates face up until the back and hips are horizontal, parallel to the floor, with the hips level with the shoulders. Hold for time, then lower the hips under control back to a hang.

Arms locked: bending the elbows turns it into a row. Hips at shoulder height, not sagging below. The back may round slightly in this first stage. Build to 3-5 sets of 10-20 second holds before moving to the advanced tuck.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, arms straight, shoulders depressed.

Lift into a tuck front lever, then push the hips back and open the hip angle to about 90 degrees so the back becomes flat and horizontal, thighs vertical or angled slightly back and knees still bent. Keep the arms locked and the shoulders, hips and back in one horizontal line. Hold, then retuck and lower to a hang.

The flat back is what distinguishes it from the tuck: the lever arm is longer, so it is much harder. Do not let the hips drop below the shoulders. Build to 10-15 second holds; then progress to one-leg, straddle or half lay.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Lift into an advanced tuck front lever, then extend one leg fully so it continues the straight line of the torso, while the other knee stays bent with the thigh vertical (advanced tuck leg). Hold with the body horizontal and the hips square, then retuck and lower. Alternate the extended leg each set.

Keep the hips level and square; the body tends to twist toward the extended leg. The extended leg stays in line with the torso, not dropping below horizontal. Bridges the gap between advanced tuck and straddle or full front lever.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

With straight arms, press the bar toward the hips and lift into a horizontal front lever with both legs straight and spread wide apart, hips extended (no pike) so the line from shoulders to hips is horizontal. Hold, then lower into a hang or retuck.

Wider legs bring the centre of mass closer to the shoulders and make it easier. Squeeze the glutes, lock the knees and point the toes. The commonest fault is piking at the hips; keep the hips open and level with the shoulders.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Lift into a horizontal front lever with the hips fully extended and the thighs in line with the torso, legs together, but with the knees bent about 90 degrees so the shins hang down. Hold, then lower to a hang.

Hips stay fully open; only the knees bend. Keep the shoulders, hips and knees in one horizontal line. Gradually straighten the knees over weeks toward the full lever; an alternative to the straddle progression for those with tight inner thighs.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

With straight arms, press the bar down toward the hips and raise the whole body into a rigid straight horizontal line, face up, legs together, from shoulders to toes. The arms make roughly a 90 degree angle with the torso at the shoulder. Hold for time, then lower back to a hang under control.

Body straight like a plank: glutes squeezed, ribs down, toes pointed, no pike and no arch. Elbows locked. A clean 5-10 second hold is an advanced standard; train it with 3-6 sets of short holds rather than one long effort.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Keeping the arms straight, raise the body (in tuck, straddle or full position) from the hang up through the horizontal lever to an inverted hang with the hips above the shoulders, then lower slowly back down to the lever, pause, and continue to the hang. A variant starts inverted and lowers to the lever and back up.

Arms stay straight; any elbow bend means the progression is too hard. Use the tuck or straddle version that matches your hold strength. Control the lowering, especially through the horizontal; avoid swinging into the rep.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Hold your front lever progression horizontally, then pull the bar toward the hips while keeping the body horizontal, so the body rises flat until the hips or upper abdomen touch the bar. Extend the arms back to the straight-arm lever and repeat.

Keep the body horizontal throughout; do not let the legs drop as you pull. Drive the elbows back toward the hips. Scale with tuck, advanced tuck or straddle legs. Distinct from the front lever row: the pull here is toward the bar from a hanging lever, ending at the hips.
Hang from a bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width and lift into a tuck or advanced tuck front lever (or harder) with straight arms.

Keeping the body horizontal, row the bar toward the lower chest and stomach by bending the elbows and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Lower back to straight arms while maintaining the horizontal lever, then repeat.

Keep the hips level with the shoulders; they drop as you tire. Elbows stay close to the sides. Use 3-8 rep sets and progress the leg position over time. Rings allow the wrists to rotate if the bar irritates the elbows.
Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip about shoulder width, arms straight and shoulders depressed.

Pull up to the top of a pull-up with the chin over the bar. Then rotate the body backward to horizontal while pushing the bar away toward the hips and straightening the arms, ending in a front lever (tuck, straddle or full) with locked elbows. Reverse: bend the arms and pull back to the top of the pull-up, then lower to the hang.
Keep the body tight and rotate smoothly rather than swinging. Lead the rotation with the hips coming up as the arms extend. Use a tuck to scale. A good dynamic lever strength builder.
Hang from a pull-up bar or rings with an overhand grip about shoulder width, thumbs wrapped, arms straight. Depress the shoulders and set a slight hollow before lifting.

Pull or roll up to an inverted hang with the body pointing straight up and the arms straight. Then slowly lower the body with straight arms through the horizontal front lever and on down to a hang over 5-10 seconds.
Fight hardest as you pass horizontal; slow down most there. Use tuck or straddle legs if the full body drops too fast. Stop the set when you cannot control the descent.
Uses gymnastic rings at about chest height (or a low bar) so the feet can touch the floor. Grip the rings, tuck the knees and rotate backward through an inverted hang.

Continue rotating until the feet point down behind you and the arms are extended behind the body with the shoulders in deep extension. Let the feet touch the floor for support or hang freely. Hold for 10-30 seconds, then tuck and reverse back through inverted to the starting hang.

Go only as deep as you control and keep the arms straight. Start with feet on the floor to scale load. Builds the shoulder extension and biceps tendon tolerance needed for back lever; avoid with recent shoulder instability.
Uses gymnastic rings set high (or a pull-up bar). Hang with straight arms and a shoulder width neutral or overhand grip, shoulders active.

Tuck the knees and pull the hips up through the arms into an inverted hang, then keep rotating backward, lowering the feet behind you into the German hang. Pause, then pull the knees back through to inverted and lower forward to the starting hang with control.
Keep the arms straight throughout. Move slowly, especially into the German hang. Stop the rotation where the shoulders are still comfortable and build depth over sessions.
Uses gymnastic rings (or a pull-up bar) set high. Hang with straight arms, tuck and roll backward into an inverted hang with the hips over the head.

Lower backward from the inverted hang with the knees tucked to the chest until the back is horizontal and face down, hips level with the shoulders and arms straight, the rings at the sides of the hips. Hold, then pull back up to inverted or continue to the German hang.

Keep the arms straight and press the rings down toward the hips. Lean the shoulders slightly forward. Hips level with the shoulders. The front of the shoulder and biceps take the load; build 10-15 second holds before advancing.
Uses gymnastic rings (or a pull-up bar) set high. Hang with straight arms, tuck and roll backward into an inverted hang with the hips over the head.

Lower into a tuck back lever, then open the hips so the back is flat and horizontal, face down, and the thighs sit roughly perpendicular to the back with the knees still bent. Arms straight with the rings beside the hips. Hold, then retuck and return to inverted.
Keep a flat back and the hips level with the shoulders. Arms locked. Build to 10-15 second holds before moving to straddle or half lay.
Uses gymnastic rings (or a pull-up bar) set high. Hang with straight arms, tuck and roll backward into an inverted hang with the hips over the head.
Lower from inverted with the legs straight and spread wide until the body is horizontal, face down, with the hips extended and level with the shoulders. Hold, then return to inverted.
Keep the body straight from shoulders to hips with no pike. Squeeze the glutes and lock the elbows. Wider legs make it easier.
Uses gymnastic rings (or a pull-up bar) set high. Hang with straight arms, tuck and roll backward into an inverted hang with the hips over the head.

Lower into a horizontal back lever with the hips fully extended and the thighs in line with the torso, legs together, but the knees bent about 90 degrees with the shins pointing up. Hold, then return to inverted.
Hips stay fully open; only the knees bend. Keep everything horizontal. Straighten the knees gradually over time.
Uses gymnastic rings (or a pull-up bar) set high. Hang with straight arms, tuck and roll backward into an inverted hang with the hips over the head.

Lower from the inverted hang with the body straight and legs together until it is horizontal, face down, with the rings beside the hips and arms locked. Hold, then pull back up to inverted with straight arms.

Body stays straight: glutes squeezed, toes pointed, no pike or excessive arch. Lean the chest slightly forward to balance. The biceps and front of the shoulder are loaded in extension; build underhand and German hang tolerance gradually to protect the biceps tendon.

Take a push-up plank on the floor or parallettes with straight arms, hands shoulder width and fingers turned out or back. Protract the shoulders, set a hollow body and rest on the toes with the ankles pointed.

Keeping the arms locked and the body hollow, lean the shoulders forward past the hands so the weight shifts onto the hands and the toes slide forward or roll onto their tops. Hold the lean for time, then return to a normal plank.

Lock the elbows and keep pushing the floor away (protraction). Lean only as far as you can hold good form; measure progress by how far the shoulders travel past the hands. Increase the lean slowly to protect the wrists and the biceps tendon.

Squat with the hands flat on the floor about shoulder width, fingers spread and pointing forward. Bend the elbows slightly and rest the inside of the knees on the backs of the upper arms just above the elbows.

Lean forward so the weight shifts from the feet onto the hands until the toes lift off the floor. Balance with the knees resting on the arms and the elbows bent, head looking slightly forward. Hold, then lower the feet.

Look slightly ahead, not straight down. Use fingertip pressure to stop tipping forward. A cushion in front helps confidence. Unlike yoga crow, the arms stay bent with knees on the elbows; it leads into tuck planche and bent-arm handstand presses.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.

Lean the shoulders forward over the hands and lift the feet, pulling the knees into the chest so only the hands touch the ground. Balance on straight arms with the hips at about shoulder height and the back rounded. Hold, then lower the feet.

Arms locked: a bent-arm version is a frog stand. Keep the shoulders protracted and the hips from dropping below shoulder height. Parallettes reduce wrist strain. Build 10-15 second holds before advanced tuck.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.

From a tuck planche, push the hips back and up so the back becomes flat and parallel to the floor, with the knees still bent and the thighs roughly perpendicular to the back. Lean further forward to balance. Hold, then lower.
The flat back lengthens the lever, so it is much harder than the tuck. Keep the arms straight and the shoulders protracted. Build to 10-15 second holds before moving to straddle or half lay.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lean well forward and lift the legs straight behind you, spread wide, keeping the hips extended so the body is horizontal and supported only by the straight arms. Hold, then lower.
Squeeze the glutes and point the toes. Keep the shoulders protracted and depressed. Wider legs make it easier. Avoid piking at the hips.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lean forward and lift into a horizontal planche with the hips fully extended and the thighs in line with the torso, legs together and the knees bent about 90 degrees. Hold, then lower.
Keep the hips open and in line with the shoulders. Arms locked. Gradually straighten the knees toward the full planche.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lean far forward over the hands and lift the whole body into a straight horizontal line, legs together, supported only by locked arms with the shoulders well in front of the hands. Hold, then lower.
Protract hard and keep a slight hollow. Arms stay locked. Elite skill; build tendon strength over years and progress patiently.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lift into a tuck planche, then bend the elbows to lower the body, keeping the knees tucked, the shoulders forward of the hands and the back horizontal. Press back up to the straight-arm tuck planche.
Keep the hips up as you lower. Elbows stay close to the sides and point back. Parallettes allow more depth.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lift into a straddle planche, lower by bending the elbows with the legs wide and the body horizontal until the chest is near hand level, then press back up to straight arms.
Keep the legs wide and up. Shoulders stay in front of the hands. Elite movement; master the straddle planche hold first.

Place the hands on the floor or on parallettes about shoulder width, fingers turned out or back to suit the wrists. Lock the elbows, protract the shoulders so the upper back is slightly rounded, and depress them away from the ears.
Lift into a full planche, lower by bending the elbows with the legs together and the body straight and horizontal, then press back up.
Body stays rigid and horizontal. Keep the elbows tight. One of the hardest push-up variations; build volume very gradually.
