Uses gymnastic rings set high, or very wide parallettes for the floor version. Start in a straight-arm support with the rings turned out.

Lean forward and lower the body while the straight arms move out wide to the sides, until the body is horizontal, face down, at the level of the hands, like a planche with arms spread. Hold, then press back to support.
Elite gymnastics skill. Keep the arms locked and the body straight. Build through full planche and iron cross work first.
Uses gymnastic rings set high. Start in a straight-arm support with the rings turned out and the body vertical.
Slowly spread the straight arms out to the sides, lowering the body until the arms are horizontal and the body hangs vertically between the rings, forming a T. Hold, then press back up to support.
Keep the elbows locked and press the rings down. Train with bands or a spotter first. Elite skill demanding huge tendon strength.
Start in a push-up position with the feet against the base of a wall and the hands on the floor shoulder width, fingers spread, roughly a body length from the wall.

Walk the feet up the wall while walking the hands back toward it until the hands are about 10-20 cm from the wall and the body is vertical, chest and toes facing the wall. Stack wrists, shoulders, hips and ankles in a line with arms locked overhead. Hold, then walk the hands out and feet down the same way.

Push the floor away so the shoulders elevate fully toward the ears; arms by the ears. Ribs down and glutes squeezed so the back does not arch. Build toward 60 seconds; this is the best wall drill for freestanding line.
Stand facing a wall and place the hands on the floor shoulder width, fingers spread, about 15-30 cm from the wall.

Kick one leg up and then the other until both heels rest lightly on the wall above you. Hold with straight arms, shoulders pushed up and the body as straight as possible, then step one foot down at a time. To practise balance, pull one heel and then both slightly off the wall.

Keep the arms locked and the shoulders elevated. Move the hands closer to the wall and squeeze the glutes to reduce the banana-shaped arch this version invites. Easier to enter than chest-to-wall, so use it for kick-up practice and short holds.
Clear space in front and use a mat. Place the hands on the floor shoulder width with fingers spread and slightly cupped, index fingers pointing forward.

Kick up into a vertical line with wrists, shoulders, hips and ankles stacked and arms locked. Balance on the hands: press through the fingertips to correct falling forward (overbalance) and shift into the heel of the palm to correct falling back. Hold, then step down one leg at a time or cartwheel out.
Learn to bail first: turn one hand out and cartwheel down. Push tall through the shoulders and keep the ribs tucked. Short, frequent practice (many 5-30 second attempts) beats long sessions.
Stand on a line with the arms straight overhead, lead leg forward in a lunge, body facing along the line.

Reach forward and place the first hand on the line, then the second hand, while kicking the back leg up and pushing off the front so the legs pass overhead in a straddle through a sideways handstand. Land the first foot then the second on the line, finishing in a lunge facing back the way you came.
Hand, hand, foot, foot in a straight line. Keep the arms straight and the hips stacked over the shoulders at the top. Also teaches the safe bail from a handstand.
Stand in a lunge stance with the arms straight overhead by the ears, the front knee bent and the back leg straight. Choose a lead leg and keep a clear space or a wall in front.

Reach the hands to the floor about shoulder width, a short step in front of the front foot, while swinging the straight back leg up and pushing off the bent front leg so the hips rise over the shoulders. Join the legs at the top and find balance, then step down the same way and repeat.
Keep the arms locked by the ears as you reach; bending them is the common fault. Use just enough kick force: too much overshoots. Practise against a wall first, then with a spotter.
Use a clear, flat floor. Kick up into a freestanding handstand, arms locked, legs together or in a slight split for balance.

Let the body tip slightly forward and catch it with small steps of the hands, shifting weight fully onto one hand while the other moves a few centimetres forward. Keep walking for distance, then step down. Advanced versions travel backward, sideways or over obstacles.

Small, quick steps and steady shoulders; the hips stay stacked just ahead of the hands. Keep the body tight. Measure progress in distance or steps without falling; in workouts, step down and re-kick when balance is lost rather than overcorrecting.
Walk up into a chest-to-wall handstand with the hands about 10-20 cm from the wall, arms straight, body vertical and hollow.
Shift the weight slowly onto one hand, then lift the other and tap the opposite shoulder, replacing the hand in the same spot before shifting to the other side. Alternate sides for reps.

Shift weight slowly and keep the hips square; the body should not swing. Keep the toes lightly in contact with the wall. Widen the hands slightly to make it easier. Builds single-arm balance for handstand walking and one-arm work.
Squat with the hands flat on the floor shoulder width, fingers spread, and set a frog stand with the knees resting on the backs of the bent arms.

From the frog stand, lean the shoulders forward and lift the hips upward, sliding the knees off the elbows while keeping the elbows bent. Continue raising the hips over the hands, then extend the legs up and straighten the arms to finish in a handstand. Reverse slowly.
Lean first, then lift. Keep the elbows tucked and pointing back. Easier than straight-arm presses; learn against a wall.
Squat with the hands on the floor shoulder width, fingers spread, and the knees tucked to the chest. Arms straight.

Lean the shoulders forward over the hands until the feet float into a straight-arm tuck balance. Keep leaning and rounding the back to raise the hips above the shoulders, then extend the hips and legs up into a handstand. Reverse slowly back to the tuck and to the feet.

Lean first, then lift: the hips must stack over the hands before the legs extend. Keep the arms straight and the shoulders pushing up. Learn with the back to a wall or a spotter; a solid tuck planche helps.
Stand in a wide straddle and fold forward, placing the hands flat on the floor between the feet about shoulder width.

Lean the shoulders forward over the hands to shift the weight off the feet. Keeping the legs straight and wide, compress hard and lift the hips over the shoulders until the feet float, then raise the legs out to the sides and bring them together overhead into a handstand. Reverse slowly to the floor.

Pancake flexibility and compression strength are key; drill straddle L-sits and seated compression lifts. Lean the shoulders forward to start rather than jumping. Keep the arms locked. Use an elevated surface or a wall to learn.
Stand with the feet together and fold forward, placing the hands flat on the floor close to the feet about shoulder width.
Lean the shoulders forward and lift the hips over the shoulders while keeping the legs straight and together close to the chest, then raise the legs into a handstand. Reverse slowly to the floor.
Requires great pike compression and flexibility. Keep the arms locked. Master the straddle press first.
Kick up into a solid freestanding handstand, usually in a straddle with the legs open, hands shoulder width or slightly narrower.

Shift the hips and shoulders over the supporting hand, keeping the body upright, and lift the other hand off the floor, first to the fingertips and then fully. Balance on one arm using the fingers and wrist, then return the hand down.
Master a 60 second freestanding handstand first. Use finger pressure to control balance. Elite skill.
Kneel and place the hands flat on the floor shoulder width with the top of the head in front of them, forming a triangle.
Walk the feet in, place the knees on the elbows, then lift the legs up to vertical. Balance the weight between head and hands. Lower with control.
Keep the neck neutral and push into the hands so the neck is not overloaded. Avoid if neck problems.

Place the hands on the floor (or a mat) slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers spread, about 15-25 cm from a wall. Kick up into a handstand with the heels resting on the wall, arms locked and the body tight.

Lower under control by bending the elbows until the top of the head touches the floor (or abmat), forming a tripod with the hands slightly in front of the head. Without kicking, press straight back up to locked elbows, pushing the shoulders tall at the top.

Elbows about 45 degrees from the body, not flared straight out. Ribs down and glutes squeezed so the back does not overarch against the wall. Scale with pike push-ups, box pike push-ups or a stack of mats under the head; progress to deficit or freestanding versions.
Uses gymnastic rings set at about hip height over a mat. Start in a ring support with the rings against the hips.

Lower into a bent-arm support, pike the hips up and roll forward so the shoulders come down in front of the hands while the hips rise overhead, then extend the legs straight up. Rest the upper arms against the ring straps and hold with the elbows bent, body vertical. Roll back down to support.
Keep the rings pressed close and the straps against the arms for stability. Lower slowly into the stand. Stepping stone to the ring handstand; learn with a spotter.
Uses gymnastic rings set low, around knee to hip height, over a mat. Grip the rings firmly and start in a straight-arm support or a ring shoulder stand, with the rings pressed against the forearms.

Press or kick the hips up over the hands and extend the legs to vertical, turning the rings slightly out and squeezing them toward the body to kill the wobble. Hold, then lower back through a shoulder stand or pike to support.
Rings stay close and arms locked. Learn with the feet against the ring straps or with a spotter. Requires a solid floor handstand, RTO support and ring shoulder stand first.
Kneel and place the hands on the floor shoulder width or a little narrower with fingers pointing back or out. Bend the elbows and press them into the stomach either side of the navel.
Lean forward and extend the legs back until the body is horizontal and balanced on the hands and elbows. Hold, then lower.
Lean forward until the body balances. Keep the body straight. A good beginner hand-balancing skill.

Stand side-on to a sturdy vertical pole. Hug the pole with the near arm so it is clamped in the armpit and wrap the hand around it at about chest height; grip the pole with the other hand overhand at about head height.

Squeeze the pole between the upper arm and ribs, pull with the top hand and lift the legs sideways off the ground, first tucked and then straight, until the body is close to horizontal. Hold, then lower the feet with control.

The armpit clamp carries much of the load, which makes it the most accessible flag. Keep the legs together and the obliques tight. Pad the pole if the clamp hurts. First step of the human flag series before vertical and tuck flags.

Stand side-on to a sturdy vertical pole. Grip it with the top hand overhand above the head and the bottom hand around chest height with the thumb pointing up or down, hands roughly shoulder width or more apart.

Lock the bottom arm and press it into the pole while pulling with the top arm as you jump the legs up, holding the body vertical and close to the pole above the hands, upside down with the top shoulder, hip and feet stacked. Hold, then lower down under control.
Lock the bottom arm and push the pole away. Keep the body straight and squeezed. Teaches the push-pull pattern before lowering the legs toward horizontal.
Stand side-on to a sturdy vertical pole. Grip with the top hand overhand above the head and the bottom hand around chest height, hands wider than the shoulders.
Push through the straight bottom arm and pull with the top arm, jumping the hips up and tucking the knees to the chest so the torso is roughly horizontal. Hold, then lower the feet down with control.
Keep both arms locked. Stack the shoulders over each other rather than letting the chest face the floor. Build to 10 second holds before opening the legs.
Stand side-on to a sturdy vertical pole. Grip with the top hand overhand above the head and the bottom hand around chest height, hands wider than the shoulders.
Push with the bottom arm and pull with the top while lifting the legs straight and spread wide so the body is horizontal. Hold, then lower down under control.
Wider legs make it easier. Keep the hips in line with the shoulders, not sagging. Point the toes and squeeze the obliques and glutes.
Stand side-on to a sturdy vertical pole. Grip it with the top hand overhand above the head and the bottom hand around hip or chest height, hands about shoulder width or wider apart.

Lock both arms, push hard through the bottom arm while pulling with the top, and lift the body sideways until it is straight and horizontal with the legs together. Hold, then lower the feet back to the floor with control.
The bottom arm pushes, the top arm pulls, both stay straight. Keep the top shoulder and hip stacked over the bottom ones. Advanced skill built through tuck and straddle flags.
Sit on the floor or between parallettes with the legs straight together and the hands flat beside the hips (or gripping the parallettes), arms straight, fingers pointing forward.
Press the hands down and depress the shoulders to lift the hips and buttocks off the floor while the heels stay on the floor and the legs stay straight. Hold for time, then lower the hips and repeat.

Shoulders pushed down away from the ears and elbows locked. Raise the hands on blocks or parallettes if arm length or wrist mobility makes lifting the hips hard. Builds the support strength for tuck and full L-sits.
Sit on the floor or between parallettes with the legs straight together and the hands beside the hips, arms straight.
Press down to lift the hips, pull one knee to the chest (tuck) and raise the other leg straight to parallel with the floor. Hold, then lower and switch legs on the next set or rep.
Keep the arms locked and shoulders depressed. Lock the knee of the extended leg and point the toes. Bridges the gap from the tuck L-sit to the full L-sit.
Uses gymnastic rings set at hip height. Jump into a straight-arm support with the rings pressed against the sides of the hips.
From the support, lift the legs straight and together until they are parallel to the floor, holding an L shape while keeping the rings steady. Hold for time, then lower the legs and step down.
Rings stay close to the body and arms locked. Turn the rings out slightly to stabilise. Harder than floor or parallette versions because of the unstable support.
Sit on the floor with the legs straight and spread wide. Place the hands flat on the floor between the legs, close to the hips, arms straight.
Press down hard, lean the shoulders slightly forward and compress the hips to lift the hips and both straight legs off the floor in a wide straddle. Hold, then lower.
Needs pancake flexibility and strong hip flexors. Point the toes and lock the knees. A key step toward the straddle press to handstand.
Sit on the floor or parallettes with the legs straight together and the hands beside or slightly behind the hips, arms straight.
Press down to lift into an L-sit, then lean the shoulders back and compress the hips to raise the legs well above parallel so the body forms a V. Hold, then lower back to the L or floor.
Push the shoulders down while leaning back. Keep the knees locked. Requires strong hip flexors and compression; drill seated leg lifts.
Sit on the floor or low parallettes with the legs straight together and the hands placed behind the hips, fingers pointing back, arms straight.
Press down and lift the hips, then drive the shoulders forward and up while lifting the legs past vertical so the hips sit behind the hands and the body is almost folded. Hold, then lower.
Elite skill needing shoulder extension strength and extreme compression. Progress through V-sit angles. Keep the arms locked.
Sit on the floor with the legs straight together and the back tall. Place the hands on the floor beside the knees or shins.
Without leaning back, contract the hip flexors and abdominals to lift both heels a few centimetres off the floor. Hold for one to two seconds, then lower. Repeat for reps.
Keep the knees locked and the back upright. Move the hands closer to the feet to make it harder. Builds the active flexibility needed for L-sit, V-sit and press handstand.
Lie face down with the arms extended overhead and the legs straight together with toes pointed.
Squeeze the glutes and lift the arms, chest and legs off the floor so only the belly area touches. Hold for time, then relax.
Keep the neck neutral and looking at the floor. Squeeze the glutes rather than cranking the lower back. Pairs with the hollow hold for gymnastic body tension.
Lie face down and set a tight arch body hold: arms overhead, chest and legs lifted, glutes squeezed.
Keeping the shape fixed, rock forward toward the chest and back toward the thighs in a smooth rhythm. Continue for reps or time, then relax to the floor.
The shape must stay rigid. Do not bend the knees or drop the arms. Squeeze the glutes and keep the head neutral.
Lie on the back in a hollow body hold with the arms overhead and legs together and lifted.
Roll onto the stomach and finish in an arch hold, without letting the arms or legs touch the floor. Roll back to the hollow. Alternate directions to train both sides.
Keep the body rigid like a pencil. Initiate with the trunk, not by kicking. Builds body tension control for kipping and levers.
Squat on a mat with the feet together and the hands on the mat shoulder width just in front of the feet.

Tuck the chin to the chest, lift the hips and bend the elbows and push from the feet so the shoulders and rounded upper back meet the mat; no weight goes on the head or neck. Roll along the rounded spine, grab the shins and roll up to a squat and stand.
Chin to chest and stay round. Push evenly through both hands. Use a soft incline mat to learn; a basic gymnastics and safe-falling skill.
Squat on a mat facing away from the direction of travel, chin tucked, hands beside the ears with palms facing up and fingers pointing back.

Sit back and roll along a rounded spine, bringing the knees to the chest. As the hips go over the head, place the hands flat on the mat and push hard to take weight off the neck, rolling over to land on the feet in a squat.
Keep the chin tucked and the body round. Push through the hands as the hips pass overhead. Learn down an incline mat; avoid with neck problems.
Sit on the floor with the knees bent, feet flat hip width apart, and the hands on the floor behind the hips with fingers pointing toward the feet.
Push through the hands and feet to lift the hips until the body forms a flat table from knees to shoulders, shins vertical and arms straight. Hold, then lower the hips back down.
Drive the hips up and squeeze the glutes. Let the head stay neutral or drop back gently. Opens the shoulders as a first bridge progression.
Sit on the floor with the legs straight together and the hands on the floor just behind the hips, fingers pointing toward the feet.
Push through the hands and heels to lift the hips until the body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders, arms straight. Hold, then lower.
Lock the knees and squeeze the glutes. Push the chest up and the shoulders back. Builds shoulder extension and posterior chain strength for full bridges.
Lie face up with the knees bent and feet flat. Place the hands on the edge of a bench or box above the head, fingers pointing toward the shoulders.
Push through the hands and feet to lift the hips and chest into a bridge with the hands supported higher than the feet. Hold or lower and repeat.
The higher the support, the easier the bridge. Push the chest toward the wall. Lower the support gradually toward the floor.
Lie face up with the knees bent, feet flat and hands flat beside the head, fingers pointing toward the shoulders.
Push through the hands and feet to lift the hips and back, then rest lightly on the crown of the head with the hands still pressing. Hold, then lower.
Protect the neck by keeping most weight on the hands. Avoid if neck problems. A step toward the full bridge.
Lie on the back with the knees bent, feet flat hip width apart, and the hands flat beside the head with fingers pointing toward the shoulders.
Push through the hands and feet to lift the body into an arch until the arms are straight, the hips high and the chest pushed toward the wall behind. Hold, then lower with control.
Push the chest toward the wall rather than just the hips to the ceiling. Keep the arms straight. Warm up shoulders, hips and spine well before training.
Stand with the back to a wall about an arm length away (roughly 60-90 cm), feet hip width apart and parallel, arms reaching straight overhead.

Push the hips forward, lift the chest and arch backward to place the hands flat on the wall, fingers pointing down. Walk the hands down the wall a few centimetres at a time, keeping the hips forward, until reaching the floor in a bridge or as low as you control. Walk the hands back up the wall to return to standing.
Push the hips forward and keep the knees slightly bent as you descend. Breathe steadily and move slowly; stop where the lower back feels pinched. A step toward the stand-to-stand bridge.
Lie on the back with the knees bent, feet flat hip width apart and hands beside the head, fingers pointing toward the shoulders. Press up into a full bridge with straight arms and the hips high.

Shift weight onto one foot and both hands, then lift the other leg and extend it straight up toward the ceiling while holding the bridge height. Hold for a few seconds, lower the foot back to the floor and switch sides.
Keep the hips level and high; do not let the unsupported side drop or rotate. Push the chest toward the wall behind. Requires a solid 20-30 second full bridge first.
Stand on a mat with plenty of space behind, feet hip width apart and parallel, arms reaching straight overhead by the ears.

Squeeze the glutes, push the hips forward and lift the chest, then arch backward, looking for the floor, and lower the hands to land in a full bridge with arms straight. To return, shift the weight toward the feet by driving the knees forward and pushing the shoulders over the hands, then lift the chest and stand up.

Push the hips forward as you descend so the knees, not the lower back, take the lean. Learn with a spotter or the wall walking bridge first. Advanced flexibility skill: build the full bridge and warm up the spine well.
Get on the hands and knees with the hands directly under the shoulders, fingers spread, and the knees under the hips, hip width apart, toes tucked under.

Press the floor away and lift the knees about 2-5 cm off the floor, keeping the back flat and the knees hovering at roughly 90 degrees at hip and knee. Hold for time while breathing behind a braced trunk, then lower the knees.
Keep the back flat and hips level, no rounding or sagging. Press the floor away so the shoulder blades do not wing. The foundational Animal Flow position; build to 30-60 seconds.
Start in a static beast hold: hands under shoulders, knees under hips hovering 2-5 cm off the floor, back flat.

Move forward by stepping the opposite hand and foot together a short distance (right hand with left foot), then the other pair. Keep the knees hovering low and the hips level. Crawl backward and laterally as well.

Keep the knees low and the hips level with the shoulders; unlike a typical bear crawl the hips do not rise. Move slowly and quietly with small steps. Keep the back flat and avoid rocking side to side.
Sit on the floor with the knees bent, feet flat about hip width, and the hands on the floor behind the hips, fingers pointing back or out (static crab position).
Drive the hips up high through the heels and reach one arm overhead and back toward the floor behind, rotating the chest toward the ceiling into an arch. Return to the crab and switch sides.
Drive the hips up high and squeeze the glutes. Follow the reaching hand with the eyes. Stretches the shoulders, chest and front of the hips.
Squat deep with the feet wider than the hips, toes turned out slightly and the knees pushed out over the toes. Place both hands on the floor in front of the feet.

Keeping one hand pressing into the floor, reach the other arm overhead and back, rotating the chest open toward that side and following the hand with the eyes. Return the hand to the floor and switch sides.
Keep the heels down and the knees out. Rotate through the upper back rather than shifting the hips. Keep the planted arm straight. Stretches the hips, groin and shoulders.
Squat deep with the feet wide, knees out and hands on the floor in front of the feet, arms straight.
Move the hands a short distance to one side and load weight onto them, then hop the feet over to land beside the hands, staying low. Repeat for distance and return the other way.
Land softly and keep the hips low throughout. Keep the arms straight as you hop. Load the weight onto the hands before the feet leave the floor. Move in both directions equally.
Start in a push-up plank with the hands shoulder width, arms straight and the body tight from head to heels.
Step one hand forward and bring the opposite knee up toward the outside of that elbow while lowering the chest close to the floor. Press forward and repeat on the other side, crawling low.
Keep the body low throughout. Move slowly. Keep the hips level, not piking up, and the elbows close to the ribs. Scale by staying higher off the floor.
Start in a static beast hold with the hands under the shoulders and the knees hovering just off the floor.
Lift one hand and pivot on the feet to rotate the hips, kicking the opposite leg through under the body to the side so the hips face sideways. Return through the same path to beast and switch sides.
Rotate fully through the hips. Keep the hips low and stay light on the hands. Reach the kicking leg long with the toes pointed.
Start in a static beast hold with the hands under the shoulders and the knees hovering just off the floor.

Lift one hand and step the opposite foot forward to land flat outside the remaining hand, sinking the hips low into a deep lunge-like position with the chest close to the knee. Return to beast and switch sides.
Keep the planted arm strong. Step the foot all the way forward. Opens the hips and groin.
Start in a static beast hold with the hands under the shoulders and the knees hovering just off the floor.
Lift one hand and thread the opposite leg under the body, pivoting on the other foot so the body turns to face up and land in a crab position. Thread back to beast and switch sides.
Rotate fully and keep the hips low. Move smoothly between positions. Keep the planted hand under the shoulder and drive the hips high once you land in the crab.
Start in a static beast hold with the hands under the shoulders and the knees hovering just off the floor.

Lift the hips and reach one leg back and up, bending the knee and rotating the hips so the foot travels over toward the opposite side, looking over the shoulder at the foot. Return to beast and switch.
Rotate through the hips and spine. Keep the arms straight. Stretches the hip flexors and front of the body.
Lie on the floor on your back with a climbing rope hanging directly above the chest, legs straight.
Grip the rope and pull hand over hand, keeping the body straight and the heels as the pivot, until you are standing. Reverse hand under hand to lower back down to the floor.
Keep the body straight. Builds rope climb grip and pulling strength. Reach high and pull smoothly, not with jerks. Bend the knees to make it easier.
Uses a wall-mounted pegboard and two wooden pegs. Hang from the board with a peg in each hand, inserted in the lowest holes, arms straight.

Pull up and lock off one arm tight to the chest, then remove the other peg and move it into a higher hole. Pull up on the new peg and move the other one higher. Continue to the top, then descend in reverse.
Move one peg at a time and keep the locked-off arm tight to the body. Place each peg fully into the hole before loading it. Scale with pegboard hangs and lock-offs.

Feet hip to shoulder width, toes turned out 10 to 15 degrees, bell about 30 cm in front. Hinge with a flat back and soft knees, grip the handle with both hands overhand, tilt the bell toward you and pull the shoulders down into the lats.

Hike the bell back high between the thighs, forearms touching the inner thighs. Snap the hips and squeeze the glutes so the bell floats to chest height with straight arms (it is weightless at the top, not lifted by the shoulders). Let it drop, wait until the forearms nearly meet the hips, then hinge sharply into the next rep. Exhale forcefully at lockout.

Hinge, not squat: shins stay close to vertical and hips travel back. Standing plank at the top, ribs down, no backward lean. The bell stops at chest or eye height; height comes from the hip snap, not the arms.

Same setup as the Russian swing: feet hip to shoulder width, bell 30 cm in front, both hands overhand on the handle, flat back and lats engaged. Requires full, comfortable overhead shoulder flexion; use a lighter bell than for the Russian swing.

Hike the bell back and drive the hips forward hard, then continue guiding the bell with straight arms until it is directly overhead, bottom of the bell pointing at the ceiling and biceps by the ears. Let it fall back through the same arc, absorbing it with a hinge.

The hips do the work; the arms only guide the last part of the arc. Do not arch the low back or flare the ribs to reach overhead. Anyone without full shoulder mobility should stop at eye level (Russian swing).

Feet hip to shoulder width, bell 30 cm in front and centred. Hinge and grip the handle with one hand, thumb wrapped and slightly toward the corner of the handle; free arm can hang or shadow the bell. Shoulders square to the front.
Hike the bell back between the legs, then snap the hips to float it to chest height with a straight arm. Let it return through the legs and hinge into the next rep. Complete the set and switch hands.

Do not let the shoulders or hips rotate toward the bell: resist with the obliques. Keep the working shoulder packed, not pulled forward at the top. Grip fatigue is the usual limiter; switch hands before form breaks.
