Set up exactly as for a single-arm swing: feet hip to shoulder width, flat-back hinge, one hand on the handle. Learn the one-arm swing first.

Swing with one hand. At the float (top of the arc, chest height) release the handle and immediately catch it with the other hand, then swing it back through the legs. Switch hands on every rep or every few reps.
Change hands only at the weightless top of the swing, never during the backswing. Keep the bell close and the arc smooth. Clear the area around you; a missed switch drops the bell.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Two equal bells side by side. Take a wider stance than usual (about 1.5 times shoulder width) so both bells pass between the legs. Hinge, grip each bell with one hand and tilt them toward you.

Hike both bells back between the legs, one hand per bell, then snap the hips to float them to chest height together. Let them fall back and hinge again. Park both bells in front at the end of the set.

Wider stance and a deeper hip hinge than the single-bell swing. Keep the bells close together and the elbows soft but not bending. Brace hard; the doubled load stresses the low back if the spine rounds.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Bell on the floor about 30 cm in front, feet hip to shoulder width. Hinge with a flat back, grip the handle with both hands and tilt the bell toward you; pull the shoulders into the lats to create tension before each rep.

Hike the bell back hard, snap the hips to float it to chest height, then guide it back through the legs and park it on the floor in its starting spot. Reset the tension and breath, then begin the next rep from a dead stop.
Each rep starts from zero momentum, so all power comes from the hike and hip snap. Good teaching drill for the hinge and for keeping the back flat. Park the bell in front, never between the feet.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Clean one bell to the rack: handle diagonal across the palm, bell resting on the outside of the forearm and against the chest, wrist neutral, elbow tucked against the ribs. Feet shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace and squat to at least parallel, knees tracking over the toes and torso upright, keeping the rack tight. Drive up through mid-foot. Complete the set, then switch sides.
The offset load tries to bend you sideways: stay level and square. Keep the elbow in contact with the ribs and the wrist straight. A unilateral loaded squat; useful for exposing asymmetries.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Two equal bells in front, stance slightly wider than shoulder width, deep flat-back hinge, one overhand grip on each handle. Only for lifters with a solid single snatch.

Hike both bells back, snap the hips and pull both elbows high, then punch both hands through to lock the bells out overhead together, biceps by the ears. Drop them back down in an arc into the next hike, or lower through the rack.
Requires full overhead mobility; do not arch the low back to finish. Bells travel close together and close to the body. Start well lighter than your single-bell snatch.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Clean or carefully lift the bell so it balances upside down, bell above the handle, at shoulder height. Grip as hard as possible, wrist straight, forearm vertical, elbow tucked in front of the ribs. Feet hip width, glutes tight.
Press the bell straight up slowly, keeping it perfectly upright, to full lockout over the shoulder. Lower slowly to the start position without letting it tip.
Crush the handle; a loose grip lets it fall. Keep the forearm vertical at all times. Use roughly half your normal press load. Builds shoulder stability and grip and corrects a wandering press path.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lift one bell into a bottoms-up hold at shoulder height: bell above the handle, forearm vertical, elbow bent about 90 degrees and close to the ribs. Squeeze the handle hard.
Walk slowly for distance or time keeping the bell perfectly upright and the torso tall. Set it down safely, switch hands and repeat. Keep breathing behind a light brace the whole walk.
Short, smooth steps. Keep the shoulder packed down and away from the ear. Do not lean away from the bell. A light bell (8 to 16 kg) is plenty; it is grip and shoulder stability work.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on your back holding the bell in one hand with the arm locked vertically over the shoulder. Bend the same-side knee with the foot flat; the other leg and arm lie on the floor at about 45 degrees.

Roll to the elbow, then the hand, then bridge the hips high. Sweep the straight leg under you to a half-kneeling position, windshield-wiper the back shin, and stand up from the lunge. Reverse every step to lie back down. Eyes stay on the bell until you are standing.
The arm stays vertical and locked throughout; the body moves under the bell. Move slowly and pause in each position. Learn it with a shoe balanced on the fist before adding load.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Start exactly as for the Turkish get-up: on your back, bell locked out vertically over the shoulder, same-side knee bent with the foot flat, other arm and leg at 45 degrees.
Roll to the elbow, press to the hand, then bridge the hips up to full hip extension. Lower the hips, return to the elbow, then to the floor. Repeat for reps on one side before switching.
Covers the hardest early portion of the get-up for higher reps. Drive through the heel of the bent leg in the bridge. Keep the arm vertical and the shoulder packed throughout.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Press or snatch the bell overhead and lock it out. Feet slightly wider than shoulder width, both turned about 45 degrees away from the bell side. Weight shifted into the hip under the bell.

Keeping the arm locked and eyes on the bell, push the hip under the bell out to the side and hinge, sliding the free hand down the inside of the front leg toward the foot. Go as low as the hamstrings allow with the back long. Drive the hip back under you to stand.
It is a hip hinge with lateral flexion, not a side bend from the waist. The bell arm stays vertical. The leg under the bell stays straight; the other may bend slightly.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Place the bell on the floor inside the front foot. Feet slightly wider than shoulder width, both turned about 45 degrees away from the free arm. Reach the free arm straight up to the ceiling.

Push the hip on the free-arm side out and hinge down, keeping the top arm vertical and eyes on the hand, until the low hand grips the bell. Drive the hip back under you to stand up with the bell hanging. Lower it along the same path.
Same windmill path, but loaded from below, so heavier bells are possible. Keep the legs mostly straight and the back long. Learn this before the overhead windmill.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand tall with feet hip width, holding the bell by the handle in one hand in front of the hips. Glutes and abs braced.
Pass the bell around the waist, transferring it from one hand to the other in front of the body and again behind the back. Keep a steady rhythm for reps or time, then reverse direction.
The hips and shoulders stay still while the bell moves. Keep the bell close to the body. Grip and core work as well as a warm-up; increase speed only once the hand-off is clean.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet wider than shoulder width, hinge to a half squat with the back flat, holding the bell by the handle in one hand.

Pass the bell between the legs from front to back, handing it to the other hand behind the leg, bring it around the outside of that leg to the front, then pass it back through. The path traces a figure 8 around the legs. Continue for reps or time.
Hold the hinge position; do not stand up between passes. Keep the back flat and the chest up. Add a hip pop to swing the bell between hands for a faster, more dynamic version.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Clean one or two bells into the rack: forearms vertical, elbows tucked onto the ribs, wrists straight. Stand tall with feet hip width.
Walk for distance or time with short controlled steps, holding a tight rack and breathing shallowly behind the brace. Clean the bells back down safely at the end.
The rack compresses the chest, so brace without holding your breath. Do not lean back to support the bells. With one bell, resist the side bend toward the loaded side.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold one bell by the horns or by the bell body against the upper chest, elbows pointing down and tucked. Stand tall with feet hip width.
Walk for distance or time with short controlled steps, keeping the bell glued to the chest. Breathe steadily behind a light brace. Set it down by squatting at the end.
Do not lean back to support the bell: stack ribs over hips. Keep the upper back tall and shoulders down. A front-loaded carry that also builds upper-back endurance for the squat.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Deadlift one bell beside the foot and stand tall holding it at the side, neutral grip, arm long. Shoulders level, free arm relaxed or out to the side.
Walk for distance or time with short controlled steps, keeping the torso perfectly upright despite the one-sided load. Set the bell down by hinging and switch hands.
Do not lean away from or toward the bell; the obliques and quadratus lumborum resist side bending. Keep the shoulder of the loaded side packed, not hanging. Squeeze the handle hard.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Deadlift two heavy bells, one beside each foot, and stand tall holding them at the sides with a neutral grip, arms long. Shoulders packed down and back.
Walk for distance or time with short, quick, controlled steps, keeping the torso upright and the bells still. Set them down with a flat-back deadlift at the end.
Crush the handles. Keep the shoulders down and away from the ears; do not let them roll forward. Walk heel to toe without letting the bells swing into the legs.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Press or snatch one or two bells overhead and lock out the arms, biceps beside the ears, bells stacked over the shoulders. Stand tall with feet hip width.
Walk for distance or time with short controlled steps, keeping the arms vertical and locked and the ribs down. Lower the bells to the rack, then to the floor, at the end.
Requires full overhead mobility; if the low back arches to get there, use the rack carry instead. Keep the shoulder packed and the elbow locked. Do not let the bell drift forward.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold one bell in the rack (or locked overhead) and the other at the side in a suitcase grip. Stand tall, racked elbow tucked against the ribs, shoulders level.
Walk for distance or time, resisting both lean and rotation from the uneven load. Breathe steadily and keep steps short. Switch arm positions and repeat for equal distance.
Keep the shoulders level and the hips square. Use the lighter bell in the higher position. Combines anti-lateral flexion and anti-rotation in one carry.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Stand in a wide sumo stance, about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width, toes out 30 degrees, with one bell on the floor between the feet. Squat down with a flat back and grip the handle with both hands overhand, close together.

Drive through the legs to stand explosively, then shrug and pull the handle up to just below the chin, elbows leading high and out above the hands. Lower the bell back to arm's length, then to the floor (or just above it) in one smooth path.
Legs first, then hips, then arms. Keep the bell close to the body. Stop the pull under the chin to protect the shoulders; elbows above wrists at the top.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Rack one or two bells, forearms vertical, elbows tucked, feet shoulder width and toes slightly out.

Squat to at least parallel with an upright torso, then drive up hard and use the momentum from the legs to press the bells overhead to lockout in one continuous movement. Bring them back to the rack as you descend into the next squat.
Do not pause between the squat and the press; the hip drive launches the bell. Keep the elbows tucked in the squat. Lock out with the biceps beside the ears and ribs down.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Swing setup: feet hip to shoulder width, bell 30 cm in front, flat-back hinge, single overhand grip.

Hike the bell back and clean it to the rack, bell on the forearm and elbow on the ribs. Pause, brace, then strict press it to lockout overhead. Lower to the rack, then drop it into the backswing for the next clean.
Clean with the arm close to the body so the bell lands softly. Pause in the rack before every press. Press strictly with no leg drive; it is a classic full-body kettlebell complex.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Rack one or two bells and squat to the bottom of a full squat: heels down, knees out over the toes, torso as upright as possible. Requires good ankle, hip and thoracic mobility.
While holding the bottom of the squat, press the bell(s) overhead to full lockout, biceps beside the ears. Lower back to the rack under control and repeat. Stand only after the set.
Keep the chest up and the lower back neutral in the hole; do not fold forward. Start very light (well under half your standing press). Named after Soviet lifter Viktor Sots.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold one bell in the goblet or rack position, or a bell in each hand at the sides. Stand tall with feet hip width.

Step one foot back about 60 to 90 cm and lower until the back knee lightly touches or hovers above the floor, front shin near vertical and front knee over mid-foot. Drive through the front heel to return to standing. Alternate legs or complete one side first.
Stepping back is easier on the knees than a forward lunge. Keep the torso tall and the hips square. Most of the weight stays on the front foot.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold a bell in the goblet position. Take a very wide stance, about twice shoulder width, toes turned out slightly.

Shift onto one leg and squat deep over it, heel flat and knee tracking over the toes, while the other leg straightens with that foot pivoting onto the heel, toes pointing up. Push back up through the bent leg and shift to the other side.
The working heel stays down. Keep the chest up and the bell close as counterbalance. Go only as low as mobility allows; it builds inner-thigh flexibility and strength together.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Two-hand swing setup with a slightly wider stance than usual (just over shoulder width) to allow a deep squat.

Swing the bell. At the float at chest height, release the handle and catch the bell by the bell body or horns in the goblet position while dropping into a goblet squat. Stand up, push the bell away and regrip the handle, then let it drop into the next hike.
Catch softly with the hands around the bell. Keep the swing a hinge and the squat a squat. An advanced coordination drill; use a light bell.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Clean the bell to the rack with the upper arm resting on the side of the torso and the elbow on the hip. Turn the feet about 45 degrees away from the bell side, stance slightly wider than shoulder width.

Keeping the forearm vertical, bend the torso away and down under the bell while pushing the hip out to the bell side, so the arm straightens because the body moves away from it. Once the arm is locked, stand up under the bell. Lower to the rack.
The body moves under the bell; the arm does not press it up. Windmill competence is a prerequisite. Eyes on the bell throughout. A classic old-time strongman lift.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set a high plank gripping the handles of two bells placed directly under the shoulders, feet wider than shoulder width.

Shift the weight slightly onto one hand, row the other bell to the lower ribs keeping the elbow close to the body, and set it down under control. Alternate sides, adding a push-up between rows if programmed.
Hips stay square to the floor: no twist or hike. Widen the feet to scale. Use stable, flat-bottomed bells or hex dumbbells; round bells can roll.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Use a dead-bounce slam ball (3 to 12 kg). Stand with feet shoulder width, holding the ball at the chest with both hands on its sides.

Rise onto the toes and drive the ball overhead with the arms nearly straight, stretching tall. Then violently flex the trunk and pull the arms down, hinging at the hips and bending the knees, to slam the ball into the floor about 30 cm in front of the feet. Squat down with a flat back to pick it up and repeat.
Power comes from the abs and lats pulling down, not just the arms. Exhale hard on the slam. Never slam a bouncy rubber medicine ball; it rebounds into the face.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet shoulder width holding a dead-bounce slam ball at the chest. Clear space on both sides.

Lift the ball overhead toward one shoulder, then rotate and pull it down diagonally across the body to slam it beside the opposite foot, pivoting the back foot as the hips turn. Pick it up with a hinge or squat and slam to the other side.
Rotate through the hips and trunk, not only the arms. Pivot the back foot to protect the knee. Keep the back flat when picking up the ball. Use a non-bouncing slam ball.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Lie on your back on the floor or a bench with the knees bent and feet flat. Hold a 1 to 4 kg medicine ball at the chest with both hands, elbows bent at about 45 degrees from the torso. A partner can stand over you to catch and drop.

Throw the ball explosively straight up from the chest, extending the arms fully. Catch it with soft elbows, absorb it back toward the chest and immediately throw again. Alone, catch and pause before each throw.
Throw straight up so it comes straight back down. Keep the head and shoulders on the floor. Use a light ball; the goal is speed of the press, not load.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Stand side-on to a wall or open space, feet wider than shoulder width. Hold a 2 to 5 kg ball against the back shoulder with the throwing hand behind it, fingers spread and elbow pointing back and down; the other hand supports the front.

Rotate away and shift weight onto the back leg, then drive off the back leg, rotate the hips and torso toward the target and punch the ball forward and slightly up with the throwing arm, like a shot put. Catch or retrieve, then repeat. Switch sides.
Push the ball, do not throw it like a baseball: the elbow stays behind the ball. The hips turn before the arm extends. Finish with the chest facing the target.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand 2 to 3 m from a solid wall or partner, feet staggered or shoulder width. Hold a 2 to 5 kg ball overhead with both hands, arms slightly bent.

Bring the ball slightly behind the head to pre-stretch the abs and lats, then step or shift forward and throw it hard toward the wall or partner, finishing with the arms pointing at the target and the trunk flexed slightly forward. Catch and repeat.
Use the stretch-reflex of the trunk; do not throw with the arms alone. Do not over-arch the low back on the wind-up. Keep the elbows pointing forward, not flared.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand facing away from an open field or high wall with feet shoulder width. Hold a 3 to 6 kg ball at arm's length in front of the hips with both hands.

Hinge and dip the ball between the knees with a flat back, then jump explosively through the hips, knees and ankles, swinging the arms up and throwing the ball backward over the head as high and far as possible. Retrieve the ball and reset.
A triple-extension power test: the legs and hips launch the ball, the arms only guide it. Release at full extension with straight arms. Always check that the landing area is clear.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand facing an open space or wall with feet shoulder width. Hold a 3 to 6 kg ball at arm's length in front of the hips with both hands.

Hinge with a flat back and lower the ball between the knees, then extend the hips, knees and ankles explosively and swing the ball forward and upward, releasing it at about 45 degrees for maximal distance. Retrieve and reset.
Arms stay long like ropes; the hips create the power. Finish tall on the toes. The forward counterpart of the backward overhead throw.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Stand about 30 to 60 cm from a wall, facing it, feet shoulder width and toes slightly out. Hold a soft wall ball (standard 9 kg men, 6 kg women) at the chest with hands under the ball, elbows down. Target is 3 m (men) or 2.7 m (women).

Squat until the hip crease is below the knee, then drive up explosively and use the leg drive to throw the ball up to hit the target, finishing with the arms extended. Catch the ball at the chest as it falls and descend directly into the next squat.
Full depth on every rep. Keep the elbows under the ball. Do not stand too far from the wall; the ball should come straight back down.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet shoulder width and toes slightly out, holding a 3 to 8 kg medicine ball at the chest with both hands on its sides, elbows down.

Squat to parallel or below with the torso tall, then stand and, as the hips extend, press the ball straight overhead to full lockout without letting go. Lower the ball to the chest as you descend into the next squat.
Unlike a wall ball the ball is not released, so it suits beginners and limited spaces. Keep the ribs down at lockout. Press through the top of the squat in one smooth motion.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand tall holding a 2 to 5 kg medicine ball at chest height with the arms bent or extended. Feet hip width.

Step forward into a lunge until both knees are bent about 90 degrees, front knee over the ankle. In the bottom position, rotate the trunk and ball toward the front leg, return to centre, then drive through the front heel to stand. Alternate legs or walk forward.
Rotate from the trunk while the pelvis and front knee stay still and pointed forward. Extend the arms to make it harder. Keep the torso tall.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set a high plank with one hand on a medicine ball and the other on the floor slightly wider than the shoulder, feet hip width, body in one straight line.

Lower the chest until it is a fist's height from the floor, elbows at about 45 degrees, and press back up. At the top, roll the ball across to the other hand, re-set and push up on the other side. Continue alternating.
Keep the hips level during the transfer. The ball hand is unstable, so control the descent. Add a lateral hop across the ball for a reactive version.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Med Ball Drop and Catch Push-Up
Set a high plank with both hands on a sturdy medicine ball under the chest, body straight and feet hip width. Requires a solid push-up base.

Release the hands off the ball and drop them to the floor slightly wider than shoulder width, landing with soft elbows and immediately lowering the chest, then push explosively so the hands leave the floor and return to the ball. Repeat.
Minimise floor contact time; absorb and reverse quickly. Keep a rigid plank with no sagging hips. Scale from the knees or with a lower ball.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet shoulder width and toes slightly out. Hold a light medicine ball (1 to 4 kg) overhead with straight arms, ball directly above the mid-foot.
Squat as deep as you can while keeping the ball over the mid-foot and the arms in line with the ears, heels down and knees over the toes. Stand back up.
An assessment and mobility drill: if the ball drifts forward, the thoracic spine or shoulders are limiting. Keep the ribs down. Use it as a warm-up for overhead squatting.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet shoulder width or slightly wider, holding a dead-bounce slam ball beside one hip with both hands.
Lift the ball up and over the head in an arc, rotating slightly, and slam it on the floor outside the opposite foot. Pick it up and arc it back over the head to slam on the other side.
Trace a rainbow: the arc goes over the head. Pivot the feet and use the hips. Keep the back flat when picking up the ball.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand over a 4 to 10 kg ball on the floor, feet shoulder width. Squat or hinge with a flat back and grip the ball on its sides.

Stand explosively, pulling the ball up close to the body to the chest (a ball clean), then press or push-press it straight overhead to lockout with the arms by the ears. Lower it back to the chest and then to the floor with a flat back.
Lift with the legs, not the back. Keep the ball close. Lock out fully overhead with the ribs down.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Kneel side-on to a wall about 1 m away, in tall kneeling (both knees down) or half kneeling (inside knee down, outside foot forward). Hold a 2 to 4 kg ball at the outside hip.

Rotate the trunk away from the wall to load, then rotate explosively toward the wall and throw the ball into it at chest height. Catch the rebound and reset. Finish each throw with the chest facing the wall. Switch sides.
Removing the legs isolates trunk rotation. Squeeze the glutes and keep the hips still. Stay tall through the spine.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Ball Bridge with Shoulders on Ball

Sit on a stability ball and walk the feet forward until the shoulders and upper back rest on the ball. Feet flat, shoulder width, knees bent about 90 degrees at the top. Hands on the hips or holding a dumbbell on the hips.

Lower the hips toward the floor while keeping the upper back on the ball, then drive through the heels to raise the hips until the torso and thighs are level with the floor (tabletop). Hold briefly, then lower.
Keep the chin tucked and the ribs down at the top. Knees stay over the ankles. The ball adds balance demand; use a bench for maximal loading.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on your back holding a stability ball overhead with both hands, legs straight on the floor, lower back pressed into the floor.

Lift the arms and legs together to meet above the hips and pass the ball from the hands to the feet, gripping it between the ankles. Lower the arms and legs toward the floor, then lift again and pass the ball back to the hands. Each pass is one rep.
Keep the low back pressed into the floor as the limbs lower. Control the descent. Bend the knees or reduce the range to scale.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on your back with the hips and knees bent at 90 degrees. Hold a stability ball between the hands and knees, pressing the hands and knees into the ball. Lower back flat on the floor.
Keeping pressure on the ball with one hand and the opposite knee, slowly extend the other arm overhead and the other leg straight out, hovering above the floor. Return and switch sides.
The squeeze on the ball keeps the abs active and the low back flat. Exhale as you extend. Move slowly; reduce the range if the back lifts.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie face down with the chest on a stability ball, legs extended and feet wide on the floor. Let the arms hang straight down, thumbs up.

Raise the arms into a Y (overhead at 45 degrees), lower, then a T (straight out to the sides), lower, then a W (elbows bent and pulled down and back to the ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades). One cycle is one rep.
Lead with the shoulder blades, not the arms. Thumbs up for the Y and T. No load or very light plates; quality over range.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie face down with the stomach and hips on a stability ball, legs straight and toes on the floor about shoulder width. Arms hang down beside the ball, palms facing in.

Squeeze the glutes, lift the chest until the body forms a straight line, and at the same time pull the shoulder blades back and down while rotating the arms so the thumbs point up and back. Hold 2 seconds, then lower under control.
Keep the chin tucked and the eyes on the floor. Drive the movement from the shoulder blades, not the low back. A corrective exercise for rounded shoulders.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand on a long loop band with the feet shoulder width, toes slightly out. Loop the top of the band over the shoulders (front rack style) or hold it at the shoulders, so it is taut at the bottom.
Squat down to parallel or below, knees tracking over the toes and torso upright. Drive up through mid-foot, fighting the band to full hip and knee extension.
The band is hardest at the top: finish tall. Keep the knees out. Hold the band so it cannot slip off the shoulders.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Anchor a band high, above head height. Stand side-on with the feet shoulder width, holding the band with both hands above the shoulder nearest the anchor, arms nearly straight.
Pull the band diagonally down across the body to the outside of the opposite knee, rotating the torso and pivoting the back foot. Return slowly to the start.
Rotate through the hips and trunk together. Keep the arms long. Reverse the anchor (low to high) for a lift pattern.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on your back with a mini band around both feet. Lift the legs so the hips and knees are bent at 90 degrees (tabletop). Arms flat on the floor and low back pressed down.
Extend one leg long against the band while the other stays in tabletop, then return and alternate legs.
The leg that stays at 90 degrees is working: its hip flexors hold against the band. Keep the low back flat on the floor. Extend slowly and exhale.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand on the middle of a long loop band with the feet hip width. Hinge with a flat back and grip the band on either side of the feet, arms straight.
Drive through the floor and extend the hips and knees to stand tall, squeezing the glutes at the top. Hinge back down along the same path.
Hips and shoulders rise together. Keep the back flat and the band close. Resistance is highest at lockout; finish tall without leaning back.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Stand facing the anchor with feet hip to shoulder width (or staggered), holding the bar end at the front of the shoulder with one hand, or both hands interlaced for the two-hand version.

Dip by bending the knees 10 to 15 cm with the torso upright, then drive explosively through the legs and use that momentum to press the bar up and forward to a locked arm. Lower it back to the shoulder, absorbing slightly with the knees, and reset.
Dip straight down, not forward. The legs launch the bar; the arm finishes it. Allows heavier loads than the strict landmine press while keeping the shoulder-friendly angle.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Straddle the bar facing away from the anchor, feet shoulder width, the plates just in front of you. Hinge to a 30 to 45 degree torso angle with a flat back and soft knees. Grip a V-handle (close neutral grip) hooked under the bar, or the bar itself, arms straight.

Row the bar up toward the lower chest by driving the elbows back past the torso and squeezing the shoulder blades together. Pause briefly, then lower to full arm extension without changing the torso angle.

Keep a flat back and a fixed hinge angle; no standing up to heave the weight. A wider grip handle shifts work toward the upper back; a close neutral grip toward the lats. Use small (25 cm) plates for more range.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Stand beside the end of the bar, facing the same way as the bar, in a staggered stance with the outside leg back. Hinge with a flat back to about 45 degrees and grip the bar just below the sleeve with the near hand, neutral grip. Free hand on the front thigh.
Row the bar toward the hip, driving the elbow back close to the body until it passes the torso. Lower to full extension, letting the shoulder blade stretch forward slightly.
Pull to the hip for lats. Do not rotate the torso to lift the weight. Use straps if the thick bar end limits grip.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Hold the free end at the upper chest with both hands (or at one shoulder with one hand), feet shoulder width and toes slightly out, leaning slightly into the bar.

Squat to parallel with the torso upright, then drive up explosively and, as the hips finish extending, press the bar up and forward to lockout in one continuous motion. Bring it back to the chest as you descend into the next squat.
No pause between squat and press; the leg drive launches the bar. Elbows stay down in the squat. Finish with the ribs down and arms straight.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Lie on your back on the floor with the head toward the anchor side of the bar end, so the sleeve is above the chest. Knees bent, feet flat. Hold the end with one or both hands at the lower chest, elbows at about 45 degrees from the torso.
Press the bar up along its arc until the arms are straight over the chest. Lower it until the upper arms lightly touch the floor, pause briefly, then press again.
The floor stops the elbows, which limits shoulder stress. Keep the elbows tucked at about 45 degrees and the wrists stacked. Set the bar down on a stop or have a partner hand it off.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Straddle the bar facing away from the anchor with the sleeve just behind the heels or between the feet, feet shoulder width. Squat-hinge with a flat back and grip the bar with both hands just below the sleeve, or use a handle.
Brace and push the floor away to stand tall, driving the hips through and squeezing the glutes. Lower the bar by hinging and bending the knees until the plates touch the floor lightly.
A beginner-friendly deadlift: the bar sits centred under the hips and the arc keeps it close. Keep the chest up and the back flat. Lockout is tall, not leaning back.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wedge one end of an Olympic barbell into a landmine attachment or a padded corner and load the free end. Stand side-on to the bar end in a hip-width stance. Hinge and bend the knees with a flat back to grip the bar just below the sleeve with the near hand, arm straight.

Drive explosively through the legs and hips, keeping the bar close to the body, then pull the elbow up, rotate under the bar toward it and catch the end at the front of the shoulder in a quarter squat, facing the anchor. Press it if programmed, then lower it back to the start under control.
Hips first, arm second. Keep the bar close and turn the body under it to catch. Reset with a flat back on every rep.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Clean the bag to the front rack so it rests across the forearms and against the upper chest, elbows high and pointing forward. Feet shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace and squat to parallel or below, keeping the bag high and the torso upright. Drive through the mid-foot to stand tall.
Elbows up so the bag does not roll forward and round the back. Keep the chest tall. Breathe at the top, not at the bottom.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold the sandbag in a bear hug against the chest, or on one shoulder for an offset load. Stand tall with feet hip width.

Step forward 60 to 90 cm and lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor, front shin near vertical. Drive through the front foot and step through into the next lunge (walking) or back to the start. If shouldered, switch shoulders halfway.
Stay tall and keep the front knee over mid-foot. When the bag is on one shoulder, resist the side lean with the obliques. Shorter, controlled steps beat long wobbly ones.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand over the bag with a wide stance, squat down and wrap both arms around it, chest close to the bag. Make sure the area behind you is clear.
Lap or lift the bag, then extend the hips explosively and throw the bag up and over one shoulder so it lands behind you. Turn, reset over the bag and repeat, alternating shoulders.
Drive with the hips, not the arms. Release the bag high and let it go; do not follow it backward. Alternate shoulders to balance the load.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on your back with the sandbag across one shoulder, held in place by the same-side arm, head tucked away from the bag. Both feet on the floor.

Get up to standing by any efficient pattern, such as rolling to the elbow and hand, then a knee, and standing from a lunge, keeping the bag on the shoulder. Return to the floor in reverse. Alternate sides each rep or set.
Keep the bag stable and close to the neck. Move with control; no rushing. Unlike the kettlebell get-up there is no fixed pattern, which trains adaptable strength.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Use furniture sliders, gliding discs or a towel on a smooth floor. Set a high plank with hands under the shoulders and both feet together on sliders, body straight.
Pull both knees toward the chest together, rounding the low back slightly, then slide them back out to a straight plank.
Hips stay level rather than piking up. Control the return without letting the hips sag. Tuck toward one elbow to bias the obliques; progress to the slider pike.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Flip the BOSU dome side down and grip the edges of the flat platform in a high plank, hands about shoulder width, feet hip width.
Alternately drive each knee toward the chest and back, keeping the platform level, for time or reps (20 to 40 seconds is typical).
Keep the platform level and the hips low. Shoulders over the hands. Hold a steady pace rather than sprinting and losing position.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand on one foot in the centre of the BOSU dome, knee slightly bent, hands on the hips. Have a wall or rail nearby.
Hold the position for time (20 to 60 seconds), keeping the hips level and the knee tracking over the second toe. Switch legs.
Fix the eyes on a point ahead. Progress by closing the eyes, adding arm reaches or catching a ball. Ankle and knee stability drill; use support at first.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand beside a BOSU with the dome up, feet hip width, knees slightly bent in an athletic stance.
Hop sideways onto the centre of the dome with both feet, then off the other side, landing softly each time. Continue back and forth for time or reps.
Land quietly on the balls of the feet with the knees tracking over the toes, not inward. Keep ground contacts short only once landings are stable. Start slowly.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand tall about one stride behind a BOSU with the dome up, feet hip width.
Step forward, placing the front foot in the centre of the dome, and lower until both knees are bent about 90 degrees. Stabilise at the bottom, then push back to standing. Alternate legs.
Keep the front knee stable over the foot without wobbling inward. Torso tall. Pause at the bottom to own the position before pushing back.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold a BOSU flat side up by the edges, arms extended overhead, feet hip width.

Squat and place the BOSU dome side down on the floor, jump the feet back into a plank on the platform, jump them back in, then stand and press the BOSU overhead. Add a push-up in the plank if programmed.
Control the platform so it does not tip. Brace in the plank. Keep transitions smooth; step back instead of jumping to scale.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Stand with feet shoulder width holding a steel mace in a stacked grip (both hands together near the end of the handle), mace head up in front of you like a sword. Start with a light mace of 4 to 7 kg.

Drop the mace head behind the back over one shoulder, let it circle behind you, then pull it over the other shoulder and back to the front, finishing in the starting position. Alternate directions each rep or set.
Keep the hands close to the head and the elbows in. Stay braced so the torso does not rotate or arch. Choke up the grip to make it easier.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand with feet shoulder width holding a steel mace in a stacked grip vertically in front of the chest, mace head up.

Drop the mace head behind one shoulder so the handle points to 10 o'clock, then swing it back up over the top and down behind the other shoulder to 2 o'clock, like a pendulum. Continue for reps without completing a full circle.
Hands stay close to the head and the elbows in. Control the swing so it does not pull you off balance. A stepping stone toward the full mace 360.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Hold a steel mace vertically in front of the chest with a stacked grip, mace head up, feet shoulder width and toes slightly out.
Squat to depth keeping the mace vertical and close to the body, then drive up to stand.

Keep the torso tall and the mace vertical; the head-heavy load challenges posture. Good for learning the squat. Progress by holding the mace farther from the body or by squatting from a 10-to-2 swing.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand tall with feet hip width, holding a light Indian club (0.5 to 2 kg) in each hand by the knob end, clubs pointing up.
Swing the clubs in controlled circles: arm circles in front of the body, out to the sides, and inward and outward patterns, in the same or opposite directions.
Use light clubs. Keep a relaxed grip and let the clubs flow. Move from the shoulder and keep the torso still; shoulder mobility and warm-up work.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Stand tall with feet hip width, holding a club in one hand with the head pointing up in front of the shoulder.

Drop the club behind the head (inside mill) or behind the shoulder (outside mill), let it circle around behind the back and bring it back up to the front in a smooth loop. Repeat for reps and switch sides; advanced users alternate both arms continuously.
Keep the club close to the head and the elbow soft. Use a smooth, continuous pattern rather than muscling it. Light club (0.5 to 2 kg); it is a shoulder mobility and grip drill.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Wear a weighted vest fitted snug against the torso so it does not bounce or shift. Start at about 5 to 10 percent of body weight and build toward 10 to 20 percent. (Rucking with a loaded backpack is the same training effect.)
Walk at a brisk pace (roughly 5 to 6.5 km/h) for time or distance on flat ground, hills or stairs, swinging the arms naturally and breathing steadily.

Stay tall with the ribs stacked over the hips; do not lean forward under the load. Increase load or duration gradually, one at a time. A low-impact way to raise walking intensity and support bone density.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Wear a fitted weighted vest. Stand facing a stable box or bench about knee height (thigh close to parallel when the foot is on it), feet hip width.

Place the whole working foot on the box, lean the torso slightly forward and drive through the heel and mid-foot to stand fully on top, bringing the trailing foot up or holding it beside the box. Step down slowly with the trailing leg. Complete reps on one side and switch, or alternate.
Drive with the top leg; do not push off the bottom foot. Knee tracks over the toes. The vest keeps the hands free for balance, so it suits higher-rep conditioning sets.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Attach a loaded sled to a waist belt or shoulder harness with a strap 2 to 3 m long, or hold the handles behind you with straight arms. Face away from the sled and walk forward until the strap is taut, torso leaning slightly forward.

Walk or march forward with long, powerful strides, driving each foot back under the hips and fully extending the hip of the trailing leg. Continue for distance or time. Lighter loads can be sprinted for acceleration work.
Lean slightly but keep the spine neutral. Push the ground back behind you. Heavy loads for strength and work capacity; light loads (10 to 20 percent of body weight) for sprint mechanics.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more

Attach a rope or straps with handles to a loaded sled. Face the sled, take the handles with straight arms and step back until the strap is taut. Stand in a half squat with a flat back, torso at about 45 degrees, feet shoulder width.

Row the handles to the lower ribs by driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades, pulling the sled toward you. Walk back to re-tension the strap and repeat for distance. Variations pull hand over hand on a rope while standing still.
Brace and hold the half-squat angle; do not stand up to pull. Elbows drive back past the ribs. Pull smoothly; a jerk loses tension and loads the low back.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Attach a single handle at chest height. Stand in a split stance facing the stack, arm extended and holding the handle. Handle at about chest height, neutral grip; stand tall with the hips square.
Row the handle to the lower ribs, squeezing the shoulder blade back, then return to full reach.
Drive the elbow back. Avoid twisting the torso. Squeeze at the end of each rep and let the shoulder blade reach forward on the return.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Attach a rope or handle at chest height. Stand facing the stack, holding the handle with arms extended, feet shoulder width. Feet shoulder width, toes slightly out, squat to parallel.
Squat down keeping the arms long, then stand and row the handle to the chest in one smooth movement. Return the arms as you descend into the next squat.
Smooth transition between squat and row. Keep the chest up. Drive the elbows back.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Attach a straight bar to the low pulley. Stand facing the stack, feet hip width, gripping the bar shoulder width.
Hinge to lower the bar toward the shins, drive the hips to stand, then pull the bar to chest height with the elbows high. Lower to the thighs and repeat.
Flat back in the hinge. Elbows lead the pull. Stop the pull at chest height if the shoulders pinch.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set the glideboard to a low or medium incline. Lie on your back on the board with the feet hip width on the squat stand, knees bent and hands on the thighs or rails.
Push through the whole foot to straighten the legs and slide the board up, then bend the knees slowly to slide back down until the thighs are about parallel to the stand.
Raise the incline to make it harder. Keep the knees in line with the toes and the lower back on the board. Do not lock the knees hard at the top.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set a low incline. Lie on the glideboard with one foot centred on the squat stand and the other knee bent up toward the chest.
Push through the working foot to slide up until the leg is straight, then lower slowly. Finish all reps, then switch legs.
Keep the knee tracking over the middle toes and the hips level. A great step toward pistol squats with less load.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set the incline. Sit on the glideboard facing away from the tower, holding a handle in each hand at chest height with the elbows bent, then lie back with the knees bent and feet on the board.
Press the handles forward until the arms are straight, which slides the board up, then bend the arms slowly to return.
Keep the shoulder blades on the board and the wrists straight. Press the hands together slightly at the end for more chest.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set the incline. Sit on the glideboard facing the tower, legs straddling or on the board, holding a handle in each hand with the arms straight in front.
Row the handles to the lower ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades together, which pulls the board up the rails. Straighten the arms slowly to return.
Sit tall and do not lean back to pull. Lead with the elbows. Raise the incline for more resistance.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Attach the pull-up bar or use the handles. Kneel or lie face down on the glideboard facing the tower, reaching up for the bar or handles with the arms straight.
Pull the elbows down toward the ribs to slide the body up the board, then lower slowly to straight arms.
Start each rep by pulling the shoulders down. Keep the body long and the core tight. A scaled pull-up that builds toward the real thing.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Sit on the glideboard facing the tower holding the handles with the palms up and the arms straight in front at about chest height.
Curl the handles toward the shoulders, keeping the elbows still, which slides the board up. Lower slowly to straight arms.
Keep the elbows in front and the torso still. Move only at the elbows.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Sit on the glideboard facing away from the tower, holding the handles beside the head with the elbows bent and pointing forward.
Straighten the arms forward and up, sliding the board, then bend the elbows slowly to return.
Keep the upper arms still and the elbows narrow. Do not let the shoulders roll forward.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Set a low incline. Lie on the glideboard head toward the tower, holding the handles with the arms straight beside the hips, knees bent and feet on the board.
Curl the head and shoulders up and press the handles toward the feet, then lower slowly.
Curl the ribs toward the hips rather than pulling with the neck. Breathe out as you crunch.
Kettlebells, med balls, bands and more
Lie on the glideboard with the legs straight and the balls of the feet on the squat stand, heels hanging off the edge.
Lower the heels for a stretch, then push up onto the toes as high as possible and pause.
Keep the knees straight but not locked. Slow down the lowering. One leg at a time makes it harder.
