Keep both feet flat and the chest up. The bent knee tracks over the second and third toes rather than caving in. Turn the straight leg's toes up to the ceiling with the heel on the floor to add a hamstring stretch; widen the stance gradually to increase the stretch.

Begin on hands and knees with hands under the shoulders and one knee under the hip. Extend the other leg straight out to the side in line with the down knee, with the foot flat and the toes pointing forward.

Keeping a neutral spine, push the hips back toward the heel of the bent leg until the inner thigh of the straight leg stretches, then return forward to the start. Perform 8-12 slow reps per side, exhaling as you rock back.

Move from the hips without rounding or arching the back. Keep the straight-leg foot flat; turning the toes up adds the hamstrings. Hold the end position for 2-3 breaths to turn it into a static stretch, and progress range by sliding the straight leg farther out over sessions.

Sit on the floor with both legs straight and spread as wide as is comfortable, usually 90-120 degrees apart, with the kneecaps and toes pointing to the ceiling. Sit tall on the front of the sit bones with the hands on the floor in front of you.

Walk the hands forward and hinge from the hips, keeping the spine long, until a stretch is felt in the inner thighs and hamstrings. Hold 30-60 seconds, then walk the hands back to sit up. To bias one side, turn the chest over one leg and hinge over it, then switch.
Sit on a cushion if the pelvis rolls back and the back rounds. Keep the knees pointing up, not rolling inward. A flat back with less depth beats a rounded back with more.

Sit in a wide straddle with legs straight, toes and kneecaps up, at the widest angle you can hold with a flat back. Tilt the pelvis forward so you sit on the front of the sit bones, hands on the floor in front of you.

Keeping the back flat, walk the hands forward and lower the belly and chest toward the floor between the legs. Hold 30-60 seconds, or actively contract the hip flexors and quads to pull yourself deeper for 5-10 seconds, relax, and sink further. Walk back up to finish.

Lead with the belly button, not the head. A flat back matters more than depth. Sit on a folded mat or low step to help the pelvis tilt forward, and keep the toes pointing up rather than letting the legs roll in.

Stand facing a wall about an arm's length away with the hands on it at shoulder height. Step one foot back about 60-90 cm with the knee straight, heel flat and toes pointing straight ahead. Bend the front knee.
Lean the hips forward toward the wall while keeping the back heel down and the back knee straight until a stretch is felt in the upper calf. Hold 30 seconds with relaxed breathing, then switch legs.

Keep the back foot pointed straight ahead, not turned out, and do not let the arch collapse. Squeeze the back glute to keep the hip and knee straight. Step farther back to deepen. The straight knee targets the gastrocnemius; bend it for the soleus stretch.

Stand facing a wall with the hands on it at chest height. Step one foot back only about 30 cm, a shorter stride than the standard calf stretch, with both heels on the floor and both feet pointing straight ahead.

Bend both knees and sink the hips straight down, driving the back knee forward toward the wall while keeping the back heel flat, until a stretch is felt low in the back calf near the Achilles tendon. Hold 30 seconds, then switch legs.

The bent knee slackens the gastrocnemius and shifts the stretch to the soleus. Keep the heel down and the foot straight with the arch lifted. Move the back foot closer to the wall if you feel nothing; a valuable stretch for runners and anyone who squats with limited ankle range.
Stand on a step, stair or aerobic step with the balls of the feet on the edge and the heels hanging off. Hold a rail or wall for balance and stand tall with the knees straight.

Slowly lower one or both heels below the level of the step until the calves stretch. Hold 20-40 seconds, then rise back to level. For the single-leg version, keep the non-working foot resting behind the working ankle.

Lower under control and do not bounce at the bottom. Doing one leg at a time increases the stretch. Bend the knees slightly to shift the stretch to the soleus. Keep the ankle from rolling out so the weight stays over the big and second toes.

Kneel on a padded surface with the knees together, the tops of the feet flat on the floor and the toes pointing straight back. Sit the hips back onto the heels and place the hands on the floor beside or slightly behind the hips.

Lean back onto the hands and gently lift the knees off the floor a few centimeters, pointing the ankles further, until a stretch is felt down the front of the shins and the top of the ankles (tibialis anterior and toe extensors). Hold 20-30 seconds, then lower the knees.

Lift the knees gradually and stop if you feel cramping in the arch or pain in the knee. Place a rolled towel under the ankles to reduce intensity. A standing option is to rest the top of the toes on the floor behind you and gently press the ankle forward.
Sit on a chair and cross one foot over the opposite knee so the sole faces in. Grasp the toes, especially the big toe, with one hand and place the thumb of the other hand along the arch.

Pull the toes back toward the shin (ankle dorsiflexed) until the arch becomes taut and a stretch is felt along the bottom of the foot; the band of fascia should be palpable under the thumb. Hold 15-30 seconds, release and repeat 3 times, then switch feet.

Pull steadily rather than jerking. Most useful first thing in the morning and before standing after long sitting for plantar heel pain. Combine with calf and soleus stretching, since a tight calf increases tension on the plantar fascia.

Stand in a doorway or at a wall corner. Place both forearms on the frame with the elbows bent to 90 degrees and level with the shoulders, palms facing forward. Step one foot through the door into a short split stance.

Keeping the trunk tall, shift the body weight forward through the doorway until a stretch is felt across the chest and front shoulders. Hold 30 seconds, then step back. Repeat with the elbows raised to about 135 degrees and lowered to about 45 degrees to stretch different fibers.

Keep the ribs down and do not arch the low back or let the head poke forward. Elbows at shoulder height target the mid pec; higher elbows bias the lower (sternal) fibers and lower elbows bias the upper (clavicular) fibers. Stop if you feel tingling into the hands.
Kneel about 60-90 cm from a flat bench with the knees hip-width apart. Place the hands on the bench edge shoulder-width apart with the arms straight, palms down or thumbs up. Brace the abs lightly.

Sit the hips back toward the heels and let the chest sink toward the floor between the arms, keeping the arms straight, until a stretch is felt along the sides of the back and into the armpits. Hold 30-60 seconds, breathing into the back. Shift the hips toward one side to bias the opposite lat.

Keep the ribs tucked; dropping the chest by arching the low back removes the stretch. Keep the arms straight with the shoulders away from the ears. For a thoracic extension emphasis, bend the elbows on the bench instead (see Bench Thoracic Extension Stretch).

Stand side-on or facing a pole or power rack upright. Grab it with one hand at about hip to chest height, the arm straight, and set the feet about hip-width apart a little more than an arm's length away.

Sit the hips back and away from the pole while letting the arm stay long and the torso curve into a C shape, so the stretch runs from the armpit down the side of the back. Hold 20-30 seconds, adjusting the hand height and hip angle to find the tightest line, then switch sides.
Let the shoulder blade glide forward and up around the rib cage. Breathe into the stretched side. Cross the outside leg behind the inside leg to lengthen the line through the hip as well.
Stand or sit tall with the abs lightly braced. Raise one arm overhead, bend the elbow fully and let the hand drop behind the head toward the upper back, the elbow pointing to the ceiling.

Place the opposite hand on the bent elbow and gently press it back and toward the midline of the head until a stretch is felt along the back of the upper arm and into the armpit. Hold 20-30 seconds, then switch arms.

Keep the head up and avoid flaring the ribs or arching the low back. Press gently on the elbow, not on the hand. If shoulder flexion is limited, hold a towel in the top hand and pull it down with the bottom hand behind the back.

Stand tall. Hold a towel or strap overhead in one hand and let it hang down the back. Reach the other hand behind the low back, palm facing out, and grab the bottom end so both hands hold the towel behind you.

Pull the top hand upward to draw the bottom hand up the back, stretching the bottom shoulder into internal rotation and extension. Hold 20-30 seconds. Then pull down with the bottom hand to stretch the top arm's triceps and lats for 20-30 seconds. Switch hands.
Move slowly and stay within a pain-free range. Keep the torso upright without leaning or arching. Walk the hands closer together on the towel over weeks as mobility improves.
Stand side-on to a wall, about a hand's length away. Extend the near arm behind you and place the palm flat on the wall at or just below shoulder height, thumb pointing up and the elbow straight.
Slowly rotate the chest and feet away from the wall until a stretch is felt along the front of the arm and shoulder. Hold 20-30 seconds, then turn back and switch arms.

Keep the elbow straight but not locked and the shoulder down away from the ear. Turning the hand so the thumb points down increases the biceps emphasis by pronating the forearm. Move gently and back off if you feel nerve tension or tingling down the arm.
Sit tall with the shoulders relaxed. Place both hands, one over the other, flat on the upper chest just below the collarbone on the side to be stretched, to hold the first ribs and collarbone down.

Tilt the head away from the hands, then slowly lift the chin to extend the neck slightly and turn the face a little toward the stretched side until a stretch is felt along the front and side of the neck. Hold 20-30 seconds, return to neutral and switch sides.

Keep the movement small and slow; do not crank the neck back or compress the back of the neck. Breathe into the belly rather than the upper chest. Stop immediately if you feel dizziness, arm tingling or visual change.

Kneel on hands and knees with the shoulders over the hands and the knees under the hips. Turn the hands so the fingers point back toward the knees with the palms flat for the flexors, or flip them palms-up with fingers pointing toward the knees for the extensors.

Slowly shift the weight back toward the heels until the forearms stretch, then forward again. Rock rhythmically for 10 reps or hold 20-30 seconds in each hand position. Also try fingers pointing sideways and forward to cover all angles.
Keep the palms pressed flat and the elbows straight. Shift weight gradually, especially in the palms-up position. A standard prep before handstands, front squats, cleans and push-ups.
Lie on your back with the arms out in a T at shoulder height, palms down. Bend one knee and place that foot on the opposite knee, or bend both knees with the feet flat together.

Let the bent knee (or both knees) drop across the body toward the floor on the opposite side, guiding it with the opposite hand, while both shoulders stay down. Turn the head away from the knee if comfortable. Hold 30-60 seconds, breathing into the back and side ribs, then return to center and switch sides.

Prioritize keeping the shoulders down over getting the knee to the floor. Place a cushion under the knee if it hovers. Stacking both knees together is the gentler version; a straighter top leg adds the outer hip and IT band area.
Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat, or with the bottom leg straight along the floor to add a stretch to the bottom hip flexor.

Draw one knee toward the chest and hug it with both hands clasped on the shin just below the kneecap, or behind the thigh, until a stretch is felt in the low back and glute. Hold 20-30 seconds with slow belly breathing, then lower and switch legs.

Keep the opposite leg relaxed and the head and shoulders down. Hold behind the thigh if pressure on the knee is uncomfortable. A gentle option for stiff low backs in the morning; if the straight leg lifts off the floor, that hip flexor is tight.
Lie on your back and bring both knees toward the chest one at a time, holding behind the thighs or over the shins with the knees hip-width apart.

Gently pull the knees in so the tailbone lifts slightly off the floor and the low back lengthens and flattens. Hold 20-40 seconds or rock slowly side to side to massage the low back, then lower the feet one at a time.

Relax the shoulders and neck and keep the head on the floor. Hold behind the thighs if knee flexion is uncomfortable. Breathe slowly into the belly. Avoid if spinal flexion aggravates disc-related back pain.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and the knees soft. Raise one arm straight overhead, palm facing in, and place the other hand on the hip.

Reach the raised arm up and then over to the opposite side, side-bending the torso until a stretch is felt along the side of the body from the hip to the armpit. Hold 20-30 seconds while breathing into the stretched ribs, then return upright and switch.

Bend straight sideways without leaning forward or back or rotating. Keep the hips level and centered over the feet. Cross the leg on the stretching side behind the other leg to extend the stretch into the outer hip.
Stand side-on to a wall about an arm's length away, the near hand on the wall at shoulder height. Cross the leg nearest the wall behind the other leg, with both feet flat and the back leg straight.

Push the hip of the back leg out toward the wall and lean the upper body away until a stretch is felt along the outer hip and upper thigh of the back leg. Hold 20-30 seconds, then turn around and switch sides.

Keep the back leg straight and the foot flat. Slide the hip sideways rather than twisting the pelvis. The IT band itself barely lengthens; this stretch mainly targets the small front-outer hip muscle (TFL) and the side glute that pull on it. Raise the far arm overhead to extend the line.

Sit on the floor with the front leg bent 90 degrees in front of you (thigh pointing forward, shin across the body) and the back leg bent 90 degrees to the side (thigh pointing out, shin pointing back), both knees at right angles and the feet relaxed.

Sit tall and hinge forward over the front shin with a flat back to stretch the front hip's external rotators and glute. Hold 30-60 seconds. Then turn the chest to face the back leg and lean gently toward it to stretch the back hip in internal rotation. Hold, then switch to the other side.

Keep the spine long; hinge rather than round. Place the hands on the floor behind you if stiff, and sit on a cushion if the back hip lifts high. Keep the back knee pressing down as much as comfortable rather than forcing it.

Lie on your right side with the head resting on a pad. Bend the top (left) hip and knee to 90 degrees and rest that knee on the floor in front of you, holding it down with the bottom hand. Bend the bottom (right) knee behind you and grab that foot or ankle with the top hand.

Exhale and rotate the upper back so the top shoulder and chest fall back toward the floor behind you, while holding the top knee down and pulling the bottom heel toward the glute. Breathe deeply for 5-10 breaths, rotating a little further on each exhale, then switch sides.

Keep the top knee pinned to the floor so the lumbar spine stays still and the rotation comes from the thoracic spine. Use a strap on the back foot if needed. Lead the rotation from the rib cage, not the arm, and keep the neck relaxed.
Kneel facing a flat bench about 60-90 cm away. Place both elbows on the bench edge about shoulder-width apart, palms together in a prayer position or holding a dowel, and the knees hip-width apart.

Sit the hips back toward the heels and let the chest drop between the arms toward the floor, extending the upper back while keeping the abs braced and ribs down. Then bend the elbows fully so the hands fall behind the head to add the triceps and lats. Hold 30-60 seconds or pulse gently for 10 reps.

Extend through the upper back, not the low back; brace as if bracing for a punch. Keep the elbows no wider than the shoulders. Breathe slowly and let the chest melt on each exhale. Differs from the kneeling lat stretch by the bent elbows and thoracic extension focus.
Stand with the feet slightly wider than shoulder-width and the toes turned out 15-30 degrees. Hold a rack or post at chest height if balance pulls you backward.

Sit straight down into the deepest squat you can hold with the heels flat and the knees tracking over the toes. Bring the palms together and press the elbows into the inner knees to pry them out. Hold 30-120 seconds while shifting the weight gently side to side and front to back.

Keep the heels down; raise them on small plates if ankle mobility is limited. Keep the chest tall and the spine as neutral as you can; a little low back rounding at the bottom is acceptable for an unloaded hold. Holding a light kettlebell at the chest helps counterbalance.
Stand side-on to a wall or rack and hold it with the near hand at shoulder height. Stand tall on the inside leg with a slight knee bend and the outside leg relaxed and just off the floor.

Swing the outside leg forward and back like a pendulum, starting small and gradually increasing the height in front (hamstring) and behind (hip flexor) as the hips loosen. Perform 10-15 swings, then turn around and switch legs.

Keep the torso upright and still; the movement comes from the hip, not from rounding forward or arching back. Stay relaxed and swing rather than kicking hard. Keep the standing foot pointing forward and the standing glute engaged.
Face a wall or rack and place both hands on it at chest height, arms slightly bent. Stand on one leg with a soft knee and the swinging leg just off the floor.
Swing the free leg across the front of the body and then out to the side in a smooth arc, increasing the range gradually. Perform 10-15 swings per leg.
Keep the hips and shoulders square to the wall and the toes of the swinging leg pointing forward. Swing from the hip rather than twisting the trunk. Keep the standing knee soft but stable.

Start in a push-up position with the hands under the shoulders. Step the right foot outside the right hand into a deep lunge so the front shin is near vertical, the back knee off the floor and the back leg straight.

Drop the right elbow toward the right instep and hold for a breath. Place the right hand back down, then rotate the chest open and reach the right arm to the ceiling, eyes following the hand. Return the hand to the floor, shift the hips back to straighten the front leg and pull the toes up for a hamstring stretch, then return to the push-up position and switch sides. 3-5 reps per side.
Keep the back leg straight and the back glute squeezed to stretch the back hip flexor. Rotate from the upper back while the hips stay level. Move slowly and own each position for 1-2 breaths.
Sit on the floor with both knees bent about 90 degrees and the feet planted wider than hip-width. Place the hands on the floor behind you for support and sit tall.

Rotate both knees to one side so they finish in a 90/90 position (front leg in external rotation, back leg in internal rotation), pause 1-2 seconds, then rotate them back through center to the other side. Perform 8-12 slow switches.

Keep the heels planted as pivot points and move from the hips. Progress by removing the hands and sitting tall, then by lifting the feet slightly. Keep the movement smooth; do not flop the knees to the floor.

Stand tall holding a rack or wall with one hand. Brace the core, squeeze the free fist and the standing glute to create full-body tension so only the moving hip travels. Lift the working knee to hip height or higher.

Slowly draw the biggest circle possible with the knee: open the knee out to the side, rotate the hip internally so the foot rises up behind you, extend the thigh back behind the body, then bring it down and forward to the start. Reverse the path. 3-5 slow circles in each direction per leg.

Only the hip should move; keep the pelvis level and the torso still. Work at the edge of your range with tension, not momentum. Quality over speed, roughly 10-20 seconds per circle. Can also be done on hands and knees for more stability.

Stand tall with the feet hip-width apart, the glutes and abs braced and the free hand making a tight fist to stop the trunk moving. Start with the working arm straight at the side, thumb pointing forward.

Raise the straight arm forward and up overhead, keeping the biceps near the ear at the top. Rotate the palm out so the thumb points back, then continue the circle down behind the body as far as possible without the torso moving, finishing with the arm at the side. Reverse the path. 3-5 slow reps each direction per arm.
Keep the ribs down and do not lean or arch to fake range. Make the circle as large as possible while staying in control. Move slowly with tension throughout, about 10-15 seconds per rep.
Stand or sit tall with the shoulders relaxed and down, the core lightly braced and the eyes level.

Tuck the chin toward the chest, then slowly roll the head toward one shoulder, back to look up, to the other shoulder and back to the chin, tracing the largest pain-free circle. 3 slow reps in each direction, about 10 seconds per circle.

Move slowly and smoothly; stop before any pinching, dizziness or arm symptoms. Keep the shoulders still. Do not force end range, especially extension; reduce the back half of the circle if looking up is uncomfortable.
Stand or sit tall. Make a fist with one hand, extend that arm in front with the elbow bent about 90 degrees, and grip the forearm just below the wrist with the other hand to stop it moving.

Slowly circle the fist through flexion, side bend toward the little finger, extension and side bend toward the thumb, making the largest circle possible. 5 circles in each direction, then switch hands.
Keep the forearm from twisting; the motion happens only at the wrist. Go slowly with tension. A common prep before front rack, handstands, cleans and push-ups.

Start on hands and knees with the hands under the shoulders and the knees under the hips. Sit the hips back halfway toward the heels to lock the lumbar spine. Place one hand behind the head with the elbow pointing out to the side.
Exhale and rotate the elbow down toward the opposite wrist, then rotate up and open the elbow toward the ceiling as far as possible, following it with the eyes. 8-10 reps per side.
Rotate through the upper back while the hips stay still and level. Keep the supporting arm straight and push the floor away. Exhale on the upward rotation to get more range.

Kneel on one knee with the other foot flat in front, both knees at 90 degrees, the down knee directly under the hip and the torso tall. Extend both arms straight in front at shoulder height with the palms together.

Rotate the upper body toward the front-leg side, sweeping the top arm back as far as comfortable while the hips stay square and the front knee stays still. Follow the hand with the eyes. Return and repeat 8-10 times, then switch sides.
Keep the pelvis facing forward; the front leg blocks the hips from turning. Lead with the chest, not just the arm. Exhale as you rotate and squeeze the down-leg glute to stay tall.
Start on hands and knees with the wrists under the shoulders, the knees under the hips and the spine neutral. Spread the fingers and press the floor away.

Exhale and round the spine toward the ceiling, tucking the chin and tailbone (cat). Then inhale and let the belly drop, lifting the chest and tailbone and looking slightly forward (cow). Flow slowly for 8-12 cycles.

Move one segment at a time, starting from the pelvis. Keep the arms straight and the weight evenly between hands and knees. Work within a comfortable range, using smaller movements for sensitive backs.

Lie on one side with the hips and knees bent to 90 degrees, a pad, roller or block under the top knee, and the head on a pillow. Extend both arms straight in front at shoulder height with the palms together.

Keeping the knees together, sweep the top arm up and over to the other side in an arc, rotating the chest open toward the ceiling and the floor behind you and following the hand with the eyes. Pause for a breath, then return. 8-10 reps per side.
Keep the top knee pinned to the pad so the low back stays still and the rotation comes from the upper back. Exhale as you open. Do not force the hand to the floor; let it hang and relax.

Start in a high plank with the hands under the shoulders. Step the right foot outside the right hand into a deep lunge so the right heel is flat, the back knee off the floor and the back leg straight.

Sink the hips toward the floor for 2 seconds, then rotate the chest and reach the right arm to the ceiling. Bring the hand down, step back to plank and repeat on the left. 5 per side, or walk forward with each step.

Keep the back leg straight and the back glute active to stretch the hip flexor. Keep the front heel flat and the front knee tracking out over the toes to open the groin. Move under control rather than bouncing. Differs from the World's Greatest Stretch by omitting the elbow drop and hamstring phase.
Stand tall with the feet hip-width apart and the arms relaxed. Clear a lane of 10-20 meters.

Step forward and lift the opposite knee, grabbing it just below the kneecap with both hands and pulling it toward the chest while rising onto the toes of the standing leg. Hold briefly, lower the foot forward into the next step and alternate legs for the distance.
Stay tall; do not round forward to reach the knee. Squeeze the standing glute to extend that hip, which adds a stretch to the standing hip flexor. Rising onto the toes adds balance and calf work.
Stand tall with the feet hip-width apart. Clear a lane of 10-20 meters.

Step forward onto one leg, bend the trailing knee and grab that ankle behind you with the same-side hand, pulling the heel to the glute while reaching the free arm overhead and rising onto the toes. Hold 1-2 seconds, release, step through and alternate for the distance.

Keep the knees close together and the bent knee pointing down. Squeeze the glute of the stretched leg to open the hip flexor. Do not arch the low back or lean forward. Stay flat-footed on the standing leg if balance is limited.
Stand tall with both arms extended straight in front at shoulder height, palms down. Clear a lane of 10-20 meters.
Walk forward kicking one straight leg up toward the opposite hand, keeping the torso upright, then lower it and step through to kick with the other leg. Continue alternating for the distance.

Kick only as high as you can with a straight leg and a tall spine. Keep the standing heel down and the standing knee soft. Increase height gradually over the first few reps rather than kicking hard from the start.
Stand tall with the feet hip-width apart, a soft bend in the knees and the arms extended straight out to the sides at shoulder height, palms down.
Make small forward circles with the arms, gradually increasing to large circles over 10-15 reps. Then reverse the direction for another 10-15 reps.

Keep the shoulders down away from the ears and the elbows straight. Progress from small to large circles. Finish with a few circles with the palms up and then down to vary the rotation. Keep the ribs down so the low back does not arch.
Stand tall with the feet hip-width apart and the arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.

Swing the arms across the chest into a hug, alternating which arm is on top, then swing them back open as far as comfortable to stretch the chest and front shoulders. Perform 10-20 swings. Variations swing one arm up and one down, then switch.
Move rhythmically and gradually increase the range. Keep the torso still and the ribs down. Let the shoulder blades wrap around the ribs on the hug and pinch together on the opening.
Stand tall with the hands on the hips or one hand on a wall for support.

Lift one knee to hip height in front, rotate it out to the side as far as possible to open the hip, then lower the foot. Repeat 8-10 times. Then reverse the motion, lifting the knee out to the side and sweeping it around to the front to close the gate. Switch legs.
Keep the pelvis level and the torso still; only the hip moves. Keep the circle large. Can be done walking forward as a warm-up, alternating legs with each step.
Lie face down with the arms out to the sides in a T, palms down, and the legs straight with the toes on the floor.

Bend one knee and rotate the hip to bring that foot up and across the back of the body toward the opposite hand, keeping the chest and both shoulders down. Return to the start and alternate for 6-10 reps per side.
Keep both shoulders pinned to the floor so the rotation stretches the hip flexors, abs and spine. Move slowly; this is not a kick. Reduce the range if the low back pinches.
Sit in a 90/90 position with both knees bent 90 degrees, the torso tall and the hands free in front of the chest.

Drive the front shin and knee into the floor and squeeze the back-leg glute to lift the hips into tall kneeling on the front shin, then lower back down with control. Switch the legs to the other side through a 90/90 switch and repeat. 5-8 per side.
Keep the chest up and avoid using the hands. Squeeze the glutes fully at the top so the hips are extended. Regress by staying seated and only switching, or by using the hands lightly on the floor.
Half-kneel facing a wall with the front foot 5-10 cm from it, the foot pointing straight ahead and the hands on the wall.

Drive the front knee forward over the middle toes toward the wall while keeping the heel flat, then return. Perform 10-15 reps, holding the end range for 2-3 seconds. Move the foot back as range improves; touching the wall from about 10 cm is a common target.
Keep the heel down and the knee tracking over the second and third toes. Do not let the arch collapse inward. Pinching at the front of the ankle suggests a joint restriction; try the banded version.

Anchor a heavy resistance band low to a rack behind you and loop it around the front of the ankle, sitting low on the joint just below the ankle bones. Step forward into a half-kneeling or split position with that foot forward and the band taut.
Drive the knee forward over the toes while the band pulls the ankle joint backward, then return. Perform 10-15 reps or hold the end range for 20-30 seconds.

Keep the heel flat. Position the band low on the ankle joint, not on the shin. Use enough band tension to feel a clear backward pull on the talus, which helps reduce a pinch at the front of the ankle.

Loop a heavy resistance band over a high anchor such as a pull-up bar. Put one hand through the loop and grip the band so it pulls at the wrist, then step back so the band is taut with the arm straight overhead.
Sit the hips back and let the band pull the arm overhead, lowering the chest toward the floor and shifting gently side to side to find tight spots. Hold 30-60 seconds, then switch arms.
Keep the ribs down. Let the band traction the shoulder; do not shrug. Rotate the torso slightly away from the working arm or step to the side to explore different angles.

Stand facing a wall with the feet a short step back. Place the forearms on the wall shoulder-width apart, elbows bent 90 degrees at shoulder height, with the little finger side of the forearms on the wall.

Press the forearms lightly into the wall and slide them up overhead while letting the shoulder blades rotate up and wrap forward around the rib cage, then return slowly. Perform 8-12 reps. Lift the forearms off the wall briefly at the top for more lower-trap work.
Do not shrug; let the shoulder blades rotate upward naturally. Keep the ribs tucked and the low back neutral. Add a mini band around the wrists to work the external rotators.

Stand with the back, head and glutes against a wall and the feet 15-30 cm out from it, knees slightly bent. Flatten the low back gently toward the wall. Place the arms in a goalpost position with the backs of the hands, forearms and elbows on the wall.
Slide the arms overhead while keeping the forearms, hands and back in contact with the wall, then slide them down until the elbows are just below shoulder height. Perform 8-12 slow reps.
Keep the ribs down and the low back from arching. Only go as high as you can while keeping contact. A good test and drill for thoracic extension and shoulder external rotation.

Start on hands and knees with the hands shoulder-width apart and slightly ahead of the shoulders, fingers spread with the middle fingers pointing forward. Knees are under the hips about hip-width apart and the toes are tucked.

Exhale and lift the hips up and back to form an inverted V, straightening the legs as far as possible and pressing the chest toward the thighs and the heels toward the floor. Hold 5-10 breaths or pedal the feet by bending one knee at a time, then lower the knees.

Prioritize a long spine over straight legs; bend the knees if the back rounds. Press through the whole hand, especially the base of the index finger. Turn the upper arms out so the shoulders broaden, and let the head hang between the arms. The heels do not need to touch the floor.
Lie face down with the legs hip-width apart and the tops of the feet on the floor. Place the hands flat beside the lower ribs with the elbows bent and close to the sides.

Press into the hands and straighten the arms, lifting the chest forward and up and the thighs and knees off the floor so only the hands and tops of the feet touch. Hold 3-5 breaths, then lower down or roll over the toes into downward dog.

Stack the shoulders over the wrists and draw them back and down, away from the ears. Engage the legs so the knees stay lifted, and spread the backbend through the upper back rather than hinging only at the low back. Keep the neck long. Use cobra instead if the low back feels compressed.
Lie face down with the legs together or hip-width apart and the tops of the feet on the floor. Place the hands under the shoulders with the fingers spread and the elbows bent, hugging the sides.

Inhale and lift the head and chest using mainly the back muscles, pressing lightly into the hands while the pubic bone, hips and lower ribs stay down and the elbows stay bent. Hold 3-5 breaths, then exhale and lower.

Keep the pubic bone on the floor; this separates cobra from upward dog, where the thighs lift. Draw the shoulders back and away from the ears. Go only as high as feels good in the low back; lifting the hands off the floor briefly checks that the back, not the arms, is doing the work.
Lie face down with the legs hip-width apart and the tops of the feet on the floor. Place the forearms on the floor with the elbows directly under the shoulders and the forearms parallel, palms down.

Press the forearms and palms down and draw them gently back to lift and lengthen the chest forward, while the hips and thighs stay grounded and the low back relaxes. Hold 1-3 minutes with slow breathing, then lower.

A gentler, supported backbend than cobra and a good restorative option. Keep the shoulders down and the neck long. Relax the glutes and legs. Move the elbows slightly forward to reduce the arch if the low back pinches.
Kneel with the big toes touching and the knees together or apart about mat-width, sitting the hips toward the heels.

Fold forward over or between the thighs and rest the forehead on the floor, with the arms extended forward palms down (extended child's pose) or resting alongside the body palms up. Hold 30 seconds to several minutes, breathing into the back of the ribs.

Widen the knees to make room for the torso and to add an inner thigh stretch. Place a cushion under the hips or forehead if they do not reach. Walk the hands to one side to stretch the opposite lat and side body. Hold the hands back by the feet if knee flexion is limited.
Start on hands and knees with the hips stacked over the knees, the knees hip-width apart and the toes untucked.

Walk the hands forward a few hand-lengths and lower the chest toward the floor while keeping the hips over the knees, resting the forehead or chin on the floor and the arms straight with the elbows lifted. Hold 5-10 breaths, then walk the hands back.

Keep the hips high over the knees; letting them sit back turns it into child's pose. Let the chest melt toward the floor for thoracic extension, but keep the abs lightly engaged so the low back does not sag. Keep the palms pressing down and elbows off the floor.

From standing, step one foot back about a leg's length (roughly 1-1.2 m) and turn the back foot out 45 degrees with the heel down. Keep the feet about hip-width apart side to side, like standing on railroad tracks, and turn the hips toward the front of the mat.

Bend the front knee toward 90 degrees with the knee over the ankle, then raise the arms overhead, shoulder-width apart with palms facing in, and lift the chest. Hold 5-8 breaths, then straighten the front leg and switch sides.

Keep the back leg straight and press the outer edge of the back foot down. Draw the tailbone down slightly so the stretch reaches the back hip flexor. Widen the stance side to side if balance or hip squaring is difficult. Differs from Warrior II by the squared hips and overhead arms.

Stand with the feet about 1-1.2 m apart. Turn the front toes to point straight forward and the back foot in about 5-15 degrees, with the front heel in line with the arch of the back foot. Open the hips and chest to face the long side of the mat.

Bend the front knee toward 90 degrees so it is over the ankle, and extend the arms out parallel to the floor, palms down, gazing over the front middle finger. Hold 5-8 breaths, then straighten and switch sides.

Keep the front knee tracking over the middle toes rather than caving in. Keep the torso stacked over the hips, not leaning toward the front leg. Press into the outer edge of the back foot and keep the back leg straight. A strength-endurance hold for the front quad and glutes as well as an inner thigh opener.
Stand tall on one leg with a soft standing knee and the foot gripping the floor. Extend the arms forward by the ears, out to the sides, or keep the hands at the chest.

Hinge forward at the standing hip while lifting the free leg straight back, until the body forms a T from hands to heel parallel to the floor. Hold 3-8 breaths, then lower the leg and come up to standing and switch.

Keep the hips level by pointing the lifted toes straight down toward the floor rather than opening the hip. Reach long through the head and heel and keep the spine neutral. Rest the fingertips on blocks or a wall to regress, and keep the arms at the chest until balance is solid.
Begin in Warrior II with the front knee bent over the ankle, the back foot turned in slightly and the arms extended at shoulder height.

Turn the front palm up and reach that arm overhead and back while the back hand slides lightly down the back leg, arching the front side body. Keep the front knee bent. Hold 3-5 breaths, then return to Warrior II and switch.

Keep the front knee bent and tracking over the toes as you lean back. Lengthen the front side of the body rather than collapsing into the back hand; the back hand carries almost no weight. Keep the neck relaxed and gaze up only if comfortable.

Stand with the feet about 1 m apart, the front toes pointing forward and the back foot turned in about 15 degrees, front heel in line with the back arch. Extend the arms out to the sides at shoulder height.

Keeping both legs straight, shift the hips back and reach the front arm forward over the front leg, then hinge down and rest the front hand on the shin, a block or the floor outside the front foot while raising the other arm to the ceiling. Stack the shoulders vertically and gaze up or forward. Hold 5 breaths, come up and switch.

Lengthen both sides of the waist equally rather than collapsing the lower side. Keep the front knee soft and avoid hyperextending it. Rest the hand higher on the shin rather than rounding to reach the floor.
Stand with the feet about 1 m apart, the front foot forward and the back foot turned out about 45 degrees. Square the hips toward the front of the mat and place the hands on the hips.

Hinge over the front leg with a long spine, then place the hand opposite the front leg on a block or the floor outside the front foot. Rotate the chest open toward the front-leg side and reach the other arm up toward the ceiling. Hold 3-5 breaths, then rise and switch.

Keep the hips level and square; the front hip tends to swing out. Use a block to avoid rounding the spine. Rotate from the rib cage, not by pulling the shoulders. Shorten the stance if balance or hip squaring is difficult.
Begin in Warrior II with the feet about 1.2 m apart, the front knee bent 90 degrees over the ankle and the arms at shoulder height.

Lower the front forearm onto the front thigh, or place the hand on a block or the floor outside the front foot. Extend the top arm over the ear, palm facing down, to create a straight line from the back heel to the fingertips. Hold 5 breaths, then come up and switch.

Keep the front knee tracking over the toes and the thigh near parallel to the floor. Rotate the chest up toward the ceiling rather than letting it drop. Press firmly through the outer edge of the back foot to lengthen the whole side body.
From downward dog or a high lunge, step one foot forward to the outside of the same-side hand so both hands are inside the front foot. Lower the back knee to the floor or keep it lifted.

Walk the front foot slightly out toward the edge of the mat and sink the hips forward and down until the back hip flexor and front inner groin stretch. Lower to the forearms on the floor or on blocks if comfortable. Hold 5-10 breaths, then switch sides.

Use blocks under the forearms if they do not reach. Keep the front foot flat and the front knee tracking over the toes. Roll onto the outer edge of the front foot and let the knee fall out to deepen the groin stretch.
Step one foot forward into a lunge with the front knee over the ankle, and lower the back knee to the floor or a folded blanket with the top of the back foot down.

Shift the hips forward until the front knee is over the ankle or slightly beyond, lift the torso upright and raise the arms overhead, lifting the chest into a gentle backbend. Hold 5-8 breaths, then switch sides.

Draw the tailbone down and lightly engage the lower abs to stretch the front of the back hip rather than compressing the low back. Keep the ribs from flaring. Rest the hands on the front thigh if balance is difficult.

From standing, step one foot back about a leg's length into a long stance, with the back heel lifted, the back toes pointing forward and both hips facing the front of the mat. Keep the feet about hip-width apart side to side.

Bend the front knee toward 90 degrees with the knee over the ankle, keep the back leg straight and lifted, and reach the arms overhead with the palms facing in. Hold 5-8 breaths, then step forward and switch.

Press back through the back heel to keep the back leg strong and stretch its hip flexor. Keep the pelvis level and square to the front. Engage the core to avoid arching the low back. Unlike Warrior I, the back heel is lifted.
Lie on your back and bring the knees toward the armpits, the knees wider than the torso and the soles of the feet facing the ceiling so the shins are vertical.

Hold the outer edges of the feet, the ankles or the backs of the knees and gently draw the knees down toward the floor beside the chest while the tailbone and sacrum stay heavy on the floor. Hold 5-10 breaths, rocking gently side to side if desired.

Keep the shins vertical and the ankles over the knees. Keep the head and shoulders relaxed on the floor. Hold behind the thighs or use a strap around the feet if the hands do not reach without the head lifting.
Start on hands and knees with the hips over the knees and the hands under the shoulders.

Slide one arm under the body along the floor, palm up, toward the opposite side, lowering that shoulder and the side of the head onto the floor while the hips stay over the knees. Hold 5-10 breaths, then press the top hand into the floor to come back up and switch.

Keep the hips stacked over the knees rather than shifting sideways. Press the top hand into the floor to rotate further, or reach it overhead to add the side body. Relax the neck and rest the head on a block if it does not reach the floor.
Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat, hip-width apart and parallel, heels close enough that the fingertips can graze them. Place the arms by the sides, palms down.

Press through the feet and lift the hips toward the ceiling, then roll the shoulders underneath one at a time and interlace the hands beneath you, pressing the arms into the floor to lift the chest toward the chin. Hold 5-8 breaths, release the hands and roll down slowly.

Keep the knees pointing forward and hip-width apart. Do not turn the head while up, as the weight is on the shoulders. Squeeze the glutes to open the front of the hips, and keep the neck relaxed with a small gap between the chin and chest.

Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat, hip-width apart and parallel, close to the glutes. Place the hands on the floor beside the ears with the fingers pointing toward the shoulders and the elbows pointing up.

Press into the feet to lift the hips, then press into the hands to lift onto the crown of the head briefly, draw the elbows in, and straighten the arms into a full backbend. Hold 3-5 breaths, then tuck the chin, bend the elbows and knees and lower the shoulders and upper back to the mat with control, without resting on the head.

Keep the feet and knees parallel rather than splaying out. Push the chest toward the wall behind you to open the shoulders. Do not take weight on the head for more than a moment. Practice bridge and wheel off a wall first if the shoulders or upper back are tight.

Kneel with the knees hip-width apart and the thighs vertical, the toes tucked under to raise the heels or the tops of the feet flat. Place the hands on the back of the pelvis with the fingers pointing down.

Press the hips forward over the knees, lift the chest and lean back, then reach the hands one at a time to the heels if possible. Keep the neck long or let the head drop back only if comfortable. Hold 3-5 breaths, then bring the hands to the low back and come up leading with the chest.

Keep the hips over the knees; they tend to drift back. Lift the chest rather than collapsing into the low back. Keep the hands on the pelvis as a regression, or tuck the toes to bring the heels closer.
Lie face down with the forehead on the floor. Bend the knees and reach back with both hands to hold the outsides of the ankles, the knees hip-width apart.
Inhale and kick the feet back into the hands, using that pull to lift the thighs and chest off the floor and balance on the belly. Hold 3-5 breaths, then exhale and release slowly.
Keep the knees no wider than the hips. Let the legs drive the lift by kicking back rather than pulling with the arms. Use a strap around the ankles if you cannot reach them.
Lie face down with the arms by the sides, palms down or up, the legs hip-width apart with the tops of the feet down and the forehead on the floor.

Inhale and lift the head, chest, arms and legs off the floor at the same time, reaching back through the fingers and toes so the body forms a long shallow arc balanced on the belly and front hips. Hold 3-5 breaths, then lower. Repeat 2-3 times.

Keep the neck long and the gaze down a little ahead of you. Reach long rather than high. Squeeze the glutes to lift the legs while keeping the knees straight. Lift only the upper or lower body to regress.
Sit with the legs extended and together, the toes pointing up and the knees straight but soft. Sit tall on the front of the sit bones with the hands beside the hips.

Inhale to lengthen the spine and raise the arms, then exhale to hinge forward from the hips, reaching for the shins, ankles or feet. Hold 5-10 breaths, lengthening on each inhale and folding a little deeper on each exhale, then roll up.

Bend the knees or sit on a folded blanket so the spine stays long. Lead with the chest and belly toward the thighs. Loop a strap around the feet if you cannot reach them. Relax the neck only once you reach your end position.
Sit with one leg straight in front, toes up, and bend the other knee so the sole rests against the inner thigh of the straight leg and the bent knee drops out to the side.
Turn the torso slightly to face the straight leg, lengthen on an inhale, then exhale and fold forward over the straight leg, reaching for the shin or foot. Hold 5-8 breaths, then sit up and switch.

Keep the straight-leg knee pointing up and the foot flexed. Lengthen before folding and keep the chest moving toward the knee rather than the head dropping. Place a cushion under the bent knee if it floats, and use a strap around the foot if needed.
Stand with the feet hip-width apart and parallel, the knees soft and the hands on the hips.

Hinge from the hips and fold forward, letting the head hang and the hands rest on the floor, shins or blocks, or hold opposite elbows (ragdoll). Hold 5-10 breaths, then bend the knees and roll up slowly, stacking the head last.

Bend the knees generously to release the low back and let the belly rest on the thighs. Shift the weight slightly toward the balls of the feet so the hips stay over the ankles. Sway gently side to side in ragdoll for relaxation. Come up slowly if prone to dizziness.
Stand with the feet about 1-1.2 m apart, toes parallel or slightly turned in, and the hands on the hips.

Inhale to lengthen the spine, then exhale and hinge forward with a flat back, placing the hands on the floor between the feet shoulder-width apart. Bend the elbows back to lower the crown toward the floor. Hold 5-8 breaths, then return the hands to the hips and rise with a flat back.
Keep the weight in the balls of the feet so the hips stay over the ankles. Keep the legs engaged with the kneecaps lifted. Use blocks under the hands if needed. Do not put weight on the head.

Stand with one foot forward and the other back about 0.9-1 m, the back foot turned in about 45 degrees and both hips squared to the front. Place the hands on the hips or on blocks either side of the front foot.
Inhale to lengthen the spine, then exhale and hinge forward over the front leg with a long back, bringing the hands to the blocks or floor. Hold 5-8 breaths, then rise with a flat back and switch.
Keep both legs straight and the hips square by drawing the front hip back. Use blocks to keep the spine long rather than rounding. Shorten the stance if the back heel lifts or the hips cannot square.
Stand with the feet together or hip-width apart and parallel, the arms by the sides.

Bend the knees and sit the hips back and down as if into a chair, aiming for thighs as close to parallel as you can control, while raising the arms overhead by the ears with the palms facing in. The torso leans forward slightly so it stays roughly parallel to the shins. Hold 5-8 breaths, then straighten up.

Keep the weight in the heels and the knees over the toes, not collapsing inward. Keep the chest lifted and draw the ribs down so the low back does not arch. Hold the hands at the chest if the shoulders are tight. Sit lower only as far as the back stays long.

Stand tall and shift the weight onto one leg, spreading the toes and grounding the standing foot. Place the sole of the other foot on the inner calf or inner thigh of the standing leg, never directly on the knee, with the bent knee opening out to the side.
Press the foot and standing leg firmly into each other, bring the hands to the chest or overhead, and balance. Hold 5-10 breaths, then switch.

Keep the hips level; the bent-leg hip tends to hike up. Fix the gaze on a still point. Keep the standing knee soft but strong. Regress by resting the heel on the standing ankle with the toes on the floor, or by touching a wall.
Stand with the feet slightly wider than hip-width and the toes turned out about 30-45 degrees. Hold a post or wall if balance pulls you backward.
Squat down as deeply as possible with the heels down, bring the palms together at the chest and press the elbows into the inner knees to widen them while lengthening the spine. Hold 5-10 breaths.

Keep the heels down or place a rolled mat under them. Lengthen the spine and lift the chest. Sit on a block for support if the hips cannot settle comfortably. Differs from a fitness deep squat hold by the turned-out feet and prayer hands pressing the knees open.
Sit and stack one knee directly on top of the other, with the feet beside the opposite hips and the sit bones evenly on the floor. Reach one arm overhead and the other arm down and behind the back.

Bend both elbows so the top hand drops between the shoulder blades and the bottom hand climbs up the back, palm out, and try to clasp the fingers. Sit tall and hold 5-8 breaths, then switch both the legs and the arms.

Use a strap between the hands if they do not meet. Sit on a cushion to level the hips. Keep the head neutral and the top elbow pointing up rather than pushing the head forward. The legs stretch the outer hip and glutes; the arms stretch the triceps and shoulder rotators.

Sit with the legs extended. Bend the right knee and step the right foot to the outside of the left thigh. Bend the left knee so the left heel rests beside the right hip, or keep the left leg straight.

Inhale to lengthen the spine, then exhale and twist to the right, placing the right hand on the floor behind you and hooking the left elbow outside the right knee or hugging the knee. Hold 5-8 breaths, lengthening on each inhale and twisting a little more on each exhale, then switch sides.
Lengthen before twisting. Rotate from the mid-back rather than levering with the arm. Keep both sit bones grounded and sit on a cushion if the spine rounds.
Stand tall with the knees slightly bent. Lift one leg and cross that thigh over the standing thigh, then hook the top foot behind the standing calf if possible.

Extend the arms forward, cross one elbow over the other (traditionally the arm opposite the top leg is on top), bend the elbows and press the palms or backs of the hands together, lifting the elbows to shoulder height. Sit lower and hold 5 breaths, then unwind and switch both legs and arms.

Keep the hips square and the standing knee over the toes. Rest the toes of the top foot on the floor if you cannot wrap the foot. Lift the elbows and draw the forearms away from the face to stretch between the shoulder blades.
From triangle or Warrior II, bend the front knee and place the front hand on a block or the floor about 30 cm ahead of and slightly outside the front little toe.

Shift the weight into the front foot and straighten the front leg while lifting the back leg until it is parallel to the floor. Stack the top hip over the bottom hip and raise the top arm to the ceiling. Hold 5 breaths, then bend the standing knee and lower the back leg to switch.

Flex the lifted foot with the toes pointing to the side, not up. Use the block to keep the chest open rather than collapsing. Look down at the floor if balance is unstable, or practice with the back against a wall.
Stand on one leg with a soft standing knee. Bend the other knee and hold the inside of that foot or ankle with the same-side hand, the knees side by side. Reach the free arm straight up.
Kick the foot back into the hand and, as the leg rises behind you, tilt the torso forward and reach the free arm forward, creating a balanced backbend. Hold 5 breaths, then come up and switch.

Keep the hips square rather than letting the lifted hip open out. Kick back into the hand rather than pulling the foot with the arm. Lift the chest as the foot rises so the backbend is shared through the spine. Use a wall or a strap around the foot to assist.
Stand with the feet about 1 m apart and the toes turned out about 45 degrees, the weight spread evenly between both feet.

Bend the knees deeply so they track over the toes and lower into a wide squat, aiming for thighs near parallel, with the arms in a goalpost position or the hands at the chest. Hold 5-8 breaths, then straighten the legs.

Keep the knees tracking over the toes and pressing back. Keep the torso upright with the tailbone pointing down rather than sticking the hips back. Lift the heels to add calf work, or pulse up and down a few centimeters between holds for strength endurance.
Kneel tall with the knees hip-width apart, then extend one leg straight out to the side in line with the kneeling knee, the foot flat and the toes pointing forward.
Raise the arm opposite the straight leg overhead and side-bend toward the straight leg, sliding the other hand down the straight leg. Hold 5 breaths, come up and switch.
Keep the hips stacked over the kneeling knee and do not let them push backward. Avoid leaning forward; bend straight sideways. Breathe into the lengthened side of the ribs. Pad the kneeling knee.

Sit tall with the knees bent. Place the left shin parallel to the front edge of the mat, then stack the right shin directly on top so the right ankle rests on the left knee and the right knee rests above the left ankle.
Sit tall, then hinge forward from the hips over the stacked shins until the outer hips stretch. Hold 5-10 breaths, then sit up and switch which leg is on top.

Keep both feet flexed to protect the knees. Place a block or cushion under a lifted top knee rather than forcing it down. Sit on a cushion if the back rounds. Stop if the knees, rather than the hips, feel the stretch.
Sit sideways with one hip against a wall, then lie back as you swing both legs up the wall so the glutes are close to it and the legs are vertical. Rest the arms by the sides or on the belly.
Relax with the legs straight up the wall for 2-10 minutes, breathing slowly into the belly, then bend the knees, roll onto one side and press up to exit.

Move the hips away from the wall if the hamstrings feel tight. Place a folded blanket under the hips for a gentle inversion. A restorative recovery pose rather than an intense stretch; let the feet fall apart into a straddle to add the inner thighs.
Lie on your back with the arms by the sides, palms down, ideally with the shoulders on a folded blanket and the head on the floor to reduce neck flexion.

Press the arms down and use the abs to lift the legs and hips overhead, then lower the toes to the floor behind the head with the legs straight, supporting the back with the hands or keeping the arms down. Hold 5-8 breaths, then roll down slowly, one vertebra at a time.

Keep the weight on the shoulders, not the neck, and never turn the head while in the pose. Rest the feet on a block or chair if the toes do not reach. Avoid with neck problems, high blood pressure or glaucoma.
Lie on your back with the legs straight and together. Slide the hands, palms down, under the hips and draw the elbows in close to the body.

Press the forearms and elbows into the floor to lift the chest, arching the upper back, then lower the crown of the head lightly to the floor. Hold 3-5 breaths, then press into the forearms, lift the head and lower the back down.
Keep most of the weight in the forearms, not the head. Place a block under the upper back for a supported version. Avoid or use the supported version with neck problems.

Squat with the feet together and the knees apart. Place the hands flat on the floor shoulder-width apart, about 30 cm in front of the feet, with the fingers spread. Bend the elbows slightly back and place the knees high on the backs of the upper arms near the armpits.

Lean forward, shifting the weight into the hands until the elbows are over the wrists, then lift one foot and then the other off the floor, drawing the heels toward the glutes and balancing. Hold 3-5 breaths, then lower the feet.

Look forward, not down at the hands. Round the upper back and pull the knees into the arms with the abs. Place a cushion in front of the head for confidence. Crow keeps the elbows bent; crane is the straight-arm progression.
Stand tall at the front of the mat with the feet together or hip-width apart and the hands at the chest.

Inhale and reach the arms up; exhale and fold forward; inhale to a half lift with a flat back; exhale and step or jump back to plank and lower through chaturanga; inhale into upward dog; exhale into downward dog and hold 5 breaths. Then step or jump forward, inhale to a half lift, exhale to fold and inhale to rise with the arms overhead. Repeat 3-5 rounds.

Link each movement to a single breath. Lower with the knees down in chaturanga to scale. Use cobra instead of upward dog if the low back or wrists complain. Bend the knees in the forward folds as needed.
Begin in a high plank with the hands under the shoulders, the fingers spread and the legs straight, hip-width apart, with the body in one line.

Shift slightly forward onto the toes so the shoulders move past the wrists, then lower with the elbows hugging the ribs and pointing back until the upper arms are parallel to the floor and the elbows are at 90 degrees. Hold 1-3 breaths, then press up or flow forward into upward dog.

Do not let the shoulders dip below the elbows, which stresses the front of the shoulder. Keep the body in one line with the abs and legs engaged. Lower the knees to the floor to scale, or stop halfway down.
From a high plank, shift onto the outer edge of one foot and turn the body to the side, stacking the feet. The bottom hand is slightly ahead of the shoulder with the arm straight.
Press the floor away and lift the hips so the body forms a straight line from head to heels, then extend the top arm to the ceiling. Hold 3-5 breaths, then return to plank and switch.

Keep the bottom hand slightly ahead of the shoulder rather than directly under or behind it. Lift the hips and avoid sagging. Drop the bottom knee to the floor to regress, or stagger the feet for balance.
Sit on the floor with the knees bent and the feet flat. Place the hands behind the thighs and lean back slightly so you balance just behind the sit bones with a long spine and the chest lifted.

Lift the feet off the floor until the shins are parallel to the floor (half boat), then extend the arms forward at shoulder height alongside the legs. Straighten the legs to about 45 degrees for full boat so the body forms a V. Hold 3-5 breaths, then lower the feet. Repeat 3-5 times.
Keep the spine long and the chest lifted; rounding the low back turns it into a different exercise. Keep the knees bent or hold the thighs to scale. Breathe steadily rather than holding the breath.
Start in a low lunge with the back knee on a pad, directly under the hip, and the front foot flat. Place the hands on blocks or the floor either side of the front foot.

Shift the hips back until they stack over the back knee, straightening the front leg with the heel on the floor and the toes pulled up. Hinge forward over the front leg with a long spine until a stretch is felt behind the front thigh. Hold 5-10 breaths, then shift forward to the lunge and switch.

Keep the hips square and the back hip stacked over the knee. Lengthen the spine forward rather than rounding down. Keep a micro bend in the front knee if the hamstring is very tight, and use blocks to bring the floor up.
Fold one or two blankets and lie with the shoulders on the folded edge and the head on the floor, so the neck has space. Arms by the sides, palms down, knees bent.

Press the arms down and lift the hips, swinging the legs over the head as in plow. Bend the elbows and place the hands on the back with the elbows shoulder-width apart, then lift the legs straight up so the body is as vertical as possible. Hold 5-10 breaths, then lower the legs overhead and roll down slowly.

Keep the weight on the shoulders and upper arms, not the neck, and never turn the head. Walk the hands toward the shoulder blades to lift the chest. Avoid with neck injuries, uncontrolled blood pressure or glaucoma. Practice legs up the wall first.
Stand tall at the front of the mat with the feet together or hip-width apart and the arms by the sides.

Inhale into Chair Pose with the arms overhead; exhale fold; inhale half lift; exhale step back and lower through chaturanga; inhale upward dog; exhale downward dog. Inhale step the right foot forward into Warrior I; exhale to chaturanga; inhale upward dog; exhale downward dog. Repeat Warrior I on the left, flow back to downward dog for 5 breaths, then step forward, fold and rise into Chair Pose. Repeat 3-5 rounds.

Link each movement to one breath. Square the hips in Warrior I and keep the back heel down. Lower the knees in chaturanga and use cobra to scale. Differs from Sun Salutation A by Chair Pose and Warrior I.
Start on hands and knees, then lower the forearms to the floor with the elbows directly under the shoulders and the forearms parallel, palms flat, or clasp the hands. Tuck the toes.
Lift the knees and press the hips up and back into an inverted V on the forearms, pressing the chest toward the thighs and walking the feet in slightly. Hold 5-10 breaths, then lower the knees.

Press the forearms down so the shoulders lift away from the floor and the head hangs free; do not sink into the shoulders. Keep the elbows from sliding wider than the shoulders. Bend the knees to keep a long spine. A common prep for forearm stands that builds shoulder flexion range and strength.
Lie on your back with the arms by the sides, palms pressing down, and the legs straight and together pointing to the ceiling at 90 degrees.

Exhale and use the abs to lift the hips and roll the legs over the head until they are parallel to the floor, weight on the shoulder blades. Open the legs shoulder-width, flex the feet and roll down one vertebra at a time, keeping the legs as close to the body as control allows. At the bottom, close the legs and lift them back to 90 degrees. 3 reps, then reverse (legs together on the way over, open on the way down) for 3.

Keep the weight on the shoulder blades, never on the neck, and do not turn the head. Control the descent with the abs and arms. Avoid with neck, osteoporosis or disc problems, and master the roll-up first.

Lie on your back with one leg straight up toward the ceiling, foot softly pointed, and the other leg extended along the mat, foot flexed. Arms rest long by the sides, palms down, and the pelvis is level and still.

Circle the raised leg across the body toward the opposite shoulder, down toward the mat, out to the same side and back up to the start, in one smooth loop. Perform 5 circles in one direction, then 5 in the other, and switch legs.

The test is a still pelvis; make the circle only as big as you can control without the hips rocking. Bend the bottom knee with the foot flat, or soften the top knee, if the hamstrings are tight. Breathe steadily, inhaling for half the circle and exhaling for the rest.

Sit near the front of the mat, hug the shins with the hands on the ankles and the elbows wide, tuck the chin, and lift the feet off the floor so you balance just behind the sit bones in a tight ball with the heels close to the glutes.

Inhale and roll back to the tips of the shoulder blades, keeping the shape, then exhale and use the abs to roll forward to balance again without the feet touching the floor. Pause for a moment at the top. 6-8 reps.

Keep the same ball shape throughout; do not throw the head back or kick the legs. Never roll onto the neck. Roll on a well-padded mat. Hold the backs of the thighs and widen the knees to make it easier, or practice just the balance first.

Lie on your back with the head and shoulders curled up and both legs straight. Raise one leg toward the face and hold behind the calf or ankle with both hands; the other leg hovers a few centimeters above the mat.
Pulse the raised leg toward you twice while exhaling, then scissor the legs to switch in one quick, controlled movement and pulse the other leg. 8-10 per side.

Keep the torso still and the shoulders lifted; do not pull the head forward. Keep the low leg off the floor and both legs long. Hold behind the thigh and bend the top knee slightly if the hamstrings are tight, or raise the low leg to protect the back.

Lie on your back with the hands stacked behind the head, the elbows wide, and the head and shoulders curled up. Extend both legs together straight up toward the ceiling with the feet softly pointed in a small turnout.

Inhale and lower the legs slowly together toward the floor only as far as the low back stays imprinted, then exhale and raise them back to vertical. 6-10 reps, lowering over about 3 seconds and lifting over about 1-2.

Keep the low back imprinted and the upper body lifted throughout. Lower slowly and lift with control rather than swinging. Keep the elbows wide so the hands support rather than pull the head. Bend the knees slightly or reduce the range to scale.

Sit tall on the sit bones with the legs extended a little wider than hip-width, the feet flexed, and the arms reaching forward at shoulder height, palms down. Sit on a cushion or bend the knees if the pelvis rolls back.

Exhale and curl forward from the head, rounding the spine into a C-shape as the arms reach forward and the abs pull in and up. Inhale and restack the spine vertebra by vertebra from the low back up to tall sitting. 5-6 reps.

Lift up out of the hips before rounding forward. Keep the hips still and the sit bones heavy; this is spinal articulation, not a hip hinge forward fold. Keep the arms parallel to the floor and the shoulders relaxed.
Sit and balance just behind the sit bones with the legs extended in a V about shoulder-width apart, holding the ankles or calves with straight arms. Lift the chest and draw the shoulders down.

Inhale and roll back to the shoulder blades, keeping the V shape and the arms straight, then exhale and use the abs to roll back up to balance in the V without the legs dropping or the feet touching the floor. 6 reps.

Keep the shape constant; initiate the roll from the abs by deepening the C-curve, not by throwing the head back. Never roll onto the neck. Bend the knees or hold the calves to scale, and practice holding the open-leg balance before adding the rock.
Lie on your back with the arms long by the sides, palms down, and the legs straight and squeezed together pointing to the ceiling.

Shift the legs to one side, circle them down toward the mat and around to the other side, then back up to center, keeping them together and the shoulders down. In the beginner version the pelvis stays still; in the advanced version the hips lift and roll slightly. Alternate directions for 3-5 circles each way.
Keep the legs glued together as one unit. Start with small circles and only enlarge them while the low back stays stable. Keep the shoulders and arms anchored. Bend the knees to scale.
Sit tall with the legs straight and wider than the hips, the feet flexed, and the arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.

Inhale and rotate the torso toward the right leg. Exhale and hinge forward over the right leg, reaching the left little finger past the right little toe as if sawing it off, while the right arm reaches long behind you, palm down. Pulse forward 3 times on the exhale, inhale to restack and return to center, then alternate. 4-5 per side.
Keep both sit bones anchored; the opposite hip tends to lift. Rotate first, then flex forward. Reach the back arm long behind and keep it lifted. Sit on a cushion if the pelvis rolls back.

Lie face down with the hands under the shoulders, the elbows bent and hugging the sides, and the legs together or hip-width apart. Press the tops of the feet, the thighs and the pubic bone lightly into the mat and draw the navel away from the floor.

Inhale and lift the head, then the chest, in a long arc, pressing lightly into the hands and extending through the upper back while the lower ribs stay near the mat. Exhale and lower with control, chest then head. 5-6 reps.

Lengthen before lifting so the extension spreads through the spine rather than pinching the low back. Keep the pubic bone down and the shoulders away from the ears. Keep the elbows slightly bent and close to the body. Swan Dive, the advanced version, rocks the body from chest to thighs without the hands.

Lie face down propped on the forearms, elbows under the shoulders, the hands in fists together or flat on the mat, and the legs straight and together. Lift the navel away from the mat, press the pubic bone down and lift the chest.
Bend one knee and kick that heel toward the glute twice in a quick double pulse (flexed foot then pointed), then lower it straight as the other leg kicks. Alternate for 8-10 per side.

Keep the abdominals lifted off the mat and the hips grounded so the low back does not sag. Press the forearms down and keep the chest lifted with the shoulders away from the ears. Keep the knees together.
Lie face down with the head turned to one cheek, the hands clasped high on the back with the elbows relaxed toward the floor, and the legs straight and together.

Kick both heels toward the glutes three times in a pulse. Then extend the legs long to the mat and lift the chest, straightening the arms and reaching the clasped hands back toward the feet while squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower and turn the head to the other cheek. 4-6 per side.

Keep the legs together and the hips down. Lift with the upper back rather than crunching the low back. Keep the neck long during the extension. Unclasp the hands and reach them alongside the body to scale.
Lie on your back with the legs extended hip-width apart, the feet flexed, and the hands stacked lightly behind the head with the elbows wide.

Inhale and nod the chin, exhale and curl up off the mat and roll forward over the legs into a C-curve. Inhale and restack the spine to tall sitting, then hinge back with a flat back a few degrees, and exhale to roll down one vertebra at a time. 4-6 reps.
Do not pull on the head; the hands only cradle it. Keep the legs heavy and the heels reaching away. A more advanced roll-up. Bend the knees or reach the arms forward to scale.

Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat, hip-width apart, and the arms by the sides, palms down. Roll up into a bridge with the weight on the shoulder blades and a straight line from knees to shoulders.

Keeping the hips high and level, extend one leg toward the ceiling with a pointed foot, then lower it with a flexed foot to knee height and kick it back up. 5 per leg, then place the foot down, switch, and finally roll down sequentially.

Keep the pelvis level and the hips high; the support glute does most of the work. Move the leg without the hips rocking or dropping. Hold the basic bridge or simply lift the foot a few centimeters to scale.

Sit tall on the sit bones with the legs straight and squeezed together, the feet flexed and the arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms down. Press the inner thighs together and reach the heels away.
Exhale and rotate the torso to one side in two pulses, the second slightly further, growing taller as you twist. Inhale and return to center. Then twist to the other side. 4-5 per side.

Keep the hips square and both sit bones grounded; the rotation comes from the rib cage. Keep the arms in line with the shoulders. Exhale fully on each pulse as if wringing the air out of the lungs. Sit on a cushion or bend the knees if the pelvis rolls back.
Lie on your back with the arms long by the sides, palms pressing down, and the legs straight and together pointing to the ceiling.

Exhale and roll the legs overhead until they are parallel to the floor, as in the roll over. Inhale and press the arms down to shoot the legs straight up toward the ceiling, lifting the hips so the body is near vertical with the weight on the shoulder blades. Exhale and roll down slowly, vertebra by vertebra, keeping the legs vertical, until the tailbone lands. 3-5 reps.
Keep the weight on the shoulder blades, never on the neck, and do not turn the head. Control the descent. Master the roll over first. Avoid with neck, spine or osteoporosis concerns.

Lie on one side with the head resting on the bottom hand, the top hand on the mat in front of the chest, and the legs straight and angled about 30 degrees forward of the body so you can see the feet. Lift the top leg to hip height.
Swing the top leg forward with a flexed foot and pulse twice, then sweep it back behind the body with a pointed foot, keeping it at hip height. 8-10 reps, then switch sides.

Keep the trunk still, stacked and long, with the waist lifted off the mat. Move the leg only as far forward and back as the pelvis stays still. Avoid arching the back as the leg goes back. Bend the bottom knee for more stability.

Lie on one side with the head supported on the bottom hand. Cross the top leg over and place the top foot flat on the floor in front of the bottom knee, or rest the top knee on a cushion. Line the shoulders and hips up, with the bottom leg straight and in line with the body.
Exhale and lift the straight bottom leg off the floor as high as you can, hold 1-2 seconds, and lower with control without fully resting. 10-15 reps, then switch sides.

Keep the bottom foot flexed and the leg straight. Lift from the inner thigh rather than rolling the pelvis back. Keep the hips stacked and the waist long. Add a light ankle weight or more reps to progress.
Lie face down with the arms extended overhead shoulder-width apart and the legs straight and hip-width apart. Draw the navel up and reach the arms and legs long so the body lengthens before it lifts.

Lift the arms, legs, head and chest a few centimeters off the mat, then flutter the opposite arm and leg up and down quickly in small movements, inhaling for 5 counts and exhaling for 5 counts. Continue for 20-30 seconds, then lower and rest in child's pose.

Keep the movements small and fast. Lengthen rather than lifting high, and keep the gaze down so the neck stays long. Keep the hips and pelvis from rocking side to side. Slow it down to an alternating bird-dog style lift to scale.
Begin in a high plank with the hands under the shoulders, the fingers spread and the legs straight and together. Press the floor away so the shoulder blades are wide and the body is in one line.

Lift one straight leg off the floor, point the foot and then flex it while pushing back through the standing heel to rock the body back slightly. Point the foot and come forward, lower the leg and switch. 3-5 per side.

Keep the hips stable and level; lift the leg only as high as the pelvis stays still. Keep the shoulders over the wrists and the core braced so the middle does not sag. Lower the knees or skip the rock to scale.
